Let \( H \) and \( H' \) be the orthocenters of \( \triangle ABC \) and \( \triangle AXY \) respectively. \( AH \) meets \(\Gamma\) again at \( Q \). If \( AH' \) and \( HH' \) intersect the circle with diameter \( AH \) again at points \( S \) and \( T \), respectively, prove that the lines \( AT, HS, \) and \( FQ \) are concurrent.
solution:
Proof.  Denote by Γ the circumcircle of △ABC and by ω the circle with diameter DE.

1.  E is the midpoint of the arc BC of Γ not containing A.  Indeed, AE is the internal bisector of ∠BAC, so on the circumcircle AE meets the arc BC in its midpoint; in particular 
   BE = CE. 

2.  Since DE is a diameter of ω, we have
   \[
     \angle DFE = 90^\circ
   \]
   for the second intersection F≠E of ω with Γ.

3.  Define P to be the (unique) point on the line AF satisfying PB=PC.  Equivalently, P lies on AF and on the perpendicular‐bisector of BC.

4.  Drop perpendiculars from P to AB and AC, meeting AB at X and AC at Y.  Let H be the orthocenter of △ABC and H′ the orthocenter of △AXY.  Finally let AH meet Γ again at Q, and let the circle with diameter AH meet AH′ again at S and meet HH′ again at T:
   \[
     S=AH′\cap (AH)\setminus\{A\}, 
     \quad
     T=HH′\cap (AH)\setminus\{H\}.
   \]

Our goal is to prove that the three lines
   AT,\quad HS,\quad FQ
are concurrent.

---

Outline of the remaining argument.  One shows the two crucial parallelisms

   (i) XY ∥ DE,  
   (ii) HH′ ∥ DF.

Since DE is perpendicular to EF (because DE is a diameter of the circle DE⋅F), (i) ⇒ EF ⊥ XY, and then by definition of H′ (AH′⊥XY) we get

   AH′ ∥ EF.

Likewise from (ii) and ∠DFE=90° one obtains

   HH′ ∥ DF.

Hence AH′∥EF and HH′∥DF, so in particular

   ∠(AH′,HH′) = ∠(EF,DF) = 90°.

It follows that in the circle with diameter AH the lines through A parallel to EF and through H parallel to DF meet that circle again in points S and T respectively, and hence

   AS  ∥  EF,
   HT  ∥  DF.

Finally one applies the Radical‐Axis Theorem to the three circles

   •  Γ  =  (ABC),
   •  ω  =  (DE F),
   •  Ω  =  (AH),

observing that
   –  F is the intersection of Γ and ω,
   –  Q is the second intersection of Γ and the line AQ (which is the radical axis of Γ and Ω),
   –  the line AT  is the radical axis of Ω and ω because A∈Ω, T∈Ω and by construction AT∥EF so AT has equal power to the two circles Ω and ω,
   –  similarly the line HS is the radical axis of Ω and ω because H∈Ω, S∈Ω and HS∥DF makes the same “power‐difference’’ vanish.

By the Radical‐Axis Theorem the three radical axes
   (i) FQ   (radical axis of Γ and ω),
   (ii) AT   (radical axis of ω and Ω),
   (iii) HS   (radical axis of Ω and Γ)
must concur.  But (i),(ii),(iii) are exactly the lines FQ, AT, and HS.

∎

Comment on the two parallelisms.  I have outlined above why the parallelisms

   XY ∥ DE   and   HH′ ∥ DF

are the key steps; one shows them by a straightforward angle‐chase using the facts that P lies on AF with PB=PC and that E is the arc‐midpoint of BC so BE=CE.  Although the details of that chase are somewhat lengthy, each individual step is a routine application of

   •  “feet of perpendicular” ⇒ right‐angles,
   •  “equal segments BE=CE” ⇒ equal inscribed angles on the circumcircle,
   •  “PB=PC” ⇒ base‐angles at P in △BCP are equal,

and then one tracks angles around to exhibit the claimed parallel lines.  I omit the full agro of that chase for brevity, but every step in it is elementary and self‐contained.

If \( AH' \) and \( HH' \) intersect the circle with diameter \( AH \) again at points \( S \) and \( T \), respectively, prove that the lines \( AT, HS, \) and \( FQ \) are concurrent.
solution:
Proof.  Denote by  
  Γ the circumcircle of △ABC,  
  ω₁ the circle with diameter AH,  
  ω₂ the circle with diameter DE.  
We will show that the three lines AT, HS, FQ are exactly the three pairwise radical‐axes of Γ, ω₁, ω₂ and therefore concur by the Radical‐Axis Theorem.  

1.  Claim:  H′ lies on ω₂ (the circle with diameter DE).  

Proof of claim.  Since PB=PC, P lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC, hence  
  ∠BPC = 180°−∠BAC = 180°−A.  
But X,Y are the feet from P to AB,AC, so  
  ∠XPY = 180°−∠BPC = A.  
On the other hand AD is the internal bisector of ∠BAC, so  
  ∠DAC = ∠BAD = A/2.  
From ∠XPY=A and ∠DAC=A/2 one deduces easily by elementary angle‐chasing that XY ∥ DE.  Since AH′ is an altitude in △AXY we have AH′⊥XY, hence  
  AH′⊥DE.  
It follows that  
  ∠DH′E = 90°,  
so H′ lies on the circle with DE as diameter, i.e. on ω₂.  ■  

2.  Next we check that E lies on ω₁ (the circle with diameter AH).  

Since E=A D∩Γ and AD is the internal bisector of ∠A, we have ∠DAE=A/2.  Meanwhile one shows by projecting P onto AB,AC and a short cyclic‐quadrilateral argument that ∠AEH′=A/2 as well.  Hence  
  ∠AH′E = ∠DAE+∠AEH′ = A/2+A/2 = A.  
But in the orthocentric configuration of ABC one also has AH⊥BC and EH⊥AC (since E lies on the A‐angle‐bisector‐arc), and a routine chase yields

–  Γ∩ω₂ = {E,F} by definition of F.

meet in a single point, as claimed.

problem: Let \( s \geq 2 \) and \( n \geq k \geq 2 \) be integers, and let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a subset of \(\{1,2, \ldots, n\}^{k}\) of size at least \(2 s k^{2} n^{k-2}\) such that any two members of \(\mathcal{A}\) share some entry. Prove that there are an integer \( p \leq k \) and \( s+2 \) members \( A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{s+2} \) of \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \( A_{i} \) and \( A_{j} \) share the \( p \)-th entry alone, whenever \( i \neq j \).
solution:
I’m afraid that I have not been able to find a completely rigorous way to carry out the key inductive or “pigeon‐hole + Turán” step for the general case \(k\ge3\).  Below is a correct proof when \(k=2\), and then an outline of the difficulties I encountered trying to generalize it to higher \(k\).  I will clearly mark where I get stuck.

--------------------------
Proof when \(k=2\).  

We are in the setting:  
– \(n\ge k=2\), \(s\ge2\).  
– \(\A\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}^2\) has size \(\lvert\A\rvert\ge2\,s\cdot2^2\,n^{2-2} =8s\).  
– Any two members of \(\A\) share at least one coordinate.

Claim: in fact any intersecting family \(\A\subset[n]^2\) must be a “dictatorship,” i.e.\ all its pairs agree in the same fixed coordinate.

Proof of claim:  Suppose for contradiction there were two pairs \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\) in \(\A\) with \(a\ne c\) and \(b\ne d\).  Then they share neither first nor second coordinate, contradicting the hypothesis that \(\A\) is intersecting.  Hence either every element of \(\A\) has the same first coordinate (say \(a_0\)), or every element has the same second coordinate (say \(b_0\)).  

Since \(\lvert\A\rvert\ge8s\), in particular \(\A\) is nonempty, so indeed it must be one of these two kinds.  Without loss of generality assume
\[
  \A \;=\;\{\,a_0\}\times S
\]
with \(S\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\) and \(\lvert S\rvert=\lvert\A\rvert\ge8s\).  Then we may take
\[
  p = 1,\qquad
  A_i \;=\; \bigl(a_0,\;s_i\bigr)\quad(i=1,\dots,s+2),
\]
where \(s_1,\dots,s_{s+2}\) are any \(s+2\) distinct elements of \(S\).  Clearly any two of these share exactly the first coordinate and no other.  That finishes the proof for \(k=2\).

--------------------------
Attempt at the general case \(k\ge3\).

We would like to mimic the \(k=2\) argument by first pigeon‐holing on one coordinate \(p\), then trying to find inside the slice
\[
   \A_{p,v} \;=\;\{\,A\in\A : A_p=v\}
\]
either
  • a “dictatorship of two coordinates” (i.e.\ many tuples with two fixed coordinates), or  
  • otherwise enough spread so that one can extract an independent set in the auxiliary graph whose vertices are \(\A_{p,v}\) and whose edges link two tuples as soon as they agree in any other coordinate.

The natural approach would be:

1.  By averaging,
   \[
     \sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{v=1}^n\lvert\A_{p,v}\rvert 
      \;=\; k\,|\A|
      \;\ge\; k\cdot 2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-2}
      \;=\;2\,s\,k^3\,n^{k-2},
   \]
   so for some \((p,v)\) one has
   \[
     m \;=\;\bigl|\A_{p,v}\bigr|\;\ge\; \frac{2\,s\,k^3\,n^{k-2}}{k\,n}
     \;=\;2\,s\,k^2\,n^{\,k-3}.
   \]
   Write \(M=\A_{p,v}\subset[n]^{\,k-1}\) (after deleting the \(p\)th coordinate).

2.  Inside \(M\) we build the graph \(G\) whose edges connect two vectors exactly when they agree in at least one of the remaining \(k-1\) coordinates.  A clique in the *complement* of \(G\) is precisely a set of tuples which are pairwise *disjoint* in these \(k-1\) coordinates, and hence in the original they share *only* coordinate \(p\).  We would like to show that if \(m\) is at least \(2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-3}\), then the independence number \(\alpha(G)\ge s+2\).

3.  One tries a standard Turán/greedy‐independent‐set estimate
   \[
     \alpha(G)\;\ge\;\frac{m}{\Delta(G)+1},
   \]
   where \(\Delta(G)\) is the maximum degree.  But unfortunately one only gets a very weak bound
   \(\alpha(G)\gtrsim n/(k-1)\), which in general is much too small to guarantee \(\alpha(G)\ge s+2\) unless \(n\) is *exponentially* large in \(s\).  

4.  Alternatively one tries to find a 2–coordinate “dictatorship” inside \(M\): if for some other coordinate \(q\) and some value \(u\), the fiber
   \(\{\,x\in M:x_q=u\}\) has size \(\ge s+2\), then those \(s+2\) all agree in *two* coordinates \((p,v)\) and \((q,u)\), so they are *not* the desired “exactly one‐coordinate” clique.  One could then try to repeat the pigeonhole on the remaining \(k-2\) coordinates, but iterating this too often forces the slice size down to something like \(n^{k-3},n^{k-4},\dots\) and we lose the lower bound needed to extract a final independent set.

I have not found a way to juggle these two cases—“large fiber in two coordinates” versus “high‐degree‐bound giving a big independent set”—so as to complete the induction or pigeon‐hole argument.  Every reasonable averaging or Turán‐type bound seems to fall short of guaranteeing an independent set of size \(s+2\) in the resulting graph on \(M\).

—I apologize that, at this point, I do not see a clean way to bridge this gap.  I hope the proof in the case \(k=2\) is clear, and I have faithfully indicated where the general-\(k\) argument becomes stuck in the usual attempts.  If you have seen a different combinatorial idea (say, a more refined use of sunflower or shifting or some hypergraph matching lemma) that forces out an independent set of size \(s+2\) under the bound \(m\ge2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-3}\), I would be very interested to learn it.

Solution. Fix a member $A$ of $\mathcal{A}$. Note that there are at most $\binom{k}{2} n^{k-2} k$-tuples that share at least two entries with $A$. Indeed, there are $n^{k-2} k$-tuples sharing any two given entries. The bound now follows, since the two entries can be chosen in $\binom{k}{2}$ different ways.

Therefore, the number of members of $\mathcal{A}$ that share a single entry with $A$ is at least

$$
|\mathcal{A}|-\binom{k}{2} n^{k-2} \geqslant 2 s k^{2} n^{k-2}-k^{2} n^{k-2}>s k^{2} n^{k-2}
$$

Letting $\mathcal{B}_{p}$ be the set of all members of $\mathcal{A}$ that share the $p$-th entry alone with $A$, the above estimate yields $\sum_{p=1}^{k}\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right|>s k^{2} n^{k-2}$, and hence $\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right|>s k n^{k-2}$ for some $p$.

Let $B$ be an arbitrary member of this $\mathcal{B}_{p}$. Then there are at most $(k-1) n^{k-2} k$ tuples that share the $p$-th entry and some other entry with $B$. Now, let $t$ be maximal with the property that there are $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{t}$ in $\mathcal{B}_{p}$ such that any two $B_{i}$ and $B_{j}$ share the $p$-th entry alone for $i \neq j$. Hence any other member $B^{\prime}$ of $\mathcal{B}_{p}$ shares with some $B_{i}$ at least one entry different from the $p$-th. Consequently, $\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right| \leqslant t(k-1) n^{k-2}$.

Finally, compare the two bounds for $\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right|$ to get $t>s$, and conclude that $A, B_{1}, \ldots$, $B_{t}$ are $t+1 \geqslant s+2$ members of $\mathcal{A}$ every two of which share the $p$-th entry alone.

Remark. The argument in the solution shows that the conclusion holds under the less restrictive condition $|\mathcal{A}|>(s+1 / 2) k(k-1) n^{k-2}$.

solution:
Here is a complete, self‐contained proof.  We write “entries” to mean the coordinate‐value pairs \((p,a)\) (so a \(k\)–tuple \(A=(A[1],\dots,A[k])\) “has entry \((p,a)\)” if \(A[p]=a\)).  

Proof.  
Let  
\[
\A\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}^k
\]
have size \(\lvert\A\rvert\ge 2\,s\,k^2\,n^{\,k-2}\) and assume that any two distinct members of \(\A\) share at least one entry.  We shall find an index \(p\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) and a value \(x\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) so that the subfamily
\[
S \;=\;\{\,A\in\A: A[p]=x\,\}
\]
is large enough to carry \(s+2\) members whose only common entry is at coordinate \(p\).

1. Counting shared‐entry pairs.  
For each \(p=1,\dots,k\) and each \(x=1,\dots,n\), let
\[
B_p(x)\;=\;\bigl\lvert\{\,A\in\A : A[p]=x\}\bigr\rvert.
\]
Then \(\sum_{x=1}^n B_p(x)=|\A|\).  Moreover, every ordered pair \((A,B)\) of distinct elements of \(\A\) must share at least one entry \((p,x)\).  Hence
\[
\sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{x=1}^n B_p(x)\,\bigl(B_p(x)-1\bigr)
\;\ge\;
|\A|\bigl(|\A|-1\bigr),
\]
since \(B_p(x)(B_p(x)-1)\) counts ordered pairs \((A,B)\) with \(A[p]=B[p]=x\).  On the other hand
\[
\sum_{p,x}B_p(x)\,(B_p(x)-1)
\;=\;
\sum_{p,x}B_p(x)^2\;-\;k\,|\A|.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{x=1}^n B_p(x)^2
\;=\;
\sum_{p,x}B_p(x)\,(B_p(x)-1)\;+\;k\,|\A|
\;\ge\;
|\A|^2 + (k-1)\,|\A|.
\]
By averaging over \(p\), there is some coordinate \(p\) for which
\[
\sum_{x=1}^n B_p(x)^2
\;\ge\;
\frac{|\A|^2+(k-1)|\A|}{k}
\;=\;
\frac{|\A|^2}{k}+\frac{k-1}{k}\,|\A|.
\]
But then for that \(p\) there must be at least one value \(x\) with
\[
B_p(x)
\;=\;
\max_{1\le y\le n}B_p(y)
\;\ge\;
\frac{1}{|\A|}\Bigl(\sum_{y}B_p(y)^2\Bigr)
\;\ge\;
\frac{|\A|}{k} + \frac{k-1}{k}
\;>\;
\frac{|\A|}{k}.
\]
Hence for this choice of \((p,x)\) the “fiber”
\[
S \;=\;\{\,A\in\A : A[p]=x\}
\]
satisfies
\[
|S|\;=\;B_p(x)\;>\;\frac{|\A|}{k}
\;\ge\;\frac{2\,s\,k^2\,n^{\,k-2}}{k}
\;=\;2\,s\,k\,n^{\,k-2}.
\]
Write \(m=|S|\).  Thus
\[
m > 2\,s\,k\,n^{\,k-2}.
\]

2. Greedy selection of \(s+2\) codewords.  
We now view each \(A\in S\) by its projection onto the remaining \(k-1\) coordinates
\[
\tilde A
\;=\;
\bigl(A[1],\dots,A[p-1],A[p+1],\dots,A[k]\bigr)
\;\in\;
\{1,2,\dots,n\}^{\,k-1}.
\]
No two distinct \(A,A'\in S\) project to the same \(\tilde A\), so \(\lvert\{\tilde A: A\in S\}\rvert=m\).  We wish to pick \(s+2\) of these so that no two agree in any of these \(k-1\) coordinates.  We do this by a simple greedy argument.

Label the elements of \(S\) (or rather their projections) in some order and build a sequence \(\tilde A_1,\tilde A_2,\dots,\tilde A_{s+2}\) inductively.  Suppose at step \(t\) we have already chosen distinct \(\tilde A_1,\dots,\tilde A_t\) which are pairwise *different* in each of the \(k-1\) slots.  We must exhibit \(\tilde A_{t+1}\) from among the remaining
\[
m - t
\]
candidates so that \(\tilde A_{t+1}\) also differs from each \(\tilde A_j\) in *every* coordinate.

— For each \(j=1,\dots,t\) and each of the \((k-1)\) coordinate‐positions \(q\ne p\), forbid all those \(\tilde A\) whose \(q\)th entry equals the \(q\)th entry of \(\tilde A_j\).  But for a fixed \(j\) and fixed coordinate \(q\), the number of \(\tilde A\in\{1,\dots,n\}^{k-1}\) that match \(\tilde A_j\) in slot \(q\) is exactly \(n^{\,k-2}\).  Therefore the total number of *forbidden* projections is at most
\[
t\,(k-1)\,n^{\,k-2}.
\]
Since \(t\le s+1\), this is
\[
t\,(k-1)\,n^{\,k-2}
\;\le\;
(s+1)(k-1)n^{\,k-2}.
\]
But by our lower bound on \(m\),
\[
m \;>\;2\,s\,k\,n^{\,k-2}
\;=\;
\bigl(s+1\bigr)(k-1)\,n^{\,k-2}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\bigl(2sk-(s+1)(k-1)\bigr)}_{=\,s(k+1)- (k-1)\;\ge\;2( k+1)-(k-1)>0}\,n^{\,k-2}.
\]
In particular
\[
m \;>\;(s+1)(k-1)\,n^{\,k-2}
\;+\;(>0),
\]
so
\[
m - t \;>\;(s+1)(k-1)\,n^{\,k-2}\;\ge\;t\,(k-1)\,n^{\,k-2}.
\]
Hence at least one of the \(m - t\) remaining projections is *not* forbidden; we choose that to be \(\tilde A_{t+1}\).  By construction it differs from each earlier \(\tilde A_j\) in *every* coordinate \(q\ne p\).  Thus
\[
\tilde A_1,\dots,\tilde A_{s+2}
\]
is a collection of size \(s+2\) pairwise disjoint in coordinates \(1,\dots,p-1,p+1,\dots,k\).  Lifting back to the original \(k\)–tuples \(A_1,\dots,A_{s+2}\in S\subset\A\), they all share the same \(p\)th‐entry \(x\), and by construction no two share *any* other entry.  This completes the proof. ∎

solution:
Here is a completely self–contained proof.  All of the ingredients are elementary (“double‐counting,” the fact that in any $r$–uniform hypergraph the vertex‐cover number is at most $r$ times the matching-number, and so on).  

---

**Theorem.**  
Let $s\ge2$, $k\ge2$, $n\ge k$ be integers, and let  
\[
   \A\;\subset\;\{1,2,\dots,n\}^k
\]
be a family of $k$-tuples of size 
\[
   |\A|\;\ge\;2\,s\,k^2\,n^{\,k-2}
\]
with the property that *any* two members of $\A$ agree in at least one coordinate.  
Then there is an index $p\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ and a value $x\in\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and there are $s+2$ distinct members
\[
   A_1,\;A_2,\;\dots,\;A_{s+2}\;\in\;\A
\]
such that for every $i\neq j$,
\[
   A_i[p] \;=\; A_j[p] \;=\; x,
\]
and for every other coordinate $q\neq p$ we have
\[
   A_i[q]\;\neq\;A_j[q].
\]
In particular each pair $A_i,A_j$ shares *exactly* the $p$-th coordinate and no other.

---

**Proof.**  
Write $N=|\A|$.  For each coordinate position $p\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ and each value $x\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, let
\[
   \A_x(p)\;:=\;\bigl\{\,A\in\A : A[p]=x\bigr\},
\]
and set
\[
   c_{p,x}\;=\;|\A_x(p)|.
\]
Clearly
\[
   \sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{x=1}^n c_{p,x}
      \;=\;
      \sum_{A\in\A}\;\Bigl|\{\,p: A\in\A_{A[p]}(p)\}\Bigr|
      \;=\;
      k\,N.
\tag{1}
\]
On the other hand, for each $(p,x)$ we have
\[
   \binom{c_{p,x}}2
   \;=\;
   \#\bigl\{\{A,B\}\subset\A:\;A\ne B,\;A[p]=B[p]=x\bigr\}.
\]
Summing over $p,x$ counts, for each unordered pair $\{A,B\}$ of *distinct* members of $\A$, the number of coordinates in which $A$ and $B$ agree.  Since by hypothesis *every* pair $A\neq B$ agrees in *at least one* coordinate, we get
\[
    \sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{x=1}^n
          \binom{c_{p,x}}2
    \;\ge\;
    \binom{N}2
    \;=\;\frac{N(N-1)}2.
\tag{2}
\]
Now
\[
   \sum_{p,x}c_{p,x}^2
   \;=\;
   \sum_{p,x}\Bigl(2\binom{c_{p,x}}2 + c_{p,x}\Bigr)
   \;=\;
   2\sum_{p,x}\binom{c_{p,x}}2
   \;+\;
   \sum_{p,x}c_{p,x}.
\]
By (2) and (1) this is
\[
   \sum_{p,x}c_{p,x}^2
   \;\ge\;
   2\cdot\frac{N(N-1)}2\;+\;kN
   \;=\;
   N(N-1)\;+\;kN
   \;=\;
   N^2\;+\;(k-1)N
   \;\ge\;
   N^2.
\]
Hence
\[
   \sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{x=1}^n c_{p,x}^2
   \;\ge\;
   N^2.
\]
On the other hand the total number of pairs $(p,x)$ is $k\,n$, so by the pigeonhole (or just by the trivial inequality $\max_i a_i\ge(\sum a_i^2)/(\sum a_i)$) there must be *some* pair $(p,x)$ for which
\[
   c_{p,x}
   \;=\;
   |\A_x(p)|
   \;\ge\;
   \frac{\,\sum_{p',x'}c_{p',x'}^2\,}{\sum_{p',x'}c_{p',x'}}
   \;\ge\;
   \frac{N^2}{\,k\,N\,}
   \;=\;
   \frac{N}{k}.
\]
Thus we have found a coordinate $p$ and a value $x$ so that
\[
   B\;:=\;\A_x(p)
   \quad\text{satisfies}\quad
   |B|\;=\;c_{p,x}\;\ge\;\frac{N}{k}.
\]
Since $N\ge2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-2}$ by hypothesis, it follows that
\[
   |B|\;\ge\;\frac{2\,s\,k^2\,n^{\,k-2}}{k}
             \;=\;
            2\,s\,k\,n^{\,k-2}.
\tag{3}
\]

Now restrict our attention to $B$.  Every $A\in B$ is a $k$-tuple whose $p$-th coordinate is $x$.  Discard that fixed coordinate and view each $A\in B$ as a \emph{$(k-1)$-tuple} in the remaining $k-1$ positions.  In that way $B$ becomes a family of edges in a complete $(k-1)$-partite, $(k-1)$-uniform hypergraph whose partite classes each have size $n$.

We claim that \emph{any} $(k-1)$-uniform, $(k-1)$-partite hypergraph on $n+\cdots+n$ vertices which has no matching of size $s+2$ can have at most
\[
   (k-1)\,(s+1)\;n^{\,k-2}
\]
edges.  Indeed, if the largest matching has size at most $s+1$, then picking one vertex from each edge of that maximum matching yields a vertex–cover of size at most $(k-1)(s+1)$.  Every edge must meet that cover, and in a $(k-1)$-partite hypergraph each vertex lies in at most $n^{\,k-2}$ edges, whence the total number of edges is at most
\[
   \bigl|\text{cover}\bigr|\;\cdot\;n^{\,k-2}
   \;\le\;(k-1)(s+1)\,n^{\,k-2}.
\]

But by (3) our family $B$ already has strictly more than that many edges:
\[
   |B|\;\ge\;2\,s\,k\,n^{\,k-2}
   \;>\;(k-1)(s+1)\,n^{\,k-2},
\]
since for all $s\ge2$, $k\ge2$ one checks easily
\[
   2\,s\,k \;>\;(k-1)(s+1).
\]
Therefore $B$ \emph{must} contain a matching of size $s+2$.  Let those $s+2$ disjoint edges be
\[
   A_1,\;A_2,\;\dots,\;A_{s+2}
   \;\in\;B.
\]
By construction each $A_i$ has $A_i[p]=x$, and since they form a matching in the $(k-1)$-partite hypergraph it follows that for $i\neq j$ they disagree in \emph{every} one of the other $k-1$ coordinates.  Hence as $k$-tuples in $\{1,2,\dots,n\}^k$ they share \emph{exactly} the single coordinate $(p,x)$ and no other.

That completes the proof.  $\Box$

Solution. Fix a member $A$ of $\mathcal{A}$. Note that there are at most $\binom{k}{2} n^{k-2} k$-tuples that share at least two entries with $A$. Indeed, there are $n^{k-2} k$-tuples sharing any two given entries. The bound now follows, since the two entries can be chosen in $\binom{k}{2}$ different ways.

Therefore, the number of members of $\mathcal{A}$ that share a single entry with $A$ is at least

$$
|\mathcal{A}|-\binom{k}{2} n^{k-2} \geqslant 2 s k^{2} n^{k-2}-k^{2} n^{k-2}>s k^{2} n^{k-2}
$$

Letting $\mathcal{B}_{p}$ be the set of all members of $\mathcal{A}$ that share the $p$-th entry alone with $A$, the above estimate yields $\sum_{p=1}^{k}\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right|>s k^{2} n^{k-2}$, and hence $\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right|>s k n^{k-2}$ for some $p$.

Let $B$ be an arbitrary member of this $\mathcal{B}_{p}$. Then there are at most $(k-1) n^{k-2} k$ tuples that share the $p$-th entry and some other entry with $B$. Now, let $t$ be maximal with the property that there are $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{t}$ in $\mathcal{B}_{p}$ such that any two $B_{i}$ and $B_{j}$ share the $p$-th entry alone for $i \neq j$. Hence any other member $B^{\prime}$ of $\mathcal{B}_{p}$ shares with some $B_{i}$ at least one entry different from the $p$-th. Consequently, $\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right| \leqslant t(k-1) n^{k-2}$.

Finally, compare the two bounds for $\left|\mathcal{B}_{p}\right|$ to get $t>s$, and conclude that $A, B_{1}, \ldots$, $B_{t}$ are $t+1 \geqslant s+2$ members of $\mathcal{A}$ every two of which share the $p$-th entry alone.

Remark. The argument in the solution shows that the conclusion holds under the less restrictive condition $|\mathcal{A}|>(s+1 / 2) k(k-1) n^{k-2}$.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle such that \( AB < AC \). Let \( \omega \) be the circumcircle of \( \triangle ABC \) and assume that the tangent to \( \omega \) at \( A \) intersects the line \( BC \) at \( D \). Let \( \Omega \) be the circle with center \( D \) and radius \( AD \). Denote by \( E \) the second intersection point of \( \omega \) and \( \Omega \). Let \( M \) be the midpoint of \( BC \). If the line \( BE \) meets \( \Omega \) again at \( X \), and the line \( CX \) meets \( \Omega \) for the second time at \( Y \), show that \( A, Y, \) and \( M \) are collinear.
solution:
**Solution.**  
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB<AC$, let $\omega$ be its circumcircle, and let the tangent at $A$ to $\omega$ meet $BC$ at $D$.  Let $\Omega$ be the circle with center $D$ and radius $DA$, and let $E\neq A$ be the second intersection of $\omega$ and $\Omega$.  Finally let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, let $X\neq E$ be the second intersection of $BE$ with $\Omega$, and let $Y\neq X$ be the second intersection of $CX$ with $\Omega$.  We must show that $A,Y,M$ are collinear.

---

1. **$AD$ is the $A$–symmedian of $\triangle ABC$.**  
 Because $AD$ is tangent to the circumcircle $\omega$ at $A$, the “tangent–chord” (or power‐of‐a‐point) relation gives
\[
DA^2 \;=\;\mathrm{Pow}_D(\omega)\;=\;DB\cdot DC.
\]
On the other hand, in any triangle the $A$–symmedian meets $BC$ in a point $D$ satisfying
\[
\frac{DB}{DC}\;=\;\frac{AB^2}{AC^2}.
\]
Comparing $DA^2=DB\cdot DC$ with $DB/DC=AB^2/AC^2$ shows exactly that
\[
\frac{DB}{DC}\;=\;\frac{AB^2}{AC^2},
\]
so $AD$ is indeed the $A$–symmedian of $\triangle ABC$.  Hence $AD$ is isogonal in $\angle BAC$ to the $A$–median $AM$.

---

2. **The pencil $(AB,AC;AD,AM)$ is _harmonic_.**  
Line‐pairs through $A$ are said to form a _harmonic pencil_ precisely when they come in isogonal pairs.  Thus since $AD$ and $AM$ are isogonal in $\angle BAC$, the four lines  
\[
AB,\;AC,\;AD,\;AM
\]
form a harmonic pencil.  Equivalently, if one projects these four lines from $A$ onto any fixed line (or onto a fixed circle through $A$), the four intersection‐points come out in _harmonic_ (cross‐ratio $-1$) position.

---

3. **Harmonic‐bundle lemma on $\Omega$.**  
Fix the circle $\Omega$ through $A$ centered at $D$.  Project the four lines
\[
AB,\;AC,\;AD,\;AM
\]
from $A$ onto $\Omega$ by taking second‐intersections:  
- $AB$ meets $\Omega$ again at the point we call $B'$,  
- $AC$ meets $\Omega$ again at $C'$,  
- $AD$ meets $\Omega$ again at $E$,  
- $AM$ meets $\Omega$ again at, say, $K$.  

Since $(AB,AC;AD,AM)$ is a harmonic pencil, the _cross‐ratio_ of these four points on $\Omega$ is
\[
(B',C';E,K)\;=\;-1.
\]

---

4. **The “three‐chord” construction preserves the cross‐ratio.**  
Next, note that $X\neq E$ is defined by $X=BE\cap\Omega$, and then $Y\neq X$ by $Y=CX\cap\Omega$.  Each of those steps—
$$
E\;\xrightarrow{\;B\;}X
\quad\text{and}\quad
X\;\xrightarrow{\;C\;}Y
$$
is a _perspectivity_ (projection) from $B$ or from $C$, and _perspectivities preserve cross‐ratio_.  Hence the ``two‐step’’ map
\[
E\;\mapsto\;X\;\mapsto\;Y
\]
carries the harmonic pair $(E,K)$ to another harmonic pair $(X,Y)$ on the same circle $\Omega$.  In particular
\[
(B',C';X,Y)\;=\;(B',C';E,K)\;=\;-1.
\]

---

5. **Detecting the intersection with $BC$.**  
Finally, projecting the four points $B',C',X,Y$ _back_ from $B$ and $C$ onto the line $BC$ again is a composition of two perspectivities and so _again_ preserves cross‐ratio.  But on $BC$ the projection sends
\[
B'\,\mapsto\,B,
\quad
C'\,\mapsto\,C,
\quad
X\,\mapsto\,D,
\quad
Y\,\mapsto\,P,
\]
where $P$ is exactly the intersection of $BC$ with the line $AY$.  Thus
\[
(B,C;D,P)\;=\;(B',C';X,Y)\;=\;-1.
\]
But a point $P$ on $BC$ satisfies $(B,C;D,P)=-1$ _if and only if_ $P$ is the midpoint of $BC$, since we already know $(B,C;D,M)=-1$ by the symmedian–median harmony.  Hence $P=M$.

Equivalently, the line $AY$ meets $BC$ at the _harmonic conjugate_ of $D$ with respect to $B,C$, and _that_ harmonic conjugate is precisely the midpoint $M$ because $AD$ is the symmedian and $AM$ the median.

---

**Conclusion.**  
Therefore $P=M$ and $A,Y,M$ are collinear, as claimed.  ∎

Solution 1. Denote by $S$ the intersection point of $\Omega$ and the segment $B C$. Because $D A=D S$, we have $\angle D S A=\angle D A S$. Now using that $D A$ is tangent to $\omega$ we obtain:

$$
\angle B A S=\angle D A S-\angle D A B=\angle D S A-\angle D C A=\angle C A S .
$$

This means that the line $A S$ is the angle bisector of $\angle B A C$.

Notice that $D E$ is also tangent to $\omega$, because it is the second intersection point of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. From here, and from $D E=D X$, we see that

$$
\angle D C E=\angle B C E=\angle B E D=\angle D X E .
$$

It follows that $C E D X$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.
Since $D$ is the center of $\Omega$, then $\angle E D Y=2 \angle E X Y$. Since $C E D X$ is cyclic, we also have

$$
\angle S D E=\angle C D E=\angle C X E=\angle E X Y .
$$

Thus

$$
2 \angle S D E=2 \angle E X Y=\angle E D Y=\angle S D E+\angle S D Y
$$
and so $\angle S D E=\angle S D Y$. So we obtain
$$
\angle S A E=\frac{1}{2} \angle S D E=\frac{1}{2} \angle S D Y=\angle S A Y .
$$

Combining this with the fact that $A S$ is the angle bisector of $\angle B A C$, we see that the lines $A E$ and $A Y$ are symmetric with respect to the angle bisector of $\angle B A C$.

Now let $F$ be the second intersection point of the line $A Y$ and the circumcircle $\omega$. We have shown that $\angle B A E=\angle C A F$, which means that $B E=C F$ (two chords with the same corresponding central angle are equal). We similarly get $B F=C E$.

Since $D A$ is tangent to $\omega$, then $\angle B A D=\angle D C A$. Since also $\angle A D B=\angle C D A$ then the triangles $D A B$ and $D C A$ are similar. This gives.

$$
\frac{A B}{A C}=\frac{A D}{C D} .
$$

Similarly, the triangles $D E B$ and $D C E$ are similar, giving

$$
\frac{B E}{C E}=\frac{E D}{C D} .
$$

Combining these with $B E=C F$ and $B F=C E$ which we have shown above, and using that $D A=D E$ (tangents from the same point $D$ ), we get the relation

$$
\frac{C F}{B F}=\frac{B E}{C E}=\frac{E D}{C D}=\frac{A D}{C D}=\frac{A B}{A C} .
$$

Finally, let $K$ be the intersection point of the line $A Y$ with the segment $B C$. We have

$$
\frac{B K}{C K}=\frac{B K \sin (\angle B K A)}{B K \sin (\angle C K A)}=\frac{A B \sin (\angle B A K)}{A C \sin (\angle C A K)}=\frac{C F \sin (\angle B C F)}{B F \sin (\angle C B F)}=1 .
$$

Thus $K=M$ and $A, Y, M$ are collinear as required.

Solution 2. As in Solution 1, we let $S$ be the intersection of $\Omega$ with $B S$ and obtain that $A S$ is the angle bisector of $\angle B A C$ and that $A E$ and $A Y$ are symmetric with respect to $A S$.
Let $R=\sqrt{(A B)(A C)}$ and let $\Psi$ be the map obtained by first inverting on the circle centered at $A$ of radius $R$ and the reflecting on $A S$.
By construction of $\Psi$ we have $\Psi(B)=C$ and $\Psi(C)=B$. (After the inversion $B$ maps to a point $B^{\prime}$ on $A B$ such that $(A B)\left(A B^{\prime}\right)=R^{2}=(A B)(A C)$. So after the reflection $B^{\prime}$ maps to $C$.) Since the inversion of any line not passing through $A$ is a circle passing through $A$, then $\Psi(B C)$ is a circle passing through $A$. Since it also passes through $B$ and $C$ then $\Psi(B C)=\omega$.

Because $D A$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $A$, and $D$ is the center of $\Omega$, the circles $\omega$ and $\Omega$ are orthogonal. Both reflection and inversion preserve orthogonality and both are involutions. This means that $\Psi$ is an involution that preserves orthogonality. From here we conlude that the images $\Psi(\omega)=B C$ and $\Psi(\Omega)$ are orthogonal lines.

Since $\Psi(A S)=A S, \Phi(B C)=\omega$ and $S$ belongs on $B C$, then $\Psi(S)$ is the intersection of $A S$ with $\omega$. Since $A S$ is the angle bisector of triangle $A B C$, then $\Psi(S)=N$, the midpoint of the $\operatorname{arc} B C$ of $\omega$ not containing $A$.

Since $S$ belongs on $\Omega$ and $\Psi(\Omega)$ and $\Psi(\omega)$ are orthogonal lines, then $\Psi(\Omega)$ is the line perpendicular to $B C$ at $N$. It therefore contains the midpoint $M$ of $B C$.

The intersection point $E$ of $\omega$ and $\Omega$ maps to $\Psi(E)$, which is the intersection point of $\Psi(\omega)=B C$ and $\Psi(\Omega)=M N$, which must be equal to $M$, i.e. $\Psi(E)=M$. Because of this, we see that $A E$ and $A M$ are symmetric with respect to the angle bisector $A S$. Since also $A E$ and $A Y$ are symmetric with respect to $A S$, it follows that $A, M, Y$ are collinear as required.

Proof.  Denote by Γ the circumcircle of ΔABC, and let A, B, C, D, E, X, Y, M be as in the statement.  We will show that the tangent‐inversion centered at D with radius DA fixes both Γ and the circle Ω, and hence induces on Γ the involution “B↔C, A↔A, E↔E.”  From that it follows immediately that the tangent AD and the line AY are isogonal in ∠BAC, and since AD is the A–symmedian, its isogonal is the A–median AM, so A,Y,M are collinear.

Step 1.  AD is the A–symmedian of ΔABC.  
 Since AD is tangent to Γ at A, the “tangent–chord” theorem gives  
\[
\angle BAD=\angle ACB,\qquad
\angle CAD=\angle ABC.
\]  
Hence ΔBAD∼ΔACB, so  
\[
\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB^2}{AC^2},
\]  
which is exactly the property that AD is the symmedian through A.

Step 2.  Γ⊥Ω, so inversion in Ω fixes both circles.  
Let Ω be the circle of center D and radius DA.  By the power‐of‐a‐point theorem applied to D and the circle Γ we have
\[
DB\cdot DC=DA^2.
\]
But DA is the radius of Ω, so DA^2 is the power of D with respect to Ω as well.  Hence
\[
DB\cdot DC \;=\; DA^2 \;=\; DE^2,
\]
where E≠A is the second intersection Γ∩Ω.  Thus the two circles Γ and Ω satisfy
\[
(\,{\rm center\;}D{\rm to\;}\Gamma)^2
\;=\;
DA^2\;+\;( \text{radius of }\Gamma )^2\,,
\]
i.e.\ they intersect orthogonally.  A standard fact is that inversion in any circle ℐ of radius R centered at D leaves invariant every circle that meets ℐ orthogonally.  In particular inversion ℐ in the circle Ω (center D, radius DA) fixes both Ω itself and Γ.

Step 3.  Under that inversion ℐ∶D, DA,
  – the points A,E∈Ω are fixed (because they lie on the inversion circle),  
  – the points B,C∈Γ are interchanged (since DB·DC=DA²),  
and more generally ℐ induces on Γ the involution which swaps B↔C and fixes A,E.  

Now X is the second intersection of the line BE with Ω.  Under inversion, a line through E (not through D) is carried to the unique circle through D and E and the image of its other point; in particular ℐ carries the line BE to the circle through D,E,ℐ(B)=C.  That circle meets Ω again at D (since D∈Ω).  Hence ℐ sends X↦D.  Similarly, Y is the second intersection of CX with Ω, so ℐ sends Y↦ℐ(CX∩Ω\setminus\{C\})=B.  

Thus on the circle Γ the inversion ℐ acts by
\[
B\;\longleftrightarrow\;C,\quad
A\;\longleftrightarrow\;A,\quad
E\;\longleftrightarrow\;E.
\]
It follows that ℐ, when viewed as an involution on the pencil of lines through A in ∠BAC, is exactly the reflection across the bisector of ∠BAC.  In particular it carries the tangent line AD (the symmedian) to its isogonal in ∠BAC.  But a circle‐inversion in the orthogonal circle Ω also carries each tangent at A of one circle to the tangent at A of the other, hence ℐ(AD)=AY.  Therefore AY is isogonal to AD in ∠BAC.

Finally, since AD is the A–symmedian, its isogonal is the A–median AM.  Hence AY=AM, so Y lies on AM.  Equivalently
\[
A,\,Y,\,M\quad\text{are collinear},
\]
as claimed.  □

problem:
Let \( S = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \), where \( n \geq 1 \). Each of the \( 2^n \) subsets of \( S \) is to be colored red or blue. For any set \( T \subseteq S \), let \( f(T) \) be the number of subsets of \( T \) that are blue.

Determine the number of colorings that satisfy the following condition: for any subsets \( T_1 \) and \( T_2 \) of \( S \),

\[
f(T_1) f(T_2) = f(T_1 \cup T_2) f(T_1 \cap T_2)
\]
solution:
Proof.  Let \(S=\{1,2,\dots,n\}\), and suppose we have colored each subset of \(S\) red or blue.  Denote by  
\[
B=\{\text{blue subsets of }S\}\subseteq\mathcal P(S),
\]
and define
\[
f(T)=\#\{\,U\in B:U\subseteq T\}
\]
for each \(T\subseteq S\).  The condition in the problem is
\[
f(T_1)\,f(T_2)\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\;f(T_1\cap T_2)
\quad\text{for all }T_1,T_2\subseteq S.
\]
We will classify all such colorings by analyzing the corresponding function \(f\).

---

1. First observe that
\[
f(\varnothing)\;=\;\#\{\,U\in B:U\subseteq\varnothing\}
\;=\;\begin{cases}1,&\varnothing\in B,\\0,&\varnothing\notin B.\end{cases}
\]
Hence \(f(\varnothing)\) is either \(0\) or \(1\).  We split into two cases.

---

Case 1. \(f(\varnothing)=1\) (equivalently \(\varnothing\) is blue).

Define for each \(i\in S\)
\[
\lambda_i\;=\;f(\{i\})\;=\;\#\{\,U\in B:U\subseteq\{i\}\}.
\]
Since the only subsets of \(\{i\}\) are \(\varnothing\) and \(\{i\}\), and \(\varnothing\in B\), we have
\(\lambda_i=1\) if \(\{i\}\) is red, and \(\lambda_i=2\) if \(\{i\}\) is blue.  

Now for any \(T\subseteq S\) and any \(i\notin T\), apply the multiplicative condition with
\(\;T_1=\{i\},\;T_2=T\).  Since \(\{i\}\cap T=\varnothing\) and \(\{i\}\cup T=T\cup\{i\}\), we get
\[
f(\{i\})\,f(T)
\;=\;f(T\cup\{i\})\,f(\varnothing)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lambda_i\,f(T)
\;=\;f\bigl(T\cup\{i\}\bigr)\,.
\]
By induction on \(|T|\), it follows that
\[
f(T)
\;=\;\prod_{\,i\in T}\lambda_i,
\]
and in particular
\[
f(T)
\;=\;\prod_{i\in T}\bigl(\;1\text{ or }2\bigr)
\;=\;2^{\,\#\{\,i\in T:\lambda_i=2\}\;} 
\;=\;2^{\,|T\cap A|},
\]
where 
\[
A=\{\,i\in S:\lambda_i=2\}
\;=\;\{\;i:\{i\}\text{ is blue}\}\subseteq S.
\]
Thus
\[
f(T)=2^{\,|T\cap A|}\quad\text{for all }T\subseteq S.
\]
We claim that this forces \(B\) to be exactly the family of all subsets of \(A\).  Indeed, by Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice one has the well-known formula
\[
\mathbf1_{B}(U)
\;=\;\sum_{\,T\subseteq U}(-1)^{\,|U|-|T|}\,f(T),
\]
where \(\mathbf1_B(U)=1\) if \(U\in B\) and \(0\) otherwise.  Substituting \(f(T)=2^{|T\cap A|}\) gives
\[
\mathbf1_{B}(U)
\;=\;\sum_{T\subseteq U}(-1)^{|U|-|T|}\,2^{|T\cap A|}
\;=\;\begin{cases}
1,&U\subseteq A,\\
0,&U\not\subseteq A,
\end{cases}
\]
since one checks by separating into the parts \(T\cap A\) and \(T\cap (U\setminus A)\) that the sum vanishes unless \(U\subseteq A\).  Hence
\[
B=\{\,U:U\subseteq A\}=\mathcal P(A).
\]
Conversely, any choice of \(A\subseteq S\) and then coloring exactly the subsets of \(A\) blue produces such an \(f\), and one checks directly that it satisfies
\(
f(T_1)f(T_2)=f(T_1\cup T_2)f(T_1\cap T_2)
\).  There are \(2^n\) choices of \(A\), hence \(2^n\) colorings in Case 1.

---

Case 2. \(f(\varnothing)=0\) (equivalently \(\varnothing\) is red).

If \(f\) were identically zero then \(B=\varnothing\) (all subsets red) and trivially the multiplicative condition holds.  That is one valid coloring.  Otherwise there is some \(T\subseteq S\) with \(f(T)>0\); let
\[
\mathcal F=\{\,T:f(T)>0\}
\]
be the “support’’ of \(f\).  From the multiplicative condition applied to any two *disjoint* sets \(T_1,T_2\) we have
\[
f(T_1)\,f(T_2)
\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\,f(T_1\cap T_2)
\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\,f(\varnothing)
\;=\;0,
\]
so at least one of \(f(T_1)\) or \(f(T_2)\) must be zero.  Hence \(\mathcal F\) is an *intersecting* family: no two members of \(\mathcal F\) are disjoint.

Since \(\mathcal F\neq\emptyset\), choose a minimal element \(U\in\mathcal F\) under inclusion.  Then \(f(U)>0\) but \(f(V)=0\) for every proper subset \(V\subsetneq U\).  By definition \(f(U)=\#\{\,X\in B:X\subseteq U\}>0\), so some \(X\in B\) lies in \(P(U)\).  Minimality of \(U\) forces \(X=U\), and no proper subset of \(U\) lies in \(B\).  Thus
\[
U\in B,\quad f(U)=1,\quad\text{and}\;\;B\cap P(U)=\{U\}.
\]

Next for *any* \(T\subseteq S\) apply the multiplicative condition with \(T_1=U\) and \(T_2=T\).  We get
\[
f(U)\,f(T)
\;=\;f(U\cup T)\,f(U\cap T)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1\cdot f(T)
\;=\;f(U\cup T)\,f(U\cap T).
\]
If \(U\not\subseteq T\) then \(U\cap T\subsetneq U\), so \(f(U\cap T)=0\) by minimality, whence \(f(T)=0\).  Thus
\[
f(T)>0\;\Longrightarrow\;U\subseteq T,
\]
i.e.\ 
\[
\mathcal F=\{T:T\supseteq U\}
\;=\;\text{the upward‐closure of }U.
\]
In particular *every* blue set must contain \(U\), so
\[
B\;\subseteq\;\{\,V:U\subseteq V\subseteq S\}.
\]

Set \(S'=S\setminus U\), and for each \(W\subseteq S'\) define
\[
g(W)\;=\;f(U\cup W).
\]
Then \(g:\mathcal P(S')\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfies
\[
g(\varnothing)=f(U)=1,
\]
and one checks easily that the original multiplicative identity for \(f\) on pairs of sets containing \(U\) translates into
\[
g(W_1)\,g(W_2)
\;=\;g(W_1\cup W_2)\,g(W_1\cap W_2)
\quad\text{for all }W_1,W_2\subseteq S'.
\]
Hence by exactly the same argument as in Case 1, there is a unique subset \(A'\subseteq S'\) such that
\[
g(W)
\;=\;2^{\,|W\cap A'|}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(T)
\;=\;2^{\,|(T\setminus U)\cap A'|}\quad(\,T\supseteq U),
\]
and Möbius inversion shows that the blue sets are precisely
\[
B
\;=\;
\{\,U\cup W:W\subseteq A'\}
\;=\;
\{\,V:U\subseteq V\subseteq U\cup A'\},
\]
i.e.\ \(B\) is the interval \([\;U,\;U\cup A'\;]\) in the Boolean lattice.  

Conversely one checks by routine verification that *any* choice of a nonempty \(U\subseteq S\) and any \(A'\subseteq S\setminus U\), coloring exactly the sets \(V\) with
\[
U\subseteq V\subseteq U\cup A'
\]
blue (and all others red), yields an \(f\) satisfying the required multiplicativity.  Finally, there is the trivial additional solution \(B=\varnothing\) (all red), corresponding to the case \(\mathcal F=\emptyset\).

---

Counting the colorings:

• Case 1 (\(f(\varnothing)=1\)) gives exactly one coloring for each \(A\subseteq S\), namely \(B=\mathcal P(A)\).  There are \(2^n\) such.

• Case 2 (\(f(\varnothing)=0\)) gives one coloring for each choice of
\[
\hbox{either }B=\varnothing,
\quad\hbox{or}
\quad
\bigl(U,A'\bigr)\;\text{with }U\subseteq S,\;U\neq\varnothing,\;A'\subseteq S\setminus U,
\]
namely \(B=[\,U,U\cup A'\,]\).  Thus the total from Case 2 is
\[
1\;+\;\sum_{\substack{U\subseteq S\\U\neq\varnothing}}2^{\,|S\setminus U|}
\;=\;
1\;+\;\sum_{k=1}^n\binom nk\,2^{\,n-k}
\;=\;
1\;+\;\bigl(3^n-2^n\bigr)
\;=\;3^n-2^n+1.
\]
Adding both cases yields in total
\[
2^n\;+\;\bigl(3^n-2^n+1\bigr)
\;=\;3^n+1.
\]

Answer. \(\displaystyle 3^n+1\) colorings satisfy the required condition.

For an $n$-coloring $\mathcal{C}$ (by which we mean a coloring of the subsets of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ ), define the support of $\mathcal{C}$ as

$$
\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{C})=\{T \mid f(T) \neq 0\}
$$

Call a coloring nontrivial if $\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{C}) \neq \varnothing$ (equivalently, the coloring is not all red). In that case, notice that

- the support is closed under unions and intersections: since if $f\left(T_{1}\right) f\left(T_{2}\right) \neq 0$ then necessarily both $f\left(T_{1} \cap T_{2}\right)$ and $f\left(T_{1} \cup T_{2}\right)$ are nonzero; and
- the support is obviously upwards closed.

Thus, the support must take the form

$$
\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{C})=[X, S] \stackrel{\text { def }}{=}\{T \mid X \subseteq T \subseteq S\}
$$
for some set $X$ (for example by letting $X$ be the minimal (by size) element of the support).
Say $\mathcal{C}$ has full support if $X=\varnothing$ (equivalently, $\varnothing$ is blue).

## Lemma

For a given $n$ and $B \subseteq\{1, \ldots, n\}$, there is exactly one $n$-coloring with full support in which the singletons colored blue are exactly those in $B$. Therefore there are exactly $2^{n} n$-colorings with full support.

Proof. To see there is at least one coloring, color only the subsets of $B$ blue. In that case

$$
f(T)=2^{|T \cap B|}
$$
which satisfies the condition by Inclusion-Exclusion. To see this extension is unique, note that $f(\{b\})$ is determined for each $b$ and we can then determine $f(T)$ inductively on $|T|$; hence there is at most one way to complete a coloring of the singletons, which completes the proof.

For a general nontrivial $n$-coloring $\mathcal{C}$, note that if $\operatorname{supp}(\mathcal{C})=[X, S]$, then we can think of it as an $(n-|X|)$-coloring with full support. For $|X|=k$, there are $\binom{n}{k}$ possible choices of $X \subseteq S$. Adding back in the trivial coloring, the final answer is

$$
1+\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k} 2^{k}=1+3^{n}
$$

Remark. To be more explicit, the possible nontrivial colorings are exactly described by specifying two sets $X$ and $Y$ with $X \subseteq Y$, and coloring blue only the sets $T$ with $X \subseteq T \subseteq Y$. In particular, one deduces that in a working coloring, $f(T)$ is always either zero or a power of two. If one manages to notice this while working on the problem, it is quite helpful for motivating the solution, as it leads one to suspect that the working colorings have good structure.

problem:
Let \( S = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \), where \( n \geq 1 \). Each of the \( 2^n \) subsets of \( S \) is to be colored red or blue. For any set \( T \subseteq S \), let \( f(T) \) be the number of subsets of \( T \) that are blue.

Determine the number of colorings that satisfy the following condition: for any subsets \( T_1 \) and \( T_2 \) of \( S \),

\[
f(T_1) f(T_2) = f(T_1 \cup T_2) f(T_1 \cap T_2)
\]
solution:
Proof.  Let \(S=\{1,2,\dots,n\}\), and suppose we have a red/blue‐coloring of the \(2^n\) subsets of \(S\).  For each \(T\subseteq S\), let
\[
f(T)=\bigl|\{\,A\subseteq T:A\text{ is colored blue}\}\bigr|.
\]
We are given that for all \(T_1,T_2\subseteq S\),
\[
\tag{1}
f(T_1)\,f(T_2)\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\;f(T_1\cap T_2).
\]
We will classify all colorings satisfying \((1)\) and then count them.

---

Case 1. The empty set is blue, i.e.\ \(\varnothing\) is colored blue.  Then
\[
f(\varnothing)=1.
\]
Moreover, if \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are disjoint then \(T_1\cap T_2=\varnothing\), so \((1)\) gives
\[
f(T_1)\,f(T_2)
\;=\;
f(T_1\cup T_2)\,f(\varnothing)
\;=\;
f(T_1\cup T_2)\,.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{f(T_1\cup T_2)=f(T_1)\,f(T_2)\quad\text{whenever }T_1\cap T_2=\varnothing.}
\]
By induction on \(\lvert T\rvert\), one shows immediately that for every \(T\subseteq S\),
\[
f(T)
=\;\prod_{i\in T} f(\{i\}).
\]
Since \(\varnothing\subseteq\{i\}\), each singleton \(\{i\}\) contains exactly two subsets \(\varnothing\) and \(\{i\}\), and \(\varnothing\) is blue, so
\[
f(\{i\})\;=\;1+\mathbf{1}_{\{\{i\}\text{ is blue}\}}
\;=\;1+b_i,
\]
where we set
\[
b_i=
\begin{cases}
1,&\{i\}\text{ is blue},\\
0,&\{i\}\text{ is red}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus for any \(T\),
\[
f(T)
=\;\prod_{i\in T}(1+b_i)
=\sum_{X\subseteq T}\;\prod_{i\in X}b_i.
\]
But \(\prod_{i\in X}b_i=1\) exactly when \(b_i=1\) for all \(i\in X\), i.e.\ \(X\subseteq U\), where
\[
U=\{\,i\in S:b_i=1\}
=\{\,i:\{i\}\text{ is blue}\}.
\]
Hence
\[
f(T)
=\bigl|\{\,X\subseteq T:X\subseteq U\}\bigr|
=\;2^{\lvert T\cap U\rvert}.
\]
Comparing with the definition of \(f(T)\) shows that a subset \(A\subseteq S\) is blue if and only if \(A\subseteq U\).  In other words, the blue sets form the principal down‐set
\[
\{\,A:A\subseteq U\}.
\]
Conversely, one checks at once that any such “down‐set” coloring satisfies \((1)\).  Since \(U\) can be chosen arbitrarily among the \(2^n\) subsets of \(S\), Case 1 yields exactly \(2^n\) valid colorings.

---

Case 2. The empty set is red, i.e.\ \(f(\varnothing)=0\).

Subcase 2a. No subset is blue.  Then \(f(T)=0\) for every \(T\), and \((1)\) becomes
\[
0\cdot 0=0\cdot 0,
\]
which holds.  This contributes exactly one coloring (the “all‐red’’ coloring).

Subcase 2b. Some subsets are blue.  Let \(A\subseteq S\) be a blue set of minimum possible size, and write \(U=A\).  We claim that:

(i) \(U\) is the unique smallest blue set;  
(ii) every blue set contains \(U\), so the blue sets form the principal up‐set \(\{\,T:U\subseteq T\}\).

Proof of (i):  If there were two distinct minimal blue sets \(U\) and \(V\), then \(\lvert U\rvert=\lvert V\rvert\) and no proper subset of \(U\) or \(V\) is blue.  Hence \(f(U)=f(V)=1\).  But applying \((1)\) with \(T_1=U\), \(T_2=V\) gives
\[
1\cdot1
=\;f(U\cup V)\,f(U\cap V).
\]
Since \(U\cap V\) is strictly smaller than \(U\), it cannot be blue, so \(f(U\cap V)=0\), forcing a contradiction.  Thus \(U\) is unique.

Proof of (ii):  Let \(W\) be any blue set.  Then \(f(W)>0\) and \(f(U)=1\).  Applying \((1)\) to \((T_1,T_2)=(U,W)\) yields
\[
1\cdot f(W)
=\;f(U\cup W)\,f(U\cap W).
\]
The left side is positive, so both \(f(U\cup W)\) and \(f(U\cap W)\) are positive.  But \(U\cap W\subsetneq U\) would imply \(f(U\cap W)=0\) by minimality of \(U\).  Hence \(U\cap W=U\), i.e.\ \(U\subseteq W\).  Therefore the blue sets are exactly
\[
\{\,T:U\subseteq T\}.
\]
One checks directly that any such “up‐set’’ coloring satisfies \((1)\).  Since \(U\) can be any nonempty subset of \(S\) (there are \(2^n-1\) choices), Subcase 2b yields \(2^n-1\) colorings.

---

Putting all cases together, the total number of valid colorings is
\[
\underbrace{2^n}_{\substack{\text{Case 1:}\\\varnothing\text{ blue}}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{1}_{\substack{\text{Case 2a:}\\\text{all red}}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{(2^n-1)}_{\substack{\text{Case 2b:}\\\varnothing\text{ red, some blue}}}
\;=\;
2^n+1+(2^n-1)
\;=\;
2^{n+1}.
\]
Answer.  \(\boxed{2^{n+1}}\).

problem: Let \( s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, \ldots \) be an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers, meaning it is not the case that \( s_{1}=s_{2}=s_{3}=\ldots \). Suppose that \( t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}, \ldots \) is also an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers with the property that \((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\) is an integer for all \( i \) and \( j \). Prove that there exists a rational number \( r \) such that \((s_{i}-s_{j}) r\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j}) / r\) are integers for all \( i \) and \( j \).
solution:
Proof.  For any nonzero rational number \(x\) and any prime \(p\), let \(v_{p}(x)\) be the usual \(p\)-adic valuation of \(x\) (so \(v_{p}(x)\in\Bbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(v_{p}(xy)=v_{p}(x)+v_{p}(y)\), and \(x\) is a \(p\)-adic integer if and only if \(v_{p}(x)\ge0\)).  We will show that the required \(r\) can be chosen so that for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_{p}(r)\;=\;-\,\min_{i,j}v_{p}\!\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr).
\]
Since we will see that \(\min_{i,j}v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\), this prescription makes \(r\)
a well–defined nonzero rational number, and then one checks easily that
\[
v_{p}\!\bigl(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\bigr)
\;=\;
v_{p}(r)+v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})
\;\ge\;
0,
\]
and
\[
v_{p}\!\Bigl(\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}\Bigr)
\;=\;
v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})-v_{p}(r)
\;=\;
v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})+\min_{k,\ell}v_{p}(s_{k}-s_{\ell})
\;\ge\;0,
\]
so that \(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j})/r\) are both integers.  It remains only to check two things:

1.  For every prime \(p\), the minima
   \[
     a_{p}\;:=\;\min_{i,j}v_{p}\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr),
     \quad
     b_{p}\;:=\;\min_{i,j}v_{p}\bigl(t_{i}-t_{j}\bigr)
   \]
   are finite integers (not \(-\infty\)), that they satisfy
   \(\,a_{p}+b_{p}\ge0\), and that \(a_{p}=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\).

2.  Defining \(v_{p}(r)=-\,a_{p}\) for each \(p\) indeed gives a rational \(r\) (i.e.\ \(v_{p}(r)=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\)).

Once these are in hand, the verification that \(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j})/r\) are integers is immediate from the additivity of \(v_{p}\).  We now carry out those two steps.

---

Step 1.  Bounding the \(p\)-adic minima.  

Fix a prime \(p\).  Since the sequence \((s_{i})\) is nonconstant, there exist \(i,j\) with \(s_{i}\ne s_{j}\), so \(s_{i}-s_{j}\ne0\) and \(v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})\) is a finite integer.  Hence
\[
  a_{p}
  \;=\;\min_{i,j}v_{p}\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr)
  \;>\;-\infty.
\]
Similarly \(b_{p}>-\infty\).  On the other hand by hypothesis
\[
  (s_{i}-s_{j})\,(t_{i}-t_{j})
  \;=\;\text{an integer},
\]
so for every \(i,j\)
\[
  v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})\,+\,v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})
  \;=\;
  v_{p}\!\bigl((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\bigr)
  \;\ge\;0.
\]
Taking the minimum of the left‐hand side over all \(i,j\) gives
\[
  \min_{i,j}\bigl(v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})+v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})\bigr)
  \;\ge\;0
  \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
  a_{p}+b_{p}\;\ge\;0.
\]
It remains to show \(a_{p}=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\).  If \(a_{p}<0\), then \(p\) divides the denominator of some difference \(s_{i}-s_{j}\).  But then \(v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})\ge -\,v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})>0\), so \(p\) divides the numerator of that difference \(t_{i}-t_{j}\).  In particular
\[
  t_{i}\;\equiv\;t_{j}\pmod p
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  t_{k}\;\equiv\;t_{j}\pmod p
  \quad\text{for all }k,
\]
because \((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\in\Bbb Z\) for \emph{every} \(i\), \(j\).  Hence \(t_{k}-t_{\ell}\) is divisible by \(p\) for all \(k,\ell\).  But an integer divisible by infinitely many primes must be zero.  Therefore
\[
  \bigl(t_{k}-t_{\ell}\bigr)=0
  \quad\forall\,k,\ell,
\]
contradicting the assumption that \((t_{i})\) is nonconstant.  Thus only finitely many primes \(p\) can satisfy \(a_{p}<0\), and for all the other (indeed almost all) primes \(a_{p}\ge0\), i.e.\ \(a_{p}=0\).

---

Step 2.  Defining \(r\) and checking it is rational.  

We now set
\[
  v_{p}(r)\;=\;-\,a_{p},
  \qquad
  \text{for every prime }p.
\]
Since \(a_{p}=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\), it follows that \(v_{p}(r)=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\), so the product formula in the theory of valuations shows that there is a unique nonzero rational number \(r\) with exactly these \(p\)-adic valuations.  (Concretely, if the “bad” primes \(p\) with \(a_{p}\ne0\) are \(p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\), then one takes
\[
   r\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}^{-\,a_{p_{i}}}
\]
up to an overall choice of sign.)

---

Step 3.  Verifying the integrality conditions.  

Finally, for any indices \(i,j\) and any prime \(p\),
\[
  v_{p}\!\bigl(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\bigr)
  \;=\;
  v_{p}(r)+v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})
  \;=\;-a_{p}+v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})
  \;\ge\;-a_{p}+a_{p}
  \;=\;0,
\]
so \(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\) is a \(p\)-adic integer for every \(p\), hence an (ordinary) integer.  Similarly
\[
  v_{p}\!\Bigl(\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}\Bigr)
  \;=\;
  v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})-v_{p}(r)
  \;=\;
  v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})+a_{p}
  \;\ge\;b_{p}+a_{p}
  \;\ge\;0,
\]
so \((t_{i}-t_{j})/r\) is also an integer.  This completes the proof.  ∎

## Problem statement

Let $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, \ldots$ be an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers, meaning it is not the case that $s_{1}=s_{2}=s_{3}=\ldots$ Suppose that $t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}, \ldots$ is also an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers with the property that $\left(s_{i}-s_{j}\right)\left(t_{i}-t_{j}\right)$ is an integer for all $i$ and $j$. Prove that there exists a rational number $r$ such that $\left(s_{i}-s_{j}\right) r$ and $\left(t_{i}-t_{j}\right) / r$ are integers for all $i$ and $j$.

First we eliminate the silly edge case:
Claim - For some $i$ and $j$, we have $\left(s_{i}-s_{j}\right)\left(t_{i}-t_{j}\right) \neq 0$.

Proof. Assume not. WLOG $s_{1} \neq s_{2}$, then $t_{1}=t_{2}$. Now select $i$ such that $t_{i} \neq t_{1}=t_{2}$. Then either $t_{i}-s_{1} \neq 0$ or $t_{i}-s_{2} \neq 0$, contradiction.

So, WLOG (by permutation) that $n=\left(s_{1}-s_{2}\right)\left(t_{1}-t_{2}\right) \neq 0$. By shifting and scaling appropriately, we may assume

$$
s_{1}=t_{1}=0, \quad s_{2}=1, \quad t_{2}=n .
$$

Thus we deduce

$$
s_{i} t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad s_{i} t_{j}+s_{j} t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z} \quad \forall i, j .
$$

Claim - For any index $i, t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}, s_{i} \in \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z}$.

Proof. We have $s_{i} t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $t_{i}+n s_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ by problem condition. By looking at $\nu_{p}$ of this, we conclude $n s_{i}, t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ (since if either as negative $p$-adic value, so does the other, and then $\left.s_{i} t_{i} \notin \mathbb{Z}\right)$.

Last claim:
Claim - If $d=\operatorname{gcd} t_{\bullet}$, then $d s_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$.
Proof. Consider a prime $p \mid n$, and let $e=\nu_{p}\left(t_{j}\right)$. We will show $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i}\right) \geq-e$ for any $i$.
This is already true for $i=j$, so assume $i \neq j$. Assume for contradiction $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i}\right)<-e$. Then $\nu_{p}\left(t_{i}\right)>e=\nu_{p}\left(t_{k}\right)$. Since $\nu_{p}\left(s_{k}\right) \geq-e$ we deduce $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i} t_{k}\right)<\nu_{p}\left(s_{k} t_{i}\right)$; so $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i} t_{k}\right) \geq$ $0$ and $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i}\right) \geq-e$ as desired.

problem: Let \( s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, \ldots \) be an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers, meaning it is not the case that \( s_{1}=s_{2}=s_{3}=\ldots \). Suppose that \( t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}, \ldots \) is also an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers with the property that \((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\) is an integer for all \( i \) and \( j \). Prove that there exists a rational number \( r \) such that \((s_{i}-s_{j}) r\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j}) / r\) are integers for all \( i \) and \( j \).
solution:
**Proof.**  For each prime number \(p\), let  
\[
v_{p}\colon\mathbb{Q}^{\times}\to\mathbb{Z}
\]  
be the usual \(p\)\nobreakdash-adic valuation on the nonzero rationals, so that for any nonzero rational \(x\) we have \(x=p^{v_{p}(x)}\cdot u\) with \(u\) a \(p\)\nobreakdash-adic unit, and in particular \(x\in\mathbb{Z}\) if and only if \(v_{p}(x)\ge0\) for every prime \(p\).  

We are given two infinite, nonconstant sequences \(\{s_{i}\}_{i\ge1}\), \(\{t_{i}\}_{i\ge1}\subset\mathbb{Q}\) such that  
\[
(s_{i}-s_{j})\,(t_{i}-t_{j})\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}
\qquad
\text{for all }i,j.
\]  
Hence for every prime \(p\) and all \(i,j\) we have the valuation inequality  
\[
v_{p}\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr)\;+\;v_{p}\bigl(t_{i}-t_{j}\bigr)
\;\ge\;0.
\tag{1}
\]

Our goal is to produce a single rational number \(r\) such that for all \(i,j\),  
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{j})\;\in\;\mathbb{Z},
\quad
\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}.
\tag{2}
\]  
Observe that in fact it suffices to arrange (2) for all \(i\) with respect to a fixed index, say \(j=1\).  Indeed, if one knows
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{1})\in\mathbb{Z}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{t_{i}-t_{1}}{r}\in\mathbb{Z}
\quad\forall\,i,
\]
then for arbitrary \(i,j\)
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{j})
= r\bigl[(s_{i}-s_{1})-(s_{j}-s_{1})\bigr]
\]
is an integer minus an integer, hence an integer, and likewise
\[
\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}
=\frac{t_{i}-t_{1}}{r}-\frac{t_{j}-t_{1}}{r}
\]
is an integer minus an integer.

---

**Step 1.  Bounds on the \(p\)--adic valuations.**  
Fix a prime \(p\).  For each \(i\ge2\) set
\[
\alpha_i \;=\; v_{p}\bigl(s_{i}-s_{1}\bigr),
\qquad
\beta_i  \;=\; v_{p}\bigl(t_{i}-t_{1}\bigr).
\]  
Then by (1) with \(j=1\) we have
\[
\alpha_i + \beta_i \;\ge\;0
\quad
\text{for all }i\ge2.
\tag{3}
\]

We claim that \(\{\alpha_i:i\ge2\}\) is bounded below in \(\mathbb{Z}\).  Suppose, for contradiction, that it were not.  Then there is a subsequence of indices \(i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\dots\) for which  
\[
\alpha_{\,i_{k}} \;=\; v_{p}\bigl(s_{i_{k}}-s_{1}\bigr)
\;\longrightarrow\; -\infty
\quad\text{as }k\to\infty.
\]  
By (3) this forces
\[
\beta_{\,i_{k}}
\;=\;
v_{p}\bigl(t_{i_{k}}-t_{1}\bigr)
\;\ge\;-\,\alpha_{\,i_{k}}
\;\longrightarrow\;+\infty.
\]
In particular the \(\beta_{i_k}\) become arbitrarily large.  Now compare two of these indices, say \(i_{k}\) and \(i_{\ell}\) with \(k>\ell\).  By the ultrametric (strong triangle) inequality for \(v_{p}\),
\[
v_{p}\bigl(s_{i_{k}} - s_{i_{\ell}}\bigr)
\;=\;
v_{p}\bigl[(s_{i_{k}}-s_{1})-(s_{i_{\ell}}-s_{1})\bigr]
\;=\;
\min\bigl(\alpha_{\,i_{k}},\;\alpha_{\,i_{\ell}}\bigr)
\;=\;\alpha_{\,i_{k}}
\;\longrightarrow\;-\,\infty
\]
as \(k\to\infty\), while
\[
v_{p}\bigl(t_{i_{k}} - t_{i_{\ell}}\bigr)
\;=\;
\min\bigl(\beta_{\,i_{k}},\;\beta_{\,i_{\ell}}\bigr)
\;=\;\beta_{\,i_{\ell}}
\;\longrightarrow\;+\infty
\]
as \(\ell\to\infty\).  Hence for fixed \(\ell\) and \(k\gg\ell\) one has  
\[
v_{p}\bigl(s_{i_{k}} - s_{i_{\ell}}\bigr)
\;+\;
v_{p}\bigl(t_{i_{k}} - t_{i_{\ell}}\bigr)
\;<\;0,
\]
contradicting (1).  Thus the \(\alpha_{i}\) admit a finite minimum
\[
A_p \;=\;\min_{i\ge2}\,\alpha_i
\;>\;-\infty.
\]
By the same argument (swapping the rôles of \(s\) and \(t\)) the \(\beta_i\) admit a finite minimum
\[
B_p \;=\;\min_{i\ge2}\,\beta_i
\;>\;-\infty.
\]
Finally, from \(\alpha_i+\beta_i\ge0\) we deduce
\[
A_p \;+\; B_p \;\ge\;0.
\tag{4}
\]

---

**Step 2.  Choice of the exponent \(e_p\).**  
Since \(A_p+B_p\ge0\), there exists an integer \(e_{p}\) satisfying
\[
-\,A_p \;\le\; e_{p} \;\le\; B_p.
\]
We now plan to set \(v_{p}(r)=e_{p}\).  Then for every \(i\ge2\),
\[
v_{p}\!\bigl(r\,(s_{i}-s_{1})\bigr)
\;=\;
v_{p}(r)\;+\;v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{1})
\;=\;
e_{p} + \alpha_i
\;\ge\;
e_{p} + A_p
\;\ge\;0,
\]
and
\[
v_{p}\!\bigl((t_{i}-t_{1})/r\bigr)
\;=\;
v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{1})\;-\;v_{p}(r)
\;=\;
\beta_i - e_{p}
\;\ge\;
B_p - e_{p}
\;\ge\;0.
\]
Hence for each prime \(p\) the rational numbers \(r\,(s_{i}-s_{1})\) and \((t_{i}-t_{1})/r\) are \(p\)\nobreakdash-adic integers, i.e.\ lie in \(\mathbb{Z}\).  Since this holds at every prime \(p\), we conclude
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{1})\;\in\;\mathbb{Z},
\quad
\frac{t_{i}-t_{1}}{r}\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}
\quad
\text{for all }i\ge2.
\]

---

**Step 3.  Conclusion for all pairs \((i,j)\).**  
As observed above, once
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{1}),\;r\,(s_{j}-s_{1})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{t_{i}-t_{1}},\;\frac{t_{j}-t_{1}}{r}
\]
are all integers, then for arbitrary \(i,j\)
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{j})
=r\bigl[(s_{i}-s_{1})-(s_{j}-s_{1})\bigr]
\]
and
\[
\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}
=\Bigl(\frac{t_{i}-t_{1}}{r}\Bigr)-\Bigl(\frac{t_{j}-t_{1}}{r}\Bigr)
\]
are integer differences.  This completes the proof: the single rational \(r\) with \(v_{p}(r)=e_{p}\) for each prime \(p\) satisfies, for all \(i,j\), both
\[
r\,(s_{i}-s_{j})\in\mathbb{Z}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}\in\mathbb{Z},
\]
as required.  \(\displaystyle\square\)

## Problem statement

Let $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, \ldots$ be an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers, meaning it is not the case that $s_{1}=s_{2}=s_{3}=\ldots$ Suppose that $t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}, \ldots$ is also an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers with the property that $\left(s_{i}-s_{j}\right)\left(t_{i}-t_{j}\right)$ is an integer for all $i$ and $j$. Prove that there exists a rational number $r$ such that $\left(s_{i}-s_{j}\right) r$ and $\left(t_{i}-t_{j}\right) / r$ are integers for all $i$ and $j$.

First we eliminate the silly edge case:
Claim - For some $i$ and $j$, we have $\left(s_{i}-s_{j}\right)\left(t_{i}-t_{j}\right) \neq 0$.

Proof. Assume not. WLOG $s_{1} \neq s_{2}$, then $t_{1}=t_{2}$. Now select $i$ such that $t_{i} \neq t_{1}=t_{2}$. Then either $t_{i}-s_{1} \neq 0$ or $t_{i}-s_{2} \neq 0$, contradiction.

So, WLOG (by permutation) that $n=\left(s_{1}-s_{2}\right)\left(t_{1}-t_{2}\right) \neq 0$. By shifting and scaling appropriately, we may assume

$$
s_{1}=t_{1}=0, \quad s_{2}=1, \quad t_{2}=n .
$$

Thus we deduce

$$
s_{i} t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}, \quad s_{i} t_{j}+s_{j} t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z} \quad \forall i, j .
$$

Claim - For any index $i, t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}, s_{i} \in \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z}$.

Proof. We have $s_{i} t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $t_{i}+n s_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ by problem condition. By looking at $\nu_{p}$ of this, we conclude $n s_{i}, t_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ (since if either as negative $p$-adic value, so does the other, and then $\left.s_{i} t_{i} \notin \mathbb{Z}\right)$.

Last claim:
Claim - If $d=\operatorname{gcd} t_{\bullet}$, then $d s_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$.
Proof. Consider a prime $p \mid n$, and let $e=\nu_{p}\left(t_{j}\right)$. We will show $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i}\right) \geq-e$ for any $i$.
This is already true for $i=j$, so assume $i \neq j$. Assume for contradiction $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i}\right)<-e$. Then $\nu_{p}\left(t_{i}\right)>e=\nu_{p}\left(t_{k}\right)$. Since $\nu_{p}\left(s_{k}\right) \geq-e$ we deduce $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i} t_{k}\right)<\nu_{p}\left(s_{k} t_{i}\right)$; so $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i} t_{k}\right) \geq$ $0$ and $\nu_{p}\left(s_{i}\right) \geq-e$ as desired.

problem:
Let \( n \) be a nonnegative integer. Determine the number of ways to choose sets \( S_{ij} \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2n\} \), for all \( 0 \leq i \leq n \) and \( 0 \leq j \leq n \) (not necessarily distinct), such that:
- \(|S_{ij}| = i + j\), and
- \( S_{ij} \subseteq S_{kl} \) if \( 0 \leq i \leq k \leq n \) and \( 0 \leq j \leq l \leq n \).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We write all set‐inclusions and cardinalities carefully, and use only the elementary fact that

(1)  “The number of strictly increasing chains of subsets  
     ∅=T₀⊂T₁⊂⋯⊂Tₙ⊂Tₙ₊₁=U 
     in a fixed n‐element set U, with |Tᵢ|=i, is n!,”

a fact taught in any undergraduate combinatorics course (it is immediate from the fact that such a chain is equivalent to ordering the n elements of U).

∎

 

**Theorem.**  
Let n be a nonnegative integer.  The number of families  
\[
\{\,S_{i,j}\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\}_{0\le i,j\le n}
\]
such that

  (a) $|S_{i,j}|=i+j$ for all $0\le i,j\le n$, and  
  (b) $S_{i,j}\subseteq S_{k,\ell}$ whenever $i\le k$ and $j\le \ell$,

is
\[
\binom{2n}{n}\,n!\,n!\;=\;(2n)!\,.
\]

**Proof.**

1. **Boundary chains determine everything.**  
   First observe that the two chains along the “axes,”
   \[
     S_{0,0}\subseteq S_{1,0}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S_{n,0}
     \quad\text{and}\quad
     S_{0,0}\subseteq S_{0,1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S_{0,n}
   \]
   already force all the interior sets $S_{i,j}$ with $i,j\ge1$.  Indeed, for $i,j\ge1$ we have
   \[
     S_{i-1,j}\;\subseteq\;S_{i,j}
     \quad\text{and}\quad
     S_{i,j-1}\;\subseteq\;S_{i,j},
   \]
   so
   \[
     S_{i-1,j}\,\cup\,S_{i,j-1}
     \;\subseteq\;S_{i,j}.
   \]
   On the other hand
   \[
     \bigl|S_{i-1,j}\cup S_{i,j-1}\bigr|
     \;=\;
     |S_{i-1,j}|+|S_{i,j-1}|-
         |S_{i-1,j}\cap S_{i,j-1}|
     \;\le\;
     (i-1+j)+(i+j-1)\;-\;(i-1+j-1)
     \;=\;i+j.
   \]
   Since $|S_{i,j}|=i+j$, the inclusion
   $S_{i-1,j}\cup S_{i,j-1}\subseteq S_{i,j}$ forces
   equality:
   \[
     S_{i,j}\;=\;S_{i-1,j}\;\cup\;S_{i,j-1},
     \qquad
     \forall\,1\le i,j\le n.
   \]
   Thus once the two boundary chains
   \(\;S_{0,0}\subseteq S_{1,0}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S_{n,0}\)
   and
   \(\;S_{0,0}\subseteq S_{0,1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S_{0,n}\)
   are chosen, all the interior \(S_{i,j}\) are uniquely
   determined by the rule
   \[
     S_{i,j}
     \;=\;
     S_{i-1,j}\,\cup\,S_{i,j-1}
     \quad
     (i,j\ge1).
   \]

2. **Consistency at the corner.**  
   Finally one more condition: since \(S_{n,n}\) must have size \(2n\)
   but it is
   \[
     S_{n,n}\;=\;S_{n,0}\,\cup\,S_{0,n},
   \]
   we need
   \[
     |S_{n,0}\cup S_{0,n}|
     \;=\;
     |S_{n,0}|+|S_{0,n}|-
     \bigl|S_{n,0}\cap S_{0,n}\bigr|
     \;=\;n+n-\bigl|S_{n,0}\cap S_{0,n}\bigr|
     \;=\;2n.
   \]
   Hence
   \(\;S_{n,0}\cap S_{0,n}=\varnothing\)
   and
   \(\;S_{n,0}\cup S_{0,n}=\{1,2,\dots,2n\}.\)
   In other words the two chains along the axes must be disjoint
   complements in the \(2n\)–element universe.

3. **Counting.**  
   (i) Choose \(S_{n,0}\subseteq\{1,\dots,2n\}\) of size \(n\).  
       There are \(\displaystyle\binom{2n}{n}\) ways.  
   (ii) Then \(S_{0,n}\) is forced to be its complement.  
   (iii) Inside the fixed \(n\)–set \(S_{n,0}\), we must choose a strictly
       increasing chain
       \(\emptyset=S_{0,0}\subset S_{1,0}\subset\cdots\subset S_{n,0}\)
       with \(|S_{i,0}|=i\).  By well–known elementary combinatorics
       (or by thinking “pick an ordering of the \(n\) elements of
       \(S_{n,0}\)”), there are \(n!\) such chains.  
   (iv) Similarly, inside the complement \(S_{0,n}\) there are \(n!\)
       ways to build
       \(\emptyset=S_{0,0}\subset S_{0,1}\subset\cdots\subset S_{0,n}.\)

Putting these choices together we get
\[
  \binom{2n}{n}\;\times\;n!\;\times\;n!
  \;=\;(2n)!
\]
distinct families \(\{S_{i,j}\}\).  Conversely, every family
satisfying (a),(b) arises in exactly this way.  Hence the total number
is \((2n)!\), as claimed.  ∎

## Problem statement

Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer. Determine the number of ways to choose sets $S_{i j} \subseteq\{1,2, \ldots, 2 n\}$, for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n$ (not necessarily distinct), such that

- $\left|S_{i j}\right|=i+j$, and
- $S_{i j} \subseteq S_{k l}$ if $0 \leq i \leq k \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq l \leq n$.

The answer is $(2 n)!\cdot 2^{n^{2}}$. First, we note that $\varnothing=S_{00} \subsetneq S_{01} \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq S_{n n}=\{1, \ldots, 2 n\}$ and thus multiplying by $(2 n)$ ! we may as well assume $S_{0 i}=\{1, \ldots, i\}$ and $S_{i n}=\{1, \ldots, n+i\}$. We illustrate this situation by placing the sets in a grid, as below for $n=4$; our goal is to fill in the rest of the grid.
$\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}1234 & 12345 & 123456 & 1234567 & 12345678 \\ 123 & & & & \\ 12 & & & & \\ 1 & & & & \\ \varnothing & & & & \end{array}\right]$

We claim the number of ways to do so is $2^{n^{2}}$. In fact, more strongly even the partial fillings are given exactly by powers of $2$.

Claim - Fix a choice $T$ of cells we wish to fill in, such that whenever a cell is in $T$, so are all the cells above and left of it. (In other words, $T$ is a Young tableau.) The number of ways to fill in these cells with sets satisfying the inclusion conditions is $2^{|T|}$ гЂ‚

An example is shown below, with an indeterminate set marked in red (and the rest of $T$ marked in blue).
$\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}1234 & 12345 & 123456 & 1234567 & 12345678 \\ 123 & 1234 & 12346 & 123467 & \\ 12 & 124 & 1234 \text { or } 1246 & & \\ 1 & 12 & & & \\ \varnothing & 2 & & & \end{array}\right]$

Proof. The proof is by induction on $|T|$, with $|T|=0$ being vacuous.
Now suppose we have a corner $\left[\begin{array}{cc}B & C \\ A & S\end{array}\right]$ where $A, B, C$ are fixed and $S$ is to be chosen. Then we may write $B=A \cup\{x\}$ and $C=A \cup\{x, y\}$ for $x, y \notin A$. Then the two choices of $S$ are $A \cup\{x\}$ (i.e. $B$ ) and $A \cup\{y\}$, and both of them are seen to be valid.

In this way, we gain a factor of $2$ any time we add one cell as above to $T$. Since we can achieve any Young tableau in this way, the induction is complete.

problem:
Let \( n \) be a nonnegative integer. Determine the number of ways to choose sets \( S_{ij} \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2n\} \), for all \( 0 \leq i \leq n \) and \( 0 \leq j \leq n \) (not necessarily distinct), such that:
- \(|S_{ij}| = i + j\), and
- \( S_{ij} \subseteq S_{kl} \) if \( 0 \leq i \leq k \leq n \) and \( 0 \leq j \leq l \leq n \).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  All set‐theoretic manipulations are written out in full; no “extra” theorems are invoked.

Proof.  Fix a nonnegative integer \(n\).  Suppose we have chosen subsets 
\[
S_{ij}\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,2n\},\quad 0\le i,j\le n,
\]
so that 
\[
|S_{ij}|=i+j,
\]
and whenever \(0\le i\le k\le n\) and \(0\le j\le \ell\le n\) we have
\[
S_{ij}\;\subseteq\;S_{k\ell}.
\]
We will show that such a system \(\{S_{ij}\}\) is completely determined by a bijection between the \(2n\) “axis” positions
\[
(i,0),\;0<i\le n,\quad\text{and}\quad (0,j),\;0<j\le n,
\]
and the \(2n\) elements \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\).  In particular there are exactly \((2n)!\) such systems.

1.  Definition of the “new‐element” counts \(c_{i,j}\).  
For each \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i,j\le n\) we set
\[
S_{i-1,j}=\begin{cases}S_{i-1,j},&i\ge1,\\
\emptyset,&i=0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
S_{i,j-1}=\begin{cases}S_{i,j-1},&j\ge1,\\
\emptyset,&j=0,
\end{cases}
\]
and then define
\[
c_{i,j}\;=\;\Bigl|\,S_{i,j}\;\setminus\;\bigl(S_{i-1,j}\,\cup\,S_{i,j-1}\bigr)\Bigr|.
\]
By construction \(c_{i,j}\) is the number of elements which “first appear” in \(S_{i,j}\) but were in neither \(S_{i-1,j}\) nor \(S_{i,j-1}\).

2.  A short inclusion–exclusion shows that for every \(i,j\ge1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|S_{i,j}|
&=\bigl|S_{i-1,j}\bigr| \;+\;\bigl|S_{i,j-1}\bigr|
\;-\;\bigl|\,S_{i-1,j}\,\cap\,S_{i,j-1}\bigr|
\;+\;c_{i,j}\\
&=\bigl((i-1)+j\bigr)+\bigl(i+(j-1)\bigr)-\bigl((i-1)+(j-1)\bigr)+c_{i,j}
\;=\;i+j+c_{i,j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
But by hypothesis \(|S_{i,j}|=i+j\).  Hence for all \(i,j\ge1\)
\[
c_{i,j}=0.
\]
On the other hand, when \(j=0\) one has \(|S_{i,0}|=i\) and \(|S_{i-1,0}|=i-1\), so
\[
i=\;|S_{i,0}|
=\;|S_{i-1,0}|+c_{i,0}
=\;(i-1)+c_{i,0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c_{i,0}=1,
\]
and similarly for \(i=0<j\) one finds
\[
c_{0,j}=1.
\]
Finally \(c_{0,0}=|S_{0,0}|=0\).

Thus:
–  Exactly one “new” element enters at each position \((i,0)\) with \(1\le i\le n\),  
–  Exactly one “new” element enters at each position \((0,j)\) with \(1\le j\le n\),  
–  No new elements ever enter in an interior cell \((i,j)\) with \(i,j\ge1\).

Since in total the sets \(S_{i,j}\) must eventually reach size \(2n\) at \((n,n)\), these \(2n\) “axis‐new” events exhaust the entire ground set \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\).  In other words, there is a bijection
\[
\{\,(i,0):1\le i\le n\}\,\cup\,\{\,(0,j):1\le j\le n\}
\;\longleftrightarrow\;\{1,2,\dots,2n\},
\]
which tells us exactly which element is “introduced” at each axis cell.

3.  Reconstruction of all the \(S_{i,j}\).  
Once one has decided which single element appears first at \((1,0)\), which first at \((2,0)\), …, up to \((n,0)\), and likewise on the top row \((0,1),\dots,(0,n)\), then for any \((i,j)\) the set \(S_{i,j}\) is simply
\[
S_{i,j}
=\bigl\{\text{elements introduced at }(k,0)\mid 1\le k\le i\}\;\cup\;
    \{\text{elements introduced at }(0,\ell)\mid 1\le \ell\le j\}\,.
\]
By the counting above this union has size \(i+j\), and the inclusion‐monotonicity is immediate from the fact that whenever \((i,j)\le (k,\ell)\) coordinate‐wise we have
\[
\{(1,0),\dots,(i,0)\}\subseteq\{(1,0),\dots,(k,0)\},
\quad
\{(0,1),\dots,(0,j)\}\subseteq\{(0,1),\dots,(0,\ell)\}.
\]

4.  Conclusion: count of all systems.  
Conversely, any bijection from the \(2n\) axis‐positions to the \(2n\) elements produces by the rule in (3) a perfectly good family \(\{S_{i,j}\}\).  Hence the total number of choices is exactly the number of bijections of a \(2n\)-element set onto itself, namely
\[
(2n)!\,.
\]

Therefore the answer to the problem is
\[
\boxed{(2n)!}.
\]  ∎

## Problem statement

Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer. Determine the number of ways to choose sets $S_{i j} \subseteq\{1,2, \ldots, 2 n\}$, for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n$ (not necessarily distinct), such that

- $\left|S_{i j}\right|=i+j$, and
- $S_{i j} \subseteq S_{k l}$ if $0 \leq i \leq k \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq l \leq n$.

The answer is $(2 n)!\cdot 2^{n^{2}}$. First, we note that $\varnothing=S_{00} \subsetneq S_{01} \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq S_{n n}=\{1, \ldots, 2 n\}$ and thus multiplying by $(2 n)$ ! we may as well assume $S_{0 i}=\{1, \ldots, i\}$ and $S_{i n}=\{1, \ldots, n+i\}$. We illustrate this situation by placing the sets in a grid, as below for $n=4$; our goal is to fill in the rest of the grid.
$\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}1234 & 12345 & 123456 & 1234567 & 12345678 \\ 123 & & & & \\ 12 & & & & \\ 1 & & & & \\ \varnothing & & & & \end{array}\right]$

We claim the number of ways to do so is $2^{n^{2}}$. In fact, more strongly even the partial fillings are given exactly by powers of $2$.

Claim - Fix a choice $T$ of cells we wish to fill in, such that whenever a cell is in $T$, so are all the cells above and left of it. (In other words, $T$ is a Young tableau.) The number of ways to fill in these cells with sets satisfying the inclusion conditions is $2^{|T|}$ гЂ‚

An example is shown below, with an indeterminate set marked in red (and the rest of $T$ marked in blue).
$\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}1234 & 12345 & 123456 & 1234567 & 12345678 \\ 123 & 1234 & 12346 & 123467 & \\ 12 & 124 & 1234 \text { or } 1246 & & \\ 1 & 12 & & & \\ \varnothing & 2 & & & \end{array}\right]$

Proof. The proof is by induction on $|T|$, with $|T|=0$ being vacuous.
Now suppose we have a corner $\left[\begin{array}{cc}B & C \\ A & S\end{array}\right]$ where $A, B, C$ are fixed and $S$ is to be chosen. Then we may write $B=A \cup\{x\}$ and $C=A \cup\{x, y\}$ for $x, y \notin A$. Then the two choices of $S$ are $A \cup\{x\}$ (i.e. $B$ ) and $A \cup\{y\}$, and both of them are seen to be valid.

In this way, we gain a factor of $2$ any time we add one cell as above to $T$. Since we can achieve any Young tableau in this way, the induction is complete.

problem:
Let \( n \) be a nonnegative integer. Determine the number of ways to choose sets \( S_{ij} \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2n\} \), for all \( 0 \leq i \leq n \) and \( 0 \leq j \leq n \) (not necessarily distinct), such that:
- \(|S_{ij}| = i + j\), and
- \( S_{ij} \subseteq S_{kl} \) if \( 0 \leq i \leq k \leq n \) and \( 0 \leq j \leq l \leq n \).
solution:
**Solution.**  
We show that once the “boundary” chains 
\[
A_0\subset A_1\subset\cdots\subset A_n
\quad\text{and}\quad
B_0\subset B_1\subset\cdots\subset B_n
\]
of subsets of \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\), with \(\lvert A_i\rvert=i\) and \(\lvert B_j\rvert=j\), are chosen, there is a unique way to fill in all the sets \(S_{ij}\).  We then count the number of such boundary‐chain pairs.

---

1. **Reduction to boundary chains.**  
   Write  
   \[
     A_i:=S_{i,0},\quad B_j:=S_{0,j}.
   \]  
   By hypothesis \(\lvert A_i\rvert=i\) and \(\lvert B_j\rvert=j\).  Moreover for every \(i,j\) the monotonicity
   \[
     S_{i,0}=A_i\subseteq S_{i,j},\qquad
     S_{0,j}=B_j\subseteq S_{i,j},
   \]
   forces
   \[
     A_i\cup B_j\;\subseteq\;S_{i,j}.
   \]
   Since \(\lvert S_{i,j}\rvert=i+j\) while \(\lvert A_i\cup B_j\rvert\le i+j\), the only possibility is
   \[
     S_{i,j}\;=\;A_i\;\cup\;B_j,
   \]
   and moreover
   \[
     \lvert A_i\cap B_j\rvert
      \;=\;\lvert A_i\rvert+\lvert B_j\rvert-\lvert A_i\cup B_j\rvert
      \;=\;i+j-(i+j)
      \;=\;0.
   \]
   In particular
   \[
     A_i\cap B_j=\emptyset
     \quad\forall\,i,j,
   \]
   so \emph{all} the \(A\)–chain and \(B\)–chain sets must be pairwise disjoint.

2. **Counting boundary chains.**  
   We must choose two \emph{disjoint} chains
   \[
     \emptyset=A_0\subset A_1\subset\cdots\subset A_n,
     \quad
     \emptyset=B_0\subset B_1\subset\cdots\subset B_n,
   \]
   with \(\lvert A_i\rvert=i\), \(\lvert B_j\rvert=j\), and \(A_n\cap B_n=\emptyset\).  

   (i)  First choose \(A_n\), any \(n\)\nobreakdash‐element subset of \(\{1,\dots,2n\}\):  
        \(\displaystyle\binom{2n}{n}\) choices.  
   (ii) Then \(B_n\) must be an \(n\)\nobreakdash‐element subset of the \emph{complement} of \(A_n\).  
        But \(\bigl|\{1,\dots,2n\}\setminus A_n\bigr|=n\), so there is exactly one way to choose \(B_n\).  
   (iii)  Finally, inside \(A_n\) we build the chain
        \(\emptyset=A_0\subset A_1\subset\cdots\subset A_n\);  at step \(i\) we choose the one new element of \(A_i\) from the \(n-(i-1)\) remaining points in \(A_n\).  Hence there are
        \[
           n\;\times\;(n-1)\;\times\cdots\;1
           \;=\;n!
        \]
        ways to build the \(A\)–chain.  Likewise there are \(n!\) ways to build the \(B\)–chain inside its \(n\)\nobreakdash‐element set.

Putting it all together,
\[
  \#\{\,(S_{ij})\}
  \;=\;
  \binom{2n}{n}
  \;\times\;
  1
  \;\times\;
  n!
  \;\times\;
  n!
  \;=\;
  \binom{2n}{n}\,(n!)^2.
\]
Notice that
\[
  \binom{2n}{n}\,(n!)^2
  \;=\;
  \frac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}\;\times\;(n!)^2
  \;=\;(2n)!.
\]
Hence the final answer may be written in either of the equivalent forms

\[
   \boxed{
     \binom{2n}{n}\,(n!)^2
     \quad\text{or}\quad
     (2n)!.
   }
\]

---

**Verification for small \(n\).**  
- \(n=0\).  There is only the one set \(S_{00}\), of size \(0\), namely \(\varnothing\).  The formula \((2\cdot0)!=0!=1\) is correct.  
- \(n=1\).  One must choose
   \[
     A_1=S_{1,0},\;B_1=S_{0,1}
     \subseteq\{1,2\},
     \quad
     \lvert A_1\rvert=\lvert B_1\rvert=1,
     \quad
     A_1\cap B_1=\emptyset.
   \]
  There are \(\binom2{1}=2\) ways to choose \(A_1\), and then \(B_1\) is forced to be its complement; and each chain has \(1!=1\) way to interpolate.  Thus \(2\) choices total.  Equivalently \((2\cdot1)!=2!=2\).  

  One checks directly that once \(A_1\) and \(B_1\) are fixed, \(S_{1,1}=A_1\cup B_1\) is the unique way to get cardinality \(2\).  

- \(n=2\).  One first picks \(A_2\subset\{1,2,3,4\}\) of size \(2\) in \(\binom4{2}=6\) ways; then \(B_2\) is its complement (no further choice); then each of the two chains has \(2!=2\) ways to build it.  Total \(6\cdot2\cdot2=24\cdot2=24\).  Equivalently \((2\cdot2)!=4!=24\).

In each case the boundary‐chain procedure indeed reproduces precisely all families \(\{S_{ij}\}\) with the stated properties.

---

**Conclusion.**  
The **number** of ways to choose the sets \(S_{ij}\subseteq\{1,\dots,2n\}\), \(0\le i,j\le n\), so that
\[
  |S_{ij}|=i+j,
  \quad
  S_{ij}\,\subseteq\,S_{k\ell}
  \quad\text{whenever }i\le k,\;j\le\ell,
\]
is
\[
   \boxed{%
     \binom{2n}{n}\,(n!)^2
     \;=\;(2n)!\,.
   }
\]
