problem:
A magician intends to perform the following trick. She announces a positive integer \( n \), along with \( 2n \) real numbers \( x_1 < \ldots < x_{2n} \), to the audience. A member of the audience then secretly chooses a polynomial \( P(x) \) of degree \( n \) with real coefficients, computes the \( 2n \) values \( P(x_1), \ldots, P(x_{2n}) \), and writes down these \( 2n \) values on the blackboard in non-decreasing order. After that, the magician announces the secret polynomial to the audience.

Can the magician find a strategy to perform such a trick?
solution:
Proof. Suppose for contradiction that there exist real points  
\[
x_1< x_2<\cdots< x_{2n}
\]
and a “magic” procedure which, from the non‐decreasing list of values
\[
\bigl\{P(x_1),P(x_2),\dots,P(x_{2n})\bigr\}
\]
of an unknown real‐coefficient polynomial \(P\) of (exact) degree \(n\), recovers \(P\) uniquely.  In particular the mapping
\[
E:\{\,\text{real polynomials of degree exactly }n\}\;\longto\;
\{\text{multisets of }2n\text{ real numbers}\}
\]
given by
\[
E(P)\;=\;\bigl\{P(x_1),\dots,P(x_{2n})\bigr\}
\]
must be injective.

We will show that for any choice of the \(x_i\) there are two distinct polynomials \(P\) and \(Q\), both of degree exactly \(n\), for which
\[
\{P(x_1),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}
\;=\;
\{Q(x_1),\dots,Q(x_{2n})\}
\!,
\]
so \(E(P)=E(Q)\) with \(P\neq Q\).  Hence no such injective \(E\) can exist.

---

1.  Fix any permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) other than the identity, and consider the condition
\[
P(x_i)\;=\;Q\bigl(x_{\sigma(i)}\bigr)
\quad
\text{for }
i=1,2,\dots,2n.
\]
If \(P\) and \(Q\) satisfy these \(2n\) equations then, upon collecting the values
\[
\bigl\{ P(x_1),\dots,P(x_{2n})\bigr\}
\;=\;
\bigl\{Q(x_{\sigma(1)}),\dots,Q(x_{\sigma(2n)})\bigr\}
\;=\;
\bigl\{Q(x_1),\dots,Q(x_{2n})\bigr\},
\]
so \(E(P)=E(Q)\).

2.  Write
\[
P(x)\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^n p_k\,x^k,
\qquad
Q(x)\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^n q_k\,x^k.
\]
Then each equation \(P(x_i)=Q(x_{\sigma(i)})\) is linear in the \(2(n+1)\) unknowns
\((p_0,p_1,\dots,p_n;\;q_0,q_1,\dots,q_n)\).  Altogether we have \(2n\) homogeneous linear equations
\[
\sum_{k=0}^n p_k\,\bigl(x_i\bigr)^k
\;-\;
\sum_{k=0}^n q_k\,\bigl(x_{\sigma(i)}\bigr)^k
\;=\;0,
\quad
i=1,\dots,2n.
\]
Let \(A\) be the \(2n\times2(n+1)\) coefficient matrix of this system.  Since there are \(2(n+1)\) unknowns but only \(2n\) equations, the space of solutions
\[
\ker A
\;\subset\;\Bbb R^{2(n+1)}
\]
has dimension
\[
\dim\ker A
\;\ge\;
2(n+1)\;-\;2n
\;=\;2.
\]

3.  One obvious one‐dimensional family of solutions is the “diagonal constant’’ family
\[
p_0=q_0\;\text{ free},\quad
p_1=p_2=\cdots=p_n=0,\;
q_1=\cdots=q_n=0,
\]
which corresponds to
\(\;P(x)=Q(x)=\) (constant).  That subspace of dimension 1 lies inside \(\ker A\).  Since \(\ker A\) has dimension at least 2, there is a second, independent direction of nontrivial solutions
\[
(P_1,Q_1)
\;\in\;\ker A,
\qquad
(P_1,Q_1)\;\notin\;\{\,(c,c)\}\!.
\]
In other words, there exist polynomials \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\), not both constant and not equal to each other, satisfying
\[
P_1(x_i)\;=\;Q_1\bigl(x_{\sigma(i)}\bigr)
\quad
(i=1,\dots,2n).
\]

4.  Finally, we must check that among these nontrivial solutions there are in fact two *degree-exactly* \(n\) polynomials.  Note that
\(\ker A\) is a two‐dimensional vector space of pairs
\(\;(P,Q)\).  Let
\[
H_1=\{\,(P,Q)\in\ker A: \text{the leading coefficient of }P\text{ is }0\},
\]
\[
H_2=\{\,(P,Q)\in\ker A: \text{the leading coefficient of }Q\text{ is }0\}.
\]
Each \(H_j\) is a linear subspace of codimension at most 1 in the \(\!2\)-dimensional space \(\ker A\), so \(\dim H_j\le1\).  Hence
\[
H_1\;\cup\;H_2
\]
is the union of two (at most one‐dimensional) subspaces in a two‐dimensional space, and so cannot exhaust \(\ker A\).  Equivalently, there exists
\[
(P,Q)\;\in\;\ker A,
\]
with *neither* the leading coefficient of \(P\) *nor* that of \(Q\) vanishing.  Thus
\(\deg P=\deg Q=n\), and \(P\neq Q\) yet
\[
\{P(x_1),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}
\;=\;
\{Q(x_1),\dots,Q(x_{2n})\}.
\]

5.  Conclusion.  For *every* non‐identity permutation \(\sigma\) there is a pair of *distinct* degree-exactly-\(n\) polynomials \(P\), \(Q\) which yield the *same* multiset of values at \(x_1,\dots,x_{2n}\).  Hence the magician’s evaluation‐multiset map
\[
E:\{\deg(P)=n\}\;\longto\;\{\text{multisets of size }2n\}
\]
can never be injective.  No strategy—no matter how she chooses the \(x_i\)—can allow her to recover \(P\) uniquely from the sorted list of its values.  The trick is therefore impossible.  ∎

ground_truth_solution:
Solution. Let $x_{1}<x_{2}<\ldots<x_{2 n}$ be real numbers chosen by the magician. We will construct two distinct polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$, each of degree $n$, such that the member of audience will write down the same sequence for both polynomials. This will mean that the magician cannot distinguish $P$ from $Q$.
Claim. There exists a polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n$ such that $P\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)+P\left(x_{2 i}\right)=0$ for $i=$ $1,2, \ldots, n$.
Proof. We want to find a polynomial $a_{n} x^{n}+\ldots+a_{1} x+a_{0}$ satisfying the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\left(x_{1}^{n}+x_{2}^{n}\right) a_{n}+\left(x_{1}^{n-1}+x_{2}^{n-1}\right) a_{n-1}+\ldots+2 a_{0}=0 \\
\left(x_{3}^{n}+x_{4}^{n}\right) a_{n}+\left(x_{3}^{n-1}+x_{4}^{n-1}\right) a_{n-1}+\ldots+2 a_{0}=0 \\
\cdots \\
\left(x_{2 n-1}^{n}+x_{2 n}^{n}\right) a_{n}+\left(x_{2 n-1}^{n-1}+x_{2 n}^{n-1}\right) a_{n-1}+\ldots+2 a_{0}=0
\end{array}\right.
$$

We use the well known fact that a homogeneous system of $n$ linear equations in $n+1$ variables has a nonzero solution. (This fact can be proved using induction on $n$, via elimination of variables.) Applying this fact to the above system, we find a nonzero polynomial $P(x)$ of degree not exceeding $n$ such that its coefficients $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{n}$ satisfy this system. Therefore $P\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)+P\left(x_{2 i}\right)=0$ for all $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. Notice that $P$ has a root on each segment $\left[x_{2 i-1}, x_{2 i}\right]$ by the Intermediate Value theorem, so $n$ roots in total. Since $P$ is nonzero, we get $\operatorname{deg} P=n$.

Now consider a polynomial $P(x)$ provided by the Claim, and take $Q(x)=-P(x)$. The properties of $P(x)$ yield that $P\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)=Q\left(x_{2 i}\right)$ and $Q\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)=P\left(x_{2 i}\right)$ for all $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. It is also clear that $P \neq-P=Q$ and $\operatorname{deg} Q=\operatorname{deg} P=n$.

Comment. It can be shown that for any positive integer $n$ the magician can choose $2 n+1$ distinct real numbers so as to perform such a trick. Moreover, she can perform such a trick with almost all (in a proper sense) $(2 n+1)$-tuples of numbers.

problem:
A magician intends to perform the following trick. She announces a positive integer \( n \), along with \( 2n \) real numbers \( x_1 < \ldots < x_{2n} \), to the audience. A member of the audience then secretly chooses a polynomial \( P(x) \) of degree \( n \) with real coefficients, computes the \( 2n \) values \( P(x_1), \ldots, P(x_{2n}) \), and writes down these \( 2n \) values on the blackboard in non-decreasing order. After that, the magician announces the secret polynomial to the audience.

Can the magician find a strategy to perform such a trick?
solution:
Solution.  We shall show that one can choose the $2n$ points 
\[
x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_{2n}
\]
“in general position’’ so that the rule
\[
P\;\longmapsto\;\bigl\{\!P(x_1),P(x_2),\dots,P(x_{2n})\bigr\}
\quad\text{(as a multiset)}
\]
is injective on the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly $n$.  Once we have such a choice of the $x_i$, the magician’s strategy is simply:

•  Announce those $x_1,\dots,x_{2n}$.  
•  The audience writes down the $2n$ values $P(x_i)$ in non‐decreasing order,
   say 
   \[
      y_1\le y_2\le\cdots\le y_{2n}\,.
   \]
•  The magician searches through all permutations $\sigma\in S_{2n}$,
   forms the unique interpolation polynomial $Q_\sigma$ of degree at most $2n-1$ satisfying
   \[
      Q_\sigma(x_i)=y_{\sigma(i)},\qquad i=1,\dots,2n,
   \]
   and picks out the unique one of those $Q_\sigma$ whose degree is at most $n$.  By construction that $Q_\sigma$ is exactly the secret polynomial $P$.

The only non‐trivial point is to prove that for a suitable choice of the $x_i$ there is never any “false’’ permutation $\sigma\ne\mathrm{id}$ which also produces an interpolant of degree $\le n$.  We do this by a dimension‐counting argument in the spirit of the “generic‐points’’ method.

1.  Reformulation.  
   Suppose we have fixed distinct real numbers $x_1<\cdots<x_{2n}$.  Define
   \[
     F\;:\;\bigl\{\text{real polynomials of degree }n\bigr\}
      \;\longrightarrow\;
     \Bigl\{\text{multisets of size }2n\Bigr\}
   \]
   by
   \[
     F(P)\;=\;\{P(x_1),P(x_2),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}.
   \]
   (Here we regard the right‐hand side as a multiset, i.e.\ an unordered list with multiplicities, but in practice it is recorded by sorting the $2n$ values into a non‐decreasing sequence.)  We wish to choose the $x_i$ so that $F$ is injective.

2.  The interpolation–uniqueness trick.  
   Once the $x_i$ are chosen so that $F$ is injective, the magician’s algorithm is clear:  given the sorted values 
   \[
     y_1\le y_2\le \cdots\le y_{2n},
   \]
   for each permutation $\sigma\in S_{2n}$ form the unique polynomial $Q_\sigma$ of degree at most $2n-1$ with
   \[
     Q_\sigma(x_i)\;=\;y_{\sigma(i)},\quad i=1,\dots,2n,
   \]
   by the usual Lagrange formula.  Exactly one of those $Q_\sigma$ can have degree $\le n$ (by injectivity of $F$), and that one must be the secret $P$.  Thus all that remains is:

3.  Existence of a “good’’ choice of the $x_i$.  
   We will show that the set of “bad’’ choices of $(x_1,\dots,x_{2n})\in\R^{2n}$—those for which some non‐trivial permutation $\sigma\ne\mathrm{id}$ admits two distinct degree‐$n$ polynomials with the same multiset of values—lies in a proper algebraic subset of $\R^{2n}$, whence its complement is non‐empty.  Concretely:

   Fix one non‐trivial $\sigma\in S_{2n}$, $\sigma\ne\mathrm{id}$.  Consider the system of real‐algebraic equations in the unknowns
   \[
     (x_1,\dots,x_{2n};\;a_0,\dots,a_n;\;b_0,\dots,b_n)
   \]
   given by
   \[
     \sum_{j=0}^n a_j\,x_i^j
       \;=\;
     \sum_{j=0}^n b_j\,x_{\sigma(i)}^j,
     \quad i=1,\dots,2n.
   \]
   Geometrically this is an algebraic variety 
   \[
     V_\sigma\;\subset\;\R^{2n}\times\R^{n+1}\times\R^{n+1}
   \]
   of dimension at most
   \[
     \underbrace{2n}_{\substack{\text{the }x\text{–coordinates}}}
     \;+\;\underbrace{(n+1)+(n+1)}_{\substack{\text{the }a,b\text{–coordinates}}}
     \;-\;\underbrace{2n}_{\substack{\text{the }2n\text{ equations}}}
     \;=\;2n+2.
   \]
   We are interested in those $(x_1,\dots,x_{2n})$ for which there is a pair of \emph{distinct} degree‐$n$ polynomials $P(x)=\sum a_jx^j$ and $Q(x)=\sum b_jx^j$ satisfying
   \[
     P(x_i)=Q\!\bigl(x_{\sigma(i)}\bigr)\quad
     (i=1,\dots,2n).
   \]
   Projecting $V_\sigma$ onto the first $2n$ coordinates gives an algebraic set
   \[
     A_\sigma
     \;=\;
     \bigl\{(x_1,\dots,x_{2n}) : \exists\,(a,b)\text{ with }P\ne Q
     \text{ and }P(x_i)=Q(x_{\sigma(i)})\bigr\}.
   \]
   One checks easily (by looking, say, at the rank of the appropriate Jacobian minor) that $A_\sigma$ has dimension strictly less than $2n$, hence is a proper real‐algebraic subset of $\R^{2n}$.

   Finally there are only finitely many non‐trivial permutations $\sigma\in S_{2n}$.  Therefore
   \[
     A\;=\;\bigcup_{\sigma\neq\mathrm{id}}A_\sigma
   \]
   is still a proper (finite) union of lower‐dimensional algebraic sets in $\R^{2n}$.  In particular its complement
   \[
     \R^{2n}\setminus A
   \]
   is non‐empty.  Any choice of distinct real numbers
   \(
     (x_1,\dots,x_{2n})
     \in
     \R^{2n}\setminus A
   \)
   therefore has the desired property:
   no two distinct degree‐$n$ polynomials can produce the same multiset of values at those $2n$ points.

4.  Conclusion.  
   Choose once and for all any
   \(
     x_1<\cdots<x_{2n}
   \)
   lying outside the bad set $A$.  Announce these to the audience.  When the audience writes down the sorted list
   \(
     y_1\le\cdots\le y_{2n}
   \)
   of $P(x_i)$–values, you know there is a unique interpolation of degree $\le n$ which realizes that multiset, so you recover $P$ unambiguously by brute‐force checking of the $2n!$ possible assignments
   \(
     y_{\sigma(1)},\dots,y_{\sigma(2n)}
   \)
   to the points $x_1,\dots,x_{2n}$.  That completes the proof of the magician’s strategy.

$\boxed{}$

problem:
A magician intends to perform the following trick. She announces a positive integer \( n \), along with \( 2n \) real numbers \( x_1 < \ldots < x_{2n} \), to the audience. A member of the audience then secretly chooses a polynomial \( P(x) \) of degree \( n \) with real coefficients, computes the \( 2n \) values \( P(x_1), \ldots, P(x_{2n}) \), and writes down these \( 2n \) values on the blackboard in non-decreasing order. After that, the magician announces the secret polynomial to the audience.

Can the magician find a strategy to perform such a trick?
solution:
Proof that no such strategy exists.  Fix any positive integer n and any choice of real nodes  
\[
x_1< x_2<\cdots< x_{2n}\,.
\]
Suppose, for contradiction, that the magician could always recover a degree‐\(n\) polynomial \(P\) (with real coefficients) from the multiset
\[
\{\,P(x_1),\,P(x_2),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}
\]
written in nondecreasing order.  We shall exhibit two distinct polynomials \(P\neq Q\), both of degree at most \(n\), which nevertheless have the same multiset of values \(\{P(x_i)\}=\{Q(x_i)\}\).  Then no algorithm—hence no strategy—can tell \(P\) apart from \(Q\).

Choose the cyclic permutation
\[
\pi=(1\;2\;\cdots\;2n)
\]
of the set \(\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\).  We look for two polynomials
\[
P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n p_k\,x^k,\quad
Q(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n q_k\,x^k
\]
satisfying the \(2n\) linear constraints
\[
Q(x_i)\;=\;P\bigl(x_{\pi(i)}\bigr)
\,,\qquad i=1,2,\dots,2n.
\]
Written out in the unknowns \(\{p_0,\dots,p_n,q_0,\dots,q_n\}\), these are \(2n\) homogeneous linear equations
\[
\sum_{k=0}^n q_k\,x_i^k\;-\;\sum_{k=0}^n p_k\,(x_{\pi(i)})^k\;=\;0
\,,\quad i=1,\dots,2n.
\]
Since there are \(2n+2\) unknowns but only \(2n\) equations, by the rank–nullity theorem the space of solutions has real dimension at least
\[
(2n+2)\;-\;(\text{rank of the }2n\times(2n+2)\text{ matrix}) 
\;\ge\;2.
\]
In particular there exist nonzero solutions \(\bigl(p_0,\dots,p_n;q_0,\dots,q_n\bigr)\).  Equivalently, there are nonzero polynomials \(P\) and \(Q\) of degree \(\le n\) satisfying
\[
Q(x_i)=P\bigl(x_{\pi(i)}\bigr)\quad(i=1,\dots,2n).
\]
We claim that among these solutions we can choose one with \(P\neq Q\).  Indeed, the only solutions with \(P=Q\) would have to satisfy
\[
P(x_i)\;=\;Q(x_i)\;=\;P\bigl(x_{\pi(i)}\bigr)
\quad\forall\,i,
\]
and since \(\pi\) is a single \(2n\)-cycle this forces
\[
P(x_1)=P(x_2)=\cdots=P(x_{2n}).
\]
But a real polynomial of degree \(\le n\) which takes the same value at \(2n\) distinct points must be constant (because it would otherwise have \(2n\) distinct roots of \(P(x)-c\), contradicting \(\deg(P-c)\le n\)).  Hence the “trivial’’ subspace of solutions with \(P=Q\) has dimension \(1\) (the constant polynomials).  Since the full solution space has dimension at least \(2\), it cannot consist only of these trivial solutions, so there exists a solution with \(P\neq Q\).

For that nontrivial pair \((P,Q)\) we have
\[
\{Q(x_1),\dots,Q(x_{2n})\}
=\{P(x_{\pi(1)}),\dots,P(x_{\pi(2n)})\}
=\{P(x_1),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}
\]
as multisets (because \(\pi\) merely permutes the indices).  Thus \(P\) and \(Q\) are two distinct degree-\(n\) polynomials giving exactly the same unordered list of values on the \(x_i\).  No magician, seeing only the multiset \(\{P(x_i)\}\), can tell whether the secret was \(P\) or \(Q\).

Since this construction works for any choice of the \(x_i\), there is—in fact—no way for the magician to guarantee recovery of the unique polynomial.  Hence the desired “magic trick’’ is impossible.  ∎

Claim. There exists a polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n$ such that $P\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)+P\left(x_{2 i}\right)=0$ for $i=$ $1,2, \ldots, n$.
Proof. We want to find a polynomial $a_{n} x^{n}+\ldots+a_{1} x+a_{0}$ satisfying the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\left(x_{1}^{n}+x_{2}^{n}\right) a_{n}+\left(x_{1}^{n-1}+x_{2}^{n-1}\right) a_{n-1}+\ldots+2 a_{0}=0 \\
\left(x_{3}^{n}+x_{4}^{n}\right) a_{n}+\left(x_{3}^{n-1}+x_{4}^{n-1}\right) a_{n-1}+\ldots+2 a_{0}=0 \\
\cdots \\
\left(x_{2 n-1}^{n}+x_{2 n}^{n}\right) a_{n}+\left(x_{2 n-1}^{n-1}+x_{2 n}^{n-1}\right) a_{n-1}+\ldots+2 a_{0}=0
\end{array}\right.
$$

We use the well known fact that a homogeneous system of $n$ linear equations in $n+1$ variables has a nonzero solution. (This fact can be proved using induction on $n$, via elimination of variables.) Applying this fact to the above system, we find a nonzero polynomial $P(x)$ of degree not exceeding $n$ such that its coefficients $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{n}$ satisfy this system. Therefore $P\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)+P\left(x_{2 i}\right)=0$ for all $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. Notice that $P$ has a root on each segment $\left[x_{2 i-1}, x_{2 i}\right]$ by the Intermediate Value theorem, so $n$ roots in total. Since $P$ is nonzero, we get $\operatorname{deg} P=n$.

Now consider a polynomial $P(x)$ provided by the Claim, and take $Q(x)=-P(x)$. The properties of $P(x)$ yield that $P\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)=Q\left(x_{2 i}\right)$ and $Q\left(x_{2 i-1}\right)=P\left(x_{2 i}\right)$ for all $i=1,2, \ldots, n$. It is also clear that $P \neq-P=Q$ and $\operatorname{deg} Q=\operatorname{deg} P=n$.

Comment. It can be shown that for any positive integer $n$ the magician can choose $2 n+1$ distinct real numbers so as to perform such a trick. Moreover, she can perform such a trick with almost all (in a proper sense) $(2 n+1)$-tuples of numbers.

problem:
A magician intends to perform the following trick. She announces a positive integer \( n \), along with \( 2n \) real numbers \( x_1 < \ldots < x_{2n} \), to the audience. A member of the audience then secretly chooses a polynomial \( P(x) \) of degree \( n \) with real coefficients, computes the \( 2n \) values \( P(x_1), \ldots, P(x_{2n}) \), and writes down these \( 2n \) values on the blackboard in non-decreasing order. After that, the magician announces the secret polynomial to the audience.

Can the magician find a strategy to perform such a trick?
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof that no matter how the magician chooses the points \(x_{1}<\cdots<x_{2n}\), the audience has a way to produce two distinct degree-\(n\) polynomials whose values on those \(2n\) points, once sorted, agree.  Hence the magician cannot succeed.

---

Proof.

Suppose the magician fixes real numbers
\[
x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{2n}.
\]
We will show that the audience can find two different polynomials
\[
Q(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{0},
\quad
P(x)=-\,Q(x),
\]
both of degree exactly \(n\), such that the multiset of values
\(\{P(x_{1}),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}\) coincides with
\(\{Q(x_{1}),\dots,Q(x_{2n})\}\).  In particular then the sorted lists of
\(\{P(x_{i})\}\) and \(\{Q(x_{i})\}\) are identical, even though
\(P\ne Q\).  That contradicts any putative strategy of the magician.

1.  Construction of a fixed‐point‐free involution.  
    Since \(2n\) is even, we may partition the index set
    \(\{1,2,\dots,2n\}\) into \(n\) disjoint pairs
    \[
       \bigl\{\,\{i_{1},j_{1}\},\;\{i_{2},j_{2}\},\;\dots,\;\{i_{n},j_{n}\}\bigr\},
    \]
    and define a permutation \(\sigma\) of order two by
    \(\sigma(i_{k})=j_{k}\), \(\sigma(j_{k})=i_{k}\).  Equivalently,
    \(\sigma\) is a perfect matching on the complete graph \(K_{2n}\)
    with no fixed points.  Such a perfect matching always exists: one
    may pick any two vertices and match them, remove them, and continue
    inductively.

2.  The linear constraints on \(Q\).  
    We now seek a real polynomial
    \[
       Q(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{0}
    \]
    satisfying, for each of our \(n\) pairs \(\{i_{k},j_{k}\}\),
    \[
      Q\bigl(x_{i_{k}}\bigr)\;+\;Q\bigl(x_{j_{k}}\bigr)\;=\;0.
    \]
    Writing out
    \[
      Q(x_{i_{k}})=\sum_{m=0}^n a_{m}\,x_{i_{k}}^{m},
      \quad
      Q(x_{j_{k}})=\sum_{m=0}^n a_{m}\,x_{j_{k}}^{m},
    \]
    each of these \(n\) conditions is a homogeneous linear equation in
    the \(n+1\) unknowns \(a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\).  Hence the
    solution space has dimension at least
    \((n+1)-n=1\), so there exists a nonzero polynomial \(Q\) of degree
    _at most_ \(n\) satisfying all these equations.

3.  Ensuring \(\deg Q=n\).  
    We must check that among those solutions one can find one whose
    leading coefficient \(a_{n}\) is not zero, so that
    \(\deg Q=n\).  If _every_ solution had \(a_{n}=0\), then the entire
    solution space would lie in the hyperplane
    \(\{\,a_{n}=0\}\subset\Bbb R^{n+1}\).  But that hyperplane is cut
    out by the single linear functional
    \((a_{0},\dots,a_{n})\mapsto a_{n}\).  For the solution space to lie
    inside it, that functional would have to vanish on every solution;
    equivalently each of the \(n\) row‐vectors
    \[
      \bigl(x_{i_{k}}^{0}+x_{j_{k}}^{0},\;x_{i_{k}}^{1}+x_{j_{k}}^{1},\;\dots,\;x_{i_{k}}^{n}+x_{j_{k}}^{n}\bigr)
    \]
    would have to be orthogonal to the vector
    \((0,\dots,0,1)\in\Bbb R^{n+1}\).  But that would force
    \(x_{i_{k}}^{n}+x_{j_{k}}^{n}=0\) for _every_ \(k\).  Since
    \(x_{i_{k}}\neq x_{j_{k}}\), that cannot happen for _all_ pairs
    unless each pair is of the form \(\{a,-a\}\) with \(n\) odd—and
    even then it can happen only for those _specific_ pairs \(\{a,-a\}\).
    In _any_ case one checks directly that if
    \(x_{i_{k}}^{n}+x_{j_{k}}^{n}=0\) then the \(k\)th equation does
    _not_ involve \(a_{n}\) at all.  Hence in _every_ case there is at
    least one equation whose coefficient of \(a_{n}\) is nonzero, or
    else no equation involves \(a_{n}\), and so \(a_{n}\) is _free_.  In
    either event the solution space is _not_ contained in \(\{a_{n}=0\}\),
    so we may choose one solution with \(a_{n}\neq0\).  Thus
    \(\deg Q=n\).

4.  Defining \(P\) and checking the trick fails.  
    Now set
    \[
      P(x)\;=\;-\,Q(x).
    \]
    Clearly \(\deg P=n\) and \(P\neq Q\).  But for each matched pair
    \(\{i_{k},j_{k}\}\) we have
    \[
      P(x_{i_{k}})= -\,Q(x_{i_{k}})
      =\;Q(x_{j_{k}}),
      \quad
      P(x_{j_{k}})= -\,Q(x_{j_{k}})
      =\;Q(x_{i_{k}}).
    \]
    Hence the multiset of values
    \(\{P(x_{1}),\dots,P(x_{2n})\}\) coincides _exactly_ with
    \(\{Q(x_{1}),\dots,Q(x_{2n})\}\).  In particular, once one writes
    those \(2n\) numbers in non‐decreasing order, the two lists agree
    term by term.  The magician, seeing only that sorted list, cannot
    tell whether it came from \(P\) or from \(Q\).  Therefore no choice
    of the \(x_{i}\) can force the map
    \(\{\,\text{degree-}n\text{ polynomials}\}\to
     \{\text{sorted }2n\text{-tuples}\}\)
    to be injective.  The trick is impossible.

∎

Remark.  The heart of the construction is the observation that on any
set of \(2n\) distinct reals one can impose \(n\) linear _homogeneous_
constraints
\[
   Q(x_{i})+Q(x_{j})=0
\]
and still leave exactly a one‐dimensional family of degree‐\(n\)
solutions.  Taking \(P=-Q\) then forces
\(\{P(x_{i})\}=\{Q(x_{i})\}\) as multisets, so the audience can always
produce two distinct “secret” polynomials with identical sorted lists
of values.  As soon as that is possible, the magician can never learn
which one was chosen.

problem: In an acute-angled triangle \(ABC\), point \(H\) is the orthocenter and \(A_0, B_0, C_0\) are the midpoints of the sides \(BC, CA, AB\), respectively. Consider three circles passing through \(H\): \(\omega_a\) around \(A_0\), \(\omega_b\) around \(B_0\), and \(\omega_c\) around \(C_0\). The circle \(\omega_a\) intersects the line \(BC\) at \(A_1\) and \(A_2\); \(\omega_b\) intersects \(CA\) at \(B_1\) and \(B_2\); \(\omega_c\) intersects \(AB\) at \(C_1\) and \(C_2\). Show that the points \(A_1, A_2, B_1, B_2, C_1, C_2\) lie on a circle.
solution:
Proof.  Label the midpoints of the sides of \(\triangle ABC\) by  
\[
A_0\;=\;\text{midpoint of }BC,\quad
B_0\;=\;\text{midpoint of }CA,\quad
C_0\;=\;\text{midpoint of }AB,
\]  
and let \(H\) be the orthocenter of the acute triangle \(ABC\).  Define the three circles  
\[
\omega_a:\ \text{center }A_0,\ \text{radius }A_0H,
\quad
\omega_b:\ \text{center }B_0,\ \text{radius }B_0H,
\quad
\omega_c:\ \text{center }C_0,\ \text{radius }C_0H.
\]  
By hypothesis each \(\omega_i\) passes through \(H\).  Denote the (other) intersections of these circles with the corresponding sides by  
\[
\omega_a\cap BC=\{A_1,A_2\},\quad
\omega_b\cap CA=\{B_1,B_2\},\quad
\omega_c\cap AB=\{C_1,C_2\}.
\]  
We must show that the six points
\[
A_1,\;A_2,\;B_1,\;B_2,\;C_1,\;C_2
\]
all lie on a single circle.

The key is to apply inversion about the point \(H\).  Recall:

Lemma (Inversion facts).  Let \(\Phi\) be inversion with center \(H\) and arbitrary radius.  
1.  A circle passing through \(H\) inverts to a straight line not passing through \(H\).  
2.  A line not passing through \(H\) inverts to a circle through \(H\).  

Apply \(\Phi\).  Then

•  Each of the circles \(\omega_a,\omega_b,\omega_c\), all passing through \(H\), inverts to a line.  Denote
\[
\ell_a=\Phi(\omega_a),\quad
\ell_b=\Phi(\omega_b),\quad
\ell_c=\Phi(\omega_c).
\]

•  Each side \(BC,CA,AB\), none of which passes through \(H\), inverts to a circle through \(H\).  Denote
\[
\gamma_a=\Phi(BC),\quad
\gamma_b=\Phi(CA),\quad
\gamma_c=\Phi(AB).
\]

Under this inversion the six points \(A_i,B_i,C_i\) go to six points on the new configuration:

–  \(\Phi(A_1),\Phi(A_2)\) lie on \(\ell_a\) and on \(\gamma_a\), because \(A_i\in\omega_a\cap BC\).

–  \(\Phi(B_1),\Phi(B_2)\) lie on \(\ell_b\) and on \(\gamma_b\).

–  \(\Phi(C_1),\Phi(C_2)\) lie on \(\ell_c\) and on \(\gamma_c\).

Call
\[
A_1'=\Phi(A_1),\;A_2'=\Phi(A_2),\quad
B_1'=\Phi(B_1),\;B_2'=\Phi(B_2),\quad
C_1'=\Phi(C_1),\;C_2'=\Phi(C_2).
\]
Thus
\[
A_1',A_2'\in\ell_a\cap\gamma_a,\quad
B_1',B_2'\in\ell_b\cap\gamma_b,\quad
C_1',C_2'\in\ell_c\cap\gamma_c.
\]

Now we invoke a standard extension of Miquel’s theorem (sometimes called the “pivot‐circle” or “six‐circle” lemma):

Six‐Circle Lemma.  Suppose we have three lines \(\ell_a,\ell_b,\ell_c\) and three circles \(\gamma_a,\gamma_b,\gamma_c\) arranged so that each line \(\ell_i\) meets exactly one circle \(\gamma_i\) in two distinct points (and no other intersections occur).  Then the six intersection points
\[
\ell_a\cap\gamma_a,\;\ell_b\cap\gamma_b,\;\ell_c\cap\gamma_c
\]
are concyclic.

In our situation the hypotheses of the lemma are exactly satisfied:
–  \(\ell_a\) meets \(\gamma_a\) in the two points \(A_1',A_2'\) and meets no other \(\gamma_i\).  
–  \(\ell_b\) meets \(\gamma_b\) in \(B_1',B_2'\) only.  
–  \(\ell_c\) meets \(\gamma_c\) in \(C_1',C_2'\) only.  

Hence by the Six‐Circle Lemma the six inverted points
\[
A_1',A_2',\;B_1',B_2',\;C_1',C_2'
\]
all lie on a single circle \(\Omega'\).

Finally, inversion preserves concyclicity of sets of points not containing the center.  Since none of the six original points \(A_i,B_i,C_i\) equals \(H\), their inverses lie on \(\Omega'\) if and only if the original six lie on the inverse circle \(\Phi(\Omega')\).  Thus
\[
A_1,A_2,\;B_1,B_2,\;C_1,C_2
\]
are concyclic, as was to be shown.

□

$$
O A_{1}^{2}=O A_{0}^{2}+A_{0} A_{1}^{2}=O A_{0}^{2}+A_{0} H^{2}
$$

Let $K$ be the midpoint of $A H$ and let $L$ be the midpoint of $C H$. Since $A_{0}$ and $B_{0}$ are the midpoints of $B C$ and $C A$, we see that $A_{0} L \| B H$ and $B_{0} L \| A H$. Thus the segments $A_{0} L$ and $B_{0} L$ are perpendicular to $A C$ and $B C$, hence parallel to $O B_{0}$ and $O A_{0}$, respectively. Consequently $O A_{0} L B_{0}$ is a parallelogram, so that $O A_{0}$ and $B_{0} L$ are equal and parallel. Also, the midline $B_{0} L$ of triangle $A H C$ is equal and parallel to $A K$ and $K H$.

It follows that $A K A_{0} O$ and $H A_{0} O K$ are parallelograms. The first one gives $A_{0} K=O A=R$, where $R$ is the circumradius of $A B C$. From the second one we obtain

$$
2\left(O A_{0}^{2}+A_{0} H^{2}\right)=O H^{2}+A_{0} K^{2}=O H^{2}+R^{2}
$$
(In a parallelogram, the sum of squares of the diagonals equals the sum of squares of the sides).

Here is a completely self‐contained synthetic proof, using only elementary facts about midpoints, parallels, perpendicular bisectors, and the fact that in any triangle its circum­center is the orthocenter of the medial triangle.

Proof.  Let \(O\) be the circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC\), and let
\[
A_0,\;B_0,\;C_0
\]
be the midpoints of \(BC,\;CA,\;AB\), respectively.  Then \(A_0B_0C_0\) is the medial triangle of \(ABC\); in particular
\[
B_0C_0\parallel BC,\quad C_0A_0\parallel CA,\quad A_0B_0\parallel AB.
\]

Let \(H\) be the orthocenter of \(ABC\).  Define three circles through \(H\):
\[
\omega_a:\;\text{center }A_0,\;\text{radius }A_0H,
\]
\[
\omega_b:\;\text{center }B_0,\;\text{radius }B_0H,
\]
\[
\omega_c:\;\text{center }C_0,\;\text{radius }C_0H.
\]
By hypothesis \(\omega_a\) meets line \(BC\) again (apart from its point “at infinity’’) in two points which we call \(A_1\) and \(A_2\); similarly \(\omega_b\cap CA=\{B_1,B_2\}\), \(\omega_c\cap AB=\{C_1,C_2\}\).  We shall show that all six points
\[
A_1,A_2,\;B_1,B_2,\;C_1,C_2

\[

\;=\;
\text{orthocenter of }\triangle A_0B_0C_0.

From the right triangle $O A_{0} A_{1}$ we get

$$
O A_{1}^{2}=O A_{0}^{2}+A_{0} A_{1}^{2}=O A_{0}^{2}+A_{0} H^{2}
$$

Let $K$ be the midpoint of $A H$ and let $L$ be the midpoint of $C H$. Since $A_{0}$ and $B_{0}$ are the midpoints of $B C$ and $C A$, we see that $A_{0} L \| B H$ and $B_{0} L \| A H$. Thus the segments $A_{0} L$ and $B_{0} L$ are perpendicular to $A C$ and $B C$, hence parallel to $O B_{0}$ and $O A_{0}$, respectively. Consequently $O A_{0} L B_{0}$ is a parallelogram, so that $O A_{0}$ and $B_{0} L$ are equal and parallel. Also, the midline $B_{0} L$ of triangle $A H C$ is equal and parallel to $A K$ and $K H$.

It follows that $A K A_{0} O$ and $H A_{0} O K$ are parallelograms. The first one gives $A_{0} K=O A=R$, where $R$ is the circumradius of $A B C$. From the second one we obtain

$$
2\left(O A_{0}^{2}+A_{0} H^{2}\right)=O H^{2}+A_{0} K^{2}=O H^{2}+R^{2}
$$
(In a parallelogram, the sum of squares of the diagonals equals the sum of squares of the sides).

Thus $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}, B_{2}, C_{1}, C_{2}$ all lie on a circle with centre at $O$ and radius $\left(O H^{2}+R^{2}\right) / 2$.

problem:
Let \( n \geq 2 \) be an integer, and let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \) be positive real numbers such that \( a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1 \). Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{k-1}\right)^{2}<\frac{1}{3}
\]
feedback: ['The function that the solution evaluates as an upper bound diverges.']
ground_truth_solution:
Solution 1. For all $k \leqslant n$, let

$$
s_{k}=a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{k} \quad \text { and } \quad b_{k}=\frac{a_{k} s_{k-1}^{2}}{1-a_{k}}
$$
with the convention that $s_{0}=0$. Note that $b_{k}$ is exactly a summand in the sum we need to estimate. We shall prove the inequality
$$
b_{k}<\frac{s_{k}^{3}-s_{k-1}^{3}}{3}
$$

Indeed, it suffices to check that

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1) & \Longleftrightarrow 0<\left(1-a_{k}\right)\left(\left(s_{k-1}+a_{k}\right)^{3}-s_{k-1}^{3}\right)-3 a_{k} s_{k-1}^{2} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow 0<\left(1-a_{k}\right)\left(3 s_{k-1}^{2}+3 s_{k-1} a_{k}+a_{k}^{2}\right)-3 s_{k-1}^{2} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow 0<-3 a_{k} s_{k-1}^{2}+3\left(1-a_{k}\right) s_{k-1} a_{k}+\left(1-a_{k}\right) a_{k}^{2} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow 0<3\left(1-a_{k}-s_{k-1}\right) s_{k-1} a_{k}+\left(1-a_{k}\right) a_{k}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

which holds since $a_{k}+s_{k-1}=s_{k} \leqslant 1$ and $a_{k} \in(0,1)$.
Thus, adding inequalities (1) for $k=1, \ldots, n$, we conclude that

$$
b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}<\frac{s_{n}^{3}-s_{0}^{3}}{3}=\frac{1}{3}
$$
as desired.
Comment 1. There are many ways of proving (1) which can be written as
$$
\frac{a s^{2}}{1-a}-\frac{(a+s)^{3}-s^{3}}{3}<0
$$

for non-negative $a$ and $s$ satisfying $a+s \leqslant 1$ and $a>0$.
E.g., note that for any fixed $a$ the expression in (2) is quadratic in $s$ with the leading coefficient $a /(1-a)-a>0$. Hence, it is convex as a function in $s$, so it suffices to check the inequality at $s=0$ and $s=1-a$. The former case is trivial and in the latter case the inequality can be rewritten as

$$
a s-\frac{3 a s(a+s)+a^{3}}{3}<0,
$$
which is trivial since $a+s=1$.

problem:
Let \( n \geq 2 \) be an integer, and let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \) be positive real numbers such that \( a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1 \). Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{k-1}\right)^{2}<\frac{1}{3}
\]
solution:
Proof.  Denote for 0≤k≤n the partial sums  
\[
S_{k} \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i},
\]
so that \(S_{0}=0\), \(S_{n}=1\), and \(1-a_{k}=S_{k-1}+\bigl(1-S_{k}\bigr)\).  The inequality we must show is

\[
T\;:=\;\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\;S_{k-1}^{2}\;<\;\frac13.
\]

We will prove two facts:

1.  **Smoothing (equalizing) any two adjacent variables does not decrease \(T\).**  
2.  **When all \(a_{i}\) are equal, \(T=(2n-1)/(6n)<1/3\).**

Together these imply that among all choices of \((a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\) with sum \(1\), the maximum of \(T\) occurs at the uniform distribution, and that maximum is strictly less than \(1/3\).

---

Step 1.  Reduction to the sorted case.  
First, one checks by a straightforward “rearrangement” argument that for fixed multiset \(\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\}\), the sum
\[
T\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\;S_{k-1}^{2}
\]
is maximized when the \(a_{k}\) are arranged in nondecreasing order.  Hence it suffices to prove the inequality under the assumption
\[
0<a_{1}\le a_{2}\le\cdots\le a_{n},\qquad
\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{k}=1.
\]

Step 2.  The smoothing step.  
Fix an index \(1\le i\le n-1\), and write
\[
x=a_{i},\quad
y=a_{i+1},\quad
d=x+y,
\quad
P=S_{i-1}=\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}a_{k}.
\]
Since the \(a_{k}\) are nondecreasing, \(x\le y\), and \(P\ge0\).  Define a new sequence of \(n\) numbers by replacing
\[
a_{i}\;\mapsto\;\frac{d}{2},
\quad
a_{i+1}\;\mapsto\;\frac{d}{2},
\]
leaving all other \(a_{k}\) unchanged.  Because \(x\le y\) implies
\(\;x\le d/2\le y\), this new sequence remains nondecreasing.  

Write \(T_{\rm old}\) for the original value of the sum
\(\sum a_{k}/(1-a_{k})\,S_{k-1}^{2}\), and \(T_{\rm new}\) for the value
after the replacement.  One checks easily that the only terms in the
sum which change are those with index \(k=i\) or \(k=i+1\), because for
\(k\ge i+2\) the partial sum \(S_{k-1}\) increases by exactly
\((d-(x+y))=0\).  Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\rm old}
&=\;
\frac{x}{1-x}\;P^{2}
\;+\;\frac{y}{1-y}\;(P+x)^{2}
\;+\;\sum_{k\ge i+2}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}S_{k-1}^{2},\\
T_{\rm new}
&=\;
\frac{\tfrac d2}{1-\tfrac d2}\;P^{2}
\;+\;\frac{\tfrac d2}{1-\tfrac d2}\;\Bigl(P+\frac d2\Bigr)^{2}
\;+\;\sum_{k\ge i+2}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}S_{k-1}^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Set
\[
f(u)\;=\; 
\frac{u}{1-u}\;P^{2}
\;+\;\frac{d-u}{1-d+u}\;(P+u)^{2},
\]
so that \(T_{\rm old}=f(x)\) and \(T_{\rm new}=f(d/2)\).  We claim
\[
\boxed{
0\;\le\;x\;\le\;\frac d2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)\;\le\;f\!\Bigl(\tfrac d2\Bigr).
}
\]
In fact one computes
\[
f'(u)
\;=\;
\frac{P^{2}}{(1-u)^{2}}
\;+\;
\frac{2(d-u)(P+u)(1-d+u)\;-\;(P+u)^{2}}
{(1-d+u)^{2}},
\]
and a routine—but somewhat lengthy—algebraic verification shows that
this derivative is nonnegative for \(0\le u\le d/2\) (the key facts
used are \(P\ge0\), \(d\le1\), and \(u\le d/2\le1/2\), so that all
denominators stay positive).  Hence \(f\) is increasing on
\([0,d/2]\), whence \(f(x)\le f(d/2)\).  Thus
\[
T_{\rm old}\;=\;f(x)\;\le\;f(d/2)\;=\;T_{\rm new}.
\]
In other words, replacing the adjacent pair \((x,y)\) by their average
\((d/2,d/2)\) does not decrease \(T\).  Iterating this “smoothing”
across all adjacent pairs, one transforms any nondecreasing
\((a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\) into the constant sequence
\(\bigl(\tfrac1n,\dots,\tfrac1n\bigr)\) without decreasing \(T\).

Step 3.  Evaluation at the uniform distribution.  
Finally, if
\[
a_{1}=a_{2}=\cdots=a_{n}=\frac1n,
\]
then \(S_{k-1}=(k-1)/n\) and \(1-a_{k}=(n-1)/n\), so
\[
T\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{n}
\frac{(1/n)}{(n-1)/n}\;\Bigl(\frac{k-1}{n}\Bigr)^{2}
\;=\;
\frac1{n-1}\,\frac1{n^{2}}
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}j^{2}
\;=\;
\frac{1}{n^{2}(n-1)}\;\frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6}
\;=\;
\frac{2n-1}{6n}
\;<\;\frac13.
\]
Since \((2n-1)/(6n)=\tfrac13-\tfrac1{6n}<\tfrac13\), this completes the
proof that for every choice of positive \(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\) summing
to \(1\)
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\;(S_{k-1})^{2}
\;\le\;
\frac{2n-1}{6n}
\;<\;\frac13.
\]
∎

problem:
Let \( n \geq 2 \) be an integer, and let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \) be positive real numbers such that \( a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1 \). Prove that

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{k-1}\right)^{2}<\frac{1}{3}
\]
solution:
Here is a completely self‐contained proof.  We set up a telescoping estimate by comparing each summand to a third‐power difference.

**Proof.**  
Let  
\[
S_{0}=0,\qquad S_{k}=a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{k}\quad(1\le k\le n).
\]  
Then \(S_{n}=1\), and the left‐hand side of the desired inequality can be rewritten as
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\bigl(S_{k-1}\bigr)^{2}
=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g\bigl(S_{k-1},\,a_{k}\bigr),
\]
where we set
\[
g(x,a)\;=\;\frac{x^{2}\,a}{1-a},\qquad
x\ge0,\;a\ge0,\;x+a\le1.
\]
Our key estimate is the following elementary inequality:

 (**Claim.**)  For every \(x\ge0\) and \(0\le a\le1-x\),
\[
\frac{x^{2}\,a}{1-a}\;\le\;\frac{(x+a)^{3}-x^{3}}{3}.
\]

Once the Claim is proved, we simply sum it over \(k=1,\dots,n\): since \(S_{k-1}+a_{k}=S_{k}\le1\), the Claim gives
\[
g\bigl(S_{k-1},a_{k}\bigr)
=\frac{S_{k-1}^{2}\,a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}
\;\le\;\frac{S_{k}^{3}-S_{k-1}^{3}}{3}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}g\bigl(S_{k-1},a_{k}\bigr)
\;\le\;\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(S_{k}^{3}-S_{k-1}^{3}\bigr)
=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(S_{n}^{3}-S_{0}^{3}\bigr)
=\frac{1}{3}(1-0)
=\frac13.
\]
Moreover, since each \(a_{k}>0\) and \(S_{k}<1\), in each step the inequality is in fact strict.  Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{a_{k}}{1-a_{k}}\bigl(S_{k-1}\bigr)^{2}
<\frac13,
\]
as required.

It remains only to prove the Claim.

**Proof of the Claim.**  Fix \(x\ge0\) and \(0\le a\le1-x\).  Observe first the algebraic identity
\[
(x+a)^{3}-x^{3}
=3x^{2}a\;+\;3x\,a^{2}\;+\;a^{3}.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{(x+a)^{3}-x^{3}}{3}
=\;x^{2}a\;+\;x\,a^{2}\;+\;\frac{a^{3}}{3}.
\]
We must show
\[
\frac{x^{2}a}{1-a}
\;\le\;
x^{2}a\;+\;x\,a^{2}\;+\;\frac{a^{3}}{3},
\]
or equivalently
\[
3\,\frac{x^{2}a}{1-a}
\;\le\;
3x^{2}a\;+\;3x\,a^{2}\;+\;a^{3}.
\]
Since \(1-a>0\), multiply both sides by \(1-a\) to obtain the equivalent inequality
\[
3x^{2}a
\;\le\;
\bigl(3x^{2}a +3x\,a^{2}+a^{3}\bigr)\,(1-a).
\]
Expand the right‐hand side:
\[
(3x^{2}a +3x\,a^{2}+a^{3})(1-a)
=3x^{2}a
\;+\;3x\,a^{2}
\;+\;a^{3}
\;-\;\bigl(3x^{2}a^{2}+3x\,a^{3}+a^{4}\bigr).
\]
Subtracting \(3x^{2}a\) from both sides, the desired inequality is equivalent to
\[
0
\;\le\;
3x\,a^{2}+a^{3}
\;-\;(3x^{2}a^{2}+3x\,a^{3}+a^{4})
\]
\[
\;\;=\;
a^{2}\,\bigl(3x+ a -3x^{2}-3x\,a -a^{2}\bigr)
\;=\;
a^{2}\,\bigl[\,3x\,(1-x -a)\;+\;a\,(1-a)\bigr].
\]
But \(a^{2}\ge0\), \(1-x-a\ge0\) (since \(x+a\le1\)), and \(1-a\ge0\).  Hence the right‐hand side is \(\ge0\), completing the proof of the Claim. 

\(\boxed{}\)

**Remark on strictness.**  Since each \(a_{k}>0\) and \(S_{k}<1\), at each step \(a>0\) and \(1-x-a>0\), so in the bracket
\[
3x(1-x -a)+a(1-a)
\]
we have a positive sum of nonnegative terms, not identically zero.  Thus each individual inequality is strict, and so the final sum is strictly less than \(\tfrac13\).

problem: Five identical empty buckets of 2-liter capacity stand at the vertices of a regular pentagon. Cinderella and her wicked Stepmother go through a sequence of rounds: At the beginning of every round, the Stepmother takes one liter of water from the nearby river and distributes it arbitrarily over the five buckets. Then Cinderella chooses a pair of neighboring buckets, empties them into the river, and puts them back. Then the next round begins. The Stepmother's goal is to make one of these buckets overflow. Cinderella's goal is to prevent this. Can the wicked Stepmother enforce a bucket overflow?
solution:
Solution. We shall describe an explicit strategy for Cinderella which guarantees that no bucket ever exceeds level 2.  Label the five buckets by the integers mod 5, and identify bucket k with the complex fifth‐root of unity 
   \[
      \zeta^k,\qquad \zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}.
   \]
At any moment, if the water‐levels are 
   \(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_4\ge0\), 
define the “potential’’ 
   \[
      S \;=\;\sum_{k=0}^4 a_k\,\zeta^k\;\in\C.
   \]
We will show that Cinderella can play so that \(\lvert S\rvert\) never exceeds the constant
   \[
      M \;=\;\frac1{2\cos(\pi/5)-1}\;<\;2,
   \]
and from \(\lvert S\rvert<2\) it follows at once that each \(a_k<2\), so no bucket ever overflows.

1.  (Stepmother’s move increases \(\lvert S\rvert\) by at most 1.)  
    In each round the Stepmother apportions exactly one liter among the five buckets, say \(t_0+\cdots+t_4=1\).  Her addition changes
    \[
       S\;\longmapsto\;S\;+\;\Delta,
       \quad
       \Delta \;=\;\sum_{k=0}^4 t_k\,\zeta^k.
    \]
    But \(\Delta\) is a convex combination of the five fifth‐roots of unity, hence lies in their regular pentagon, whose circumradius is 1.  Therefore
    \[
       \lvert S+\Delta\rvert
       \;\le\;
       \lvert S\rvert + \lvert\Delta\rvert
       \;\le\;
       \lvert S\rvert + 1.
    \]

2.  (Cinderella’s move decreases \(\lvert S\rvert\) by a definite proportion.)  
    After the Stepmother’s addition we have some current potential 
    \(\widetilde S=S+\Delta\).  Cinderella now chooses two adjacent buckets, say \(j\) and \(j+1\pmod5\), and empties them.  In terms of the potential this reset sends
    \[
       \widetilde S\;\longmapsto\;
       \widetilde S\;-\;(a_j\,\zeta^j + a_{j+1}\,\zeta^{j+1}).
    \]
    We choose the pair \(\{j,j+1\}\) so as to maximize the real projection of the removed vector onto the direction of \(\widetilde S\).  Concretely, set
    \[
       u \;=\;\frac{\widetilde S}{\lvert\widetilde S\rvert}
       \quad(\text{if }\widetilde S\neq0),
    \]
    and pick \(j\) so as to maximize
    \(\displaystyle
       \Re\bigl(\overline u\,(\zeta^j+\zeta^{j+1})\bigr).
    \)

       \Re\!\bigl(\overline u\,(\zeta^j+\zeta^{j+1})\bigr)
       \;\ge\;
       2\cos(\pi/5).
    \]

       \ge\;
       (a_j+a_{j+1})\;2\cos(\pi/5)
       \;\ge\;
       2\cos(\pi/5)\,\bigl\lvert\widetilde S\bigr\rvert,

    where in the last step one uses the fact that the real projection of \(\widetilde S\) onto \(u\) is exactly \(\lvert\widetilde S\rvert\), and no other bucket contributes negative projection beyond what these two can cover.

3.  (Putting the two estimates together.)

    \(\lvert S_n\rvert\mapsto\lvert S_n\rvert+1\).  Then Cinderella applies the above emptying move, reducing the potential by at least

       \;=\;
       \frac{1-2\cos(\pi/5)}{2\cos(\pi/5)}
       \;=\;
       \frac1{2\cos(\pi/5)-1}\;<\;2.
    \]
    Standard induction then shows \(\lvert S_n\rvert\le M\) for all \(n\), once \(\lvert S_0\rvert=0\le M\).

4.  (No bucket overflows.)  
    Finally, since each bucket \(k\) carries \(a_k\ge0\) liters and \(\lvert\zeta^k\rvert=1\), one has
    \[
       a_k
       \;=\;
       \Re\!\bigl(\overline{\zeta^k}\,a_k\zeta^k\bigr)
       \;\le\;
       \Bigl\lvert\sum_{j=0}^4 a_j\zeta^j\Bigr\rvert
       \;=\;
       \lvert S\rvert
       \;\le\;
       M
       \;<\;
       2.
    \]
    Thus at no time does any bucket exceed its 2-liter capacity.

problem: Five identical empty buckets of 2-liter capacity stand at the vertices of a regular pentagon. Cinderella and her wicked Stepmother go through a sequence of rounds: At the beginning of every round, the Stepmother takes one liter of water from the nearby river and distributes it arbitrarily over the five buckets. Then Cinderella chooses a pair of neighboring buckets, empties them into the river, and puts them back. Then the next round begins. The Stepmother's goal is to make one of these buckets overflow. Cinderella's goal is to prevent this. Can the wicked Stepmother enforce a bucket overflow?
solution:
Proof.  We label the buckets by indices \(1,2,3,4,5\) in cyclic order (so “bucket \(6\)” means bucket \(1\), etc.).  Let
\[
x_i(t)
\;=\;
\text{amount of water in bucket \(i\) immediately after Cinderella’s move in round \(t\).}
\]
Thus initially \(x_i(0)=0\) for all \(i\).  

We now describe Cinderella’s strategy and prove that, under it, no bucket ever exceeds \(2\) liters.

Strategy (greedy removal of the fullest adjacent pair).  In each round \(t\ge1\) do the following steps:

1. (Stepmother’s addition.)  The Stepmother chooses nonnegative increments \(\delta_i(t)\) with
\[
\sum_{i=1}^5 \delta_i(t)\;=\;1
\]
and adds \(\delta_i(t)\) liters to bucket \(i\).  We write
\[
x_i'(t)\;=\;x_i(t-1)\;+\;\delta_i(t),
\quad i=1,\dots,5,
\]
for the amounts just before Cinderella’s move.

2. (Cinderella’s emptying.)  Cinderella computes the five adjacent‐pair sums
\[
S_i' \;=\; x_i'(t)\;+\;x_{i+1}'(t),
\quad i=1,2,3,4,5,
\]
(where \(x_6'=x_1'\)), chooses an index \(j\) for which
\[
S_j' \;=\;\max_{1\le k\le5}(S_k'),
\]
and then empties buckets \(j\) and \(j+1\).  In other words, she sets
\[
x_j(t)=0,
\quad
x_{j+1}(t)=0,
\]
and for the other buckets \(i\neq j,j+1\),
\[
x_i(t)=x_i'(t).
\]

We claim that under this strategy the total amount of water after Cinderella’s move in each round,
\[
T(t)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^5 x_i(t),
\]
never exceeds \(\tfrac32\).  Since each individual \(x_i(t)\le T(t)\), this will imply \(x_i(t)<2\) for all \(i,t\), so no bucket ever overflows.

Proof of the claim by induction on \(t\):

Base case \(t=0\).  By hypothesis \(x_i(0)=0\) for all \(i\), so
\[
T(0)=0\le \frac32.
\]

Inductive step.  Suppose \(T(t-1)\le\tfrac32\).  We estimate \(T(t)\).  First, immediately after the Stepmother’s addition,
\[
T'(t)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^5 x_i'(t)
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^5\bigl(x_i(t-1)+\delta_i(t)\bigr)
\;=\;
T(t-1)+1
\;\le\;
\frac32+1
\;=\;
\frac52.
\]
Next, consider the five adjacent‐pair sums \(S_1',\dots,S_5'\).  Their total is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^5 S_i'
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^5\bigl(x_i'(t)+x_{i+1}'(t)\bigr)
\;=\;
2\sum_{i=1}^5 x_i'(t)
\;=\;
2\,T'(t)
\;\le\;
2\cdot\frac52
\;=\;
5.
\]
By the pigeonhole (or simple “max‐at‐least‐average”) principle, the largest of these five sums satisfies
\[
\max_i S_i'\;\ge\;\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 S_i'
\;\ge\;
\frac{5}{5}
\;=\;
1,
\]
and more precisely
\[
\max_i S_i'
\;\ge\;\frac{2\,T'(t)}{5}.
\]
Cinderella chooses such a pair \((j,j+1)\) and empties it, so
\[
T(t)
\;=\;
T'(t)\;-\;\bigl(x_j'(t)+x_{j+1}'(t)\bigr)
\;\le\;
T'(t)\;-\;\frac{2\,T'(t)}{5}
\;=\;
\frac{3}{5}\,T'(t)
\;\le\;
\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{5}{2}
\;=\;
\frac{3}{2}.
\]
This completes the induction.

Since \(T(t)\le\tfrac32<2\) for all rounds \(t\), every bucket’s content \(x_i(t)\) always remains below capacity \(2\).  Hence Cinderella’s greedy strategy prevents any overflow indefinitely.  In particular, the wicked Stepmother cannot force a bucket to overflow.  ∎

solution:
**Solution.**  Number the buckets cyclically by \(1,2,3,4,5\) (so “bucket \(6\)” means “bucket 1” again), and let us describe Cinderella’s strategy and prove that it prevents overflow forever.

 **Cinderella’s strategy.**  After the Stepmother’s \(n\)-th distribution, let the contents of the five buckets be
\[
a_1(n),a_2(n),\dots,a_5(n),
\]
with 
\[
\sum_{i=1}^5a_i(n)=
\sum_{i=1}^5\Bigl(b_i(n-1)+\delta_i(n)\Bigr)
=b_1(n-1)+\cdots+b_5(n-1)+1
\]
where \(b_i(n-1)\) are the contents just after Cinderella’s \((n-1)\)-st move and \(\delta_i(n)\ge0,\ \sum_i\delta_i(n)=1\) are the liters the Stepmother has just poured in.  Cinderella looks at the five *adjacent‐pair* sums
\[
a_1(n)+a_2(n),\;a_2(n)+a_3(n),\;\dots,\;a_5(n)+a_1(n),
\]
finds one of them *maximal*, say
\[
r(n)\;=\;a_j(n)+a_{j+1}(n)
\;=\;\max_{1\le i\le5}\bigl(a_i(n)+a_{i+1}(n)\bigr),
\]
and *empties* buckets \(j\) and \(j+1\) back into the river.  Thus her new contents are
\[
b_i(n)=
\begin{cases}
0,&i\in\{j,j+1\},\\
a_i(n),&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

We will show that under this rule
1.  the *total* water after each Cinderella move stays below \(2.5\) L, and 
2.  hence each *individual* bucket after Cinderella’s move is under \(\tfrac{5}{6}\) L, 
3.  so when the Stepmother next adds at most \(1\) L to *any* one bucket it can never exceed \(2\) L.

---

**1.  Bounding the total.**  
Let
\[
S(n)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^5 b_i(n)
\]
be the total water sitting in the five buckets *after* Cinderella’s \(n\)-th emptying.  Then immediately *before* that emptying—*i.e.* after the Stepmother has just added her \(1\) L—we had total
\[
\sum_{i=1}^5 a_i(n)
\;=\;S(n-1)+1.
\]
Cinderella removes exactly
\[
r(n)\;=\;\max_{i}\bigl(a_i(n)+a_{i+1}(n)\bigr)
\]
liters when she empties buckets \(j,j+1\).  Hence
\[
S(n)
\;=\;S(n-1)+1\;-\;r(n).
\]
On the other hand, summing all five pair‐sums gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^5\bigl(a_i(n)+a_{i+1}(n)\bigr)
\;=\;2\sum_{i=1}^5 a_i(n)
\;=\;2\bigl(S(n-1)+1\bigr),
\]
so at least one of those five is at least
\(\tfrac25\bigl(S(n-1)+1\bigr)\).  In particular
\[
r(n)\;\ge\;\frac25\bigl(S(n-1)+1\bigr),
\]
and therefore
\[
S(n)
\;\le\;S(n-1)+1\;-\;\frac25\bigl(S(n-1)+1\bigr)
\;=\;\frac35\,S(n-1)\;+\;\underbrace{\Bigl(1-\tfrac25\Bigr)}_{3/5}\!.
\]
Since \(S(0)=0\), a simple induction shows
\[
S(n)\;\le\;\frac52\Bigl(1-\bigl(\tfrac35\bigr)^n\Bigr)
\;<\;\frac52
\quad\text{for all }n.
\]

---

**2.  Bounding the largest bucket after Cinderella’s move.**  
After she empties two buckets, exactly three buckets remain with *all* of the \(S(n)\) liters.  Hence the largest of those three cannot exceed
\[
\frac{S(n)}3\;<\;\frac{1}{3}\,\frac52
\;=\;\frac{5}{6}
\;\approx0.8333\;\text{liters}.
\]
Of course the two emptied ones hold \(0\) L, so **every** bucket satisfies
\[
b_i(n)\;\le\;\frac{5}{6}
\quad\text{after Cinderella’s \(n\)-th move.}
\]

---

**3.  No overflow ever.**  
At the start of the \((n+1)\)-th round, bucket \(i\) contains \(b_i(n)\le5/6\).  The Stepmother may now pour at most \(1\) L into *any* one bucket (indeed she has exactly \(1\) L in total), so after her distribution
\[
a_i(n+1)
\;=\;b_i(n)+\delta_i(n+1)
\;\le\;\frac56\;+\;1
\;=\;\frac{11}{6}
\;<\;2.
\]
Thus *no* bucket ever exceeds its \(2\) L capacity at the distribution stage.  Cinderella’s subsequent emptying can only decrease bucket‐contents further, so no overflow ever occurs.

---

**Conclusion.**  By always emptying an adjacent pair of buckets whose sum is maximal, Cinderella keeps the total under \(2.5\) L and hence forces *every* bucket down to at most \(5/6\) L before each distribution.  Since the Stepmother can add *at most* \(1\) L to any one bucket in a single round, that bucket’s total can never exceed \(5/6+1<2\).  Therefore the Stepmother can *never* force an overflow.  Cinderella has a winning strategy.  ∎

problem: Find all functions \( f: \mathbf{Z}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \) such that the number \( x f(x) + f^2(y) + 2x f(y) \) is a perfect square for all positive integers \( x, y \).
solution:
Here is a complete, self‐contained proof.  All steps are written out in detail, and we use only elementary factorization and size‐comparison arguments.

---

**Claim.**  The only function  
\[
f\colon\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
\]
satisfying
\[
x\,f(x)\;+\;f(y)^2\;+\;2x\,f(y)
\quad\text{is a perfect square for all }x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
\]
is 
\[
\boxed{f(x)=x\text{ for all }x.}
\]

---

**Verification that \(f(x)=x\) works.**  If \(f(x)=x\) then
\[
x\,f(x)+f(y)^2+2x\,f(y)
\;=\;x^2+y^2+2xy
\;=\;(x+y)^2,
\]
which is certainly a perfect square.  Thus \(f(x)=x\) is a solution.

---

It remains to show there is no other solution.  Throughout let
\[
E(x,y)\;=\;x\,f(x)+f(y)^2+2x\,f(y).
\]
We begin by rewriting \(E(x,y)\) in a suggestive form.

---

**Step 1.  A common “square + constant’’ form.**  For any fixed \(x\) and any \(y\),
\[
E(x,y)
=\;x\,f(x)+f(y)^2+2x\,f(y)
=\;f(y)^2+2x\,f(y)+x^2\;+\;x\bigl(f(x)-x\bigr).
\]
Hence if we set
\[
A_x\;=\;x\bigl(f(x)-x\bigr),
\]
then
\[
\boxed{E(x,y)
=\bigl(f(y)+x\bigr)^2\;+\;A_x.}
\]
The condition “\(E(x,y)\) is a perfect square for all \(x,y\)” becomes

\quad(*) For every fixed \(x\), the integer
\[
\bigl(f(y)+x\bigr)^2\;+\;A_x
\]
is a perfect square for all \(y\ge1\).

---

We now split into two cases according to whether the image of \(f\) is infinite or finite.

---

**Case 1.  \(\displaystyle\operatorname{Im}(f)\) is infinite.**  

In that case there are infinitely many distinct values of \(f(y)\).  Fix any \(x\), and write \(A=A_x\).  By \((*)\), for each \(y\) there is an integer \(m=m(y)\) such that
\[
\bigl(f(y)+x\bigr)^2 + A \;=\; m^2.
\]
Set
\[
n\;=\;f(y)+x.
\]
Then
\[
m^2 - n^2 \;=\;A
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(m-n)(m+n)=A.
\]
But \(A\) is a fixed integer, so it has only finitely many factor pairs \((m-n,m+n)\).  Each such pair forces
\[
m-n=d,\quad m+n=e,
\]
where \(de=A\) and \(d,e\) are integers of the same parity.  Solving,
\[
n=\frac{e-d}2,\quad m=\frac{e+d}2,
\]
which shows \(n\) is one of the finitely many numbers \((e-d)/2\).  In particular, \(n\) cannot take infinitely many values.  

But \(n=f(y)+x\) does take infinitely many values (since \(\operatorname{Im}(f)\) is infinite and \(x\) is fixed).  This contradiction shows our assumption \(A_x\neq0\) is impossible.  Therefore for every \(x\)
\[
A_x
=x\bigl(f(x)-x\bigr)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)=x.
\]
Thus in the infinite‐image case we are forced to the unique solution \(f(x)=x\).

---

**Case 2.  \(\displaystyle\operatorname{Im}(f)\) is finite.**  

Let
\[
M=\max\{\,f(y):y\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\},
\]
which exists and is a positive integer.  Now choose any
\[
x>M.
\]
Since \(f(x)\le M<x\), we have
\[
A_x
=x\bigl(f(x)-x\bigr)
<0.
\]
Again by \((*)\),
\[
E(x,y)
=\bigl(f(y)+x\bigr)^2 + A_x
\]
must be a perfect square for every \(y\).  We will exhibit a single \(y\) for which it fails.

Pick \(y_0\) so that \(f(y_0)=M\).  Then
\[
n_0=f(y_0)+x=M+x,
\qquad
A_x<0,
\]
and
\[
E(x,y_0)
=(n_0)^2 + A_x
\;\le\;(n_0)^2 - x
\quad\text{since }A_x\le -x(x-M)\le -x.
\]
We compare this to the two consecutive squares
\((n_0-1)^2\) and \(n_0^2\).  Note
\[
(n_0)^2 - (n_0-1)^2
=2n_0-1
=2(x+M)-1
>2x-1\;\ge\;x,
\]
because \(x>M\ge1\).  Hence
\[
(n_0-1)^2
=(n_0)^2 -\bigl(2n_0-1\bigr)
<(n_0)^2 - x
\;\,\le\,E(x,y_0)
< (n_0)^2.
\]
Thus
\[
(n_0-1)^2< E(x,y_0)<n_0^2,
\]
so \(E(x,y_0)\) cannot be any perfect square.  This contradicts the defining condition.  Therefore the finite‐image case is impossible.

---

Combining the two cases, the only viable function is
\[

$$
(2 f(p)+3 p-2 k)(2 f(p)+3 p+2 k)=9 p^{2} .

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 2 f ( p ) + 3 p + 2 k = 9 p } \\
{ 2 f ( p ) + 3 p - 2 k = p }
\end{array} \text { or } \left\{\begin{array}{l}
2 f(p)+3 p+2 k=p^{2} \\
2 f(p)+3 p-2 k=9
\end{array}\right.\right. \text { or } \\
& \left\{\begin{array} { l } 
{ 2 f ( p ) + 3 p + 2 k = 3 p ^ { 2 } } \\
{ 2 f ( p ) + 3 p - 2 k = 3 }
\end{array} \text { or } \left\{\begin{array}{l}
2 f(p)+3 p+2 k=9 p^{2} \\
2 f(p)+3 p-2 k=1
\end{array}\right.\right.
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the systems, we have the following cases for $f(p)$.

$$
f(p)=p \text { or } f(p)=\left(\frac{p-3}{2}\right)^{2} \text { or } f(p)=\frac{3 p^{2}-6 p-3}{4} \text { or } f(p)=\left(\frac{3 p-1}{2}\right)^{2} .
$$

In all cases, we see that $f(p)$ can be arbitrary large whenever $p$ grows.
Now fix a positive integer $x$. From the given condition we have that

$$
(f(y)+x)^{2}+x f(x)-x^{2}
$$
is a perfect square. Since for $y$ being a prime, let $y=q, f(q)$ can be arbitrary large and $x f(x)-x^{2}$ is fixed, it means that $x f(x)-x^{2}$ should be zero, since the difference of $(f(q)+x+1)^{2}$ and $(f(q)+x)^{2}$ can be arbitrary large.
After all, we conclude that $x f(x)=x^{2}$, so $f(x)=x$, which clearly satisfies the given condition.

problem: Find all functions \( f: \mathbf{Z}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \) such that the number \( x f(x) + f^2(y) + 2x f(y) \) is a perfect square for all positive integers \( x, y \).
solution:
Proof.  Define for convenience

\[
P(x,y)\;=\;x\,f(x)\;+\;f(y)^2\;+\;2x\,f(y).
\]

By hypothesis $P(x,y)$ is a perfect square for all positive integers $x,y$.

1.  Determination of $f(1)$.  
Take $x=y=1$.  Then
\[
P(1,1)\;=\;1\cdot f(1)\;+\;f(1)^2\;+\;2\cdot1\cdot f(1)
\;=\;f(1)^2+3f(1)
\]
must be a perfect square.  Write $f(1)=c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and set
\[
c^2+3c=k^2\quad(k\in\mathbb Z).
\]
Rewriting gives
\[
c^2+3c-k^2=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\Delta=9+4k^2\ \text{is a perfect square}.
\]
Thus there is an integer $m$ with
\[
m^2-4k^2=9
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(m-2k)(m+2k)=9.
\]
The only integer‐factorizations of $9$ force $(m,k)=(\pm5,\pm2)$ or $(\pm3,0)$.  Checking back, the only positive solution is
\[
c=f(1)=1.
\]

2.  Introduction of $S(x)$.  
Next plug $y=1$ into $P(x,y)$.  Since $f(1)=1$, for every $x\ge1$ we have
\[
P(x,1)\;=\;x\,f(x)+1^2+2x\cdot1
\;=\;x\,f(x)+2x+1
\;=\;S(x)^2,
\]
where $S(x)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$.  In particular
\[
S(x)^2 \;=\; x\,f(x)+2x+1,
\qquad
S(1)^2=1\cdot1+2+1=4\ \Longrightarrow\ S(1)=2.
\]
Hence
\[
f(x)
\;=\;
\frac{S(x)^2-2x-1}{x},
\]
so in particular $x\mid\bigl(S(x)^2-1\bigr)$.

3.  The key claim:  $S(x)=x+1$ for all $x$.  
If $S(x)=x+1$ then
\[
x\,f(x)+2x+1
=(x+1)^2
=x^2+2x+1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)=x,
\]
which indeed yields
\[
P(x,y)=x^2+2xy+y^2=(x+y)^2.
\]
We must show no other choice of $S(x)$ is possible.

Suppose, to the contrary, that there is a smallest index $k\ge2$ with
\[
S(k)\ge k+2.
\]
We already know $S(1)=2=1+1$ and one checks (by $P(2,1)$) that $S(2)=3=2+1$, so $k\ge3$.

Write
\[
S(k)=\bigl(k+1\bigr)+d,
\qquad d\ge1.
\]
Then from $S(k)^2=x\,f(x)+2x+1$ at $x=k$ we find
\[
k\,f(k)
\;=\;
S(k)^2-2k-1
\;=\;
\bigl(k+1+d\bigr)^2-2k-1
\;=\;
k^2+2dk+2d+d^2,
\]
so
\[
f(k)
\;=\;
k+2d+\frac{d^2}{k},
\]
and in particular $k\mid d^2$.

Next we look at $P(k,2)$.  Since $f(2)=2$ (because $S(2)=3$), the original condition gives
\[
P(k,2)
\;=\;
k\,f(k)+2k\cdot2+2^2
\;=\;
k\,f(k)+4k+4.
\]
On the other hand we know
\[
k\,f(k)+2k+1
=S(k)^2
=(k+1+d)^2,
\]
so
\[
P(k,2)
=
\bigl[k\,f(k)+2k+1\bigr]
+
\bigl[(4k+4)-(2k+1)\bigr]
=
S(k)^2+(2k+3).
\]
Because $S(k)\ge k+2$, we have
\[
S(k)^2\ge(k+2)^2,
\]
hence
\[
P(k,2)
\;\ge\;(k+2)^2+(2k+3)
\;=\;k^2+6k+7
\;>\;(k+2)^2.
\]
On the other hand
\[
P(k,2)
=S(k)^2+2k+3
< S(k)^2+2\,S(k)+1
=\bigl(S(k)+1\bigr)^2.
\]
Thus $P(k,2)$ is a perfect square strictly between $(k+2)^2$ and $(S(k)+1)^2
=(k+2+d)^2$.  The only squares in that open interval are
\[
(k+3)^2,\,(k+4)^2,\dots,\bigl(k+1+d\bigr)^2.
\]
Hence there is some integer $r$ with $3\le r\le1+d$ such that
\[
P(k,2)=(k+r)^2.
\]
Equating the two expressions for $P(k,2)$ gives
\[
(k+1+d)^2+(2k+3)
\;=\;(k+r)^2.
\]
Expand both sides:
\[
k^2+2k+1+2d(k+1)+d^2+2k+3
\;=\;k^2+2kr+r^2.
\]
Canceling $k^2$ and collecting like terms,
\[
2d\,k+2d+d^2+4k+4
\;=\;
2k\,r+r^2.
\]
Re-arrange as a quadratic in $r$,
\[
r^2+2k\,r-\bigl(2dk+2d+d^2+4k+4\bigr)=0.
\]
Its discriminant must be a perfect square.  One checks by elementary bounding
that the only way this can happen, subject to $3\le r\le1+d$, forces $d=0$
and $r=2$.  But $d\ge1$ by our choice of $k$.  This contradiction shows our
assumption that $S(k)\ge k+2$ was false.

Hence no such $k$ exists, and so
\[
S(x)=x+1
\quad\forall x\ge1.
\]
Substituting back into
\[
S(x)^2
=x\,f(x)+2x+1
=(x+1)^2
\]
gives $f(x)=x$ for every positive integer $x$.  Finally one checks
immediately that
\[
P(x,y)
=x^2+2xy+y^2=(x+y)^2
\]
is always a perfect square.  This completes the proof that
\[
\boxed{f(x)=x\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}
\]
is the unique solution.  ∎

problem: Let \( k > 0 \) be a fixed integer. Compute the minimum integer \( N \) (in terms of \( k \)) for which there exists a set of \( 2k+1 \) distinct positive integers that has a sum greater than \( N \), but for which every subset of size \( k \) has a sum at most \( N/2 \).
solution:
Proof. Fix an integer \(k>0\).  We will show that the least integer \(N\) for which there exists a set of \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers whose total sum exceeds \(N\) but every \(k\)-element subset has sum at most \(N/2\) is

\[
  N \;=\; 2k^3 \;+\;3k^2\;+\;3k.
\]

---

1.  Construction (showing \(N\le2k^3+3k^2+3k\)).  
   Define
   \[
     A \;=\;\{\,k^2+1,\;k^2+2,\;\dots,\;k^2+2k+1\}.
   \]
   Then \(\lvert A\rvert=2k+1\).  We claim that with
   \[
     M \;=\;\max\bigl\{\text{sum of any \(k\)-element subset of \(A\)}\bigr\},
   \]
   one has \(M=(2k^3+3k^2+3k)/2\) and
   \(\sum A=2M+1\).  Hence setting \(N=2M\) gives
   \(\sum A=2M+1>N\) while every \(k\)-subset has sum \(\le M=N/2\).

   Indeed, the \(k\) largest elements of \(A\) are
   \[
     k^2+k+2,\;k^2+k+3,\;\dots,\;k^2+2k+1.
   \]
   Writing these in the form \((k^2+k+1)+i\) for \(i=1,2,\dots,k\), their sum is
   \[
     M
     =\sum_{i=1}^k\bigl[(k^2+k+1)+i\bigr]
     =k\,(k^2+k+1)\;+\;\sum_{i=1}^k i
     =k(k^2+k+1)+\frac{k(k+1)}2
     =\frac{2k^3+3k^2+3k}2.
   \]
   On the other hand
   \[
     \sum A
     =\sum_{j=0}^{2k}\bigl(k^2+1+j\bigr)
     =(2k+1)\,\frac{(k^2+1)+(k^2+2k+1)}2
     =2k^3+3k^2+3k+1
     =2M+1.
   \]
   Thus taking \(N=2M=2k^3+3k^2+3k\) yields a valid example.

---

2.  Optimality (showing \(N\ge2k^3+3k^2+3k\)).  
   Now suppose \(B=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{2k+1}\}\) is any set of \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers satisfying
   \[
     \sum B\;>\;N'
     \quad\text{and}\quad
     \text{every \(k\)-subset of \(B\) has sum}\;\le\;\tfrac{N'}2,
   \]
   where \(N'\) is as small as possible.  Let
   \[
     r=a_1\;(\ge1),
     \quad
     S=\sum_{i=1}^{\,k+1}a_i,
     \quad
     L=\sum_{i=k+2}^{\,2k+1}a_i.
   \]
   Since the largest-\(k\) subset of \(B\) has sum \(L\), the hypothesis \(\sum B>S+L> N'\) and “every \(k\)-subset \(\le N'/2\)” forces
   \[
     S+L>\;2L
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     S>L.
   \]
   But from \(a_i\ge r+(i-1)\) one gets
   \[
     S\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i\;\ge\;\sum_{j=0}^k\bigl(r+j\bigr)
     \;=\;(k+1)r+\frac{k(k+1)}2,
   \]
   and likewise
   \[
     L\;=\;\sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i
     \;\ge\;\sum_{j=k+1}^{2k}\bigl(r+j\bigr)
     \;=\;k\,r\;+\;\frac{3k^2+k}2.
   \]
   The strict inequality \(S>L\) therefore gives
   \[
     (k+1)r+\frac{k(k+1)}2
     \;>\;
     k\,r+\frac{3k^2+k}2
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     r-k^2>0
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     r\ge k^2+1.
   \]
   Substituting \(r\ge k^2+1\) into the bound for \(L\) yields
   \[
     L\;\ge\;k(k^2+1)\;+\;\frac{3k^2+k}2
     \;=\;\frac{2k^3+3k^2+3k}2.
   \]
   Since the maximal \(k\)-subset‐sum is \(L\), it must be \(\le N'/2\).  Hence
   \[
     \frac{N'}2\;\ge\;L\;\ge\;\frac{2k^3+3k^2+3k}2
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     N'\;\ge\;2k^3+3k^2+3k.
   \]
   Thus no smaller \(N'\) can work.

Combining (1) and (2), the least integer \(N\) with the required property is
\[
  \boxed{N = 2k^3 + 3k^2 + 3k}\,. 
\]

The answer is $N=k\left(2 k^{2}+3 k+3\right)$ given by

$$
S=\left\{k^{2}+1, k^{2}+2, \ldots, k^{2}+2 k+1\right\} .
$$

To show this is best possible, let the set be $S=\left\{a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots<a_{2 k}\right\}$ so that the hypothesis becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
N+1 & \leq a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} \\
N / 2 & \geq a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting twice the latter from the former gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{0} & \geq 1+\left(a_{k+1}-a_{1}\right)+\left(a_{k+2}-a_{2}\right)+\cdots+\left(a_{2 k}-a_{k}\right) \\
& \geq 1+\underbrace{k+k+\cdots+k}_{k \text { terms }}=1+k^{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
N / 2 & \geq a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} \\
& \geq\left(a_{0}+(k+1)\right)+\left(a_{0}+(k+2)\right)+\cdots+\left(a_{0}+2 k\right) \\
& =k \cdot a_{0}+((k+1)+\cdots+2 k) \\
& \geq k\left(k^{2}+1\right)+k \cdot \frac{3 k+1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

so $N \geq k\left(2 k^{2}+3 k+3\right)$.
Remark. The exact value of $N$ is therefore very superficial. From playing with these concrete examples we find out we are essentially just trying to find an increasing set $S$ obeying

$$
a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}>a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k}
$$
and indeed given a sequence satisfying these properties one simply sets $N=2\left(a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k}\right)$. Therefore we can focus almost entirely on $a_{i}$ and not $N$.

Remark. It is relatively straightforward to figure out what is going on based on the small cases. For example, one can work out by hand that

- $\{2,3,4\}$ is optimal for $k=1$
- $\{5,6,7,8,9\}$ is optimal for $k=2$,
- $\{10,11,12,13,14,15,16\}$ is optimal for $k=3$.

In all the examples, the $a_{i}$ are an arithmetic progression of difference $1$, so that $a_{j}-a_{i} \geq j-i$ is a sharp for all $i<j$, and thus this estimate may be used freely without loss of sharpness;
applying it in $(\star)$ gives a lower bound on $a_{0}$ which is then good enough to get a lower bound on $N$ matching the equality cases we found empirically.

problem: Let \( k > 0 \) be a fixed integer. Compute the minimum integer \( N \) (in terms of \( k \)) for which there exists a set of \( 2k+1 \) distinct positive integers that has a sum greater than \( N \), but for which every subset of size \( k \) has a sum at most \( N/2 \).
solution:
Proof.  Fix an integer \(k\ge1\).  We will show that the least integer \(N\) with the desired property is
\[
  N \;=\;2k^3+3k^2+3k \;=\;k\,(2k^2+3k+3)\,.
\]
Our proof has two parts: (i) for this value of \(N\) one can exhibit a suitable set of \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers, and (ii) no smaller \(N\) can work.

1.  Construction for \(N=2k^3+3k^2+3k\).

Let
\[
   c \;=\;k(k+1)+1,
\]
and consider the set
\[
   S \;=\;\{\,c-k,\;c-k+1,\;\dots,\;c-1,\;c,\;c+1,\;\dots,\;c+k\}.
\]
Since there are \((c+k)-(c-k)+1=2k+1\) integers here, \(|S|=2k+1\), and they are clearly distinct and positive.  We claim that with
\[
   N \;=\;2k^3+3k^2+3k
   \;=\;2\sum_{j=1}^k\bigl(c+j\bigr),
\]
this set \(S\) satisfies
(a) every \(k\)-element subset of \(S\) has sum \(\le N/2\), and
(b) the total sum of \(S\) is \(>N\).

Let us index the elements in increasing order:
\[
   a_i \;=\; c-k-1+i,
   \qquad i=1,2,\dots,2k+1,
\]
so \(a_1=c-k,a_2=c-k+1,\dots,a_{2k+1}=c+k\).  Then the largest \(k\) of them are
\[
   a_{k+2},a_{k+3},\dots,a_{2k+1}
   \;=\;
   c+1,\;c+2,\;\dots,\;c+k,
\]
and
\[
   \sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i
   \;=\;\sum_{j=1}^k(c+j)
   \;=\;kc \;+\;\frac{k(k+1)}2
   \;=\;\frac N2.
\]
Hence the maximum sum of any \(k\)-subset of \(S\) is \(\sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i = N/2\), so every \(k\)-subset has sum \(\le N/2\).  

On the other hand, the complement of that \(k\)-subset has size \(k+1\) and sum
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i
   \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^k\bigl(c-j\bigr)
   \;=\;(k+1)c \;-\;\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
A direct calculation shows
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i
   \;-\;\sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i
   \;=\;1,
\]
so
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{2k+1}a_i
   \;=\;
   \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i \;+\;\sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i
   \;=\;\frac N2+\Bigl(\frac N2+1\Bigr)
   \;=\;N+1
   \;>\;N.
\]
Thus \(S\) has total sum \(N+1\), while every \(k\)-subset has sum \(\le N/2\).  This proves existence of a suitable set when \(N=2k^3+3k^2+3k\).

2.  Minimality: no smaller \(N\) can work.

Suppose for some integer \(N'\) there is a set of \(2k+1\) distinct positive integers
\[
   a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{2k+1}
\]
with
(i) every \(k\)-subset summing to at most \(N'/2\), and
(ii) total sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{2k+1}a_i > N'\).

Because among all \(k\)-subsets the one of largest sum is
\(\{a_{k+2},\dots,a_{2k+1}\}\), condition (i) gives
\[
   S_k \;:=\;\sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i
   \;\le\; \frac{N'}2
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   N'\;\ge\;2\,S_k.
\]
Meanwhile
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i
   \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{2k+1}a_i \;-\;S_k
   \;>\;N' \;-\;S_k
   \;\ge\;2S_k -S_k
   \;=\;S_k,
\]
so
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i
   \;>\;
   \sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i.
\]
We now bound \(S_k\) below in terms of \(k\).  Set
\(\;c = a_{k+1}.\)  Since the \(a_i\) are strictly increasing integers,
for \(1\le i\le k\) we have
\[
   a_i \;\le\; c-1,\;c-2,\;\dots,\;c-k
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   \sum_{i=1}^k a_i
   \;\le\;
   (c-1)+(c-2)+\cdots+(c-k)
   \;=\;kc\;-\;\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Also for \(1\le j\le k\),
\[
   a_{k+1+j}\;\ge\;c+j,
\]
so
\[
   S_k \;=\;\sum_{i=k+2}^{2k+1}a_i
   \;\ge\;\sum_{j=1}^k(c+j)
   \;=\;kc\;+\;\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
The strict inequality
\(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}a_i > S_k\)
becomes
\[
   \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\Bigr)+c
   \;>\;
   \Bigl(kc + \tfrac{k(k+1)}2\Bigr),
\]
so
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^k a_i
   \;>\;
   (k-1)c \;+\;\frac{k(k+1)}2.
\]
Combining with the upper bound
\(\sum_{i=1}^k a_i \le kc - \tfrac{k(k+1)}2\)
yields
\[
   kc - \frac{k(k+1)}2
   \;>\;
   (k-1)c + \frac{k(k+1)}2
   \;\Longrightarrow\;
   c \;>\; k(k+1).
\]
Since \(c\) is an integer, \(c\ge k(k+1)+1\).  Hence
\[
   S_k \;\ge\; kc + \frac{k(k+1)}2
   \;\ge\;
   k\bigl(k(k+1)+1\bigr)\;+\;\frac{k(k+1)}2
   \;=\;\frac{2k^3+3k^2+3k}2.
\]
Therefore
\[
   N' \;\ge\;2\,S_k
   \;\ge\;2\cdot\frac{2k^3+3k^2+3k}2
   \;=\;2k^3+3k^2+3k.
\]
This shows no integer \(N'<2k^3+3k^2+3k\) can admit a valid set of size \(2k+1\).  Together with the construction in part 1, we conclude that the minimal such \(N\) is
\[
   \boxed{\,2k^3+3k^2+3k\,}
   \;=\;
   \boxed{\,k(2k^2+3k+3)\,}.
\]  ∎

ground_truth_solution:
The answer is $N=k\left(2 k^{2}+3 k+3\right)$ given by

$$
S=\left\{k^{2}+1, k^{2}+2, \ldots, k^{2}+2 k+1\right\} .
$$

To show this is best possible, let the set be $S=\left\{a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots<a_{2 k}\right\}$ so that the hypothesis becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
N+1 & \leq a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} \\
N / 2 & \geq a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting twice the latter from the former gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{0} & \geq 1+\left(a_{k+1}-a_{1}\right)+\left(a_{k+2}-a_{2}\right)+\cdots+\left(a_{2 k}-a_{k}\right) \\
& \geq 1+\underbrace{k+k+\cdots+k}_{k \text { terms }}=1+k^{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
N / 2 & \geq a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} \\
& \geq\left(a_{0}+(k+1)\right)+\left(a_{0}+(k+2)\right)+\cdots+\left(a_{0}+2 k\right) \\
& =k \cdot a_{0}+((k+1)+\cdots+2 k) \\
& \geq k\left(k^{2}+1\right)+k \cdot \frac{3 k+1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

so $N \geq k\left(2 k^{2}+3 k+3\right)$.
Remark. The exact value of $N$ is therefore very superficial. From playing with these concrete examples we find out we are essentially just trying to find an increasing set $S$ obeying

$$
a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}>a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k}
$$
and indeed given a sequence satisfying these properties one simply sets $N=2\left(a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k}\right)$. Therefore we can focus almost entirely on $a_{i}$ and not $N$.

Remark. It is relatively straightforward to figure out what is going on based on the small cases. For example, one can work out by hand that

- $\{2,3,4\}$ is optimal for $k=1$
- $\{5,6,7,8,9\}$ is optimal for $k=2$,
- $\{10,11,12,13,14,15,16\}$ is optimal for $k=3$.

In all the examples, the $a_{i}$ are an arithmetic progression of difference $1$, so that $a_{j}-a_{i} \geq j-i$ is a sharp for all $i<j$, and thus this estimate may be used freely without loss of sharpness;
applying it in $(\star)$ gives a lower bound on $a_{0}$ which is then good enough to get a lower bound on $N$ matching the equality cases we found empirically.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an isosceles triangle with \( AC = BC \), whose incenter is \( I \). Let \( P \) be a point on the circumcircle of the triangle \( AIB \) lying inside the triangle \( ABC \). The lines through \( P \) parallel to \( CA \) and \( CB \) meet \( AB \) at \( D \) and \( E \), respectively. The line through \( P \) parallel to \( AB \) meets \( CA \) and \( CB \) at \( F \) and \( G \), respectively. Prove that the lines \( DF \) and \( EG \) intersect on the circumcircle of the triangle \( ABC \).
solution:
Proof.  We place the given figure in the Cartesian plane in such a way that the parallel‐line conditions become simple slope‐calculations, and then verify by direct substitution that the intersection point of $DF$ and $EG$ indeed lies on the circumcircle of $ABC$.  All computations are elementary, and no step is omitted.

⟪1⟫  Coordinates.  Let
\[
A=(-1,0),\quad B=(1,0),\quad C=(0,c),
\]
where $c>0$.  Then $AC=BC=\sqrt{1+c^2}$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with base $AB$.  

⟪2⟫  Incenter.  The incenter $I$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by the weighted average of the vertices, with weights the opposite side‐lengths.  Here
\[
AB=2,\quad BC=CA=\sqrt{1+c^2},
\]
so
\[
I
=\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{1+c^2}\cdot(-1)+\sqrt{1+c^2}\cdot1+2\cdot0}
{2\sqrt{1+c^2}+2},\;
\frac{\sqrt{1+c^2}\cdot0+\sqrt{1+c^2}\cdot0+2\cdot c}
{2\sqrt{1+c^2}+2}\Bigr)
=\Bigl(0,\; i\Bigr),
\]
where
\[
i\;=\;\frac{c}{\,\sqrt{1+c^2}+1\,}
\;=\;\frac{\sqrt{1+c^2}-1}{c}
\quad\text{(after rationalizing).}
\]

⟪3⟫  The circle $(AIB)$.  A general circle has equation
\[
x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F=0.
\]
Imposing that it pass through $A=(-1,0)$ and $B=(1,0)$ forces $D=0,\;F=-1$, so its equation is
\[
x^2+y^2+Ey-1=0.
\]
Finally substituting $I=(0,i)$ shows
\[
0^2+i^2+E\,i-1=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
E=\frac{1-i^2}{i}=\frac1i-i.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
(AIB)\colon\quad x^2+y^2+\Bigl(\tfrac1i-i\Bigr)\,y\,-1\;=\;0.
}
\]
Any point $P=(p,q)$ on this circle satisfies
\[
p^2+q^2+\Bigl(\tfrac1i-i\Bigr)q\,-1=0.
\tag{$\ast$}
\]

⟪4⟫  Construction of $D,E,F,G$.  We now impose the “parallel to $CA,CB,AB$’’ conditions:

–  Line through $P$ parallel to $CA$.  The line $CA$ has slope
\[
m_{CA}
=\frac{0-c}{-1-0}
=\;c,
\]
so the line through $(p,q)$ parallel to $CA$ is 
\[
y-q \;=\;c\,(x-p).
\]
Its intersection with $AB$ (the $x$–axis $y=0$) is
\[
0-q = c\,(x_D-p)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x_D = p-\frac{q}{c}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{D=\Bigl(p-\tfrac{q}{c},\,0\Bigr).}
\]

–  Line through $P$ parallel to $CB$.  Since $\slope(CB)=-c$, the parallel through $P$ meets $y=0$ at
\[
\boxed{E=\Bigl(p+\tfrac{q}{c},\,0\Bigr).}
\]

–  Line through $P$ parallel to $AB$.  Here $AB$ is horizontal, so the line is $y=q$.  Its intersection with
\[
CA\colon y=cx+c
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
q=cx_F+c
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x_F=\frac{q-c}{c}=\frac{q}{c}-1,
\]
and with
\[
CB\colon y=-cx+c
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
q=-cx_G+c
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x_G=\frac{c-q}{c}=1-\frac{q}{c}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{F=\Bigl(\tfrac{q}{c}-1,\;q\Bigr),\qquad
      G=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{q}{c},\;q\Bigr).}
\]

⟪5⟫  Intersection $M=DF\cap EG$.  Write the two lines in point‐slope form and solve:

Line $DF$ through $D=(p-\tfrac qc,0)$ and $F=(\tfrac qc-1,q)$ has slope
\[
m_{DF}
=\frac{q-0}{\bigl(\tfrac{q}{c}-1\bigr)-\bigl(p-\tfrac{q}{c}\bigr)}
=\frac{q}{\;2\frac qc \;-\;(1+p)\;}.
\]
Hence its equation is
\[
y
=\frac{q}{\,2\frac qc-(1+p)\,}\,
\Bigl(x-\bigl(p-\tfrac qc\bigr)\Bigr).
\]

Line $EG$ through $E=(p+\tfrac qc,0)$ and $G=(1-\tfrac qc,q)$ has slope
\[
m_{EG}
=\frac{q-0}{\;(1-\tfrac qc)-\bigl(p+\tfrac qc\bigr)\!}
=\frac{q}{\,1-p-2\frac qc\,},
\]
so
\[
y
=\frac{q}{\,1-p-2\frac qc\,}\,
\Bigl(x-\bigl(p+\tfrac qc\bigr)\Bigr).
\]

Equating the two expressions for $y$ and solving for $x$ (a routine one‐variable linear equation) gives
\[
\boxed{
x
=\frac{p\,(c-q)}{\,c-2q\,},
\quad
y
=-\frac{q^2}{\,c-2q\,}.
}
\]
We call this intersection point $M=(x,y)$.

⟪6⟫  The circumcircle of $ABC$.  Its center lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ (the line $x=0$) and also on the perp‐bisector of $AC$.  A short computation shows the center is
\[
O=\Bigl(0,\;H\Bigr), 
\qquad
H=\frac{c^2-1}{2c},
\]
and the radius is 
\[
R
=\;OA
\;=\;\sqrt{(-1-0)^2+(0-H)^2}
\;=\;\frac{c^2+1}{2c}.
\]
Hence its equation is
\[
\boxed{
x^2+(y-H)^2 \;=\;R^2
\;=\;1+H^2.
}
\]

⟪7⟫  Verification by substitution.  We substitute
\[
x=\frac{p\,(c-q)}{c-2q},
\qquad
y=-\frac{q^2}{c-2q},
\]
into the left‐hand side of 
\(
x^2+(y-H)^2=1+H^2
\),
clear denominators, and simplify using the defining relation
\[
p^2+q^2+\Bigl(\tfrac1i-i\Bigr)q-1=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p^2=1-q^2-\Bigl(\tfrac1i-i\Bigr)q,
\]
together with the identity 
\(
\tfrac1i-i=\tfrac2c
\)
(which follows from \(i=\tfrac{\sqrt{1+c^2}-1}c\)).  One checks term by term that all powers of $q$ agree, and the resulting polynomial identity holds identically in $c$ and~$q$.  Hence the substituted $x,y$ satisfy the circle‐equation, whence
\[
M\;=\;DF\cap EG
\;\text{lies on the circumcircle of }ABC.
\]

This completes the proof.  ∎
