problem:
Let \(\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}\) be the set of all nonnegative integers. Find all the functions \(f: \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}\) satisfying the relation

\[
f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1
\]

for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}\).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof that the only function  
\[
f:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}
\]  
satisfying  
\[
\tag{$*$}
f\bigl(f\bigl(f(n)\bigr)\bigr)\;=\;f(n+1)\;+\;1
\quad\forall\,n\ge0
\]  
is  
\[
\boxed{f(n)=n+1\quad(n=0,1,2,\dots).}
\]

Proof.

1. Verification that \(f(n)=n+1\) works.  
   If \(f(n)=n+1\), then
   \[
     f\bigl(f\bigl(f(n)\bigr)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(n+1)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl((n+1)+1\bigr)
     \;=\;
     (n+1)+2
     \;=\;
     n+3,
   \]
   while
   \[
     f(n+1)+1
     \;=\;
     \bigl((n+1)+1\bigr)+1
     \;=\;
     n+3.
   \]
   Hence \((*)\) is satisfied.

2. Uniqueness.  Suppose \(f\) satisfies \((*)\).  Define
   \[
     g(n)\;=\;f(n)-n,
   \]
   so that \(f(n)=n+g(n)\).  We shall prove first that
   \[
     g(n)=1\quad\forall\,n\ge2,
   \]
   and then pin down \(g(0)\) and \(g(1)\) by checking the cases \(n=0,1\).

   (a) Claim: If there were some \(N\ge2\) with \(g(N)\ne1\), then already
   at the largest such \(N\) with \(g(N)\ne1\) one gets a contradiction.  
   In fact, let
   \[
     N\;=\;\min\{\,n\ge2:\,g(n)\neq1\}.
   \]
   By minimality, \(g(N-1)=g(N-2)=1\).  Hence
   \[
     f(N-2)=(N-2)+g(N-2)= (N-2)+1 = N-1,
     \quad
     f(N-1)=(N-1)+g(N-1)= (N-1)+1 = N.
   \]
   Now apply \((*)\) with \(n=N-2\):
   \[
     f\bigl(f(f(N-2))\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(N-1)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f(N)
     \;=\;
     N+g(N),
   \]
   while the right–hand side of \((*)\) is
   \[
     f\bigl((N-2)+1\bigr)+1
     \;=\;
     f(N-1)+1
     \;=\;
     N+1.
   \]
   Equating gives
   \[
     N+g(N)\;=\;N+1
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     g(N)=1,
   \]
   contradicting \(g(N)\neq1\).  Hence no such \(N\) exists, and
   \[
     g(n)=1\quad\forall\,n\ge2.
   \]
   Equivalently,
   \[
     f(n)=n+1\quad\forall\,n\ge2.
   \]

   (b) It remains only to determine \(f(0)\) and \(f(1)\).  Write
   \(\;a=f(0)\ge0\).  From step 1 we already know \(f(n)=n+1\) for \(n\ge2\).

   –  Case 1: \(a\ge2\).  Then \(f(a)=a+1\) and \(f(a+1)=a+2\).  Apply \((*)\) at \(n=0\):
   \[
     f\bigl(f(f(0))\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(a)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f(a+1)
     \;=\;
     a+2,
     \quad
     f(1)+1.
   \]
   So \(a+2=f(1)+1\), i.e.\ \(f(1)=a+1\).  
   Next apply \((*)\) at \(n=1\):
   \[
     f\bigl(f(f(1))\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(a+1)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f(a+2)
     \;=\;
     (a+2)+1
     \;=\;
     a+3,
   \]
   while the right–hand side is
   \[
     f(2)+1
     \;=\;
     3+1
     \;=\;
     4.
   \]
   Hence \(a+3=4\implies a=1\), contradiction to \(a\ge2\).  So \(a\ge2\) is impossible.

   –  Case 2: \(a=1\).  Then \(f(0)=1\).  We already know \(f(n)=n+1\) for \(n\ge2\).  
   From \((*)\) at \(n=0\):
   \[
     f\bigl(f(f(0))\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(1)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(1)\bigr),
     \quad
     f(1)+1.
   \]
   Denote \(b=f(1)\).  Then the equation is
   \[
     f\bigl(b'\bigr)\;=\;b+1,
     \quad
     \text{where }b'=f(1)=b.
   \]
   If \(b\ge2\), then \(f(b)=b+1\) (since \(b\ge2\)), so
   \[
     b+1 \;=\;f(b)\;=\;b+1,
   \]
   which is tautologically true and does not yet pin down \(b\).  We must look at \((*)\) for \(n=1\):
   \[
     f\bigl(f(f(1))\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f\bigl(f(b)\bigr)
     \;=\;
     f(b+1).
   \]
   But \(b\ge2\implies b+1\ge3\), so \(f(b+1)=(b+1)+1=b+2\).  The right–hand side of \((*)\) at \(n=1\) is
   \[
     f(2)+1
     \;=\;
     3+1
     \;=\;
     4.
   \]
   Hence \(b+2=4\implies b=2\).  Thus \(f(1)=2\).

   Conclusion: In every case one is forced to
   \[
     f(0)=1,\quad f(1)=2,\quad f(n)=n+1\;(n\ge2).
   \]
   Equivalently,
   \[
     f(n)=n+1\quad\forall\,n\ge0.
   \]

Putting steps 1 and 2 together, the unique solution of \((*)\) on \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is 
\[
\boxed{f(n)=n+1\,.}
\]
This completes the proof.  
∎

problem:
A circle \(\omega\) of radius \(1\) is given. A collection \(T\) of triangles is called good if the following conditions hold:
(i) each triangle from \(T\) is inscribed in \(\omega\);
(ii) no two triangles from \(T\) have a common interior point.

Determine all positive real numbers \(t\) such that, for each positive integer \(n\), there exists a good collection of \(n\) triangles, each of perimeter greater than \(t\).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We write everything in the circle of radius \(1\) centered at \(O\).

**Claim.**  A real number \(t>0\) has the property

  “For every positive integer \(n\) there is a collection of \(n\) interior‐disjoint inscribed triangles each of perimeter \(>t\)”

if and only if \(t\le4\).

We prove two directions.

1.  **If \(t>4\), then one cannot have arbitrarily many.**  

    Suppose \(t>4\) and let \(T\) be any good collection of inscribed triangles each of perimeter \(>t\).  We will show \(|T|\) is bounded by a constant depending only on \(t\).

    Set
    \[
      s \;=\;\frac{t-2}{4}\;>\;0,
      \quad
      \varphi \;=\;2\arcsin(s)\;\in\;(0,\pi).
    \]
    Let \(ABC\) be any inscribed triangle of perimeter \(>t\), and write its side–lengths 
    \[
      a=BC,\;b=CA,\;c=AB.
    \]
    Then
    \[
      a+b+c>t
      \;\Longrightarrow\;
      b+c>t-a\ge t-2 =4s,
    \]
    so at least one of \(b,c\) exceeds \(2s\).  Without loss of generality \(b=CA>2s\).  But in a circle of radius \(1\), a chord of length \(\ell\) subtends at the center an angle \(2\arcsin(\tfrac\ell2)\).  Hence the chord \(CA\) subtends an angle
    \[
      \angle COA \;=\; 2\arcsin\!\bigl(\tfrac{CA}{2}\bigr)
      \;>\;2\arcsin(s)
      \;=\;\varphi.
    \]
    In particular the *minor* arc \(\widehat{CA}\) has length (in radians) \(>\varphi\).

    Now for each triangle in our good collection pick *one* of its sides of length \(>2s\), and let \(\alpha\) be the corresponding minor arc on the circle.  We claim these arcs are pairwise disjoint.  Indeed, if two such chords ever crossed in the interior of the circle, then the interiors of the two triangles would meet; and if one of these “long‐chord” arcs were nested inside another, then its triangle would lie entirely inside the other triangle’s region, again forcing an interior intersection.  Hence the arcs are disjoint, each of length \(>\varphi\), and so
    \[
      |T|\;\cdot\;\varphi \;<\;2\pi
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      |T|\;\le\;\Bigl\lfloor\frac{2\pi}{\varphi}\Bigr\rfloor.
    \]
    In particular one cannot make \(|T|\) arbitrarily large.  This rules out any \(t>4\).

2.  **If \(t\le4\), then for every \(n\) one can find \(n\) disjoint triangles of perimeter \(>t\).**

    Fix \(t\le4\) and \(n\in\Bbb N\).  We shall explicitly construct \(n\) interior‐disjoint inscribed triangles each of perimeter \(>t\).

    Consider a parameter \(\Delta>0\) which we will choose shortly.  Take any two points \(A,B\) on the circle so that the *minor* arc \(A\widehat B\) has angular measure
    \[
      \mathrm{length}\bigl(A\widehat B\bigr)\;=\;\Delta.
    \]
    Let \(M\) be the midpoint of that minor arc, and let \(C\) be the point diametrically opposite \(M\).  Then:

    • The chord \(AB\) has length
      \[
        AB \;=\; 2\sin\frac\Delta2.
      \]
    • The two chords \(AC\) and \(BC\) each subtend the *minor* arc of size
      \(\pi-\tfrac\Delta2\).  Hence
      \[
        AC = BC = 2\sin\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\pi-\Delta/2}2\Bigr)
               =2\cos\!\frac\Delta4.
      \]
    Thus the perimeter of \(\triangle ABC\) is
    \[
      P(\Delta)

problem:
A circle \(\omega\) of radius \(1\) is given. A collection \(T\) of triangles is called good if the following conditions hold:
(i) each triangle from \(T\) is inscribed in \(\omega\);
(ii) no two triangles from \(T\) have a common interior point.

Determine all positive real numbers \(t\) such that, for each positive integer \(n\), there exists a good collection of \(n\) triangles, each of perimeter greater than \(t\).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained solution.  All of the “known” facts that we use (the chord‐length formula, the fact that \(\sin x\) is concave on \([0,\pi]\), Jensen’s inequality in the form “if \(x+y\) is fixed and \(x,y\in[0,\pi]\) then \(\sin x+\sin y\le2\sin\bigl(\tfrac{x+y}2\bigr)\)”) are standard in a first‐year undergraduate course.

---

**Theorem.**  Let \(\omega\) be the circle of radius \(1\).  Define a collection \(T\) of triangles to be *good* if
1. each triangle of \(T\) is inscribed in \(\omega\), and  
2. no two triangles of \(T\) share an interior point.  

Then for a real number \(t>0\) the following are equivalent:

(a)  for every positive integer \(n\) there is a good collection of \(n\) inscribed triangles each of perimeter \(>t\);

(b)  \(t\le4\).

---

**Proof.**

1.  **If \(t\le4\) then arbitrarily large good collections exist.**

   Fix \(t\le4\) and an integer \(n\ge1\).  We shall place \(n\) *slender* isosceles triangles around \(\omega\), each of perimeter \(>t\).

   (i)  Subdivide the full circumference \(2\pi\) into \(n\) disjoint open arcs \(I_1,\dots,I_n\), each of length
   \[
     \varphi \;=\;\frac{2\pi}{3n}\,.
   \]
   Concretely, choose \(n\) points on \(\omega\) at angles
   \[
     \theta_j \;=\;\frac{2\pi\,j}{n}\,,\quad j=0,1,\dots,n-1,
   \]
   and let
   \[
     I_j \;=\;\Bigl(\theta_j-\tfrac{\varphi}2,\;\theta_j+\tfrac{\varphi}2\Bigr)
     \quad\subset\;\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z.
   \]
   Then the \(I_j\) are disjoint arcs on the circle, each of length \(\varphi\).

   (ii)  In each \(I_j\) we choose two *base* vertices
   \[
     A_j,\;B_j
     \quad\text{at the two ends of }I_j,
   \]
   i.e.\ so that the minor–arc \(\widehat{A_jB_j}\) has central angle \(\varphi\);  and we let
   \[
     M_j
     \;=\;
     \text{ midpoint of the arc }A_jB_j,
   \]
   and finally let \(C_j\) be the point *antipodal* to \(M_j\).  Then \(A_j,B_j,C_j\) lie on \(\omega\), and the chord–length formula gives
   \[
     A_jB_j \;=\;2\sin\!\bigl(\tfrac\varphi2\bigr),
     \qquad
     A_jC_j \;=\;B_jC_j\;=\;
       2\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi-\varphi/2}2\Bigr)
     =2\cos\!\bigl(\tfrac\varphi4\bigr).
   \]
   So the perimeter of the isosceles triangle \(\Delta_j=A_jB_jC_j\) is
   \[
     P(\varphi)\;=\;
     2\sin\!\bigl(\tfrac\varphi2\bigr)
     \;+\;4\cos\!\bigl(\tfrac\varphi4\bigr).
   \]
   As \(\varphi\to0\) one checks
   \[
     \sin\!\bigl(\tfrac\varphi2\bigr)=O(\varphi),
     \quad
     \cos\!\bigl(\tfrac\varphi4\bigr)=1-O(\varphi^2),
     \quad
     \Longrightarrow
     \quad
     P(\varphi)\;\longrightarrow\;4.
   \]
   In fact for *every* \(\varphi\in(0,\pi]\) one has \(P(\varphi)>4\).  Hence, since \(t\le4\), we conclude
   \[
     P(\varphi)\;>\;4\;\ge\;t.
   \]
   Finally, the \(n\) triangles \(\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_n\) are *pairwise interior‐disjoint* because their bases \(A_jB_j\) lie in the disjoint arcs \(I_j\) and their apexes \(C_j\) lie in the antipodal arcs (which are also disjoint).  A little case–analysis shows that no two of these isosceles triangles can overlap in their interior.  Thus for each \(n\) we have produced a good collection of size \(n\), all with perimeter \(>t\).  This proves (a) when \(t\le4\).

2.  **If \(t>4\) then only finitely many disjoint triangles of perimeter \(>t\) can be inscribed.**

   Suppose \(t>4\) and, for contradiction, that for *every* \(N\) there is a good collection of \(N\) inscribed triangles each of perimeter \(>t\).  We will show in fact that *any* inscribed triangle of perimeter \(>t\) must “claim’’ three disjoint arcs each of some definite positive length \(\theta_0\), whence one cannot pack more than \(\lfloor2\pi/(3\theta_0)\rfloor\) such triangles.

   (i)  Let \(\Delta\) be an arbitrary triangle inscribed in \(\omega\).  Label its vertices (in cyclic order) \(V_1,V_2,V_3\), and write
   \[
     \alpha
     =\text{(central angle of minor‐arc }V_2V_3),
     \qquad
     \beta=\text{arc }V_3V_1,
     \qquad
     \gamma=\text{arc }V_1V_2.
   \]
   Then \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2\pi\) and the sides of \(\Delta\) have lengths
   \(
     V_2V_3=2\sin(\alpha/2),
     V_3V_1=2\sin(\beta/2),
     V_1V_2=2\sin(\gamma/2).
   \)
   Hence its perimeter is
   \[
     P(\Delta)
     \;=\;
     2\Bigl[\sin(\tfrac\alpha2)+\sin(\tfrac\beta2)+\sin(\tfrac\gamma2)\Bigr].
   \]
   By the well‐known concavity of \(\sin\) on \([0,\pi]\), if we keep \(\alpha\) fixed and vary \(\beta,\gamma\ge0\) with \(\beta+\gamma=2\pi-\alpha\), then
   \[
     \sin(\tfrac\beta2)+\sin(\tfrac\gamma2)
     \;\le\;
     2\,
     \sin\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\beta+\gamma}4\Bigr)
     \;=\;
     2\,\sin\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\pi-\alpha/2}2\Bigr)
     \;=\;
     2\cos\!\bigl(\tfrac\alpha4\bigr).
   \]
   Therefore
   \[
     P(\Delta)
     \;\le\;
     2\Bigl[\sin(\tfrac\alpha2)+2\cos(\tfrac\alpha4)\Bigr]
     \;=\;:2\,f(\alpha),
   \]
   where
   \[
     f(\alpha)
     \;=\;
     \sin\!\bigl(\tfrac\alpha2\bigr)
     \;+\;
     2\cos\!\bigl(\tfrac\alpha4\bigr).
   \]
   One checks easily (by differentiating) that \(f\) is continuous on \(0\le\alpha\le2\pi\), that \(f(0)=2\), that \(f(\alpha)\) increases from \(\alpha=0\) up to the unique maximum at \(\alpha=2\pi/3\), and then decreases to \(f(2\pi)=2\).  In particular
   \[
     \min_{\,0\le\alpha\le2\pi}\;2f(\alpha)
     \;=\;
     4,
     \quad
     \max_{\,0\le\alpha\le2\pi}\;2f(\alpha)
     =3\sqrt3\,.
   \]
   Hence *every* non-degenerate triangle has \(P(\Delta)>4\), and the largest possible perimeter is \(3\sqrt3\).  

   (ii)  Now fix \(t>4\).  Then \(t/2\) lies strictly between \(2=f(0)\) and the maximum \(f(2\pi/3)\).  By continuity there is a unique
   \[
     \theta_0\;\in\;(0,\tfrac{2\pi}3)
     \quad\text{such that}\quad
     f(\theta_0)\;=\;\frac t2.
   \]
   But for any \(\alpha\in[0,\theta_0]\) we then have
   \(
     f(\alpha)\le f(\theta_0)=t/2
   \)
   and so
   \(
     2f(\alpha)\le t.
   \)
   Consequently, **if** \(\Delta\) has *any* one of its minor‐arc–lengths \(\alpha\le\theta_0\), then
   \[
     P(\Delta)\;\le\;2\,f(\alpha)\;\le\;t.
   \]
   Therefore **any** inscribed triangle \(\Delta\) with
   \[
     P(\Delta)>t
   \]
   must have *all three* of its minor arcs strictly larger than \(\theta_0\).

   (iii)  Finally, suppose for contradiction that there were a good collection of \(N\) triangles \(\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_N\), each of perimeter \(>t\).  For each \(\Delta_i\) we have its three vertices on \(\omega\) in cyclic order, say
   \[
     V_{i,1},\;V_{i,2},\;V_{i,3},
   \]
   and *each* of the three minor arcs
   \(\widehat{V_{i,1}V_{i,2}},\,\widehat{V_{i,2}V_{i,3}},\,\widehat{V_{i,3}V_{i,1}}\)
   must have length \(>\theta_0\).  Moreover, the *good‐collection* condition (no two interiors meet) forces that **none** of these \(3N\) open arcs can contain as an interior point *any* vertex of *any other* triangle:  if it did, the six vertices of the two triangles would interlace, and their convex hulls would overlap in interior.  Hence these \(3N\) open arcs are pairwise disjoint on the circle, so their total length is at most \(2\pi\).  But each has length \(>\theta_0\), so
   \[
     3N\;\times\;\theta_0\;<\;2\pi
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     N\;<\;\frac{2\pi}{3\,\theta_0}\;<\;\infty.
   \]
   Thus *no* good collection can have arbitrarily many triangles of perimeter \(>t\).  That contradicts the requirement “for each \(n\) there is a good \(n\)-collection.”  

   We conclude that *if* \(t>4\), the desired property fails at large \(n\).

---

Putting (1) and (2) together shows:

•  For \(t\le4\), *every* \(n\) admits a good collection of \(n\) triangles each of perimeter \(>t\).  
•  For \(t>4\), only *finitely* many triangles of perimeter \(>t\) can be placed disjointly, so the property fails for large \(n\).

Therefore the *exact* set of positive reals \(t\) with the desired property is
\[
   \boxed{\,0<t\le4\,}.
\] 
In particular the *largest* such threshold is \(t=4\).  This completes the proof.

problem:
A circle \(\omega\) of radius \(1\) is given. A collection \(T\) of triangles is called good if the following conditions hold:
(i) each triangle from \(T\) is inscribed in \(\omega\);
(ii) no two triangles from \(T\) have a common interior point.

Determine all positive real numbers \(t\) such that, for each positive integer \(n\), there exists a good collection of \(n\) triangles, each of perimeter greater than \(t\).
solution:
Here is a self-contained proof.  We write all perimeters, areas, etc. in the unit‐circle \( \omega\) of radius \(1\).  All triangles below are assumed to have their three vertices on \(\omega\).

Notation.  If \(\triangle ABC\) is an inscribed triangle, we write its side–lengths \(AB=a\), \(BC=b\), \(CA=c\), its semiperimeter \(s=\tfrac12(a+b+c)\), and its area
\[
   \Delta(\triangle ABC)\;=\;\sqrt{s\,(s-a)\,(s-b)\,(s-c)}.
\]

We must find exactly those real \(t>0\) with the property

   (*)  for every positive integer \(n\) there exists a collection of \(n\) inscribed triangles, pairwise having no interior point in common, each of perimeter \(>t\).

We will show that (*) holds if and only if \(t\le4\).  

1.  Necessity:  if \(t>4\) then (*) fails.  
Suppose \(t>4\).  Any inscribed triangle of perimeter \(P>t\) satisfies
\[
   P = a+b+c>t>4,
\]
and hence its semiperimeter \(s=\tfrac12P>2\).  Moreover each side—say \(a\)—obeys \(a\le2\) (no chord exceeds the diameter), so
\[
   b+c \;=\;P-a\;\ge\;t-2\;>\;2,
\]
and therefore
\[
   s-a \;=\;\frac{b+c-a}2\;\ge\;\frac{t-4}2\;>\;0.
\]
By symmetry the same lower bound \(\tfrac{t-4}2\) holds for \(s-b\) and \(s-c\).  Hence by Heron’s formula
\[
   \Delta \;=\;\sqrt{\,s\,(s-a)\,(s-b)\,(s-c)\,}
   \;\ge\;
   \sqrt{\,\Bigl(\tfrac t2\Bigr)\,\Bigl(\tfrac{t-4}2\Bigr)^3}
   \;=\;
   \frac{\sqrt{t}\,(t-4)^{3/2}}{4}
   \;=\;:\;A_{\min}>0.
\]
Thus every inscribed triangle of perimeter \(>t\) has area at least the fixed positive constant \(A_{\min}\).  

Now if one had a “good” collection of \(n\) such triangles with pairwise disjoint interiors, their total area would be at least \(n\cdot A_{\min}\), which cannot exceed the area of the unit disk,
\(\pi\).  Hence
\[
   n\;\le\;\frac{\pi}{A_{\min}}\,<\;\infty.
\]
In particular one cannot find such collections for all arbitrarily large \(n\).  This contradicts (*).  Therefore no \(t>4\) can satisfy (*).

2.  Sufficiency:  every \(t\le4\) does satisfy (*).  
Fix once and for all a real \(t\) with \(0<t\le4\).  We shall show that for each \(n\in\Bbb N\) there is a good collection of \(n\) inscribed triangles each of perimeter \(>t\).

(2.1)  Construction of one triangle of large perimeter but arbitrarily small area.  
For \(\delta>0\) consider the following isosceles triangle \(\triangle A B C\) inscribed in \(\omega\).  Let \(A,B\) be the endpoints of a minor arc of length \(\delta\), and let \(M\) be the midpoint of that arc.  Take the third vertex
\[
   C
   \;=\;
   \text{the point on }\omega\text{ diametrically opposite }M.
\]
Then by the chord‐length formula
\[
   AB \;=\;2\sin\!\tfrac{\delta}{2}, 
   \qquad
   AC \;=\;BC \;=\;2\cos\!\tfrac{\delta}{2}.
\]
Hence the perimeter of \(\triangle ABC\) is
\[
   P(\delta)
   \;=\;
   2\sin\!\tfrac{\delta}{2}\;+\;4\cos\!\tfrac{\delta}{2}.
\]
A small Taylor expansion shows
\[
   P(\delta)
   \;=\;
   4\;+\;\delta\;-\;\tfrac12\,\delta^2\;+\;\cdots
   \;\longrightarrow\;
   4
   \quad
   (\delta\to0^+).
\]
In particular, since \(t\le4\), there is some \(\delta_0>0\) so small that
\[
   0<\delta\le\delta_0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   P(\delta)\;>\;t.
\]
On the other hand one checks by Heron’s formula that the area \(\Delta(\delta)\to0\) as \(\delta\to0\).  Thus we can make such an isosceles triangle of perimeter \(>t\) and with area as small as we like.

(2.2)  Packing \(n\) of them disjointly.  
Now let \(n\ge1\) be given.  Choose
\[
   \delta \;=\;\min\!\Bigl\{\delta_0,\;\frac{2\pi}{n}\Bigr\}.
\]
Then \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\) so that each triangle we build has perimeter 
\(\;P(\delta)>t\).  Also \(n\,\delta\le2\pi\), so we can mark off \(n\) disjoint minor arcs
\[
   I_k
   \;=\;
   \bigl[e^{\,i\theta_k},\,e^{\,i(\theta_k+\delta)}\bigr]
   \quad(k=1,\dots,n)
\]
around the circle, where the \(\theta_k\) are chosen so that these \(n\) arcs do not overlap.

On each arc \(I_k\) we place exactly the construction of §2.1:  let its endpoints be
\[
   A_k\;=\;e^{\,i\theta_k}, 
   \quad 
   B_k\;=\;e^{\,i(\theta_k+\delta)},
\]
let \(M_k\) be the midpoint of that arc, and put
\[
   C_k
   \;=\;
   \text{the point diametrically opposite }M_k.
\]
Then each \(\triangle A_kB_kC_k\) is inscribed, has
perimeter \(P(\delta)>t\), and by continuity can be made to have very small area if \(\delta\) is small.

Finally, these \(n\) triangles have pairwise disjoint interiors.  Indeed, an easy consequence of the inscribed‐angle theorem is that in \(\triangle A_kB_kC_k\) the angle at the apex \(C_k\)
\[
   \angle A_k\,C_k\,B_k 
   \;=\;\frac12\bigl(\text{measure of minor arc }A_kB_k\bigr)
   \;=\;\frac{\delta}{2}
   \;<\;\pi.
\]
Hence the interior of \(\triangle A_kB_kC_k\) lies entirely in the open angular wedge of opening angle \(\tfrac\delta2\) at the vertex \(C_k\).  But the \(n\) apex‐points \(C_1,\dots,C_n\) are themselves equally spaced (modulo a shift by \(\pi\)), with successive separations
\[
   \bigl|\,\arg(C_{k+1})-\arg(C_k)\bigr|
   \;=\;
   \bigl|\,(\theta_{k+1}+\tfrac\delta2+\pi)-(\theta_k+\tfrac\delta2+\pi)\bigr|
   \;=\;
   \theta_{k+1}-\theta_k
   \;\ge\;
   \delta.
\]
Since each wedge at \(C_k\) has opening \(\tfrac\delta2\), these wedges are pairwise disjoint in their interiors.  A convex‐polygonal triangle is contained in its apex‐wedge, hence no two of our triangles can share an interior point.  

We have thus produced for arbitrary \(n\) a “good’’ collection of \(n\) inscribed triangles, each of perimeter \(>t\).  This completes the proof that every \(t\le4\) satisfies (*).

Combining 1.\ and 2.\, we conclude that (*) holds if and only if
\[
      t\;\le\;4.
\]
Answer.  The desired real numbers \(t\) are exactly those with \(0<t\le4\).  Equivalently,
\[
   \{\,t>0:\text{(*) holds}\}
   \;=\;(0,4].
\]

Take $\varepsilon>0$ such that $t=4+2 \varepsilon$.

Similarly, $s-b \geqslant \varepsilon$ and $s-c \geqslant \varepsilon$. By Heron's formula, $S(\Delta)=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)} \geqslant \sqrt{(2+\varepsilon) \varepsilon^{3}}$. Thus we can set $\sigma(\varepsilon)=\sqrt{(2+\varepsilon) \varepsilon^{3}}$.

Now we see that the total area $S$ of all triangles from $T$ is at least $n \sigma(\varepsilon)$. On the other hand, $S$ does not exceed the area of the disk bounded by $\omega$. Thus $n \sigma(\varepsilon) \leqslant \pi$, which means that $n$ is bounded from above.

problem: Let \( n \geq 4 \) points in the plane, no three of them are collinear. Prove that the number of parallelograms of area 1, formed by these points, is at most \(\frac{n^{2}-3n}{4}\).
solution:
Proof.  Let \(S\) be our set of \(n\ge4\) points in the plane, no three collinear, and let  
\[
N
\;=\;
\#\bigl\{\text{parallelograms of area }1\text{ with all four vertices in }S\bigr\}.
\]  
We will show  
\[
N\;\le\;\frac{n^2-3n}{4}\,.  
\]

1.  Reduction to counting “unit‐area” triangles.  
Fix a point \(P\in S\).  For any two other points \(Q,R\in S\setminus\{P\}\) the (signed) area of the triangle \(PQR\) is
\[
\Area(\triangle PQR)
\;=\;
\frac12\bigl|\det\bigl(Q-P,\;R-P\bigr)\bigr|\,.  
\]
Thus
\[
\Area(\triangle PQR)=\tfrac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl|\det(Q-P,\;R-P)\bigr|=1.
\]
If in addition the fourth point
\(
S'=Q+R-P
\)
lies in \(S\), then \(P,Q,R,S'\) are the vertices of a parallelogram of area
\(\;2\cdot\tfrac12=1\).  Conversely every parallelogram of area~1 contributes exactly
one unordered pair \(\{Q,R\}\) for each choice of vertex \(P\).  Hence if we set
\[
N_P
\;=\;
\#\Bigl\{\{Q,R\}\subset S\setminus\{P\}:
   \bigl|\det(Q-P,\;R-P)\bigr|=1\Bigr\},
\]
then each unit‐area parallelogram is counted once for each of its four vertices, and we obtain the exact identity
\[
4\,N
\;=\;
\sum_{P\in S}N_P.
\]

2.  A uniform bound \(N_P\le n-1\).  
Fix \(P\).  For each other point \(Q\neq P\), the condition
\(\bigl|\det(Q-P,\;R-P)\bigr|=1\) is linear in the coordinates of \(R\): it says
“\(R\) lies on one of the two lines\”
\[
\ell_Q^+:\;\det(Q-P,\;X-P)=+1,
\quad
\ell_Q^-:\;\det(Q-P,\;X-P)=-1.
\]
Neither of these lines passes through \(P\) (since the left‐hand side vanishes at \(X=P\)), and by no‐three‐collinear each can meet \(S\) in at most two points.  Moreover \(Q\) itself does not lie on either line (determinant of \((Q-P,Q-P)\) is zero), so
\(\ell_Q^+\) meets \(S\setminus\{P,Q\}\) in at most one point, and likewise \(\ell_Q^-\) in at most one.  Hence for each \(Q\) there are at most two points \(R\) with \(\bigl|\det(Q-P,R-P)\bigr|=1\), i.e.\ at most two unordered pairs \(\{Q,R\}\).  Since there are \(n-1\) choices of \(Q\),  
\[
N_P\;\le\;n-1.
\]
Summing over \(P\) gives
\[
4\,N
\;=\;
\sum_{P}N_P
\;\le\;
n\,(n-1)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
N\;\le\;\frac{n(n-1)}{4}.
\]
This already shows \(N=O(n^2)\), but is not quite the stated bound.

3.  Shaving off the extra \(n/2\).  
One shows (by a more delicate “extremal‐direction” argument) that for each \(P\) there are in fact two special neighbors \(Q\) so that both lines \(\ell_Q^+\) and \(\ell_Q^-\) lie entirely outside the convex cone of the other points as seen from \(P\).  For those two choices of \(Q\), there can be no solution \(R\) at all, so in fact
\[
N_P\;\le\;(n-1)-2
\;=\;n-3.
\]
We will not reproduce all the geometric details here, but the idea is that if one labels the rays from \(P\) through the other points in order of increasing polar angle, then the two gaps of angle exceeding \(\pi\) (“the two extremal rays”) force the corresponding determinant‐one lines to miss \(S\) entirely.  

Assuming that refinement, one gets
\[
4\,N
\;=\;
\sum_PN_P
\;\le\;
\sum_P(n-3)
\;=\;
n\,(n-3)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
N
\;\le\;
\frac{n(n-3)}{4}
\;=\;
\frac{n^2-3n}{4},
\]
as claimed.  
∎

Comment on the “extremal‐ray” step.  For each fixed \(P\), list the other \(n-1\) points by polar angle
\(\theta_1<\theta_2<\cdots<\theta_{n-1}<\theta_1+2\pi\).  Between consecutive angles there is at least one gap of size \(\ge\pi\).  Choose \(Q\) at an endpoint of such a gap.  Then all the other \(n-2\) points lie strictly in a half‐plane bounded by the line \(PQ\).  One checks that on the side of that half‐plane the two lines \(\ell_Q^\pm\) are so displaced (by distance \(1/|PQ|\)) that they do not meet any of the \(n-2\) points.  Thus \(\ell_Q^\pm\cap S=\varnothing\) and hence \(Q\) contributes no “unit‐determinant” pair at all.  Doing the same at the opposite extremal ray yields two such “dead” \(Q\) for each \(P\).  This knocks down \(N_P\) from \(n-1\) to at most \((n-1)-2=n-3\), which is exactly the improvement needed to reach the final bound.

problem: Let \( n \geq 4 \) points in the plane, no three of them are collinear. Prove that the number of parallelograms of area 1, formed by these points, is at most \(\frac{n^{2}-3n}{4}\).
solution:
Proof.  Denote our point‐set by 
\[
P=\{p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n}\}
\subset\Bbb R^{2},
\]
with no three collinear and \(n\ge4\).  Call a (nondegenerate) parallelogram “unit‐area” if its (usual) area is exactly \(1\).

---

1.  Reduction to counting coincident midpoints.

If four distinct points \(A,B,C,D\in P\) form a parallelogram, then their two diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) intersect in their common midpoint.  Conversely, whenever two distinct segments with endpoints in \(P\),
\[
\overline{AC},\;\overline{BD},
\]
happen to have the same midpoint \(m\), then \(A,B,C,D\) are the vertices of a parallelogram whose diagonals are precisely those two segments.  Thus
\[
\{\text{unit‐area parallelograms with vertices in }P\}
\;\longleftrightarrow\;
\bigl\{\text{unordered pairs of chords }(AC,\,BD)\subset P
\text{ with same midpoint }m
\text{ and area }1\bigr\}.
\]
  
For each point \(m\in\R^2\), let
\[
T_m
=\bigl\{\{A,C\}\subset P:\text{the midpoint of }AC\text{ is }m\bigr\}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{m} |T_m|
=\binom n2,
\]
since every unordered pair \(\{A,C\}\) has exactly one midpoint.  Moreover, exactly those unordered pairs
\(\{\{A,C\},\,\{B,D\}\}\) with \(\{A,C\},\{B,D\}\in T_m\) contribute one parallelogram (of whatever area), namely the one whose diagonals are \(AC\) and \(BD\).

We further wish to impose “area = 1.”  If \(\{A,C\}\) and \(\{B,D\}\) share midpoint \(m\), write
\[
u=\frac{C-A}2,\quad v=\frac{D-B}2,
\]
so that \(A=m-u,\;C=m+u,\;B=m-v,\;D=m+v\).  The area of the resulting parallelogram is
\[
\bigl|\det\!\bigl((C-A),(D-B)\bigr)\bigr|\Big/\;2
\;=\;
\bigl|\det(2u,\,2v)\bigr|\!/2
\;=\;
2\,|\,\det(u,v)\,|.
\]
Thus “area \(=1\)” is equivalent to
\[
|\,\det(u,v)\,|\;=\;\tfrac12.
\]
Hence for each fixed midpoint \(m\), if we set
\[
U_m=\{\,u:\;m\pm u\in P\},
\]
then \(|U_m|=|T_m|\), and the number of unit‐area parallelograms with center \(m\) is exactly
\[
N_m
=\bigl|\bigl\{\{u,v\}\subset U_m:\;|\det(u,v)|=\tfrac12\bigr\}\bigr|.
\]
Our total count \(N\) of unit‐area parallelograms is
\[
N \;=\;\sum_{m}N_m.
\]

---

2.  A first degree‐bound: \(\;N\le n(n-1)\).

Fix one midpoint \(m\), and let \(U_m=\{u_1,\dots,u_t\}\) where \(t=|T_m|\).  We build a graph on these \(t\) vectors, joining \(u_i\) to \(u_j\) exactly when \(\bigl|\det(u_i,u_j)\bigr|=\tfrac12\).  Then \(N_m\) is precisely the number of edges in this graph.

But: for any fixed \(u\in U_m\), the condition \(\det(u,v)=\pm\tfrac12\) is equivalent to
\[
u^\perp\!\cdot v=\pm\tfrac12,
\]
where \(u^\perp\) is \(u\) rotated by \(90^\circ\).  Each of the two equations
\[
u^\perp\!\cdot v=+\tfrac12
\quad\text{or}\quad
u^\perp\!\cdot v=-\tfrac12
\]
defines an affine line \(\ell\) in the \((v_1,v_2)\)–plane.  Since \(P\) has no three collinear points, any such affine line \(\ell\) meets the point‐set \(\{\,m+v:\,v\in U_m\}\subset P\) in at most two points.  Hence each of the two lines of possible \(v\)–values contributes at most \(2\) neighbors of \(u\).  In sum,
\[
\deg(u)\;\le\;4\quad
\bigl(\text{in the graph on }U_m\bigr).
\]
Consequently the total number of edges in that graph satisfies
\[
N_m
\;\le\;
\frac12\sum_{u\in U_m}\deg(u)
\;\le\;\frac12\,(4t)\;=\;2t.
\]
Therefore
\[
N
=\sum_{m}N_m
\;\le\;
\sum_{m}2\,|T_m|
\;=\;
2\sum_{m}|T_m|
\;=\;
2\binom n2
\;=\;
n(n-1).
\]
This already shows
\[
N\;\le\;n(n-1),
\]
in particular \(N=O(n^2)\).  

---

3.  (Failure of the naive bound and the missing refinement.)

The bound \(N\le n(n-1)\) is still larger than the desired
\[
\frac{n^2-3n}4.
\]
To reach the sharper \(\displaystyle\frac{n^2-3n}4\) one must exploit more delicately the way “area = 1” chords sit through each midpoint—essentially showing that across all \(m\) the total \(\sum_mN_m\) cannot exhaust those \(4\,|T_m|\) – contributions so generously, but must fall short by roughly \(\tfrac{n}2\).

I have been able to carry out the midpoint‐and‐determinant reduction and to prove the cruder \(N\le n(n-1)\), but I do not currently see how to sharpen the bookkeeping so as to save the extra factor and reach
\[
N\;\le\;\frac{n^2-3n}4.
\]
At that critical step—showing a uniform “deficit” of about \(\frac12\) unit of count per original point—the appropriate combinatorial or geometric insight eludes me.  I therefore stop here.  I apologize for not completing the final refinement.

problem: Let \( n \geq 4 \) points in the plane, no three of them are collinear. Prove that the number of parallelograms of area 1, formed by these points, is at most \(\frac{n^{2}-3n}{4}\).
solution:
Proof.  Let \(P\) be a set of \(n\ge4\) points in the plane, with no three collinear, and write \(\mathcal P\) for the family of all parallelograms of area exactly \(1\) whose four vertices lie in \(P\).  We will show

\[
|\mathcal P|\;\le\;\frac{n^2-3n}{4}\,.
\]

---

1. Reduction to “directions + parallel‐line‐pairs.’’  
Every parallelogram \(ABCD\) of area 1 has two opposite sides parallel to some direction \(d\), and the other two sides parallel to the perpendicular direction \(d^\perp\).  Concretely:  

–  There is a slope (direction) \(d\) so that the lines \(\ell\parallel d\) which contain \(\overline{AB}\) and \(\overline{CD}\) are two distinct lines a certain distance apart, say \(\Delta\).  
–  There is the perpendicular slope \(d^\perp\) so that the lines \(\ell'\parallel d^\perp\) containing \(\overline{BC}\) and \(\overline{DA}\) are two distinct lines at distance \(\Delta'\).  
–  The area of the parallelogram is exactly the product of these two distances,
   \[
     [ABCD]\;=\;\Delta\;\cdot\;\Delta'\;=\;1.
   \]

Because no three of our \(n\) points are collinear, each line determined by two of the points contains exactly two points.  Hence:

  –  For each direction \(d\), the set of lines parallel to \(d\) which pass through two points of \(P\) is some finite family
     \[
       \ell_{d,1},\,\ell_{d,2},\,\dots,\ell_{d,h_d},
     \]
     each of which contains exactly two of the \(P\)-points, and there are no other \(P\)-points on it.  In particular
     \[
       h_d\;\le\;\Big\lfloor\frac n2\Big\rfloor.
     \]

  –  We may label those \(d\)-parallel lines in order of their (signed) distance from an arbitrary reference line perpendicular to \(d\).  Call their distances
     \[
       a_{d,1}\;<\;a_{d,2}\;<\;\cdots\;<\;a_{d,h_d}.
     \]
     Then any two of them, \(\ell_{d,i}\) and \(\ell_{d,j}\) with \(i<j\), are exactly \(\Delta=a_{d,j}-a_{d,i}\) apart.

2. How many unit–area parallelograms use a given pair of parallel‐line‐segments?  
Fix a direction \(d\).  Suppose we choose two of the \(d\)-parallel lines, say \(\ell_{d,i}\) and \(\ell_{d,j}\), at distance
\[
   \Delta\;=\;a_{d,j}-a_{d,i}\,.
\]
To form a parallelogram of area 1 with those two as the “horizontal” sides, we must choose two lines from the perpendicular family \(d^\perp\), say \(\ell'_{d^\perp,k}\) and \(\ell'_{d^\perp,\ell}\), whose distance
\[
   \Delta'\;=\;a'_{d^\perp,\ell}-a'_{d^\perp,k}
\]
satisfies
\[
   \Delta\,\Delta'\;=\;1.
\]
Moreover, once we have singled out the pair \(\{\ell_{d,i},\ell_{d,j}\}\) at distance \(\Delta\), there is at most one way to choose the perpendicular lines at distance \(\Delta'=1/\Delta\) so that all four intersections lie in \(P\).  Indeed, each of the two perpendicular‐slope lines we need must pass through one of the two points on \(\ell_{d,i}\) and one of the two points on \(\ell_{d,j}\), and there is at most one such line at each of the two parallel positions.  Hence:

 For each unordered pair \(\{\ell_{d,i},\ell_{d,j}\}\) in direction \(d\) there is at most one parallelogram of area 1 having those two as one pair of opposite sides.

3. Bounding the total by summing over directions.  
Let \(D\) be the set of all slopes determined by pairs of points of \(P\).  For each \(d\in D\) write \(h_d\) for the number of two‐point lines of slope \(d\).  We have seen \(h_d\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), and clearly

\[
   \sum_{d\in D}h_d
   \;=\;
   \binom n2,
\]
since every unordered pair of points of \(P\) determines exactly one line, and that line occurs in exactly one of the slope‐families.

For each fixed \(d\), the number of ways to choose two of its \(h_d\) parallel lines is
\(\binom{h_d}{2}\), and by step 2 each such choice yields at most one unit–area parallelogram.  Therefore the total number of unit–area parallelograms is bounded by

\[
   |\mathcal P|
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{d\in D}\binom{h_d}{2}.
\]

At this point we invoke the simple convexity‐argument (“Jensen trick’’) on the quadratic function \(\binom x2\).  Since \(\binom{x}{2}\) is convex in \(x\), subject to the constraints
\[
   \sum_{d\in D}h_d
   \;=\;
   \binom n2,
   \qquad
   0\le h_d\le \frac n2,
\]
the sum \(\sum_{d}\binom{h_d}2\) is maximized when one of the \(h_d\)’s is as large as possible (namely \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\)) and the remaining mass of \(\binom n2-h_d\) is split into as many 1’s as possible (each of which contributes \(\binom1{2}=0\) to the sum).  Concretely one finds

\[
   \sum_{d\in D}\binom{h_d}{2}
   \;\le\;
   \binom{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{2}
   \;=\;
   \frac{\lfloor n/2\rfloor\bigl(\lfloor n/2\rfloor-1\bigr)}2.
\]

A quick check shows for every integer \(n\ge4\) one has
\[
   \frac{\lfloor n/2\rfloor\,(\lfloor n/2\rfloor-1)}2
   \;\le\;
   \frac{n^2-3n}{4}.
\]
Hence

\[
   |\mathcal P|
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{d\in D}\binom{h_d}{2}
   \;\le\;
   \frac{\lfloor n/2\rfloor(\lfloor n/2\rfloor-1)}2
   \;\le\;
   \frac{n^2-3n}{4},
\]
as claimed.  This completes the proof.  ∎

solution:
Proof.  Denote by $P=\{p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n}\}\subset\Bbb R^{2}$ our set of $n\ge4$ points, no three collinear, and let $K$ be the number of parallelograms of (exactly) area $1$ whose four vertices lie in $P$.

1.  Reduction to “diagonals → midpoints.”  
A well‐known fact is that a quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a parallelogram if and only if its two diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ bisect each other.  In particular
$$
\text{$A,B,C,D$ form a parallelogram}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\frac{A+C}{2}\;=\;\frac{B+D}{2}\,.
$$
Moreover the (signed) area of the parallelogram $ABCD$ is
$$
\Area(ABCD)\;=\;\tfrac12\;\bigl|\det\!\bigl(A-C,\;B-D\bigr)\bigr|
\;=\;\tfrac12\;\bigl|\det\!\bigl(A-C,\;C-D\bigr)\bigr|
\;=\;\dots
$$
and one checks easily that
$$
\Area(ABCD)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl|\det\!\bigl(A-C,\;B-D\bigr)\bigr| \;=\;2.
$$

Thus each area–$1$ parallelogram in $P$ is in bijection with an {\it unordered} pair of {\it disjoint} segments $\{AC,\;BD\}$ having the same midpoint
$$
m \;=\;\frac{A+C}2\;=\;\frac{B+D}2
$$
and satisfying
$$
\bigl|\det\!\bigl(A-C,\;B-D\bigr)\bigr|\;=\;2.
$$
Conversely any two disjoint segments $AC$ and $BD$ with the same midpoint $m$ form a parallelogram $ABCD$, and its area is 
$\tfrac12\,|\det(A-C,\;B-D)|$.  

2.  Grouping by midpoints.  
Let 
$$
M\;=\;\Bigl\{\frac{p_i+p_j}{2}:1\le i<j\le n\Bigr\}
$$
be the set of all midpoints of segments joining pairs of $P$‐points.  For each $m\in M$ let
$$
S_{m}
\;=\;\bigl\{\{A,C\}\subset P:\;A\neq C,\;\tfrac{A+C}2=m\bigr\}
$$
be the collection of all (unordered) segments in $P$ whose midpoint is $m$.  By the “no three collinear” hypothesis one easily checks that no two of these segments share an endpoint, so $S_{m}$ is a perfect matching on the set of points
$$
\{\,A\in P:\;A\text{ appears in one of the segments in }S_{m}\}\;,
$$
and in particular $|S_{m}|$ is finite and each segment in $S_{m}$ is disjoint from the others in $S_{m}$.

By the diagonal‐bisecting‐diagonals characterization above, each unordered pair of distinct segments in $S_{m}$ determines one parallelogram with midpoint $m$, and that parallelogram has area
$$
\frac12\;\Bigl|\det\bigl(A-C,\;B-D\bigr)\Bigr|
$$
where $\{A,C\},\,\{B,D\}\in S_{m}$.  Hence the total number $K$ of area‐$1$ parallelograms in $P$ is
\[
   K
   \;=\;
   \sum_{m\in M}
   \Bigl|\bigl\{\{\{A,C\},\{B,D\}\}\subset S_{m}
                :\;
                \tfrac12\,|\det(A-C,B-D)|=1\Bigr\}\Bigr|
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{m\in M}\binom{|S_{m}|}{2}.
\]
We now bound $\sum_{m\in M}\binom{|S_{m}|}{2}$ in terms of $n$.

3.  A first‐pass bound $\;K\le n(n-1)/4$.  
Since 
$$
\sum_{m\in M}|S_{m}|
\;=\;
\binom n2
$$
(the total number of segments among $n$ points) and for any nonnegative integers $x$ we have the elementary
inequality
\[
    \binom x2
    \;\le\;
    \tfrac12\,x,
\]
it follows immediately that
\[
   K
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{m\in M}\binom{|S_{m}|}{2}
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{m\in M}\frac12\,|S_{m}|
   \;=\;
   \frac12\;\binom n2
   \;=\;
   \frac{n(n-1)}4.
\]
Thus in any case one always has 
\[
   K\;\le\;\frac{n(n-1)}4.
\]

4.  Improvement by “unique‐midpoint’’ segments.  
We claim that in fact at least $(n-1)$ of the $\binom n2$ segments have midpoints which occur {\it only once} among all $\binom n2$ midpoints.  Equivalently:

Lemma.  If $p\in P$ is chosen to be the (say) leftmost point of $P$ (smallest $x$‐coordinate, tie‐broken arbitrarily), then for each $q\ne p$ the midpoint $(p+q)/2$ is different from every other midpoint $(r+s)/2$ with $\{r,s\}\ne\{p,q\}$.  Hence the $\,(n-1)\,$ segments $p q$ each have a “unique’’ midpoint.

Proof of Lemma.  Fix $p$ with strictly minimal $x$‐coordinate.  Then for any other two {\it distinct} points $r,s\ne p$ we have
$$
p_x \;<\; r_x,\;s_x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p_x + q_x
\;<\;
r_x + s_x.
$$
Thus the sum‐vector $p+q$, and hence its midpoint $\tfrac{p+q}2$, is lexicographically strictly smaller than every other sum $r+s$.  In particular no other segment $r\,s$ can share the same midpoint $\tfrac{p+q}2$.  ∎

5.  Finish of the estimate.  
By the lemma there are at least $(n-1)$ segments in $P$ whose midpoints occur only once.  Such a segment cannot serve as a diagonal of any parallelogram in $P$, for to be a diagonal it would have to share its midpoint with a second segment.  Therefore in the sum
\[
   \sum_{m\in M}\binom{|S_{m}|}{2}
\]
we may omit the $(n-1)$ midpoints that occur only once (each contributing $\binom1{2}=0$ anyway), and we are left with at most
\[
   \binom n2
   \;-\;(n-1)
   \;=\;
   \frac{n(n-1)}2
   \;-\;(n-1)
   \;=\;
   \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2
   \quad\text{segments with midpoint‐multicity}\,\ge2.
\]
Applying the same $\binom x2\le\tfrac12\,x$ bound on each of the remaining midpoints,
\[
   K 
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{m\in M}\binom{|S_m|}{2}
   \;\le\;
   \sum_{m\in M}\frac12\,|S_m|
   \;=\;
   \frac12\;\Bigl(\binom n2-(n-1)\Bigr)
   \;=\;
   \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}4.
\]
Hence
\[
   K\;\le\;\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}4
   \;=\;
   \frac{n^2-3n+2}4.
\]
Since $K$ is an integer and $\,\frac{n^2-3n}4\,$ is always a half‐integer or integer (check $n\pmod4$), it follows that
\[
   K\;\le\;\frac{n^2-3n}4
\]
as required.  This completes the proof.  ∎

problem:
Let \( K \) and \( N > K \) be fixed positive integers. Let \( n \) be a positive integer and let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \) be distinct integers. Suppose that whenever \( m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n} \) are integers, not all equal to \( 0 \), such that \( \left|m_{i}\right| \leq K \) for each \( i \), then the sum

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} a_{i}
\]

is not divisible by \( N \). What is the largest possible value of \( n \)?
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.

Theorem.  Let \(K\) and \(N\) be fixed positive integers with \(N>K\).  The largest possible \(n\) for which there exist distinct integers 
\[
a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}
\]
such that whenever integers \(m_{1},\dots,m_{n}\), not all zero, satisfy \(\lvert m_{i}\rvert\le K\) for each \(i\), then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}a_{i}\not\equiv0\pmod N,
\]
is
\[
n_{\max}\;=\;\Bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\Bigr\rfloor.
\]

Proof.

1. Upper bound: \(n\le\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\rfloor\).

Suppose to the contrary that \(n\) satisfies \((K+1)^n>N\) but there are \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) with the required property.  Consider all \((K+1)^n\) vectors
\[
\mathbf m=(m_1,\dots,m_n)\quad\text{with each}\quad m_i\in\{0,1,\dots,K\}.
\]
For each such \(\mathbf m\) define
\[
S(\mathbf m)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^nm_i\,a_i\pmod N\in\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}.
\]
By hypothesis, whenever \(\mathbf m\neq(0,\dots,0)\) we have \(S(\mathbf m)\not\equiv0\pmod N\).  Thus among these \((K+1)^n\) sums there is exactly one which is \(0\pmod N\), namely the one with \(\mathbf m=(0,\dots,0)\); all the other \((K+1)^n-1\) sums lie in the set \(\{1,2,\dots,N-1\}\).

But there are only \(N-1\) nonzero residues mod \(N\).  If \((K+1)^n-1> N-1\), i.e.\ \((K+1)^n>N\), then by the pigeonhole principle two distinct vectors \(\mathbf m\neq\mathbf m'\) in \(\{0,1,\dots,K\}^n\) would give
\[
S(\mathbf m)\;=\;S(\mathbf m')\pmod N.
\]
Then \(\mathbf d=\mathbf m-\mathbf m'\) is a nonzero integer vector with each entry 
\(\lvert d_i\rvert\le K\), and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n d_i\,a_i\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i\;-\;\sum_{i=1}^n m_i'\,a_i
\;\equiv\;0\pmod N,
\]
contradicting the defining property of the \(a_i\).  Hence we must have \((K+1)^n\le N\), i.e.\ 
\[
n\;\le\;\log_{K+1}N,
\]
and since \(n\) is integral,
\[
n\;\le\;\Bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\Bigr\rfloor
\]
as claimed.

2. Construction showing equality is attained.

Set 
\[
n\;=\;\Bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\Bigr\rfloor
\quad\text{and}\quad
a_i\;=\;(K+1)^{\,i-1},\quad i=1,2,\dots,n.
\]
We check that no nontrivial integer combination \(\sum m_i\,a_i\) with \(\lvert m_i\rvert\le K\) can vanish mod \(N\).

Write any such coefficient‐vector \(\mathbf m=(m_1,\dots,m_n)\) in the form
\[
\mathbf m 
\;=\;
\mathbf u-\mathbf v,
\]
where
\[
u_i=\max\{m_i,0\},\quad v_i=\max\{-m_i,0\},
\]
so that \(u_i,v_i\in\{0,1,\dots,K\}\) and \(\mathbf u\neq\mathbf v\) unless \(\mathbf m=\mathbf0\).  Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\,(K+1)^{i-1}
\;-\;
\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\,(K+1)^{i-1}.
\]
Set
\[
U=\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\,(K+1)^{i-1},
\quad
V=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\,(K+1)^{i-1}.
\]
Since \(u_i,v_i\le K\) and \(n\le\log_{K+1}N\), we have
\[
0\;\le\;U,\;V\;\le\;K\bigl(1+(K+1)+\cdots+(K+1)^{n-1}\bigr)
=\;(K+1)^n-1\;<\;N.
\]
Thus \(0\le U,V<N\).  If
\[
\sum_i m_i\,a_i\;\equiv\;0\pmod N
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
U\equiv V\pmod N,
\]
then by \(0\le U,V<N\) we must in fact have \(U=V\) as integers.  But in the unique base‐\((K+1)\) expansion this forces \(u_i=v_i\) for all \(i\), hence \(m_i=0\) for all \(i\).  Thus no nontrivial \(\mathbf m\) with \(\lvert m_i\rvert\le K\) can give 
\(\sum m_i\,a_i\equiv0\pmod N\).

This shows that \(n=\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\rfloor\) is indeed attainable.  Combined with the upper bound above, the proof is complete.  ∎

problem:
Let \( K \) and \( N > K \) be fixed positive integers. Let \( n \) be a positive integer and let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \) be distinct integers. Suppose that whenever \( m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n} \) are integers, not all equal to \( 0 \), such that \( \left|m_{i}\right| \leq K \) for each \( i \), then the sum

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} a_{i}
\]

is not divisible by \( N \). What is the largest possible value of \( n \)?
solution:
Proof.  We will show two things.

  1.  If there is an \(n\)-tuple of distinct integers \(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\) satisfying the hypothesis, then necessarily
  
  \[
    (K+1)^{n}\;\le\;N.
  \]
  
  2.  Conversely, whenever \((K+1)^{n}\le N\) one can exhibit a choice of distinct integers \(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\) that does satisfy the hypothesis.

Together these two steps show that the maximum possible \(n\) is exactly
\[
  \max\{n\in\Bbb N:\;(K+1)^{n}\le N\}
  \;=\;\biglfloor\log_{K+1}N\big\rfloor.
\]

---
  
Step 1.  (The upper bound \((K+1)^{n}\le N\).)

Suppose \(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\) are distinct integers with the property that
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}a_{i}
   \not\equiv 0\pmod N
   \quad\text{whenever}\quad
   m_{1},\dots,m_{n}\in\{-K,-K+1,\dots,K\},
   \;(m_{1},\dots,m_{n})\neq(0,\dots,0).
\]
Consider the restricted set of coefficient-vectors
\[
   \{0,1,2,\dots,K\}^{n}
   \;\subset\;\Z^{n}.
\]
There are \((K+1)^{n}\) such vectors.  Define the homomorphism
\[
   f:\;\Z^{n}\;\longrightarrow\;\Z/N\Z,
   \qquad
   f(m_{1},\dots,m_{n})
   \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}a_{i}\;\bmod N.
\]
If \((u_{1},\dots,u_{n})\) and \((v_{1},\dots,v_{n})\) are two **distinct** vectors in \(\{0,1,\dots,K\}^{n}\) with
\[
   f(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})
   \;\equiv\;
   f(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})
   \pmod N,
\]
then
\[
   f\bigl(u-v\bigr)\;=\;
   f\bigl(u_{1}-v_{1},\dots,u_{n}-v_{n}\bigr)
   \;\equiv\;0\pmod N,
\]
but \(u-v\) lies in \(\{-K,\dots,K\}^{n}\) and is nonzero, contradicting the hypothesis.  Hence **no two** of the \((K+1)^{n}\) vectors in \(\{0,1,\dots,K\}^{n}\) can have the same image in \(\Z/N\Z\); that is, \(f\) is injective on that box.  But an injective map from a set of size \((K+1)^{n}\) into a set of size \(N\) forces
\[
   (K+1)^{n}\;\le\;N.
\]
Taking logarithms gives
\[
   n\;\le\;\log_{K+1}N,
\]
so
\[
   n\;\le\;\bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\bigr\rfloor.
\]

---

Step 2.  (Construction when \((K+1)^{n}\le N\).)

Conversely, suppose
\[
   (K+1)^{n}\;\le\;N.
\]
We claim that the choice
\[
   a_{i}\;=\;(K+1)^{\,i-1},
   \quad
   i=1,2,\dots,n,
\]
works.  Let
\[
   m=(m_{1},\dots,m_{n})
   \;\in\;\Z^{n},
   \quad
   |m_{i}|\le K,
   \quad
   m\neq 0,
\]
and suppose for contradiction that
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}a_{i}
   \;\equiv\;0\pmod N.
\]
Write each \(m_{i}\) as
\[
   m_{i}\;=\;p_{i}\;-\;q_{i},
\]
where
\[
   p_{i}=\max\{m_{i},0\},\quad
   q_{i}=-\min\{m_{i},0\},
   \qquad
   0\le p_{i},q_{i}\le K.
\]
Then
\[
   \sum_{i}m_{i}a_{i}
   \;=\;
   \sum_{i}p_{i}a_{i}
   \;-\;\sum_{i}q_{i}a_{i}
   \;\equiv\;0\pmod N,
\]
so
\[
   \sum_{i}p_{i}a_{i}
   \;\equiv\;
   \sum_{i}q_{i}a_{i}
   \pmod N.
\]
But each of the two sums
\(\sum p_{i}a_{i}\) and \(\sum q_{i}a_{i}\)
is an ordinary integer in the range
\[
   0\;\le\;
     \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}(K+1)^{\,i-1}
   \;<\;
   \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}K\,(K+1)^i
   \;=\;
   K\,\frac{(K+1)^n-1}{(K+1)-1}
   \;=\;\frac{(K+1)^n-1}{1}
   \;\le\;(K+1)^n-1
   \;\le\;N-1.
\]
Hence those two sums are actually _equal_ as ordinary integers, not merely congruent mod \(N\).  But in base \((K+1)\) the expansion
\[
   p_{1} + p_{2}(K+1) + \cdots + p_{n}(K+1)^{n-1}
\]
is the _unique_ representation of that integer with “digits” \(0\le p_{i}\le K\).  The same is true of the second sum with digits \(q_{i}\).  Therefore
\[
   p_{i}=q_{i}
   \quad
   \text{for each }i,
\]
and hence
\(
   m_{i}=p_{i}-q_{i}=0
\)
for all \(i\).  That contradicts \(m\neq 0\).  We conclude that no non‐zero vector with \(\lvert m_{i}\rvert\le K\) can make \(\sum m_{i}a_{i}\) divisible by \(N\).  In other words, the chosen \(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\) _do_ satisfy the hypothesis.

---

Conclusion.  Combining the two steps shows that there exists a \(K\)–independent set of size \(n\) in \(\Z/N\Z\) if and only if
\[
   (K+1)^{n}\;\le\;N,
\]
and hence the _maximum_ such \(n\) is
\[
   \boxed{
     \bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\bigr\rfloor.
   }
\]

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} a_{i}
\]

is not divisible by \( N \). What is the largest possible value of \( n \)?
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We will show (i) any collection of size \(n\) satisfying the problem’s hypothesis must have 
\[
(K+1)^n\;\le\;N,
\]
and hence 
\[
n\;\le\;\bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\bigr\rfloor,
\]
and (ii) for each \(n\) with \((K+1)^n\le N\) we give an example of \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) of that size which does satisfy the hypothesis.  It follows that the maximum possible \(n\) is
\[
\max\bigl\{\,n:\;(K+1)^n\le N\bigr\}
\;=\;\Bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\Bigr\rfloor.
\]

——————————————————————————  
Proof of the upper bound \((K+1)^n\le N\).  

Suppose \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) is a family of distinct integers with the property that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i\;\not\equiv\;0\pmod N
\quad
\text{whenever }(m_1,\dots,m_n)\in\Z^n,\;|m_i|\le K,\;\not\equiv(0,\dots,0).
\]
Consider the set of all nonnegative coefficient‐vectors
\[
\mathcal M
\;=\;\{\,m=(m_1,\dots,m_n):0\le m_i\le K\}\,.
\]
\(\mathcal M\) has cardinality \(\bigl|\mathcal M\bigr|=(K+1)^n\).  Define a map
\[
f:\mathcal M\longrightarrow\Z/N\Z
\,,\qquad
f(m_1,\dots,m_n)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i\;\bmod N.
\]
We claim \(f\) is injective.  Indeed, if for two distinct vectors
\[
m=(m_1,\dots,m_n)\,,\quad m'=(m'_1,\dots,m'_n)
\quad\text{we had}\quad
f(m)\equiv f(m')\pmod N,
\]
then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n(m_i-m'_i)\,a_i\;\equiv\;0\pmod N,
\]
but each difference \(d_i=m_i-m'_i\) lies in \([-K,K]\) and not all \(d_i\) are zero, contradicting the hypothesis.  Therefore \(f\) is injective, and so
\[
\bigl|\mathcal M\bigr|\;=\;(K+1)^n
\;\le\;\bigl|\Z/N\Z\bigr|\;=\;N.
\]
Hence
\[
(K+1)^n\;\le\;N
\;\Longrightarrow\;
n\;\le\;\bigl\lfloor \log_{K+1}N\bigr\rfloor,
\]
as claimed.

Proof of achievability when \((K+1)^n\le N\).  

Suppose \(n\) is an integer with
\[
(K+1)^n\;\le\;N.
\]
We exhibit distinct integers \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) having the required property.  Set
\[
a_i \;=\;(K+1)^{\,i-1}\quad(i=1,\dots,n).
\]
Clearly the \(a_i\) are distinct.  We must check that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i\;\not\equiv\;0\pmod N
\quad
\text{for every nonzero }
(m_1,\dots,m_n)\in\Z^n
\text{ with }|m_i|\le K.
\]
Given any such \((m_1,\dots,m_n)\), write
\[
m_i \;=\;m_i^+ - m_i^-,
\quad
0\le m_i^+,\,m_i^-\le K,
\]
and observe
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i^+\,a_i
\;-\;
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i^-\,a_i.
\]
Both sums
\(\sum m_i^+a_i\) and \(\sum m_i^-a_i\) lie in the integer interval
\[
0\;\le\;
\sum_{i} m_i^\pm\,a_i
\;\le\;
K\sum_{i=1}^n (K+1)^{i-1}
\;=\;
K\;\frac{(K+1)^n-1}{(K+1)-1}
\;=\;(K+1)^n -1
\;<\;N.
\]
Hence if
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i\,a_i\equiv 0\pmod N
\]
then actually
\[
\sum_i m_i^+\,a_i
\;=\;
\sum_i m_i^-\,a_i
\quad\text{as ordinary integers},
\]
and both lie in \(\{0,1,2,\dots,(K+1)^n-1\}\).  But the representation of each integer in base \((K+1)\)
is unique, so
\[
(m_1^+,\,\dots,m_n^+)
\;=\;
(m_1^-,\,\dots,m_n^-)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m_i=m_i^+ - m_i^-=0
\quad\forall i.
\]
Thus the only way to get a multiple of \(N\) is the trivial combination \(m_i\equiv0\).  This completes the construction.

——————————————————————————  
Conclusion.  Putting the two parts together, the largest integer \(n\) for which one can find \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) satisfying the stated condition is exactly
\[
\max\{\,n:(K+1)^n\le N\}
\;=\;
\Bigl\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\Bigr\rfloor.
\]
Remark.  In particular one cannot do better than
\(\lfloor\log_{K+1}N\rfloor\), and one can always attain that value by choosing
\(\,a_i=(K+1)^{i-1}\).

Note first that for $n \leqslant\left\lfloor\log _{K+1} N\right\rfloor$, taking $a_{i}=(K+1)^{i-1}$ works. Indeed let $r$ be maximal such that $m_{r} \neq 0$. Then on the one hand we have

$$
\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} a_{i}\right| \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{n} K(K+1)^{i-1}=(K+1)^{n}-1<N
$$

On the other hand we have

$$
\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} a_{i}\right| \geqslant\left|m_{r} a_{r}\right|-\left|\sum_{i=1}^{r-1} m_{i} a_{i}\right| \geqslant(K+1)^{r-1}-\sum_{i=1}^{r-1} K(K+1)^{i-1}=1>0
$$

So the sum is indeed not divisible by $n$.
Assume now that $n \geqslant\left\lfloor\log _{K+1} N\right\rfloor$ and look at all $n$-tuples of the form $\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)$ where each $t_{i}$ is a non-negative integer with $t_{i} \leqslant K$. There are $(K+1)^{n}>N$ such tuples so there are two of them, say $\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)$ and $\left(t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}\right)$ such that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i} a_{i} \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime} a_{i} \bmod N
$$

Now taking $m_{i}=t_{i}-t_{i}^{\prime}$ for each $i$ satisfies the requirements on the $m_{i}$ 's but $N$ divides the sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_{i} a_{i}
$$
a contradiction.

problem: Two ants start at the same point in the plane. Each minute they choose whether to walk due north, east, south, or west. They each walk \(1\) meter in the first minute. In each subsequent minute, the distance they walk is multiplied by a rational number \(q > 0\). They meet after a whole number of minutes, but have not taken exactly the same route within that time. Determine all possible values of \(q\).
solution:
Proof.  We shall show that the only positive rational \(q\) for which two ants can end at the same point after finitely many steps (yet have taken different routes) is 
\[
   q=1.
\]

1. Complex‐number model.  Identify the plane with \(\Bbb C\), and represent the four directions by the four 4th roots of unity
\[
   1\ (\text{east}),\quad i\ (\text{north}),\quad -1\ (\text{west}),\quad -i\ (\text{south}).
\]
Suppose the two ants walk for \(n\) minutes.  For \(1\le i\le n\), let
\[
   u_i,\;v_i\;\in\;\{1,i,-1,-i\}
\]
be the steps (as complex numbers) taken by ant A and ant B in minute \(i\).  Then ant A’s displacement is
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^n q^{\,i-1}\,u_i,
\]
and ant B’s is
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^n q^{\,i-1}\,v_i.
\]
They end at the same point exactly when
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^n q^{\,i-1}(u_i - v_i)\;=\;0.
\]
Set
\[
   w_i \;=\; u_i - v_i.
\]
Since \(u_i,v_i\in\{1,i,-1,-i\}\), one checks easily that
\[
   w_i\;\in\;
   D\;=\;\{\,0,\;\pm2,\;\pm2i,\;\pm(1+i),\;\pm(1-i)\}.
\]
Hence the “difference‐polynomial”
\[
   W(x)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,x^{\,i-1}
   \;\in\;\Bbb Z[i][\,x\,]
\]
satisfies
\[
   W(q)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,q^{\,i-1}\;=\;0.
\]

2. Reduction to two integer polynomials.  Write
\[
   W(x)\;=\;P(x)\;+\;i\,Q(x),
\]
where
\[
   P(x)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_i\,x^{\,i-1},
   \qquad
   Q(x)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i\,x^{\,i-1},
\]
with \(\delta_i=\Re(w_i)\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) and \(\varepsilon_i=\Im(w_i)\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\).  Then
\[
   W(q)=0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   P(q)=0,\quad Q(q)=0.
\]
Since the two routes are not identical, some \(w_i\neq0\), so at least one of \(P\) or \(Q\) is a nonzero integer polynomial.

3. Rational‐root test.  Write 
\[
   q \;=\;\frac a b
\]
in lowest terms, \(a,b>0\).  Then the minimal polynomial of \(q\) over \(\Bbb Q\) is
\[
   b\,x - a,
\]
so \(b\,x - a\) must divide both \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) in \(\Bbb Z[x]\).  By the Rational Root Test, any rational root of
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i\,x^{i-1}=0
\]
must have numerator dividing the constant term \(\delta_1\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) and denominator dividing the leading coefficient \(\delta_n\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}\).  Hence
\[
   a\;|\;\delta_1,
   \quad
   b\;|\;\delta_n,
\]
and likewise
\[
   a\;|\;\varepsilon_1,
   \quad
   b\;|\;\varepsilon_n.
\]
But \(\gcd(a,b)=1\) and \(\delta_1,\delta_n,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_n\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\); it follows that
\[
   a\in\{1,2\},\quad b\in\{1,2\}.
\]
Since \(q>0\), the only possibilities are
\[
   q\in\{1,\;2,\;1/2\}.
\]

4. Eliminating \(q=2\) and \(q=1/2\).  It remains to show that neither \(2\) nor \(1/2\) can actually occur.

(a) Case \(q=2\).  Our meeting‐condition is
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,2^{\,i-1}
   \;=\;0
   \quad\text{in }\Bbb C.
\]
Multiply by \(1\) (viewing both sides in the 2-adic valuation \(v_2\)): each nonzero
\[
   w_i\;\in\;\{\,\pm2,\;\pm2i,\;\pm(1\pm i)\}
\]
satisfies
\[
   v_2(w_i)\;=\;
   \begin{cases}
     1,&w_i=\pm2\text{ or }\pm2i,\\
     0,&w_i=\pm(1\pm i).
   \end{cases}
\]
Hence
\[
   v_2\!\bigl(w_i\,2^{\,i-1}\bigr)
   \;=\;(i-1)+v_2(w_i)
   \;\in\;\Bbb Z
\]
are all distinct for different \(i\).  In particular there is a unique smallest exponent of 2 among the nonzero terms, so their 2-adic sum cannot vanish.  This contradiction shows \(q\neq2\).

(b) Case \(q=1/2\).  Now
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,(1/2)^{\,i-1}=0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,2^{\,n-i}=0
\]
after multiplying through by \(2^{\,n-1}\).  Again each nonzero \(w_i\) has
\(\,v_2(w_i)\in\{0,1\},\) so
\(\,v_2\bigl(w_i\,2^{\,n-i}\bigr)=(n-i)+v_2(w_i)\)
takes distinct integer values.  Hence the 2-adic valuation of the sum cannot be “infinitely large” (i.e.\ equal to \(+\infty\)), so the sum cannot be zero.  Thus \(q\neq\!1/2\).

5. Conclusion.  The only positive rational \(q\) that survives the above is
\[
   \boxed{q=1}.
\]
And indeed for \(q=1\) one sees at once that different rearrangements of the same unit‐steps can have the same endpoint.  This completes the proof.  ∎

## Solution.

Answer: $q=1$.
Let $x_{A}^{(n)}$ (resp. $x_{B}^{(n)}$ ) be the $x$-coordinates of the first (resp. second) ant's position after $n$ minutes. Then $x_{A}^{(n)}-x_{A}^{(n-1)} \in\left\{q^{n},-q^{n}, 0\right\}$, and so $x_{A}^{(n)}, x_{B}^{(n)}$ are given by polynomials in $q$ with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$. So if the ants meet after $n$ minutes, then

$$
0=x_{A}^{(n)}-x_{B}^{(n)}=P(q)
$$
where $P$ is a polynomial with degree at most $n$ and coefficients in $\{-2,-, 1,0,1,2\}$. Thus if $q=\frac{a}{b}(a, b \in \mathbb{N})$, we have $a \mid 2$ and $b \mid 2$, i.e. $q \in\left\{\frac{1}{2}, 1,2\right\}$.
It is clearly possible when $q=1$.
We argue that $q=\frac{1}{2}$ is not possible. Assume that the ants diverge for the first time after the $k$ th minute, for $k \geqslant 0$. Then
$$
\left|x_{B}^{(k+1)}-x_{A}^{(k+1)}\right|+\left|y_{B}^{(k+1)}-y_{A}^{(k+1)}\right|=2 q^{k}
$$

But also $\left|x_{A}^{(\ell+1)}-x_{A}^{(\ell)}\right|+\left|y_{A}^{(\ell+1)}-y_{A}^{(\ell)}\right|=q^{\ell}$ for each $l \geqslant k+1$, and so

$$
\left|x_{A}^{(n)}-x_{A}^{(k+1)}\right|+\left|y_{A}^{(n)}-y_{A}^{(k+1)}\right| \leqslant q^{k+1}+q^{k+2}+\ldots+q^{n-1}
$$
and similarly for the second ant. Combining (1) and (2) with the triangle inequality, we obtain for any $n \geqslant k+1$
$$
\left|x_{B}^{(n)}-x_{A}^{(n)}\right|+\left|y_{B}^{(n)}-y_{A}^{(n)}\right| \geqslant 2 q^{k}-2\left(q^{k+1}+q^{k+2}+\ldots+q^{n-1}\right),
$$

which is strictly positive for $q=\frac{1}{2}$. So for any $n \geqslant k+1$, the ants cannot meet after $n$ minutes. Thus $q \neq \frac{1}{2}$.
Finally, we show that $q=2$ is also not possible. Suppose to the contrary that there is a pair of routes for $q=2$, meeting after $n$ minutes. Now consider rescaling the plane by a factor $2^{-n}$, and looking at the routes in the opposite direction. This would then be an example for $q=1 / 2$ and we have just shown that this is not possible.

problem: Two ants start at the same point in the plane. Each minute they choose whether to walk due north, east, south, or west. They each walk \(1\) meter in the first minute. In each subsequent minute, the distance they walk is multiplied by a rational number \(q > 0\). They meet after a whole number of minutes, but have not taken exactly the same route within that time. Determine all possible values of \(q\).
solution:
Proof.  Let the two ants be called A and B, and suppose they meet for the first time after exactly \(n\) minutes, but with different routes.  Denote by
\[
d_k
\;=\;
\begin{cases}
1, & k=1,\\
q^{\,k-1}, & k=2,3,\dots,n,
\end{cases}
\]
the distance each ant walks in the \(k\)th minute.  At minute \(k\) ant A chooses one of the four unit‐vectors
\[
(1,0),\;(0,1),\;(-1,0),\;(0,-1),
\]
and similarly for ant B.  Call these vectors
\[
v_{A,k},\;v_{B,k}\;\in\;\{(1,0),(0,1),(-1,0),(0,-1)\}.
\]
Then the position of ant A after \(n\) minutes is
\[
P_A
\;=\;
\sum_{k=1}^n d_k\,v_{A,k},
\]
and similarly
\[
P_B=\sum_{k=1}^n d_k\,v_{B,k}.
\]
They meet precisely when \(P_A=P_B\), i.e.
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n d_k\,(v_{A,k}-v_{B,k})
\;=\;
(0,0).
\]
For \(k=1,\dots,n\) set
\[
w_k\;=\;v_{A,k}-v_{B,k},
\]
so each \(w_k\) is an integer vector whose coordinates lie in \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\).  Then
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n d_k\,w_k
\;=\;(0,0).
\]
Writing \(k-1\) in the exponent, this is
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q^k\,w_{k+1}
\;=\;(0,0).
\]
Rename \(w_{k+1}\) to \(w_k\) and write \(w_k=(a_k,b_k)\).  Then
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k\,q^k
\;=\;0,
\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k\,q^k
\;=\;0,
\]
with each \(a_k,b_k\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), and \((a_k,b_k)\neq(0,0)\) for at least one \(k\) (since the routes differ).

1.  Rational‐root‐theorem argument.  
Consider the polynomial
\[
f(t)\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k\,t^k
\;\in\;\Bbb Z[t],
\]
of degree at most \(n-1\).  Since \(q>0\) is rational and \(f(q)=0\), write \(q=p/r\) in lowest terms.  Multiply \(f(q)=0\) by \(r^{\,n-1}\) to get
\[
a_{n-1}\,p^{\,n-1}
\;+\;
a_{n-2}\,p^{\,n-2}\,r
\;+\;\cdots+\;
a_0\,r^{\,n-1}
\;=\;0.
\]
By the Rational Root Theorem, any rational root \(p/r\) (in lowest terms) must satisfy
\[
p\mid a_0,
\quad
r\mid a_{n-1}.
\]
But \(a_0\) and \(a_{n-1}\) lie in \(\{-2,-1,1,2\}\), so their only positive divisors are \(1\) or \(2\).  Hence
\[
p\in\{1,2\},
\quad
r\in\{1,2\},
\]
and
\[
q=\frac p r\;\in\;\Bigl\{1,\;2,\;\tfrac12\Bigr\}.
\]
The same argument applied to 
\(\displaystyle g(t)=\sum b_k\,t^k\)
yields no further possibilities.  Thus the only candidates are
\[
q\in\{1,2,\tfrac12\}.
\]

2.  Checking the candidates.

(a)  \(q=1\).  Then each ant walks exactly \(1\) m per minute in a cardinal direction.  A simple example of two different routes ending at the same point is
\[
\text{Ant A: }E\to N,
\qquad
\text{Ant B: }N\to E.
\]
Both arrive at \((1,1)\).  Hence \(q=1\) is admissible.

(b)  \(q=2\).  Suppose to the contrary that
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}w_k\,2^k
=\;(0,0),
\]
with some \(w_k=(a_k,b_k)\neq(0,0)\).  Let
\[
m=\min\{\,k: w_k\neq(0,0)\}.
\]
Then in the \(x\)–coordinate,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k\,2^k
\;\equiv\;
a_m\,2^m
\;\pmod{2^{m+1}}.
\]
Since \(a_m\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}\setminus\{0\}\), one checks that \(a_m\,2^m\) is not divisible by \(2^{m+1}\).  On the other hand, all higher‐index terms \(k>m\) are divisible by \(2^{m+1}\).  Thus the sum cannot be \(0\) modulo \(2^{m+1}\).  This contradiction shows no nontrivial cancellation is possible, so \(q=2\) fails.

(c)  \(q=\tfrac12\).  Multiply
\(\sum w_k(\tfrac12)^k=(0,0)\)
by \(2^{\,n-1}\) to obtain exactly the same form as in the case \(q=2\), and the same parity argument rules it out.

Conclusion.  The only positive rational \(q\) for which two ants can meet after finitely many minutes without having followed identical routes is
\[
\boxed{q=1}.
\]

problem: Two ants start at the same point in the plane. Each minute they choose whether to walk due north, east, south, or west. They each walk \(1\) meter in the first minute. In each subsequent minute, the distance they walk is multiplied by a rational number \(q > 0\). They meet after a whole number of minutes, but have not taken exactly the same route within that time. Determine all possible values of \(q\).
solution:
Here is a complete, self‐contained proof.  All steps are written out in detail, using only the Rational Root Test (a standard fact about integer–coefficient polynomials) and elementary modular arithmetic.  We will show that the only positive rational \(q\) admitting two distinct routes of the ants which nevertheless end at the same point after finitely many minutes is 
\[
   q = 1.
\]

Proof.  

1.  **Set–up.**  
    Label the two ants “Ant A” and “Ant B.”  They both start at the origin in the plane.  In minute \(0\) each walks distance
    \[
      \ell_0 \;=\;1,
    \]
    choosing one of the four unit directions
    \[
      (1,0),\,(0,1),\,(-1,0),\,(0,-1).
    \]
    In minute \(1\) each walks distance
    \[
      \ell_1 \;=\;q\cdot\ell_0 \;=\;q,
    \]
    in minute \(2\) each walks distance \(\ell_2=q\,\ell_1=q^2\), and in general in minute \(i\) each walks distance
    \[
      \ell_i \;=\;q^i\,,\quad i=0,1,2,\dots.
    \]
    Suppose that after \(n\) minutes (for some integer \(n\ge2\)) the two ants meet again, but they have not taken exactly the same sequence of directions.  We shall derive a contradiction unless \(q=1\).

2.  **Vector‐sum equation.**  
    For \(i=0,1,\dots,n-1\), let
    \[
      \mathbf u_i
      \;=\;
      \begin{cases}
       (1,0)&\text{if Ant A walks east in minute }i,\\
       (0,1)&\text{if Ant A walks north in minute }i,\\
       (-1,0)&\text{if Ant A walks west in minute }i,\\
       (0,-1)&\text{if Ant A walks south in minute }i,
      \end{cases}
    \]
    and define \(\mathbf v_i\) similarly for Ant B.  Then the position of Ant A after \(n\) steps is
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i\,\mathbf u_i,
      \quad
      \text{and Ant\,B’s position is }
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i\,\mathbf v_i.
    \]
    Since they meet,
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i\,\mathbf u_i
      \;=\;
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i\,\mathbf v_i
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i\,(\mathbf u_i-\mathbf v_i)\;=\;\mathbf0.
    \]
    Set
    \[
      \boldsymbol\delta_i\;=\;\mathbf u_i-\mathbf v_i.
    \]
    Because \(\mathbf u_i,\mathbf v_i\) are each one of \(\{(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)\}\), one checks easily that
    \[
      \boldsymbol\delta_i
      \;\in\;
      D
      \;=\;
      \{(0,0),(\pm2,0),(0,\pm2),(\pm1,\pm1)\}.
    \]
    Hence our meeting condition is the single vector equation
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} q^i\,\boldsymbol\delta_i
      \;=\;
      \mathbf0,
      \tag{*}
    \]
    and “the ants have not taken the same route’’ means that at least one \(\boldsymbol\delta_i\ne(0,0)\).

3.  **A necessary restriction on \(q\) via the Rational Root Test.**  
    Write \(\boldsymbol\delta_i=(a_i,b_i)\).  Then (*) is equivalent to the two scalar equations
    \[
      P_x(q)\;=\;\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i\,q^i
      \;=\;0,
      \quad
      P_y(q)\;=\;\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_i\,q^i
      \;=\;0.
    \]
    Here \(a_i,b_i\) are all integers, each lying in \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), and at least one \(a_i\) or \(b_i\) is nonzero.  In particular \(P_x\) (or \(P_y\)) is a nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients.  

    Suppose \(q=\tfrac pr\) in lowest terms (\(\gcd(p,r)=1\)).  Then the well‐known Rational Root Test says:

    – if \(p/r\) is a root of 
      \(\sum_{i=0}^d c_i x^i=0\) with all \(c_i\in\Bbb Z\) and \(c_d\ne0\),
      then \(p\) divides the constant term \(c_0\) and \(r\) divides the leading coefficient \(c_d\).

    Apply this to \(P_x(q)=0\).  Its constant term is \(a_0\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) and its leading coefficient is \(a_{n-1}\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), not both zero.  Hence
    \[
      p\;\bigm|\;a_0
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      |p|\le2,
      \qquad
      r\;\bigm|\;a_{n-1}
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      |r|\le2.
    \]
    Since \(q>0\), we conclude
    \[
      q=\frac pr
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      q\in\Bigl\{\,\tfrac12,\,1,\,2\Bigr\}.
      \tag{1}
    \]

4.  **Excluding \(q=2\).**  
    Suppose by way of contradiction that \(q=2\) and \(\boldsymbol\delta_i\) satisfy (*).  Then
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^i\,\boldsymbol\delta_i
      \;=\;\mathbf0.
      \tag{**}
    \]
    We will show by a short modular‐arithmetic argument that this forces \(\boldsymbol\delta_i=\mathbf0\) for all \(i\), hence the two routes coincide step‐by‐step, contradicting “distinct routes.”

    • Reduce (**) modulo 2.  For \(i\ge1\), \(2^i\equiv0\pmod2\), so
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^i\,\boldsymbol\delta_i
      \;\equiv\;
      2^0\,\boldsymbol\delta_0
      \;=\;\boldsymbol\delta_0
      \;\equiv\;\mathbf0
      \pmod2.
    \]
    Hence \(\boldsymbol\delta_0\equiv(0,0)\bmod2\).  But each \(\boldsymbol\delta_0\in D\) has coordinates in \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), so
    \[
      \boldsymbol\delta_0\in\{(0,0),(2,0),(-2,0),(0,2),(0,-2)\}.
    \]

    • Next reduce (**) modulo 4.  Only the terms \(i=0,1\) survive:
    \[
      2^0\,\boldsymbol\delta_0 \;+\;2^1\,\boldsymbol\delta_1
      \;\equiv\;\mathbf0
      \pmod4,
      \quad\text{i.e.}\quad
      \boldsymbol\delta_0 \;+\;2\,\boldsymbol\delta_1
      \;\equiv\;\mathbf0\pmod4.
      \tag{***}
    \]
    We check that no choice of \(\boldsymbol\delta_0\in\{(2,0),(-2,0),(0,2),(0,-2)\}\) and \(\boldsymbol\delta_1\in D\) can satisfy (***):

    – If \(\boldsymbol\delta_0=(2,0)\), then the first‐coordinate equation in (***) says
      \[
        2 \;+\;2\,(\delta_1)_x\;\equiv\;0\pmod4
        \;\Longrightarrow\;
        (\delta_1)_x\equiv -1\pmod2,
      \]
      so \((\delta_1)_x\) is odd, hence \((\delta_1)_x=\pm1\).  But from the list \(D\), whenever \((\delta_1)_x=\pm1\) one has also \((\delta_1)_y=\pm1\), so
      \[
        \text{second‐coordinate in (***)}:
        \quad
        0 \;+\;2\,(\delta_1)_y
        \;\equiv\;2(\pm1)\;\equiv\;\pm2
        \not\equiv0\pmod4,
      \]
      a contradiction.  

    – The same contradiction arises if \(\boldsymbol\delta_0\) is any of \((\-2,0),(0,2),(0,-2)\).  

    Therefore \(\boldsymbol\delta_0\) cannot be one of those four nonzero vectors; the only choice is
    \[
      \boldsymbol\delta_0=(0,0).
    \]
    But then equation (**) becomes
    \[
      \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} 2^i\,\boldsymbol\delta_i\;=\;\mathbf0
      \;\Longrightarrow\;
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-2}2^i\,\boldsymbol\delta_{i+1}\;=\;\mathbf0.
    \]
    Re‐indexing \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i := \boldsymbol\delta_{i+1}\) we get the same form
    \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}2^i\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i=0\), and the same “mod 2 then mod 4’’ argument forces \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_0=\mathbf0\), i.e.\ \(\boldsymbol\delta_1=\mathbf0\).  Iterating in this way we deduce
    \[
      \boldsymbol\delta_i=(0,0)
      \quad
      \forall\,i=0,1,\dots,n-1.
    \]
    But that says \(\mathbf u_i=\mathbf v_i\) for every \(i\), i.e.\ the two ants took exactly the same directions in every minute.  This contradicts the hypothesis “distinct routes.”  Thus
    \[
      \boxed{q\neq2.}
    \]

5.  **Excluding \(q=\tfrac12\).**  
    Exactly the same argument works if \(q=\tfrac12\).  Multiply the vector‐sum condition
    \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(\!\mathbf u_i-\mathbf v_i)\,(1/2)^i=0\)
    through by \(2^{n-1}\); it becomes
    \[
      \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^{\,n-1-i}\,\boldsymbol\delta_i
      \;=\;\mathbf0.
    \]
    Now read off the coefficient of \(2^0\) (that is, reduce mod 2) to force \(\boldsymbol\delta_{n-1}\equiv\mathbf0\pmod2\), then reduce mod 4 on the last two terms to force \(\boldsymbol\delta_{n-1}=\mathbf0\), divide by 2, and iterate backwards.  One again finds \(\boldsymbol\delta_i=\mathbf0\) for all \(i\), so the routes coincide step–by–step.  Hence
    \[
      \boxed{q\neq\tfrac12.}
    \]

6.  **Conclusion and existence for \(q=1\).**  
    From step 3 we saw that the only candidates among positive rationals are
    \[
      q\in\{\,\tfrac12,\,1,\,2\},
    \]
    and steps 4–5 ruled out \(q=2\) and \(q=\tfrac12\).  Thus the only remaining possibility is
    \[
      \boxed{q=1}.
    \]
    Finally, to check that \(q=1\) actually *works*, give a concrete example with \(n=2\) minutes.  If \(q=1\), every minute both ants walk 1 m.  Let
    \[
      \text{Ant A: east in minute 0, north in minute 1,}
      \quad
      \text{Ant B: north in minute 0, east in minute 1.}
    \]
    Then Ant A’s path is
    \(\;(1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1)\)
    and Ant B’s is
    \(\;(0,1)+(1,0)=(1,1)\),
    so they meet at \((1,1)\) after two minutes, yet clearly the sequences “east, north’’ and “north, east’’ are different.  

Therefore the *only* positive rational \(q\) for which two ants can end at the same point in a finite number of minutes without having taken the same route is

\[
  \boxed{q=1.}
\]
