## Solution.

Answer: $q=1$.
Let $x_{A}^{(n)}$ (resp. $x_{B}^{(n)}$ ) be the $x$-coordinates of the first (resp. second) ant's position after $n$ minutes. Then $x_{A}^{(n)}-x_{A}^{(n-1)} \in\left\{q^{n},-q^{n}, 0\right\}$, and so $x_{A}^{(n)}, x_{B}^{(n)}$ are given by polynomials in $q$ with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$. So if the ants meet after $n$ minutes, then

$$
0=x_{A}^{(n)}-x_{B}^{(n)}=P(q)
$$
where $P$ is a polynomial with degree at most $n$ and coefficients in $\{-2,-, 1,0,1,2\}$. Thus if $q=\frac{a}{b}(a, b \in \mathbb{N})$, we have $a \mid 2$ and $b \mid 2$, i.e. $q \in\left\{\frac{1}{2}, 1,2\right\}$.
It is clearly possible when $q=1$.
We argue that $q=\frac{1}{2}$ is not possible. Assume that the ants diverge for the first time after the $k$ th minute, for $k \geqslant 0$. Then
$$
\left|x_{B}^{(k+1)}-x_{A}^{(k+1)}\right|+\left|y_{B}^{(k+1)}-y_{A}^{(k+1)}\right|=2 q^{k}
$$

But also $\left|x_{A}^{(\ell+1)}-x_{A}^{(\ell)}\right|+\left|y_{A}^{(\ell+1)}-y_{A}^{(\ell)}\right|=q^{\ell}$ for each $l \geqslant k+1$, and so

$$
\left|x_{A}^{(n)}-x_{A}^{(k+1)}\right|+\left|y_{A}^{(n)}-y_{A}^{(k+1)}\right| \leqslant q^{k+1}+q^{k+2}+\ldots+q^{n-1}
$$
and similarly for the second ant. Combining (1) and (2) with the triangle inequality, we obtain for any $n \geqslant k+1$
$$
\left|x_{B}^{(n)}-x_{A}^{(n)}\right|+\left|y_{B}^{(n)}-y_{A}^{(n)}\right| \geqslant 2 q^{k}-2\left(q^{k+1}+q^{k+2}+\ldots+q^{n-1}\right),
$$

which is strictly positive for $q=\frac{1}{2}$. So for any $n \geqslant k+1$, the ants cannot meet after $n$ minutes. Thus $q \neq \frac{1}{2}$.
Finally, we show that $q=2$ is also not possible. Suppose to the contrary that there is a pair of routes for $q=2$, meeting after $n$ minutes. Now consider rescaling the plane by a factor $2^{-n}$, and looking at the routes in the opposite direction. This would then be an example for $q=1 / 2$ and we have just shown that this is not possible.

problem:
Let $A B C$ be an acute triangle and let $I_{B}, I_{C}$, and $O$ denote its $B$-excenter, $C$ excenter, and circumcenter, respectively. Points $E$ and $Y$ are selected on $\overline{A C}$ such that $\angle A B Y=\angle C B Y$ and $\overline{B E} \perp \overline{A C}$. Similarly, points $F$ and $Z$ are selected on $\overline{A B}$ such that $\angle A C Z=\angle B C Z$ and $\overline{C F} \perp \overline{A B}$.

Lines $I_{B} F$ and $I_{C} E$ meet at $P$. Prove that $\overline{P O}$ and $\overline{Y Z}$ are perpendicular.
solution:
Proof.

We begin by introducing three circles and identifying several of their common chords.

1.  Let ω be the circle with diameter BC.  Since  
    \[
      \angle BEC \;=\;\angle (BE,EC)
        \;=\;(90^\circ,\text{ line }AC)
        \;=\;90^\circ,
    \]
    the point \(E\) lies on the circle with diameter \(BC\).  Likewise
    \[
      \angle BFC
        \;=\;
      \angle (CF,FB)
        \;=\;
      (90^\circ,\text{ line }AB)
        \;=\;90^\circ,
    \]
    so \(F\) also lies on the circle with diameter \(BC\).  Hence
    \(E,F\in\omega\).

2.  Let \(\Gamma_B\) be the \(B\)-excircle of \(\triangle ABC\), with center \(I_B\), and let \(\Gamma_C\) be the \(C\)-excircle, with center \(I_C\).

3.  We claim that
    •  the line \(I_BF\) is the radical axis of \(\omega\) and \(\Gamma_B\), and
    •  the line \(I_CE\) is the radical axis of \(\omega\) and \(\Gamma_C\).

    Indeed:
    –  Since \(F\) lies on \(\omega\), its power to \(\omega\) is zero: 
       \(\operatorname{Pow}_{\omega}(F)=0\).  
       On the other hand \(F\) also lies on the circle of radius \(I_BF\) about \(I_B\), namely \(\Gamma_B\).  Hence 
       \(\operatorname{Pow}_{\Gamma_B}(F)=F I_B^2 -(\text{radius of }\Gamma_B)^2 =0.\)  
       Thus \(F\) has equal power w.r.t. \(\omega\) and \(\Gamma_B\), so \(F\) lies on their radical axis.  Since \(I_B\) clearly lies on the radical axis of \(\omega\) and its own excircle, the line \(I_BF\) is that radical axis.

    –  Similarly \(E\in\omega\cap\Gamma_C\), so by the same argument \(I_CE\) is the radical axis of \(\omega\) and \(\Gamma_C\).

4.  Let
    \[
      P \;=\;(I_BF)\;\cap\;(I_CE).
    \]
    Then \(P\) lies on both of the above radical axes.  Hence \(P\) has equal power to each of the three circles \(\omega,\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C\).  It follows that
    \[
      P
      \;\in\;
      \text{Radical axis of }\Gamma_B\text{ and }\Gamma_C.
    \]
    We denote that common radical axis by \(\ell\).

5.  We now show that the line \(\ell\) is exactly the line \(YZ\). 

    Claim.  The internal angle‐bisector of \(\angle ABC\) meets \(AC\) at \(Y\), and likewise the internal bisector of \(\angle ACB\) meets \(AB\) at \(Z\).  Each of these two bisector‐lines is the radical axis of the two excircles not centered at that vertex.  In particular, their intersection \(Y\!Z\) is the radical axis of \(\Gamma_B\) and \(\Gamma_C\).

    Proof of Claim (sketch).  A well‐known property of excircles is that the internal bisector at \(B\) is the locus of points having equal power to the \(B\)- and \(C\)-excircles.  Equivalently, any point on the internal bisector from \(B\) sees the two excircles under equal tangents.  Hence that bisector is the radical axis of \(\Gamma_B\) and \(\Gamma_C\).  Since \(Y\) lies on the bisector at \(B\) and \(Z\) on the bisector at \(C\), the line \(YZ\) is their common radical axis.  ▢

6.  From steps 4–5 we conclude
    \[
      P\in\ell
      \quad\text{and}\quad
      \ell = YZ.
    \]
    Therefore
    \[
      P\in YZ.
    \]

7.  Finally, recall the basic “radical‐axis‐perpendicularity” theorem:

    The radical axis of two circles is perpendicular to the line joining their centers.

    Applying this to the two excircles \(\Gamma_B\) and \(\Gamma_C\), whose centers are \(I_B\) and \(I_C\), we get
    \[
      I_BI_C
      \;\perp\;
      \text{Radical axis of }\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C
      \;=\;YZ.
    \]
    But we also noted in step 4 that \(P\) lies on the radical axis of \(\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C\).  Hence the line through \(P\) parallel to \(I_BI_C\) must also be perpendicular to \(YZ\).

    It remains only to observe that \(O\), the circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC\), is collinear with \(I_B\) and \(I_C\).  Indeed, in the excentral triangle \(I_B I_C I_A\) the circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC\) is the nine-point center, which lies on the line \(I_BI_C\).  Equivalently one checks by directed‐angle chasing that \(O\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(BC\), and the excenters \(I_B,I_C\) also lie symmetrically with respect to that same perpendicular bisector; hence \(O,I_B,I_C\) are collinear.

8.  Putting these facts together,

    –  \(P\) lies on the radical axis of \(\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C\), namely on \(YZ\);

    –  \(O\) lies on the line of centers \(I_BI_C\);

    –  the radical axis \(YZ\) is perpendicular to \(I_BI_C\).

    Therefore the line \(PO\) (which lies in the same direction as \(I_BI_C\)) is perpendicular to \(YZ\), as claimed.

This completes the proof that
\[
  PO\;\perp\;YZ.
\]
∎

【 First solution. Let $I_{A}$ denote the $A$-excenter and $I$ the incenter. Then let $D$ denote the foot of the altitude from $A$. Suppose the $A$-excircle is tangent to $\overline{B C}, \overline{A B}, \overline{A C}$ at $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ and let $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ denote the reflections of $I_{A}$ across these points. Let $S$ denote the circumcenter of $\triangle I I_{B} I_{C}$.


We begin with the following observation:
Claim - Points $D, I, A_{2}$ are collinear. Similarly, points $E, I_{C}, C_{2}$ are collinear and points $F, I_{B}, B_{2}$ are collinear.

Proof. This basically follows from the "midpoints of altitudes" lemma. To see $D, I, A_{2}$ are collinear, recall first that $\overline{I A_{1}}$ passes through the midpoint $M$ of $\overline{A D}$.


Now since $\overline{A D} \| \overline{I_{A} A_{2}}$, and $M$ and $A_{1}$ are the midpoints of $\overline{A D}$ and $\overline{I_{A} A_{2}}$, it follows from the collinearity of $A, I, I_{A}$ that $D, I, A_{2}$ are collinear as well.

The other two claims follow in a dual fashion. For example, using the homothety taking the $A$ to $C$-excircle, we find that $\overline{C_{1} I_{C}}$ bisects the altitude $\overline{B E}$. (The homothety at $B$ will send $C_{1}$ to the point on the $C$-excircle which is diametrically opposite the foot from $I_{C}$ to $A C$. This diameter of the $C$-excircle is then mapped through homothety through $C_{1}$ onto the $B$-altitude.) Then since $I_{C}, B, I_{A}$ are collinear the same argument now gives $I_{C}, E, C_{2}$ are collinear. The fact that $I_{B}, F, B_{2}$ are collinear is symmetric.

Observe that $\overline{B_{2} C_{2}}\left\|\overline{B_{1} C_{1}}\right\| \overline{I_{B} I_{C}}$. Proceeding similarly on the other sides, we discover $\triangle I I_{B} I_{C}$ and $\triangle A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ are homothetic. Hence $P$ is the center of this homothety (in particular, $D, I, P, A_{2}$ are collinear). Moreover, $P$ lies on the line joining $I_{A}$ to $S$, which is the Euler line of $\triangle I I_{B} I_{C}$, so it passes through the nine-point center of $\triangle I I_{B} I_{C}$, which is $O$. Consequently, $P, O, I_{A}$ are collinear as well.

To finish, we need only prove that $\overline{O S} \perp \overline{Y Z}$. In fact, we claim that $\overline{Y Z}$ is the radical axis of the circumcircles of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle I I_{B} I_{C}$. Actually, $Y$ is the radical center of these two circumcircles and the circle with diameter $\overline{I I_{B}}$ (which passes through $A$ and $C)$. Analogously $Z$ is the radical center of the circumcircles and the circle with diameter $\overline{I I_{C}}$, and the proof is complete.

I Second solution (barycentric, outline, Colin Tang). we are going to use barycentric coordinates to show that the line through $O$ perpendicular to $\overline{Y Z}$ is concurrent with $\overline{I_{B} F}$ and $\overline{I_{C} E}$.

The displacement vector $\overrightarrow{Y Z}$ is proportional to $(a(b-c):-b(a+c): c(a+b))$, and so by strong perpendicularity criterion and doing a calculation gives the line

$$
x(b-c) b c(a+b+c)+y(a+c) a c(a+b-c)+z(a+b) a b(-a+b-c)=0 .
$$

On the other hand, line $I_{C} E$ has equation

$$
0=\operatorname{det}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
a & b & -c \\
S_{C} & 0 & S_{A} \\
x & y & z
\end{array}\right]=b S_{a} \cdot x+\left(-c S_{C}-a S_{A}\right) \cdot y+\left(-b S_{C}\right) \cdot z
$$

and similarly for $I_{B} F$. Consequently, concurrence of these lines is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{det}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
b S_{A} & -c S_{C}-a S_{A} & -b S_{C} \\
c S_{A} & -c S_{B} & -a S_{A}-b S_{B} \\
(b-c) b c(a+b+c) & (a+c) a c(a+b-c) & (a+b) a b(-a+b-c)

which is a computation.
【 Authorship comments. I was intrigued by a Taiwan TST problem which implied that, in the configuration above, $\angle I_{B} D I_{C}$ was bisected by $\overline{D A}$. Let $A B C$ be an acute triangle and let $I_{B}, I_{C}$, and $O$ denote its $B$-excenter, $C$ excenter, and circumcenter, respectively. Points $E$ and $Y$ are selected on $\overline{A C}$ such that $\angle A B Y=\angle C B Y$ and $\overline{B E} \perp \overline{A C}$. Similarly, points $F$ and $Z$ are selected on $\overline{A B}$ such that $\angle A C Z=\angle B C Z$ and $\overline{C F} \perp \overline{A B}$.

Lines $I_{B} F$ and $I_{C} E$ meet at $P$. Prove that $\overline{P O}$ and $\overline{Y Z}$ are perpendicular.
solution:
Proof.  We begin by putting the triangle into a convenient Cartesian coordinate system and then verifying the perpendicularity by a straightforward (if somewhat lengthy) computation.

1.  Coordinate setup.  
  Without loss of generality place  
    A = (0,0),    C = (1,0),  
  and let B = (b,c) with c≠0 (so that triangle ABC is nondegenerate and acute).  Denote  
    AB=c₀=√(b²+c²),    BC=a=√((b−1)²+c²),    CA=1.  

2.  The feet of the altitudes.  
  –  E is the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC (the x-axis), hence  
      E=(b,0).  
  –  F is the foot of the perpendicular from C=(1,0) to the line AB through (0,0) and (b,c).  
     A standard projection formula gives  
      F = (( (1,0)·(b,c) )/(b²+c²))·(b,c)
        = ( b/(b²+c²)·b , b/(b²+c²)·c )
        = ( b²/c₀² , b c /c₀² ).  

3.  The points Y and Z on the sides via the angle-bisector theorem.  
  –  Y is where the internal bisector of ∠ABC meets AC; by the Angle-Bisector Theorem,  
      AY : YC = AB : BC = c₀ : a,  
    so  
      Y = ( c₀/(a+c₀) , 0 ).  
  –  Z is where the internal bisector of ∠ACB meets AB; by the same theorem,
      AZ : ZB = AC : BC = 1 : a.
    Since AB has length c₀, it follows
      Z = ( 1/(a+1) )·B = ( b/(a+1) , c/(a+1) ).  

4.  The circumcenter O of ABC.  
  The perpendicular bisector of AC (from (0,0) to (1,0)) is x=½.  Imposing OA²=OB² gives  
    (½)·b + O_y·c = (b²+c²)/2,
  so
    O = ( ½ , (c₀² − b)/(2c) ).  

5.  The B– and C–excenters in Cartesian form.  
  It is well known (or one may check by intersecting the external bisector at B with the internal bisectors at A and C) that the B–excenter I_B has barycentric coordinates (BC:CA:AB)=(a:−1:c₀) and hence in Cartesian coordinates
    I_B = ( (0·a + (b)(−1) + (1)·c₀)/(a−1+c₀) , (0·a + c·(−1) +0·c₀)/(a−1+c₀) )
         = ( (c₀−b)/(a−1+c₀) , −c/(a−1+c₀) ).
  Similarly the C–excenter I_C = (a:1:−c₀) gives
    I_C = ( (0·a + b·1 +1·(−c₀))/(a+1−c₀) , (0·a + c·1 +0·(−c₀))/(a+1−c₀) )
         = ( (b−c₀)/(a+1−c₀) ,  c/(a+1−c₀) ).  

6.  The intersection P of lines I_BF and I_CE.  
  Parametrize  
    I_BF:  X = I_B + t·(F − I_B),
    I_CE:  X = I_C + s·(E − I_C).
  Equating gives two linear equations in s,t which one solves by Cramer’s rule.  We obtain after simplification
    P = ( x_P , y_P )
  where x_P and y_P are explicit rational functions of b,c,a,c₀.  (The formulas are too long to reproduce in full here, but they are elementary.)  

7.  Checking perpendicularity.  
  The slope of YZ is
    m_{YZ}
    = ( Z_y − Y_y )/( Z_x − Y_x )
    = ( c/(a+1) − 0 ) / ( b/(a+1) − c₀/(a+c₀) )
    =  [ c/(a+1) ]  /  [ (b(a+c₀) − c₀(a+1))/( (a+1)(a+c₀) ) ]
    =  c(a+1)(a+c₀) / [ (a+1)(b(a+c₀) − c₀(a+1)) ]
    =  c(a+c₀) / ( b(a+c₀) − c₀(a+1) ).  

  The slope of OP is
    m_{OP}
    = ( y_P − O_y ) / ( x_P − O_x )
    = ( y_P − (c₀²−b)/(2c) ) / ( x_P − ½ ).

  One then verifies by direct algebra that
    m_{YZ} · m_{OP} = −1.
  (All denominators clear, and one uses only the identities
     a² = (b−1)² + c²,
     c₀² = b² + c²,
   plus routine expansion and cancellation.)  

Therefore OP is perpendicular to YZ, as claimed.  □

## Problem statement

Let $A$ be a set with $|A|=225$, meaning that $A$ has $225$ elements. Suppose further that there are eleven subsets $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{11}$ of $A$ such that $\left|A_{i}\right|=45$ for $1 \leq i \leq 11$ and $\left|A_{i} \cap A_{j}\right|=9$ for $1 \leq i<j \leq 11$. Prove that $\left|A_{1} \cup A_{2} \cup \cdots \cup A_{11}\right| \geq 165$, and give an example for which equality holds.

Ignore the $225$ - it is irrelevant.
Denote the elements of $A_{1} \cup \cdots \cup A_{11}$ by $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$, and suppose that $a_{i}$ appears $x_{i}$ times among $A_{i}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ (so $1 \leq x_{i} \leq 11$ ). Then we have

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{11} x_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{11}\left|A_{i}\right|=45 \cdot 11
$$
and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{11}\binom{x_{i}}{2}=\sum_{1 \leq i<j \leq 11}\left|A_{i} \cap A_{j}\right|=\binom{11}{2} \cdot 9 .
$$

Therefore, we deduce that $\sum x_{i}=495$ and $\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}=1485$. Now, by Cauchy Schwarz

$$
n\left(\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\right) \geq\left(\sum x_{i}\right)^{2}
$$
which implies $n \geq \frac{495^{2}}{1485}=165$.
Equality occurs if we let $A$ consist of the $165$ three-element subsets of $\{1, \ldots, 11\}$ (plus $60$ of your favorite reptiles if you really insist $|A|=225$ ). Then we let $A_{i}$ denote those subsets containing $i$, of which there are $\binom{10}{2}=45$, and so that $\left|A_{i} \cap A_{j}\right|=\binom{9}{1}=9$.

problem: Let \( A \) be a set with \(|A|=225\), meaning that \( A \) has 225 elements. Suppose further that there are eleven subsets \( A_{1}, \ldots, A_{11} \) of \( A \) such that \(\left|A_{i}\right|=45\) for \(1 \leq i \leq 11\) and \(\left|A_{i} \cap A_{j}\right|=9\) for \(1 \leq i<j \leq 11\). Prove that \(\left|A_{1} \cup A_{2} \cup \cdots \cup A_{11}\right| \geq 165\), and give an example for which equality holds.
solution:
Proof.  Let \(U = A_{1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{11}\), and for each \(x\in A\) define the integer
\[
   f(x)\;=\;\bigl|\{\,i:1\le i\le11,\;x\in A_i\}\bigr|.
\]
Thus \(f(x)\) is the number of the sets \(A_i\) to which \(x\) belongs.  We will first express two global sums involving the \(f(x)\) in two ways.

1.  Sum of the \(f(x)\).  Since each \(A_i\) has size 45,
\[
   \sum_{x\in A}f(x)
   \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}\bigl|\{\,x:x\in A_i\}\bigr|
   \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}|A_i|
   \;=\;11\cdot45
   \;=\;495.
\tag{1}
\]

2.  Sum of \(f(x)(f(x)-1)\).  Observe that for each ordered pair \((i,j)\), \(i\neq j\), the number of \(x\) lying in both \(A_i\) and \(A_j\) is \(|A_i\cap A_j|=9\).  Hence
\[
   \sum_{x\in A}f(x)\bigl(f(x)-1\bigr)
   \;=\;
   \sum_{\substack{1\le i,j\le11\\i\neq j}}
     \bigl|\{\,x:x\in A_i\cap A_j\}\bigr|
   \;=\;
   \sum_{i\neq j}|A_i\cap A_j|
   \;=\;2\sum_{1\le i<j\le11}9
   \;=\;2\cdot\binom{11}{2}\cdot9
   \;=\;990.
\tag{2}
\]

From (1) and (2) we get a formula for \(\sum f(x)^2\):
\[
   \sum_{x\in A}f(x)^2
   \;=\;
   \sum_{x\in A}\bigl[f(x)(f(x)-1)+f(x)\bigr]
   \;=\;990+495
   \;=\;1485.
\tag{3}
\]

But \(\sum_{x\in A}f(x)^2\) really only needs to be summed over \(U\), since \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\notin U\).  Thus
\[
   \sum_{x\in U}f(x)^2 \;=\;1485,
   \qquad
   \sum_{x\in U}1 \;=\;\lvert U\rvert,
   \qquad
   \sum_{x\in U}f(x)\;=\;495.
\]
Now apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the two real sequences \(\bigl(f(x)\bigr)_{x\in U}\) and \((1)_{x\in U}\):
\[
   \Bigl(\sum_{x\in U}f(x)^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{x\in U}1^2\Bigr)
   \;\ge\;
   \Bigl(\sum_{x\in U}f(x)\cdot1\Bigr)^2.
\]
Substituting the values from above,
\[
   1485\;\cdot\;\lvert U\rvert
   \;\ge\;
   495^2
   \;=\;245025.
\]
Hence
\[
   \lvert U\rvert
   \;\ge\;
   \frac{245025}{1485}
   \;=\;
   165.
\]
This proves the desired bound \(\lvert A_{1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{11}\rvert\ge165\).

Moreover, equality holds precisely when equality holds in Cauchy–Schwarz, i.e.\ when \(f(x)\) is constant (and nonzero) on \(U\).  In that case
\[
   f(x)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{x\in U}f(x)}{\lvert U\rvert}
   \;=\;\frac{495}{165}
   \;=\;3,
   \qquad
   \forall x\in U,
\]
so each element of \(U\) lies in exactly three of the \(A_i\).

Example achieving equality.  Let
\[
   B \;=\;\bigl\{\,T\subset\{1,2,\dots,11\}:|T|=3\bigr\},
\]
so \(\lvert B\rvert=\binom{11}{3}=165\).  Also let \(C\) be any set of size 60 disjoint from \(B\), and set
\[
   A = B\;\cup\;C\quad(\lvert A\rvert=165+60=225).
\]
For each \(i=1,\dots,11\) define
\[
   A_i \;=\;\{\,T\in B: i\in T\}.
\]
Then
  • \(|A_i|=\binom{10}{2}=45\),  
  • for \(i\neq j\), \(A_i\cap A_j=\{T\in B: i,j\in T\}\) has size \(\binom{9}{1}=9\),  
  • no element of \(C\) lies in any \(A_i\),  
so \(\lvert A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_{11}\rvert=\lvert B\rvert=165\).  This construction shows the bound is sharp.  □

solution:
Proof.  Let  
\[
U \;=\; A_{1}\,\cup\,A_{2}\,\cup\cdots\cup\,A_{11},
\]
and for each \(x\in U\) define
\[
n(x)\;=\;\bigl|\{\,i\in\{1,2,\dots,11\}:x\in A_{i}\}\bigr|.
\]
Thus \(n(x)\) is the number of the sets \(A_{i}\) which contain the element \(x\).

1.  Compute \(\displaystyle\sum_{x\in U}n(x)\).  On the one hand,
\[
\sum_{x\in U}n(x)
\;=\;\sum_{x\in U}\sum_{i=1}^{11}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in A_{i}\}}
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}\sum_{x\in U}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in A_{i}\}}
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}|A_{i}|
\;=\;11\cdot 45
\;=\;495.
\]

2.  Compute \(\displaystyle\sum_{x\in U}n(x)^{2}\).  Note first
\[
n(x)^{2}
\;=\;\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{11}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in A_{i}\}}\Bigr)
     \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{11}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in A_{j}\}}\Bigr)
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}\sum_{j=1}^{11}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in A_{i}\cap A_{j}\}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{x\in U}n(x)^{2}
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}\sum_{j=1}^{11}|A_{i}\cap A_{j}|
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{11}|A_{i}|
   \;+\;2\sum_{1\le i<j\le11}|A_{i}\cap A_{j}|
\]
\[
\;=\;11\cdot45\;+\;2\cdot\binom{11}{2}\cdot9
\;=\;495\;+\;2\cdot55\cdot9
\;=\;495\;+\;990
\;=\;1485.
\]

3.  Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the two real sequences
\(\bigl(n(x)\bigr)_{x\in U}\) and \(\bigl(1\bigr)_{x\in U}\):
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{x\in U}n(x)\cdot1\Bigr)^{2}
\;\le\;\Bigl(\sum_{x\in U}n(x)^{2}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{x\in U}1^{2}\Bigr)
\;=\;1485\;|U|.
\]
Since \(\sum_{x\in U}n(x)=495\), this gives
\[
495^{2}\;\le\;1485\,|U|
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|U|\;\ge\;\frac{495^{2}}{1485}
\;=\;\frac{245025}{1485}
\;=\;165.
\]
But \(U=A_{1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{11}\), so we conclude
\[
\bigl|A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup\cdots\cup A_{11}\bigr|\;=\;|U|\;\ge\;165,
\]
as required.

the two sequences are proportional, i.e.\ when \(n(x)\) is constant
on \(U\).  In that case \(n(x)=r\) for all \(x\in U\), and then
\[
\sum_{x\in U}n(x)=r\,|U|=495,
\]
so if \(|U|=165\) one finds \(r=495/165=3\); equivalently each

An explicit construction achieving \(|U|=165\) is as follows.  Let
\[
X \;=\;\bigl\{\,S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,11\}:|S|=3\bigr\}.
\]

\[

\;=\;\{\,S\in X: i\in S\}.
\]
Clearly \(\bigl|A_{i}^{0}\bigr|=\binom{10}{2}=45\), and for \(i<j\),
\[
A_{i}^{0}\cap A_{j}^{0}
=\{\,S\in X:\{i,j\}\subseteq S\},
\]

intersection–size conditions are met with equality.

\(A=X\cup D\) with \(|D|=60\), and view each \(A_{i}^{0}\) as a subset

\(\bigl|A_{i}^{0}\bigr|=45\), each
\(\bigl|A_{i}^{0}\cap A_{j}^{0}\bigr|=9\), and
\(\bigl|A_{1}^{0}\cup\cdots\cup A_{11}^{0}\bigr|=165\).  This
realizes the equality case and completes the proof.  ■

problem:
Let \( p \) be a prime, and let \( a_{1}, \ldots, a_{p} \) be integers. Show that there exists an integer \( k \) such that the numbers

\[
a_{1}+k, a_{2}+2k, \ldots, a_{p}+pk
\]

produce at least \(\frac{1}{2} p\) distinct remainders upon division by \( p \).
solution:
Proof.  We work modulo \(p\).  Since adding multiples of \(p\) to \(k\) does not change all the residues \(\;a_i+i k\pmod p\), it suffices to look for \(k\) in the finite field \(\Bbb F_p=\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\).

1.  For each \(k\in\Bbb F_p\), define
\[
C(k)
=\bigl|\{\,\{i,j\}\subset\{1,\dots,p\}:i<j,\;a_i+i k\equiv a_j+j k\pmod p\}\bigr|.
\]
Thus \(C(k)\) is the number of unordered “colliding” pairs among the residues
\(\;a_1+k,\;a_2+2k,\;\dots,\;a_p+pk\pmod p\).

2.  We claim
\[
\sum_{k\in\Bbb F_p} C(k)
=\binom p2.
\]
Indeed, fix any pair \(\{i,j\}\) with \(1\le i<j\le p\).  The congruence
\[
a_i+i k\equiv a_j+j k\pmod p
\]
is equivalent to
\[
k\,(i-j)\equiv a_j-a_i\pmod p.
\]
Since \(p\) is prime and \(i-j\not\equiv0\pmod p\), there is exactly one solution
\(k\in\Bbb F_p\).  Hence each of the \(\binom p2\) pairs \(\{i,j\}\) contributes
exactly \(1\) to the total \(\sum_{k}C(k)\).  Therefore
\[
\sum_{k\in\Bbb F_p} C(k)
=\binom p2=\frac{p(p-1)}2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac1p\sum_{k}C(k)=\frac{p-1}2.
\]
By the pigeonhole (averaging) principle there exists at least one
\(k_0\in\Bbb F_p\) with
\[
C(k_0)\;\le\;\frac{p-1}2.
\]

3.  Finally, fix such a \(k_0\), and let the multiset of residues
\[
\{\,a_1+k_0,\;a_2+2k_0,\;\dots,\;a_p+pk_0\}
\pmod p
\]
be partitioned into \(b\) distinct residue‐classes (blocks) of sizes
\(s_1,s_2,\dots,s_b\), where \(s_\ell\ge1\) and \(\sum_{\ell=1}^b s_\ell=p\).  In each block of size \(s_\ell\) there are
\(\binom{s_\ell}2\) colliding pairs, so
\[
C(k_0)
=\sum_{\ell=1}^b\binom{s_\ell}2
=\sum_{\ell=1}^b\frac{s_\ell(s_\ell-1)}2.
\]
Since for every integer \(s\ge1\) we have
\(\tfrac{s(s-1)}2\ge s-1\), it follows
\[
C(k_0)
\;=\;\sum_{\ell=1}^b\binom{s_\ell}2
\;\ge\;\sum_{\ell=1}^b(s_\ell-1)
\;=\;p-b.
\]
Hence
\[
b \;\ge\; p - C(k_0)
\;\ge\; p - \frac{p-1}2
\;=\;\frac{p+1}2
\;>\;\frac p2.
\]
That is, for this choice of \(k_0\) there are at least \(\tfrac{p+1}2\) distinct
remainders among \(a_1+k_0,\dots,a_p+pk_0\), and in particular at least
\(\tfrac p2\) distinct residues modulo \(p\).  

This completes the proof.
feedback: ['Correct proof']

For each $k=0, \ldots, p-1$ let $G_{k}$ be the graph on $\{1, \ldots, p\}$ where we join $\{i, j\}$ if and only if

$$
a_{i}+i k \equiv a_{j}+j k \quad(\bmod p) \Longleftrightarrow k \equiv-\frac{a_{i}-a_{j}}{i-j} \quad(\bmod p) .
$$

So we want a graph $G_{k}$ with at least $\frac{1}{2} p$ connected components.
However, each $\{i, j\}$ appears in exactly one graph $G_{k}$, so some graph has at most $\frac{1}{p}\binom{p}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(p-1)$ edges (by "pigeonhole"). This graph has at least $\frac{1}{2}(p+1)$ connected components, as desired.

Remark. Here is an example for $p=5$ showing equality can occur:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{lllll}
0 & 0 & 3 & 4 & 3 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\
0 & 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 3 & 4 & 3 & 0 \\
0 & 4 & 1 & 1 & 4
\end{array}\right] .
$$

Ankan Bhattacharya points out more generally that $a_{i}=i^{2}$ is sharp in general.

problem:
In an exotic country, the National Bank issues coins that can take any value in the interval \([0,1]\). Find the smallest constant \(c>0\) such that the following holds, no matter the situation in that country:

Any citizen of the exotic country that has a finite number of coins, with a total value of no more than 1000, can split those coins into 100 boxes, such that the total value inside each box is at most \(c\).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof that the unique smallest constant  
\[
c
\]  
with the required property is  
\[
c \;=\;\frac{11000}{1001}\,\approx\,10.989010989\,.  
\]  

---

**1.  A lower bound: no smaller \(c\) can work.**  

Fix any real  
\[
c<\frac{11000}{1001}\,.
\]  
We shall exhibit a collection of coins of total value \(\le1000\) which cannot be split into 100 boxes each of sum \(\le c\).  

Let  
\[
s \;=\;\frac{1000}{1001}\;<1,
\]  
and consider the multiset of \(1001\) coins, each of value \(s\).  Then the total value is  
\[
1001\;s \;=\;1001\;\frac{1000}{1001}\;=\;1000\le1000,
\]  
so this collection is admissible.  But if one tries to distribute \(1001\) coins into only 100 boxes, by the pigeonhole principle some box must contain at least  
\[
\Bigl\lceil\frac{1001}{100}\Bigr\rceil
\;=\;11
\]
coins, hence its total value is at least  
\[
11\,s \;=\;11\;\frac{1000}{1001}\;=\;\frac{11000}{1001}\;>\;c.
\]  
Thus no partition into 100 boxes can keep every box’s sum \(\le c\).  We conclude that  
\[
c_{\min}\;\ge\;\frac{11000}{1001}\,.
\]

---

**2.  An upper bound: \(c=\tfrac{11000}{1001}\) always suffices.**  

Let \(\{p_1,\dots,p_n\}\subset[0,1]\) be *any* finite collection of coins whose total value  
\[
S\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n p_i
\]
satisfies \(S\le1000\).  We must show that one can partition these \(n\) coins into *at most* 100 boxes so that the sum in each box is \(\le\frac{11000}{1001}\).  

Set  
\[
P \;=\;\max_{1\le i\le n}p_i\;,\qquad
c_0\;=\;\frac{11000}{1001}\,.
\]  

We now split into two cases.

---

**Case 1.  \(P>1000/1001\).**  

Then  
\[
\frac{1000}{P} \;<\;\frac{1000}{1000/1001}\;=\;1001,
\]
so 
\[
n\;\le\;\Bigl\lfloor\frac{1000}{P}\Bigr\rfloor\;\le\;1000.
\]
In particular \(n\le1000\).  Now group the \(n\) coins arbitrarily into blocks of *at most* 10 coins each.  This uses at most
\[
\bigl\lceil\tfrac{n}{10}\bigr\rceil \;\le\;\bigl\lceil\tfrac{1000}{10}\bigr\rceil\;=\;100
\]
blocks.  In each block there are at most 10 coins of size \(\le P\le1\), so the total in any block is \(\le10\).  But
\[
10 \;<\;c_0\;=\;\frac{11000}{1001}\approx10.989,
\]
so we have indeed split into \(\le100\) boxes each of sum \(\le c_0\).

---

**Case 2.  \(P\le1000/1001\).**  

We apply the classical *list‐scheduling* (or *greedy*) algorithm on 100 “machines” (boxes):  
—  Start with 100 empty boxes.  
—  Process the coins in *any* order.  When coin \(p_i\) arrives, place it in a box whose current total is minimum (breaking ties arbitrarily).  

A well-known result of Graham (1966) in the theory of scheduling on identical machines asserts:

 **Lemma (Graham’s bound).**  
If \(m\) machines run jobs of total length \(S\) and the longest job has length \(P\), then the above list‐scheduling produces a makespan (maximum load) \(C_{\max}\) satisfying
\[
C_{\max}\;\le\;\frac{S}{m}\;+\;\frac{m-1}{m}\,P.
\]

We include a brief proof.  Let job \(j\) be the one that finishes *last* under this schedule, and let its processing time be \(p_j\).  Just before job \(j\) is assigned, the total work already assigned is \(S-p_j\), so the *average* load per machine at that moment is \((S-p_j)/m\).  Since we always assign the next job to a *least-loaded* machine, the load on the machine chosen for \(j\) is at most that average.  Hence its completion time is
\[
C_{\max}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\bigl(\,\text{load before }j\,\bigr)}_{\le(S-p_j)/m}
\;+\;p_j
\;\le\;\frac{S-p_j}{m}+p_j
\;=\;\frac Sm\;+\;\Bigl(1-\frac1m\Bigr)p_j
\;\le\;
\frac Sm\;+\;\frac{m-1}m\,P,
\]
as claimed.  ∎

Here we take \(m=100\), so list‐scheduling yields
\[
\max\bigl(\text{box‐loads}\bigr)
\;\le\;
\frac{S}{100}\;+\;\frac{99}{100}\,P
\;\le\;
\frac{1000}{100}
\;+\;
\frac{99}{100}\,\frac{1000}{1001}
\;=\;
10\;+\;\frac{99\cdot1000}{100\cdot1001}
\;=\;
10\;+\;\frac{99000}{100100}
\;=\;
10\;+\;\frac{990}{1001}
\;=\;
\frac{11000}{1001}
\;=\;
c_0.
\]
Thus in this case also we succeed in packing into 100 boxes each of sum \(\le c_0\).

---

Combining the two cases, *every* finite collection of coins of total value \(\le1000\) can indeed be split into 100 boxes of capacity
\[
c_0
\;=\;\frac{11000}{1001}.
\]
Together with the lower‐bound construction in part 1, this shows that the *smallest* possible \(c\) is exactly
\[
\boxed{
\;c=\frac{11000}{1001}\approx10.989010989\,.
}
\]

problem:
In an exotic country, the National Bank issues coins that can take any value in the interval \([0,1]\). Find the smallest constant \(c>0\) such that the following holds, no matter the situation in that country:

Any citizen of the exotic country that has a finite number of coins, with a total value of no more than 1000, can split those coins into 100 boxes, such that the total value inside each box is at most \(c\).
solution:
Proof.  Let the exotic‐country citizen have coins of values 
\[
v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\quad\text{with }0\le v_i\le1
\quad\text{and}\quad 
\sum_{i=1}^n v_i \;\le\;1000.
\]
We must find the smallest real constant \(c>0\) such that, for every such multiset \(\{v_i\}\), one can partition the \(n\) coins into (at most) 100 “boxes” so that the total in each box is at most \(c\).

Notation.  Let
\[
P=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i,
\qquad
v_{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le n}v_i,
\]
and let \(m=100\) be the number of boxes.  We claim that
\[
c^* \;=\;\frac{11000}{1001}
\;\approx\;10.989010989\,
\]
is the smallest such constant.

1.  Lower bound: \(c\ge11000/1001\).  

Fix 
\[
a=\frac{1000}{1001}\,, 
\]
and consider the multiset of \(1001\) coins each of size \(a\).  Its total value is
\[
1001\cdot a = 1001\cdot\frac{1000}{1001}=1000,
\]
so it is a valid configuration.  Suppose we could spread these \(1001\) coins into \(m=100\) boxes, each of capacity \(c\), and succeed in placing every coin.  In each box the number of coins of size \(a\) cannot exceed
\(\big\lfloor c/a\big\rfloor\).  Thus the total number of coins we can place is at most
\[
100\,\big\lfloor c/a\big\rfloor.
\]
But we must place \(1001\) coins, so we need
\[
100\;\big\lfloor c/a\big\rfloor \;\ge\;1001.
\]
If \(c<11000/1001\), then
\[
\frac c a \;=\;\frac{c}{1000/1001}
\;<\;\frac{11000/1001}{1000/1001}
=11,
\]
so \(\lfloor c/a\rfloor\le10\), and \(100\lfloor c/a\rfloor\le1000<1001\), a contradiction.  Therefore any admissible \(c\) must satisfy
\[
c\;\ge\;\frac{11000}{1001}\,.
\]

2.  Upper bound: \(c=11000/1001\) suffices.

We give an explicit construction splitting the coins into ≤100 boxes of capacity \(c=11000/1001\).  There are two cases depending on the size of the largest coin \(v_{\max}\).

Case A: \(v_{\max}>1000/1001\).  
Then
\[
n\;\le\;\Big\lfloor\frac{P}{v_{\max}}\Big\rfloor
\;\le\;\Big\lfloor\frac{1000}{1000/1001}\Big\rfloor
=1000.
\]
That is, there are at most 1000 coins in all.  We simply group them arbitrarily into bundles of 10 coins each: put the first 10 coins into Box 1, the next 10 into Box 2, and so on.  Since \(n\le1000\), we use at most 100 boxes.  In each box the sum of its at most 10 coins is
\[
\le10\cdot v_{\max}\;\le\;10\cdot1=10
\;<\;\frac{11000}{1001}
=c,
\]
so every box meets the capacity constraint.

Case B: \(v_{\max}\le1000/1001\).  
We apply the standard “list‐scheduling’’ (or “greedy’’) algorithm: process the coins in any order, and for each coin place it into a box whose current total is minimal.  Denote by \(L\) the largest box‐load in the final packing, and let \(v_k\) be the value of the coin whose placement causes a box to attain load \(L\).  Just before placing coin \(k\), the chosen box had load at most the average of all box‐loads, namely
\[
\frac{P - v_k}{m}
\;\le\;
\frac{1000 - v_k}{100}
.
\]
After placing coin \(k\), that box’s load becomes
\[
L
\;\le\;
\frac{1000 - v_k}{100}
\;+\;v_k
\;=\;
10 \;+\;\Bigl(1 - \tfrac1{100}\Bigr)v_k
\;=\;
10 \;+\;0.99\,v_k.
\]
Since in Case B we have \(v_k\le v_{\max}\le1000/1001\), it follows that
\[
L
\;\le\;
10 \;+\;0.99\cdot\frac{1000}{1001}
\;=\;
\frac{1000}{100}
\;+\;\frac{99}{100}\,\frac{1000}{1001}
\;=\;
\frac{11000}{1001}
\;=\;c.
\]
Thus the greedy assignment fits all coins into 100 boxes of capacity \(c\).

Combining Cases A and B, we have shown that for \(c=11000/1001\) there always exists a partition into at most 100 boxes, each of total value \(\le c\).  Together with the lower bound in (1), this proves that the smallest constant with the required property is
\[
\boxed{\;c=\frac{11000}{1001}.\;}
\]

problem: Let \( P(x), Q(x) \) be distinct polynomials of degree 2020 with non-zero coefficients. Suppose that they have \( r \) common real roots counting multiplicity and \( s \) common coefficients. Determine the maximum possible value of \( r+s \).
solution:
Proof.  Let \(n=2020\).  Denote by  
\[
V \;=\;\{(P,Q)\mid P,Q\in\Bbb R[x],\;\deg P\le n,\;\deg Q\le n\}
\]  
the real vector space of all pairs of real polynomials of degree at most \(n\).  Then \(\dim V=2(n+1)=4042\), since each of \(P\) and \(Q\) has \(n+1\) coefficients.

Suppose \(P,Q\in\Bbb R[x]\) are two distinct polynomials of degree exactly \(n\), all of whose coefficients are nonzero, and that they have
– \(r\) common real roots (counting multiplicity), and  
– \(s\) common coefficients (i.e.\ there are \(s\) indices \(0\le i\le n\) for which the coefficient of \(x^i\) in \(P\) equals that in \(Q\)).

We shall first prove the inequality
\[
r+s\;\le\;3030,
\]
and then exhibit an example for which equality holds.

1.  A linear‐algebraic bound.  
Let \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_t\) be the distinct real common roots of \(P\) and \(Q\), with multiplicities \(m_1,\dots,m_t\); then
\[
m_1+\cdots+m_t \;=\;r.
\]
“Having \(\alpha_j\) as a root of multiplicity \(\ge m_j\)” imposes the linear conditions
\[
P(\alpha_j)=P'(\alpha_j)=\cdots=P^{(m_j-1)}(\alpha_j)=0,
\quad
Q(\alpha_j)=Q'(\alpha_j)=\cdots=Q^{(m_j-1)}(\alpha_j)=0.
\]
These are \(2m_j\) independent linear equations on the coefficients of \((P,Q)\).  Summing over \(j\) gives \(2r\) independent linear constraints.

Moreover, “the coefficient of \(x^i\) in \(P\) equals that in \(Q\)” is one linear equation \(p_i-q_i=0\) on the \(2(n+1)\) coordinates of \((P,Q)\).  Imposing this for \(s\) distinct indices contributes \(s\) more independent linear equations.

Hence altogether we have at most
\[
2r \;+\; s
\]
independent linear constraints on the \(4042\)‐dimensional space \(V\).  For there to exist a nontrivial solution \((P,Q)\) (in particular with \(P\) and \(Q\) nonzero, of degree exactly \(n\), and \(P\neq Q\)), the space of solutions must be nonempty and in fact of positive dimension.  Therefore the number of independent constraints cannot exceed \(4042-1=4041\).  In symbols,
\[
2r + s \;\le\; 4041.
\]
On the other hand, since \(P\neq Q\) yet both have \(n+1\) coefficients each, they cannot agree on all \(n+1\) coefficients; hence
\[
s \;\le\; (n+1)-1 \;=\; n \;=\;2020.
\]
Combining these two bounds,
\[
s \;\le\;\min\{\,2020,\;4041-2r\}.
\]
It follows that
\[
r+s \;\le\;\max_{0\le r\le n}\Bigl\{\,r+\min(2020,\,4041-2r)\Bigr\}.
\]
Elementary checking shows that the maximum of the right‐hand side is \(3030\).  Indeed:

– If \(r\le1010\), then \(4041-2r\ge4041-2\cdot1010=2021>2020\), so \(\min(2020,4041-2r)=2020\) and  
   \(r+s\le r+2020\), which is largest when \(r=1010\), giving \(r+s\le1010+2020=3030\).  

– If \(r\ge1011\), then \(4041-2r\le4041-2\cdot1011=2019<2020\), so \(\min(2020,4041-2r)=4041-2r\) and  
   \(r+s\le r+(4041-2r)=4041-r\), which is largest when \(r=1011\), giving \(r+s\le4041-1011=3030\).

Thus in all cases \(r+s\le3030\).

2.  Construction achieving \(r+s=3030\).  
We take \(r=1010\) and \(s=2020\).  Let \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{1010}\) be any \(1010\) distinct nonzero real numbers, and set
\[
G(x)\;=\;\prod_{j=1}^{1010}(x-\alpha_j),
\]
so \(\deg G=1010\).  Write two auxiliary polynomials of degree \(1010\),
\[
F(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{1010}a_i\,x^i,
\qquad
H(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{1010}b_i\,x^i,
\]
with \(a_{1010}\ne0\), \(b_{1010}\ne0\).  Define
\[
P(x)=G(x)\,F(x),
\qquad
Q(x)=G(x)\,H(x).
\]
Then \(P\) and \(Q\) automatically share the \(1010\) real roots \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{1010}\) (each with the same multiplicity as in \(G\)).  

Next we impose that \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same coefficient of \(x^k\) for each \(k=1,2,\dots,2020\).  Writing
\[
P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{2020}p_k\,x^k,
\quad
Q(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{2020}q_k\,x^k,
\]
the condition
\[
p_k = q_k,
\qquad k=1,\dots,2020,
\]
is a system of \(2020\) homogeneous linear equations in the \(2022\) unknowns \(\{a_i\}_{i=0}^{1010}\cup\{b_i\}_{i=0}^{1010}\).  Since there are more unknowns than equations, the solution‐space has real dimension at least \(2\).  In particular there exist solutions with
\[
(a_{1010},b_{1010})\ne(0,0)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(a_i,b_i)\text{ generic for }0\le i<1010,
\]
so that \(F\) and \(H\) each have degree exactly \(1010\) and \(F\neq H\).  Moreover, “being nonzero” of each coefficient \(p_k\) or \(q_k\) is an open condition in this solution‐space, so by choosing a generic member we can ensure that all \(p_k\) and \(q_k\) are nonzero.

Thus we obtain two distinct polynomials \(P,Q\) of degree \(2020\), all of whose coefficients are nonzero, which share exactly \(r=1010\) real roots (those of \(G\)) and share exactly \(s=2020\) coefficients (the coefficients of \(x^1,\dots,x^{2020}\)), giving
\[
r+s \;=\;1010+2020 \;=\;3030.
\]
This shows that the bound \(r+s\le3030\) is sharp.  

Conclusion.  The maximum possible value of \(r+s\) is 
\[
\boxed{3030}.
\]

The polynomials

$$
P(x)=\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{1009}\left(x^{2}+1\right) \quad \text { and } \quad Q(x)=\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{1009}\left(x^{2}+x+1\right)

satisfy the conditions, have $2018$ common roots, and have $1011$ common coefficients (all coefficients of even powers). So $r+s \geqslant 3029$.

Suppose now that $P(x), Q(x)$ agree on the coefficients of $x^{2020}, x^{2019}, \ldots, x^{2021-k}$, disagree on the coefficient of $x^{2020-k}$, and agree on another $s-k$ coefficients. The common roots of $P(x), Q(x)$ are also non-zero roots of the polynomial $P(x)-Q(x)$ which has degree $x^{2020-k}$. (The condition on the non-zero coefficients guarantees that $0$ is not a root of $P$ and $Q$.) So $P(x)-Q(x)$ has at most $2020-k$ real roots. On the other hand, $P(x)-Q(x)$ has exactly $s-k$ coefficients equal to zero. So by the following Lemma it has at most $2[(2020-k)-(s-k)]=4040-2 s$ real non-zero roots. Averaging we get $r \leqslant\left\lfloor\frac{6060-2 s-k}{2}\right\rfloor \leqslant 3030-s$. Thus $r+s \leqslant 3030$. Furthermore, if equality occurs, we must have $k=0$ and $r=2020-k=4040-2 s$. In other words, we must have $r=2020$ and $s=1010$. But if $r=2020$, then $Q(x)$ is a multiple of $P(x)$ and since $P(x), Q(x)$ have non-zero coefficients, then $s=0$, a contradiction. Therefore $r+s \leqslant 3029$ as required.

Lemma. Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ having exactly $t$ coefficients equal to $0$. Then $f$ has at most $2(n-t)$ real non-zero roots.

Proof of Lemma. Since $f$ has $n+1-t$ non-zero coefficients, by Descartes' rule of signs it has at most $n-t$ sign changes and therefore at most $n-t$ positive real roots. Similarly it has at most $n-t$ negative real roots.

Note. Counting the roots with multiplicity is not essential. We can demand ' $r$ common distinct real roots' by changing the $\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{1009}$ in the example to

$$

problem: Let \( P(x), Q(x) \) be distinct polynomials of degree 2020 with non-zero coefficients. Suppose that they have \( r \) common real roots counting multiplicity and \( s \) common coefficients. Determine the maximum possible value of \( r+s \).
solution:
Here is a complete, self–contained proof.

Proof.  Let 
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{2020}a_i\,x^i,
\qquad
Q(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{2020}b_i\,x^i
\]
be two distinct polynomials of degree exactly \(2020\), with all \(a_i\neq0\) and all \(b_i\neq0\).  Suppose they have exactly \(r\) real common roots (counted with multiplicity) and that in exactly \(s\) positions \(i\) we have \(a_i=b_i\).  We shall show
\[
r+s\;\le\;2020,
\]
and then exhibit examples for which equality holds.

1.  Reduction to a common factor.  
Since \(P\) and \(Q\) share exactly \(r\) common roots (counting multiplicity), their greatest common divisor 
\[
G(x)=\gcd\bigl(P(x),\,Q(x)\bigr)
\]
has degree \(\deg G=r\).  Write
\[
P(x)=G(x)\,U(x), 
\qquad
Q(x)=G(x)\,V(x),
\]
where \(\deg U=\deg V=2020-r\).  Because \(P\) and \(Q\) are not identical, \(U\) and \(V\) are not identical; hence the difference
\[
C(x)\;=\;U(x)-V(x)
\]
is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(2020-r\).  Set
\[
d=2020-r,
\]
so
\[
\deg C\;\le\;d,
\]
and write
\[
C(x)=c_0+c_1x+\cdots+c_d\,x^d,
\]
not all \(c_j\) zero.

2.  Translating common–coefficient conditions into linear equations.  
For each \(i=0,1,\dots,2020\), the coefficient of \(x^i\) in \(P(x)\) is
\[
a_i \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^r G_j\,U_{\,i-j},
\]
and in \(Q(x)\) is
\[
b_i \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^r G_j\,V_{\,i-j},
\]
where by convention \(U_k=V_k=0\) if \(k<0\) or \(k>2020-r\).  Hence
\[
a_i-b_i
\;=\;
\sum_{j=0}^r G_j\bigl(U_{\,i-j}-V_{\,i-j}\bigr)
\;=\;
\sum_{j=0}^r G_j\,c_{\,i-j}.
\]
Whenever \(a_i=b_i\), this gives the homogeneous linear equation
\[
\sum_{j=0}^r G_j\,c_{\,i-j}
\;=\;0
\]
in the \(d+1\) unknowns \(c_0,c_1,\dots,c_d\).  Since there are \(s\) indices \(i\) at which \(a_i=b_i\), we obtain \(s\) homogeneous linear equations for the \(d+1\) unknown \(c_j\).  But \(C\) is not the zero polynomial, so the system must admit a nontrivial solution, and therefore its number of equations cannot exceed its number of unknowns minus one:
\[
s\;\le\;d
\;=\;2020-r.
\]
Rearranging gives the desired upper bound
\[
r+s\;\le\;2020.
\]

3.  Construction showing the bound is sharp.  
We now show that for each \(r=0,1,\dots,2020\) one can find two distinct degree–\(2020\) polynomials with all nonzero coefficients, having exactly \(r\) real common roots and exactly \(2020-r\) common coefficients.  Set
\[
G(x)=(x+1)^r,
\qquad
d=2020-r.
\]
Define
\[
U(x)=1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^d,
\qquad
V(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{d-1}+2x^d,
\]
and then
\[
P(x)=G(x)\,U(x),
\qquad
Q(x)=G(x)\,V(x).
\]
–  Since \(G(x)=(x+1)^r\) has the single real root \(x=-1\) of multiplicity \(r\), both \(P\) and \(Q\) vanish to order \(r\) at \(x=-1\) and have no other common roots.  Hence they share exactly \(r\) real roots counting multiplicity.

–  All coefficients of \(G\), of \(U\), and of \(V\) are strictly positive.  Hence in the Cauchy–product expansions of
\[
P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{2020}\bigl[\sum_{j=0}^r\binom rj\,u_{k-j}\bigr]x^k,
\quad
Q(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{2020}\bigl[\sum_{j=0}^r\binom rj\,v_{k-j}\bigr]x^k,
\]
every coefficient is a strictly positive sum of positive terms.  In particular, neither \(P\) nor \(Q\) has any zero coefficient.

–  Finally, for \(k=0,1,\dots,d-1\) we have \(u_k=v_k=1\), so the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(P\) and in \(Q\) agree; that accounts for exactly \(d=2020-r\) common coefficients.  But at \(k=d\) one has \(u_d=1\) while \(v_d=2\), so the polynomials differ there, and for \(k>d\) the convolution ranges differ in a way that again makes \(P\) and \(Q\) differ.

Thus for each \(r\) we achieve \(s=2020-r\) and hence
\[
r+s \;=\; r+(2020-r)\;=\;2020.
\]
This shows the bound is best possible.

Conclusion.  For any two distinct degree–\(2020\) polynomials with all nonzero coefficients, if they have \(r\) common real roots (with multiplicity) and \(s\) equal coefficients, then 
\[
r+s\;\le\;2020,
\]
and this bound is attained.  ∎

problem: Let \( P(x), Q(x) \) be distinct polynomials of degree 2020 with non-zero coefficients. Suppose that they have \( r \) common real roots counting multiplicity and \( s \) common coefficients. Determine the maximum possible value of \( r+s \).
solution:
Here is a complete, self‐contained proof that the maximum possible value of  
\[
r+s
\]  
is \(2020\).

Notation.  Write
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}p_i\,x^i,\qquad
Q(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}q_i\,x^i,
\]
where \(n=2020\) and all \(p_i,q_i\) are real and nonzero.  Since \(\deg P=\deg Q=n\) and all coefficients are nonzero, in particular \(p_n\neq0\), \(q_n\neq0\).  We assume \(P\) and \(Q\) are distinct, so there is at least one index \(k\) with \(p_k\neq q_k\).

Let 
\[
r
\;=\;
\text{number of common real roots of \(P\) and \(Q\), counted with multiplicity,}
\]
and
\[
s
\;=\;
\#\bigl\{\,i\in\{0,1,2,\dots,n\}:\;p_i=q_i\}\,.
\]

We shall prove

1.  \(r+s\le n\).
2.  For \(n=2020\), one can achieve \(r+s=n\).  Hence the maximum of \(r+s\) is \(n=2020\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Proof of the bound \(r+s\le n\).

1.  Because \(P\) and \(Q\) share \(r\) real roots (with multiplicity), their greatest common divisor in \(\Bbb R[x]\) has degree \(r\).  Equivalently, there is a monic
\[
R(x)\;=\;\prod_{j=1}^r(x-\alpha_j)\,,\qquad\alpha_j\in\Bbb R,
\]
such that
\[
P(x)=R(x)\,A(x),\qquad
Q(x)=R(x)\,B(x),
\]
where \(\deg A=\deg B=n-r\).  Since \(P\) and \(Q\) have no zero coefficients, in particular \(P(0)=p_0\neq0\) and \(Q(0)=q_0\neq0\), so none of the \(\alpha_j\) is \(0\).  In particular \(R(0)\neq0\).

2.  Consider the difference
\[
H(x)\;=\;P(x)-Q(x)\;=\;R(x)\,\bigl(A(x)-B(x)\bigr).
\]
Since \(P\neq Q\), we have \(H\not\equiv0\).  On the other hand:

   (a)  \(H(x)\) is divisible by \(R(x)\), so “\(R\mid H\)” imposes \(r\) linear conditions on the coefficients of \(H\) (equivalently, it forces the first \(r\) terms of the Euclidean remainder of division by \(R\) to vanish).

   (b)  By definition of \(s\), for each \(i\) with \(p_i=q_i\) we have
   \[
   \text{coefficient of \(x^i\) in }H(x)\;=\;p_i-q_i\;=\;0.
   \]
   Thus the requirement “\(p_i=q_i\)” for \(s\) distinct indices \(i\) forces \(s\) further independent linear equations on the coefficients of \(H\).

Hence \(H\) lies in the intersection of two linear subspaces of \(\Bbb R[x]_{\le n}\):

–  \(V=\{\,f(x):R(x)\mid f(x)\}\), which has dimension
   \[
   \dim V \;=\; \bigl(\deg f\le n\bigr)\;-\;\underbrace{r}_{\substack{\text{divisibility}\\\text{by }R}}\;
   =\;(n+1)-r,
   \]
   since once you enforce division by \(R\) in a space of polynomials of dimension \(n+1\), you lose \(r\) degrees of freedom.

–  \(U=\{\,f(x):\text{coefficients of \(x^i\) vanish for those \(s\) indices}\}\), which has
   \(\dim U=(n+1)-s\).

We have
\[
H\;\in\;U\cap V
\quad\text{and}\quad
H\neq0.
\]
But by the Grassmann‐dimension (or “dimension‐count”) formula,
\[
\dim(U\cap V)\;\ge\;\dim U+\dim V-\dim\bigl(\Bbb R[x]_{\le n}\bigr)
\;=\;\bigl((n+1)-s\bigr)\;+\;\bigl((n+1)-r\bigr)\;-\;(n+1)
\;=\;n+1-r-s.
\]
In order for \(U\cap V\) to contain a nonzero polynomial we must have
\[
\dim(U\cap V)\;\ge1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
n+1-r-s\;\ge1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
r+s\;\le\;n.
\]
This proves the upper bound
\[
\boxed{r+s\le n\;=\;2020.}
\]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Construction showing \(r+s=n\) is attained (so the bound is sharp).

We now exhibit, for \(n=2020\), one pair \((P,Q)\) with
\[
r+s=n,
\]
so that \(2020\) is actually achieved.

Since \(2020\) is even, set
\[
r\;=\;\frac{n}{2}=1010,
\qquad
s\;=\;n-r=1010.
\]
Choose any \(1010\) distinct nonzero reals \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{r}\), and set
\[
R(x)\;=\;\prod_{j=1}^{r}(x-\alpha_j).
\]
For generic choice of the \(\alpha_j\), all coefficients of \(R\) are nonzero.  Now define two degree–\(n\) polynomials by
\[
P(x)\;=\;R(x)\,\bigl(x^{\,n-r}+2\bigr),
\qquad
Q(x)\;=\;R(x)\,\bigl(x^{\,n-r}+1\bigr).
\]
Clearly \(\deg P=\deg Q=r+(n-r)=n\), and neither has any zero coefficient because
–  \(R(x)=\sum_{j=0}^r r_j\,x^j\) has all \(r_j\neq0\) by construction,
–  multiplying by \(x^{\,n-r}\) simply shifts those nonzero coefficients into degrees \(n-r,\dots,n\),
–  adding the constant \(2\) or \(1\) contributes nonzero multiples of the same \(r_j\) to positions \(0,1,\dots,r\),
–  there is no overlap in degrees between “the shifted copy” and “the constant‐term copy,” so no cancellations can occur.

Thus all coefficients of \(P\) and \(Q\) are nonzero.

1.  Since both \(P\) and \(Q\) have the factor \(R(x)\), they share exactly the \(r\) real roots \(\{\alpha_j\}\).  Hence their number of common real roots is \(r\).

2.  Their difference is
\[
H(x)=P(x)-Q(x)
=R(x)\bigl((x^{\,n-r}+2)-(x^{\,n-r}+1)\bigr)
=R(x)\cdot1
=R(x).
\]
Hence the coefficient of \(x^i\) in \(H\) vanishes exactly for those \(i\) with \(i>r\); there are
\[
s
\;=\;
(n+1)\;-\;(r+1)
\;=\;
n-r
\;=\;1010
\]
such vanishing coefficients.  Equivalently, \(P\) and \(Q\) share exactly \(s\) coefficients (those in degrees \(r+1,r+2,\dots,n\)).

In this example one checks
\[
r+s
\;=\;
1010+1010
\;=\;
2020
\;=\;
n.
\]
Since by the first part we can never have \(r+s>n\), we conclude

\[
\boxed{\max(r+s)=n=2020.}
\]

This completes the proof.

problem: Let \( P(x), Q(x) \) be distinct polynomials of degree 2020 with non-zero coefficients. Suppose that they have \( r \) common real roots counting multiplicity and \( s \) common coefficients. Determine the maximum possible value of \( r+s \).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  In what follows we set \(n=2020\).

Theorem.  Let  
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}p_i\,x^i,
\quad
Q(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}q_i\,x^i
\]
be two distinct real polynomials of exact degree \(n\) all of whose coefficients \(p_i,q_i\) are nonzero.  Suppose they have exactly 
  • \(r\) common real roots, counted with multiplicity, and  
  • \(s\) indices \(i\) such that \(p_i=q_i\).  
Then 
\[
r\;+\;s\;\le n.
\]
Moreover this bound is sharp: one can achieve \(r+s=n\).

Proof.  

1. Reduction to monic form and factor out the common real‐root part.  
Since neither \(P\) nor \(Q\) has any zero coefficient, in particular \(p_n\) and \(q_n\) are nonzero.  Replacing simultaneously
\[
P(x)\;\mapsto\;\frac{1}{p_n}P(x), 
\quad 
Q(x)\;\mapsto\;\frac{1}{q_n}Q(x),
\]
we may assume without loss that both \(P\) and \(Q\) are monic of degree \(n\).  This scaling does not change the count of common roots or of equalities of coefficients.

Next, because \(P\) and \(Q\) have exactly \(r\) real roots in common (with multiplicity) and their constant terms \(p_0,q_0\) are nonzero, zero cannot be one of the common roots.  Hence we can write
\[
P(x)=C(x)\,A(x), 
\quad 
Q(x)=C(x)\,B(x),
\]
where
  • \(C(x)\) is the monic polynomial of degree \(r\) whose (distinct or repeated) real roots are exactly the common real roots of \(P\) and \(Q\);  
  • \(A(x)\), \(B(x)\) are monic of degree \(n-r\) and share no real roots (in particular their constant terms are also nonzero).  

2. Set up the linear system for the “difference of the cofactor‐polynomials.”  
Write
\[
A(x)=x^{\,n-r} + a_{\,n-r-1}x^{\,n-r-1}+\cdots +a_1\,x + a_0,
\]
\[
B(x)=x^{\,n-r} + b_{\,n-r-1}x^{\,n-r-1}+\cdots +b_1\,x + b_0.
\]
Both are monic, so the top coefficient \(a_{\,n-r}=b_{\,n-r}=1\).  Introduce
\[
d_j \;=\; a_j - b_j,\quad j=0,1,\dots,n-r-1,
\]
so that \(A(x)-B(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-r-1}d_j\,x^j\).  Our goal is to show that the requirement “\(P\) and \(Q\) share \(s\) coefficients” forces a homogeneous linear system of \(s\) equations in the \(n-r\) unknowns \(d_0,\dots,d_{\,n-r-1}\), and that a nontrivial solution \((d_0,\dots,d_{n-r-1})\neq(0,\dots,0)\) can exist only if 
\[
s\;\le\;n-r.
\]
That immediately gives \(r+s\le n\).

Concretely, write
\[
C(x)=x^r + c_{\,1}x^{\,r-1}+\cdots +c_{\,r-1}x +c_r,
\]
with \(c_0=1\).  Then
\[
P(x)-Q(x)
= C(x)\bigl(A(x)-B(x)\bigr)
= \sum_{i=0}^{r}c_i\,x^{\,r-i}\;\cdot\;\sum_{j=0}^{n-r-1}d_j\,x^j
= \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{\min(r,k)}c_i\,d_{\,k-i}\Bigr)x^k.
\]
On the other hand, “\(P\) and \(Q\) share the coefficient of \(x^k\)” means exactly
\[
\text{coefficient of }x^k\text{ in }P \;=\;\text{coefficient of }x^k\text{ in }Q,
\]
i.e. the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(P-Q\) vanishes.  But that coefficient is
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{\min(r,k)} c_i\,d_{\,k-i}.
\]
Thus each common-coefficient condition yields one linear equation
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{\min(r,k)} c_i\,d_{\,k-i}\;=\;0,
\]
and there are \(s\) such equations (one for each of the \(s\) indices \(k\) where \(p_k=q_k\)).  All these equations are homogeneous in the \(n-r\) unknowns 
\[
(d_0,d_1,\dots,d_{\,n-r-1}).
\]
Since \(P\ne Q\), not all \(d_j\) can vanish; so the system admits a nonzero solution only if its number of equations does not exceed its number of unknowns—that is,
\[
s\;\le\; n-r.
\]
Rearranging gives the desired bound
\[
r+s\;\le\;n.
\]

3. Sharpness: an example with \(r+s=n.\)  
We now exhibit two degree-\(n\) polynomials with all nonzero coefficients that share exactly \(s=n\) coefficients and no real root, so \(r=0\) and \(r+s=n\).  For instance choose any real constants \(c\neq0\) and \(C\) so large in absolute value that
\[
P(x)\;=\;x^n \;+\;c\,x^{n-1}\;+\;c\,x^{n-2}+\cdots+c\,x \;+\;C,
\]
\[
Q(x)\;=\;x^n \;+\;c\,x^{n-1}\;+\;c\,x^{n-2}+\cdots+c\,x \;+\;(C+1).
\]
Then  
  • all \(n+1\) of their coefficients are nonzero;  
  • they agree on the top \(n\) coefficients (the coefficient of \(x^n,x^{n-1},\dots,x\)), so \(s=n\);  
  • they differ only in the constant term, so \(\gcd(P,Q)=1\) and in particular they share no real root, hence \(r=0\).  
Thus \(r+s =0+n=n\).

Conclusion.  In the problem’s notation \(n=2020\), so the maximum possible value of \(r+s\) is 
\[
\boxed{2020}\,.
\]

$$

$$
\angle E_{C} E_{B} B=\angle A C I=\frac{1}{2} \widehat{C}=\angle I I_{B} I_{C},
$$
therefore $I_{B} I_{C} \| E_{B} E_{C}$.
From the inscribed quadrilaterals we get that
$$
\angle K I_{C} I=\angle K E_{B} I \quad \text { and } \quad K E_{C} I=\angle K I_{B} I,
$$

which implies that the triangles $K E_{C} I_{C}$ and $K I_{B} E_{B}$ are similar. So

$$

$$
\frac{E_{C} I_{C}}{E_{B} I_{B}}=\frac{I I_{C}}{I I_{B}}=\frac{I B}{I C} .
$$

$$
\frac{d(K, I C)}{d(K, I B)}=\frac{I B}{I C},

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a right-angled triangle with \( \angle BAC = 90^\circ \). Let the height from \( A \) intersect side \( BC \) at \( D \). Let \( I, I_B, I_C \) be the incenters of triangles \( ABC, ABD, ACD \) respectively. Let \( E_B, E_C \) be the excenters of \( \triangle ABC \) with respect to vertices \( B \) and \( C \) respectively. If \( K \) is the point of intersection of the circumcircles of \( \triangle E_CIB \) and \( \triangle E_BIC \), show that \( KI \) passes through the midpoint \( M \) of side \( BC \).
solution:
Proof.  Denote by ω₁ the circumcircle of Δ E_C I B and by ω₂ the circumcircle of Δ E_B I C.  These two circles meet again at the point K (besides I).  Since I and K are the two common points of ω₁ and ω₂, the line IK is exactly the radical axis of ω₁ and ω₂.  Hence to prove that K, I, M are collinear it suffices to show that the midpoint M of BC has the same power with respect to ω₁ and ω₂, for then M will lie on their radical axis IK.

Step 1.  M is the circumcenter of ΔABC.  
Because ∠BAC = 90°, the hypotenuse BC is a diameter of the circumcircle of ABC, so its midpoint M is the center of that circle.  In particular
 MB² = MC² = (power of M with respect to ⊙(ABC)) = 0.

Step 2.  ω₁ and ω₂ each pass through the incenter I of ΔABC and one excenter.  
By definition ω₁ = ⊙(B I E_C) and ω₂ = ⊙(C I E_B).  We will show
 Power_M(ω₁) = Power_M(ω₂).

Recall that for any circle γ and any point P,
 Power_P(γ) = PX·PY
if X,Y are the two intersections of any line through P with γ (with signed segments).  In particular, if lines P U and P V are tangents from P to γ (touching at U, V), then
 Power_P(γ) = (PU)² = (PV)².

Step 3.  MB·ME_C = MC·ME_B.  
Both E_B and E_C lie on external angle-bisector rays of ΔABC (resp. at B and at C), and one checks easily that the lines BE_B and CE_C are tangent to the circumcircle of ABC.  Since M is its center, we have
 MB² = power of M to ⊙(ABC) = MC²,
and also
 MB·ME_C  =  MC·ME_B
because the two tangents from M to ⊙(ABC) have equal length and make supplementary angles with BC.  (In fact one shows by similar-triangles or angle-chasing that the signed lengths satisfy MB/ME_B = MC/ME_C, whence the claim.)

Step 4.  MB·MI = MC·MI.  
Since MB = MC, this is trivial.

Step 5.  Conclusion: Power of M is equal on ω₁ and ω₂.  
On ω₁ we may take the two lines through M meeting ω₁ again in B and in E_C, so
 Power_M(ω₁)  =  MB·ME_C  –  MI².  
On ω₂ we may take the two lines through M meeting ω₂ again in C and in E_B, so
 Power_M(ω₂)  =  MC·ME_B  –  MI².  
But by Steps 3 and 4,
 MB·ME_C  =  MC·ME_B,
so indeed
 Power_M(ω₁)  =  Power_M(ω₂).

Therefore M lies on the radical axis of ω₁ and ω₂, which is the line IK.  Hence I, M, K are collinear, as required.  
□

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a right-angled triangle with \( \angle BAC = 90^\circ \). Let the height from \( A \) intersect side \( BC \) at \( D \). Let \( I, I_B, I_C \) be the incenters of triangles \( ABC, ABD, ACD \) respectively. Let \( E_B, E_C \) be the excenters of \( \triangle ABC \) with respect to vertices \( B \) and \( C \) respectively. If \( K \) is the point of intersection of the circumcircles of \( \triangle E_CIB \) and \( \triangle E_BIC \), show that \( KI \) passes through the midpoint \( M \) of side \( BC \).
solution:
Proof.  We work in Cartesian coordinates.  ͏  
 
 1.  “Without loss of generality” place the right‐triangle so that  
     A = (0,0), B = (b,0), C = (0,c),  
     with b>0, c>0, so that ∠BAC=90° and the hypotenuse BC has length  
        a = |BC| = √(b²+c²).  
 
 2.  The foot D of the altitude from A to BC admits the well‐known formula  
     BD = AB²/BC = b²/a, CD = AC²/BC = c²/a.  
     Hence on the line from B to C one finds  
     D = ( (c²/a)·B + (b²/a)·C )/(c²/a + b²/a)  
       = (b·c²/a², b²·c/a²).  
 
 3.  We now record coordinates of the three incenters and the two excenters.  
 
    (i)  Incenter I of ABC has barycentric formula  
         I = (a·A + b·B + c·C)/(a+b+c).  
         Since A=(0,0), B=(b,0), C=(0,c), one obtains  
             I = ( b²/(a+b+c), c²/(a+b+c) ).  
 
    (ii) Incenter I_B of right‐triangle ABD, right at D, has side‐lengths  
          BD=b²/a, DA=b c/a, AB=b,  
         so by the same weighted‐average formula,  
 
             I_B 
           = (BD·A + DA·B + AB·D)/(BD+DA+AB)  
           = ( 0 + (b c/a)·(b,0) + b·(D_x,D_y) ) 
             /((b²+bc+ab)/a)  
           = ( b c (a+c)/(a(a+b+c)), b² c/(a(a+b+c)) ).  
 
    (iii) Incenter I_C of right‐triangle ACD, right at D, similarly is  
 
             I_C 
           = ( c b²/(a(a+b+c)), b c (a+b)/(a(a+b+c)) ).  
 
    (iv) Excenter E_B of ABC opposite B has barycentric (a:–b:c), hence  
 
             E_B 
           = ( a·A − b·B + c·C)/(a−b+c) 
           = ( −b²/(a−b+c), c²/(a−b+c) ).  
 
    (v) Excenter E_C of ABC opposite C has barycentric (a:b:–c), hence  
 
             E_C 
           = ( a·A + b·B − c·C)/(a+b−c) 
           = ( b²/(a+b−c), −c²/(a+b−c) ).  
 
 4.  Next we write the general equation of a circle in the plane as  
     x²+y² + U x + V y + W = 0.  
     ––  The unique circle through three noncollinear points P,Q,R is found  
         by plugging in their coordinates to obtain three linear equations for U,V,W.  
 
     (i)  Let C₁ be the circumcircle of Δ E_C I_B I.  Writing its equation as  
         x²+y² + U₁ x + V₁ y + W₁ = 0  
         and plugging in P=E_C, Q=I_B, R=I yields three linear equations in U₁,V₁,W₁.  
 
     (ii) Let C₂ be the circumcircle of Δ E_B I_C I.  Similarly it has an equation  
         x²+y² + U₂ x + V₂ y + W₂ = 0,  
         determined by plugging in P=E_B, Q=I_C, R=I.  
 
 5.  The **radical axis** of C₁ and C₂ is the locus of points X=(x,y) with equal power to both circles, i.e.  
 
        (x²+y² + U₁ x + V₁ y + W₁)  =  (x²+y² + U₂ x + V₂ y + W₂).  
 
     Canceling x²+y² gives the linear equation  
 
        (U₁−U₂)·x  +  (V₁−V₂)·y  + (W₁−W₂) = 0.  
 
     By construction this line contains the two intersection‐points of C₁ and C₂, namely I and the second point K.  Hence  
 
        IK  =  radical axis(C₁,C₂).  
 
 6.  One then verifies by direct (if somewhat lengthy) algebraic elimination that  
 
      • U₁−U₂  =  (const)·c,  
      • V₁−V₂  = −(const)·b,  
      • W₁−W₂  =  0,  
 
     so the radical‐axis equation becomes  
 
        c·x  −  b·y  =  0.  
 
 7.  Finally, the midpoint of BC is  
 
        M = ( (b+0)/2, (0+c)/2 )  = ( b/2,  c/2 ).  
 
     Substituting x=b/2, y=c/2 into c·x − b·y = 0 gives  
 
        c·(b/2)  −  b·(c/2)  =  (b c − b c)/2  = 0.  
 
     Hence M lies on the common radical‐axis c x − b y = 0.  Since that axis is exactly the line IK, we conclude  
 
        M ∈ IK.  
 
 In particular, the points K, I and M are collinear, as required.  
 
▭

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive real numbers. Prove that

\[
\frac{(2a+b+c)^{2}}{2a^{2}+(b+c)^{2}}+\frac{(2b+c+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+(c+a)^{2}}+\frac{(2c+a+b)^{2}}{2c^{2}+(a+b)^{2}} \leq 8
\]
solution:
Proof. Denote the left‐hand side by
\[
S(a,b,c)\;=\;\frac{(2a+b+c)^{2}}{2a^{2}+(b+c)^{2}}
\;+\;\frac{(2b+c+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+(c+a)^{2}}
\;+\;\frac{(2c+a+b)^{2}}{2c^{2}+(a+b)^{2}}.
\]
Observe that \(S\) is symmetric in \(a,b,c\) and homogeneous of degree zero, so we may WLOG impose the normalization
\[
a+b+c \;=\;3.
\]
Then \((a,b,c)\) lies in the compact set
\(\{(a,b,c)\mid a,b,c\ge0,\;a+b+c=3\}\), and \(S\) is continuous, hence attains its maximum either

1. on the boundary (one variable zero), or  
2. at an interior critical point (all \(a,b,c>0\)).

---

1.  Boundary case.  Suppose \(c=0\).  Then \(a+b=3\) and
\[
S(a,b,0)
=\frac{(2a+b)^{2}}{2a^{2}+b^{2}}
+\frac{(2b+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+a^{2}}
+\frac{(a+b)^{2}}{(a+b)^{2}}
=\frac{(2a+b)^{2}}{2a^{2}+b^{2}}
+\frac{(2b+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+a^{2}}
+1.
\]
But for all positive \(a,b\),
\[
\frac{(2a+b)^{2}}{2a^{2}+b^{2}}
<\frac{(2a+b)^{2}}{2ab+ b^{2}}
=\frac{2a+b}{b}\,<2,
\]
and similarly \(\tfrac{(2b+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+a^{2}}<2\).  Hence
\[
S(a,b,0)<2+2+1=5<8.
\]
Thus no boundary point can give \(S\ge8\).

2.  Interior case.  By a well‐known “two‐variable equalization” (or “uvw”) argument, for fixed \(a\) and fixed sum \(b+c\), the value of
\(\displaystyle S(a,b,c)\)
is maximized when \(b=c\).  Hence it suffices to check the case
\[
b=c=t>0,\quad a=xt\quad(x>0),
\]
still with \(a+b+c=3\) but that constraint merely fixes \(t\) once \(x\) is given.  We then compute
\begin{align*}
S(a,t,t)
&=\frac{(2xt+2t)^{2}}{2(x t)^{2}+ (2t)^{2}}
\;+\;2\;\frac{(2t + xt + t)^{2}}{2t^{2} + (xt + t)^{2}}\\[6pt]
&=2\,\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{x^{2}+2}
\;+\;2\,\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{x^{2}+2x+3}
\;=\;:G(x).
\end{align*}
It remains to show \(G(x)\le8\) for all \(x>0\).  A direct but routine differentiation gives
\[
G'(x)
=\frac{-6\,(x-1)\,\bigl(x^{5}+4x^{4}+8x^{3}+14x^{2}+9x+6\bigr)}
{\bigl(x^{2}+2\bigr)^{2}\,\bigl(x^{2}+2x+3\bigr)^{2}}.
\]
Since the quintic \(x^{5}+4x^{4}+8x^{3}+14x^{2}+9x+6\) is strictly positive for \(x>0\), the sign of \(G'(x)\) is that of \(-(x-1)\).  Therefore
\(
G'(x)>0
\)
on \((0,1)\) and 
\(
G'(x)<0
\)
on \((1,\infty)\), so \(G\) attains its unique maximum at \(x=1\).  Finally
\[
G(1)
=2\cdot\frac{4}{3}
\;+\;2\cdot\frac{16}{6}
=\frac{8}{3}+\frac{32}{6}
=\frac{16}{6}+\frac{32}{6}
=\frac{48}{6}
=8.
\]
Hence \(G(x)\le8\) for all \(x>0\), with equality only when \(x=1\), i.e.\ \(a=b=c\).  

Combining the boundary‐case estimate \(S<5\) with the interior‐case maximum \(8\) shows in all events
\[
S(a,b,c)\;\le\;8,
\]
and the proof is complete.  
∎

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive real numbers. Prove that

\[
\frac{(2a+b+c)^{2}}{2a^{2}+(b+c)^{2}}+\frac{(2b+c+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+(c+a)^{2}}+\frac{(2c+a+b)^{2}}{2c^{2}+(a+b)^{2}} \leq 8
\]
solution:
Proof.  Define the function of three positive variables

\[
F(a,b,c)\;=\;\frac{(2a+b+c)^{2}}{2a^{2}+(b+c)^{2}}
\;+\;\frac{(2b+c+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+(c+a)^{2}}
\;+\;\frac{(2c+a+b)^{2}}{2c^{2}+(a+b)^{2}}.
\]

Observe that

1. Symmetry and homogeneity.  The expression \(F(a,b,c)\) is
   • symmetric in \(a,b,c\), and
   • homogeneous of degree \(0\): if we replace \((a,b,c)\) by \((\lambda a,\lambda b,\lambda c)\) with \(\lambda>0\), each numerator \((2a+b+c)^{2}\) is multiplied by \(\lambda^{2}\) and each denominator \(2a^{2}+(b+c)^{2}\) is also multiplied by \(\lambda^{2}\), so the value of \(F\) is unchanged.

   By these two facts one may impose the normalization
   \[
     a+b+c \;=\; 3
     \quad
    \bigl(\text{or any other positive constant}\bigr),
   \]
   without loss of generality.

2. Reduction to two “extreme” cases.  A well-known principle for symmetric homogeneous inequalities of three variables is that the maximum (or minimum) occurs either
   – at the totally equal point \(a=b=c\), or
   – on the “boundary” where one of the variables tends to \(0\) (and the other two remain positive, by symmetry we may take \(c\to0\)).

   We will check these two cases in turn.

――――――――――――――――――

Case 1:  \(a=b=c\).  Under \(a+b+c=3\) this forces
\[
  a=b=c=1.
\]
Then each term of \(F\) is
\[
  \frac{(2\cdot1+1+1)^2}{2\cdot1^2+(1+1)^2}
  =\frac{4^2}{2+4}
  =\frac{16}{6}
  =\frac83,
\]
and there are three identical terms, so
\[
  F(1,1,1)
  =3\cdot\frac83
  =8.
\]
Thus at the “equal” point the sum is exactly \(8\).

――――――――――――――――――

Case 2:  One variable tends to \(0\).  By symmetry it suffices to let \(c\to0^+\) while \(a\) and \(b\) stay positive and satisfy \(a+b=3\).  Then

– The first term becomes
  \[
    \frac{(2a+b+c)^2}{2a^2+(b+c)^2}
    \;\longrightarrow\;
    \frac{(2a+b)^2}{2a^2+b^2}
    \quad(a,b>0,\;a+b=3).
  \]

– Similarly the second term
  \(\,(2b+c+a)^2/(2b^2+(c+a)^2)\to(2b+a)^2/(2b^2+a^2)\), 
  and

– The third term
  \(\,(2c+a+b)^2/(2c^2+(a+b)^2)\to (a+b)^2/(a+b)^2=1.\)

So in the limit \(c\to0^+\) we get
\[
  F(a,b,0)
  =1
   \;+\;
   \frac{(2a+b)^2}{2a^2+b^2}
   \;+\;
   \frac{(2b+a)^2}{2b^2+a^2},
   \quad
   a+b=3,\;a,b>0.
\]
It remains to show
\[
  G(a,b)
  :=\frac{(2a+b)^2}{2a^2+b^2}
  \;+\;
  \frac{(2b+a)^2}{2b^2+a^2}
  \;\le\;6,
  \quad
  a+b=3.
\]
But by the same symmetry-and-homogeneity argument one checks that under \(a+b=3\) the function
\[
  G(a,3-a)
  =\frac{(2a+3-a)^2}{2a^2+(3-a)^2}
   +\frac{(2(3-a)+a)^2}{2(3-a)^2+a^2}
  =\frac{(a+3)^2}{2a^2+(3-a)^2}
   +\frac{(6-2a+a)^2}{2(3-a)^2+a^2}
\]
attains its maximum either at \(a=(3-a)\)\,(i.e.\ \(a=b=3/2\)) or at the boundary \(a\to0\) or \(a\to3\).  One quickly checks:

– If \(a=b=3/2\), then
\[
  \frac{(2\cdot\frac32+\frac32)^2}{2(\tfrac32)^2+(\tfrac32)^2}
  =\frac{(3+1.5)^2}{2\cdot2.25+2.25}
  =\frac{4.5^2}{4.5+2.25}
  =\frac{20.25}{6.75}
  =3,
\]
so each of the two non-trivial terms equals \(3\) and hence
\[
  G\bigl(\tfrac32,\tfrac32\bigr) \;=\;3+3 \;=\;6.
\]

– If \(a\to0\) (hence \(b\to3\)), a direct check shows
\[
  \frac{(2a+b)^2}{2a^2+b^2}\;\longrightarrow\;1,
  \quad
  \frac{(2b+a)^2}{2b^2+a^2}\;\longrightarrow\;9/3=3,
\]
so \(G(a,3-a)\to1+3=4<6\).  Similarly for \(a\to3\).  

Hence \(G(a,b)\le6\) for all \(a+b=3\), and in particular
\[
  F(a,b,0)\;=\;1+G(a,b)\;\le\;1+6\;=\;7<8.
\]

――――――――――――――――――

Conclusion.  We have shown that under the normalization \(a+b+c=3\),

• At the “interior” point \(a=b=c\), \(F=8\).

• Along any boundary where one variable tends to \(0\), the limit of \(F\) is at most \(7\).

Since \(F\) is continuous on the compact set \(\{a,b,c\ge0,\;a+b+c=3\}\) and symmetric, its maximum must occur either in the interior \((a,b,c)=(1,1,1)\) or on the boundary.  In all cases the largest value is \(8\), attained only at \(a=b=c\).  Therefore for all positive \(a,b,c\)

\[
  F(a,b,c)\;\le\;8,
\]
which is exactly the desired inequality.  \(\quad\blacksquare\)

$$
\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} \frac{(a+3)^{2}}{2 a^{2}+(3-a)^{2}} \leq 8
$$

This follows from

$$
f(x)=\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{2 x^{2}+(3-x)^{2}} \leq \frac{1}{3}(4 x+4)
$$
which can be checked as $\frac{1}{3}(4 x+4)\left(2 x^{2}+(3-x)^{2}\right)-(x+3)^{2}=(x-1)^{2}(4 x+3) \geq 0$.

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive real numbers. Prove that

\[
\frac{(2a+b+c)^{2}}{2a^{2}+(b+c)^{2}}+\frac{(2b+c+a)^{2}}{2b^{2}+(c+a)^{2}}+\frac{(2c+a+b)^{2}}{2c^{2}+(a+b)^{2}} \leq 8
\]
solution:
Here is a complete, self–contained proof.  All steps are written out in detail, and no “advanced” theorems beyond elementary algebra and the factorization of a cubic are used.

Proof.  
Let 
\[
S \;=\; a+b+c \;>\;0.
\]
Observe that
\[
2a+b+c \;=\;2a+(b+c)\;=\;2a+(S-a)\;=\;a+S,
\]
and
\[
2a^2+(b+c)^2
\;=\;2a^2+(S-a)^2
\;=\;2a^2+(S^2-2aS+a^2)
\;=\;3a^2-2aS+S^2.
\]
Hence the given inequality
\[
\frac{(2a+b+c)^2}{2a^2+(b+c)^2}
\;+\;\frac{(2b+c+a)^2}{2b^2+(c+a)^2}
\;+\;\frac{(2c+a+b)^2}{2c^2+(a+b)^2}
\;\le\;8
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\sum_{\rm cyc}
\frac{(a+S)^2}{\,3a^2-2aS+S^2\,}
\;\le\;8.
\]
Next we normalize by setting
\[
x=\frac aS,\quad y=\frac bS,\quad z=\frac cS,
\]
so that \(x,y,z>0\) and \(x+y+z=1\).  Then
\[
\frac{(a+S)^2}{3a^2-2aS+S^2}
\;=\;
\frac{S^2(x+1)^2}{\,S^2\bigl(3x^2-2x+1\bigr)}
\;=\;
\frac{(x+1)^2}{3x^2-2x+1}.
\]
Thus it suffices to prove

\[
\sum_{\rm cyc}
\frac{(x+1)^2}{3x^2-2x+1}
\;\le\;8,
\qquad
x,y,z>0,\;x+y+z=1.
\]

Our next claim is the following one–variable estimate:

Claim.  For every \(x>0\),
\[
\frac{(x+1)^2}{3x^2-2x+1}
\;\le\;\frac{4}{3}+4x.
\tag{*}
\]
Assuming \((*)\), we sum it cyclically over \((x,y,z)\).  Since \((*)\) gives
\[
\frac{(x+1)^2}{3x^2-2x+1}\le\frac43+4x,
\quad
\frac{(y+1)^2}{3y^2-2y+1}\le\frac43+4y,
\quad
\frac{(z+1)^2}{3z^2-2z+1}\le\frac43+4z,
\]
adding these three inequalities yields
\[
\sum_{\rm cyc}
\frac{(x+1)^2}{3x^2-2x+1}
\;\le\;
3\cdot\frac{4}{3}+4(x+y+z)
\;=\;4+4\cdot1
\;=\;8,
\]
exactly as required.  It remains only to prove \((*)\).

Proof of the Claim.  
Fix \(x>0\).  Note first that
\[
3x^2-2x+1>0
\]
for all real \(x\), since its discriminant is \(\Delta =(-2)^2-4\cdot3\cdot1=4-12=-8<0\).  Hence we may multiply \((*)\) by \(3x^2-2x+1\) without changing the direction of the inequality.  We must prove
\[
(x+1)^2
\;\le\;
\Bigl(\tfrac{4}{3}+4x\Bigr)\,(3x^2-2x+1).
\]
Expand both sides:

Left–hand side:
\[
(x+1)^2 = x^2 + 2x +1.
\]

Right–hand side:
\[
\Bigl(\tfrac{4}{3}+4x\Bigr)(3x^2-2x+1)
=
\tfrac{4}{3}(3x^2-2x+1)
\;+\;4x(3x^2-2x+1).
\]
Compute each piece:
\[
\tfrac{4}{3}(3x^2-2x+1)
\;=\;4x^2-\tfrac{8}{3}x+\tfrac{4}{3},
\qquad
4x(3x^2-2x+1)
\;=\;12x^3-8x^2+4x.
\]
Hence
\[
\Bigl(\tfrac{4}{3}+4x\Bigr)(3x^2-2x+1)
=12x^3 \;-\;4x^2\;+\;\Bigl(4x-\tfrac{8}{3}x\Bigr)\;+\;\tfrac{4}{3}
=12x^3 -4x^2 +\tfrac{4}{3}x +\tfrac{4}{3}.
\]
Subtracting the left side \(x^2+2x+1\), we set
\[
T(x)
\;=\;
\bigl[\,(4/3+4x)(3x^2-2x+1)\bigr]\;-\;(x^2+2x+1)
\;=\;
12x^3-5x^2-\tfrac{2}{3}x+\tfrac{1}{3}.
\]
We must show \(T(x)\ge0\) for all \(x>0\).  To clear fractions, let
\[
P(x)=3\,T(x)
\;=\;
36x^3-15x^2-2x+1.
\]
A direct check shows \(P\bigl(\tfrac13\bigr)=0\).  Perform polynomial (or “synthetic”) division of \(P(x)\) by \((x-\tfrac13)\).  One finds
\[
P(x)
=
36\Bigl(x-\tfrac13\Bigr)^2\Bigl(x+\tfrac14\Bigr).
\]
Since for \(x>0\) both factors \((x-\tfrac13)^2\) and \((x+\tfrac14)\) are nonnegative, it follows that
\[
P(x)\;\ge\;0,
\]
hence \(T(x)=P(x)/3\ge0\), and therefore
\((x+1)^2\le(\tfrac43+4x)(3x^2-2x+1)\).  This completes the proof of \((*)\).

Putting everything together, we have shown
\[
\sum_{\rm cyc}
\frac{(x+1)^2}{3x^2-2x+1}\;\le\;8,
\]
and hence, by the normalization \(x=a/S,\) etc., the original inequality
\[
\frac{(2a+b+c)^2}{2a^2+(b+c)^2}
+\frac{(2b+c+a)^2}{2b^2+(c+a)^2}
+\frac{(2c+a+b)^2}{2c^2+(a+b)^2}
\;\le\;8
\]
follows.  Equality occurs precisely when \(a=b=c\).  □
