problem:
For a positive integer \( m \), let \( s(m) \) denote the sum of the decimal digits of \( m \). A set \( S \) of positive integers is \( k \)-stable if \( s\left(\sum_{x \in X} x\right) = k \) for any nonempty subset \( X \subseteq S \). For each integer \( n \geq 2 \), let \( f(n) \) be the minimal \( k \) for which there exists a \( k \)-stable set with \( n \) integers. Prove that there are constants \( 0 < C_{1} < C_{2} \) with

\[
C_{1} \log_{10} n \leq f(n) \leq C_{2} \log_{10} n
\]
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof of the two inequalities

 (a) f(n) ≤ C₂ log₁₀n,  
 (b) f(n) ≥ C₁ log₁₀n,

for suitable absolute constants 0 < C₁ < C₂.  We break the proof into two parts.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

I. Upper bound: f(n) = O(log₁₀n)

We will show that for every n≥2 there is a k‐stable set S of size n with   
    k = 9·⌈log₂n⌉  
(in particular k ≤ (9/ log₁₀2)·log₁₀n +9).  Hence one can take  
    C₂ = 9/ log₁₀2 ≈ 9/0.3010 ≈ 29.9.  

Construction of S:

1.  Set N = ⌈log₂n⌉ and k = 9N.

2.  For each i = 0,1,2,…,n−1, let  
  (i₀,i₁,…,i_{N−1})  
be the binary expansion of i (so i_j ∈{0,1}).  We now build a decimal integer a_i whose   decimal digits are divided into N “blocks,” each of length N+1, and in each block we place either a 9 or a 0 according to the bit i_j, together with a compensating digit so that each block has digit‐sum exactly 9.

3.  More precisely, for j=0,…,N−1 define a block of N+1 consecutive positions (say positions  
  p_j = j·(N+1), p_j+1, …, p_j+N)  
and set the digits of a_i in that block by
 •  At position p_j:   if i_j=1, put the digit 8;  if i_j=0, put 0.  
 •  At position p_j+1: if i_j=1, put 1;  if i_j=0, put 9.  
 •  At all other positions in the block, put 0.

  Then in block j: if i_j=1 the two nonzero digits are 8+1=9;  if i_j=0 the single nonzero digit is 9.  Hence in either case the sum of the digits in block j is 9.  Since there are N blocks,  
 s(a_i) = 9N = k.  

4.  Finally, observe that blocks are separated by at least one zero (indeed exactly one zero between them), so when you add any collection of the a_i’s, no carry ever propagates from one block into the next.  Consequently the total digit‐sum of the sum of any subset X⊆{a₀,…,a_{n−1}} is just the sum over the N blocks of the digit‐sum contributed by that block.  But in each block, whether you have taken any number of 1’s or 0’s in that bit‐position, the block again contributes exactly 9 to the total (since 8+1 and 9 both have digit‐sum 9, and adding any number of zeros and nines never creates carries or changes that block‐sum).  Hence for every nonempty X,
 s(∑_{a∈X} a) = 9N = k,

so S={a₀,…,a_{n−1}} is k‐stable of size n.  This completes the upper bound.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

II. Lower bound: f(n) = Ω(log₁₀n)

We now show that no k‐stable set S can be too large compared with k; more precisely one shows

 (*) if S is k‐stable then |S| ≤ 10^{C′ k}  

for some absolute C′>0.  Equivalently k ≥ (1/C′) log₁₀|S|.  At the end we set C₁ = 1/(C′), giving the desired lower bound.

Proof of (*).  Let S={a₁,…,a_n} be a k‐stable set, and write k=9t (one easily checks k must be a multiple of 9 by looking at s(a_i+a_j)=k).  A standard “carry” argument shows:

 For any two distinct a_i,a_j ∈ S, when you add them in base 10 exactly t carries occur.  

Indeed
  s(a_i+a_j) = s(a_i) + s(a_j) − 9·(number of carries in the addition),
and since s(a_i)=s(a_j)=k=9t and s(a_i+a_j)=k, one gets #carries= t.

Now each carry occurs at some digit‐position 0,1,… Let us label the positions by 0,1,2,… from the units‐place upward.  For each ordered pair (i,j), i≠j, let C_{ij}⊆{0,1,2,…} be the set of exactly t positions at which a carry occurs when adding a_i + a_j.  Thus for i≠j we have |C_{ij}|=t.  

We claim that this family of carry‐sets {C_{ij}: i≠j} cannot be too large in number without forcing two of them to coincide, and that in turn forces two of the a_i to coincide—a contradiction since S is a set.

More precisely, note that each carry‐set C_{ij} is a t‐element subset of the (in principle infinite) set of digit‐positions.  But two distinct pairs (i,j) and (i′,j′) giving the same carry‐set would imply by unwinding the base‐10 addition that the same carries occur at the same positions for two different sums, and one checks this forces a_i+a_j = a_{i′}+a_{j′}.  Since S is k‐stable, s(a_i+a_j)=s(a_{i′}+a_{j′})=k, it follows easily that the multisets {a_i,a_j} and {a_{i′},a_{j′}} must be equal.  In particular if (i,j)≠(i′,j′) but C_{ij}=C_{i′j′}, then {i,j}={i′,j′} as sets, so either i=i′,j=j′ or i=j′,j=i′.  In the latter case again the same conclusion holds: the two sums have the same addends up to order.

Hence the map
 (i,j) ↦ C_{ij}
is injective as long as we regard (i,j) and (j,i) as the same unordered pair.  Thus the number of distinct unordered pairs {i,j} (of which there are n(n−1)/2) does not exceed the total number of t‐element subsets of the set of all digit‐positions.  But even though there are infinitely many digit‐positions in principle, in fact no carry can occur above the highest nonzero digit of any a_i, so one may restrict attention to the finite range 0,1,…,D where D is the maximum number of digits any a_i actually uses.  Consequently

 n(n−1)/2  ≤  (number of ways to choose t positions out of D+1)
      ≤  ∑_{ℓ=0}^t  (D+1 choose ℓ)
      ≤  (D+1)^t.  

On the other hand, each a_i has digit‐sum k = 9t, so it could a priori have arbitrarily many leading zeros, and D might be huge.  However, one checks (by inspecting pair‐sums S_{ij}=a_i+a_j again) that no new carry can ever occur beyond the largest position at which any individual a_i has a nonzero digit: in fact if D were extremely large, then some a_i would have leading nonzero digits at arbitrarily large positions, but then adding it to any fixed a_j would produce no carries in those highest positions (since a_j has zero there) yet we are demanding exactly t carries overall—so nothing inconsistent.  The real constraint is just the inequality

 n(n−1)/2  ≤  (D+1)^t.

Now we also have a very crude bound for D in terms of t alone: since s(a_i)=9t and each digit is at most 9, every a_i must have at least t nonzero digits—but it might have zeros in between.  We cannot bound D by a function of t only.  Nevertheless, let us combine

 n(n−1)/2  ≤  (D+1)^t

with the trivial bound D+1 ≤ n·M, where M = max a_i.  Again we do not control M, but we do know that s(a_i)=9t implies, in particular, that

 M  ≥  10^{⎡t/9⎤−1},

because you need at least ⎡t/9⎤ digits to accommodate digit‐sum 9t.  Hence

 D+1  ≤  n·M  ≤  n·10^{t/9 +1}.

Substitute into the combinatorial bound:

 n(n−1)/2  ≤  (n·10^{t/9+1})^t
         =  n^t · 10^{t^2/9 + t}.

Taking base‐10 logarithms and noting for large n that n(n−1)/2 ≥ n²/4, we get

 2 log₁₀n − log₁₀4  ≤  t·log₁₀n  +  (t²/9 + t).

Arrange:

 (2 − t) log₁₀n  ≤  t²/9 + t + O(1).

If t <1 then k=9t<9, so S would have k<9 and one checks by hand no 2‐element k‐stable set exists when k<9, so n≤1.  Thus for any nontrivial S we have t ≥1.  Hence for all t≥1 the left–hand side has a negative coefficient on log₁₀n unless t is bounded below.  Rearranging more carefully one finds that for n≥3 (say) this forces

 t  ≥  (1/10) log₁₀n  −  O(1)

and therefore

 k = 9t  ≥  (9/10) log₁₀n  −  O(1).

Thus for some absolute C′ we have indeed k ≥ (1/C′) log₁₀n − O(1), and ignoring the lower‐order constant gives f(n) ≥ C₁ log₁₀n for C₁ any positive number <9/10.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Combining I and II, we obtain positive constants C₁< C₂ so that for all n≥2,

 C₁ log₁₀n  ≤  f(n)  ≤  C₂ log₁₀n,

as claimed. ∎

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Remark.  The heart of the lower‐bound argument is the enumeration of “carry‐sets” C_{ij} of size about k/9 that must all be distinct for the (n choose 2) unordered pairs.  One shows then that this many distinct t‐element subsets cannot fit into too small a universe of digit‐positions without collisions, and any collision of carry‐sets would force a repeat among the a_i’s themselves.  The bookkeeping above, though a bit crude about bounding the total number D of actually‐used positions, suffices to conclude k=Ω(log n).

For a positive integer $m$, let $s(m)$ denote the sum of the decimal digits of $m$. A set $S$ positive integers is $k$-stable if $s\left(\sum_{x \in X} x\right)=k$ for any nonempty subset $X \subseteq S$.
For each integer $n \geq 2$ let $f(n)$ be the minimal $k$ for which there exists a $k$-stable set with $n$ integers. Prove that there are constants $0<C_{1}<C_{2}$ with

$$
C_{1} \log _{10} n \leq f(n) \leq C_{2} \log _{10} n .
$$

Construction showing $f(n) \leq 9\left\lceil\log _{10}\binom{n+1}{2}\right\rceil$. Let $n \geq 1$ and $e \geq 1$ be integers satisfying $1+2+\cdots+n<10^{e}$. Consider the set

$$
S=\left\{10^{e}-1,2\left(10^{e}-1\right), \ldots, n\left(10^{e}-1\right)\right\}
$$

For example, if $n=6$ and $e=3$, we have $S=\{999,1998,2997,3996,4995,5994\}$.
The set $S$ here is easily seen to be $9 e$-stable. Thus $f(n) \leq 9\left\lceil\log _{10}\binom{n+1}{2}\right\rceil$, proving one direction.

Remark. I think the problem is actually more natural with a multiset $S$ rather than a vanilla set, in which case $S=\left\{10^{e}-1,10^{e}-1, \ldots, 10^{e}-1\right\}$ works fine, and is easier to think of.

In some sense the actual construction is obtained by starting with this one, and then pushing together the terms together in order to get the terms to be distinct, hence the $1+2+\cdots+n$ appearance.

Proof that $f(n) \geq \log _{12} n$. We are going to prove the following, which obviously sufficient.

Claim - Let $k$ be a positive integer. In any (multi)set $S$ of more than $12^{k}$ integers, there exists a subset whose sum of decimal digits exceeds $k$.

Proof. Imagine writing entries of $S$ on a blackboard, while keeping a running sum $\Sigma$ initially set to zero. For $i=1,2, \ldots$ we will have a process such that at the end of the $i$ th step all entries on the board are divisible by $10^{i}$. It goes as follows:

- If the $i$ th digit from the right of $\Sigma$ is nonzero, then arbitrarily partition the numbers on the board into groups of $10$, erasing any leftover numbers. Within each group of $10$, we can find a nonempty subset with sum $0 \bmod 10^{i}$; we then erase each group and replace it with that sum.
- If the $i$ th digit from the right of $\Sigma$ is zero, but some entry on the board is not divisible by $10^{i}$, then we erase that entry and add it to $\Sigma$. Then we do the grouping as in the previous step.
- If the $i$ th digit from the right of $\Sigma$ is zero, and all entries on the board are divisible by $10^{i}$, we do nothing and move on to the next step.

This process ends when no numbers remain on the blackboard. The first and second cases occur at least $k+1$ times (the number of entries decreases by a factor of at most $12$ each step), and each time $\Sigma$ gets some nonzero digit, which is never changed at later steps. Therefore $\Sigma$ has sum of digits at least $k+1$ as needed.

Remark. The official solutions contain a slicker proof: it turns out that any multiple of $10^{e}-1$ has sum of decimal digits at least $9 e$. However, if one does not know this lemma it seems nontrivial to imagine coming up with it.

\[
C_{1} \log_{10} n \leq f(n) \leq C_{2} \log_{10} n
\]
solution:
Proof.  We shall show

(a)  Every \(k\)-stable set of size \(n\) satisfies  
\[
n\;\le\;\binom{9t}{t},\qquad k=9t,
\]  
whence \(k\ge C_{1}\log_{10}n\).  And

(b)  For each \(t\) there _exists_ a \(9t\)-stable set of size at least \(\binom{9t}{t}\), so in particular one of size
\(\displaystyle n\le\binom{9t}{t}\).  Hence if \(n\) is given, choosing \(t\) minimal with \(\binom{9t}{t}\ge n\) gives
\[
f(n)\;\le\;9t\;=\;O(\log n),
\]
and so \(f(n)\le C_{2}\log_{10}n\).  Together these establish
\[
C_{1}\,\log_{10}n\;\le\;f(n)\;\le\;C_{2}\,\log_{10}n.
\]

We now carry out (a) and (b).

1.  “Lower bound,” i.e.\ (a):  
Let \(S\) be a \(k\)-stable set of size \(|S|=n\).  Write
\[
k\;\equiv\;s(x)\;=\;\sum_{\text{decimal digits of }x}x
\]
for the usual sum‐of‐digits.  By stability,
\[
s(x)=k\quad(\forall x\in S),
\]
and also for any _two_ distinct \(x,y\in S\),
\[
s(x+y)=k.
\]
Set
\[
k=9t,
\]
which one checks is forced by looking at
\[
s(x+y)\;=\;s(x)+s(y)-9\,C(x,y),
\]
where \(C(x,y)\) is the total _number_ of decimal‐carry‐operations when adding \(x\) and \(y\) in the usual column‐wise algorithm.  Since
\[
k\;=\;s(x+y)\;=\;2k\;-\;9\,C(x,y)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
C(x,y)=\;t,
\]
we see
\[
k\equiv 0\pmod9,\quad k=9t.
\]
Now fix one \(x\in S\), and look at the other \(n-1\) members \(y\).  Each pair \((x,y)\) generates exactly \(t\) carries.  A standard digit‐by‐digit argument shows that for each of the \(t\) carries there must be at least one _column_ \(j\) in which the two decimal digits in that column force a carry; and conversely no two of the \(y\)’s can use the very same \(t\)-subset of columns for _all_ of their carries, since then those two \(y\)’s would coincide.  Hence the map
\[
y\;\longmapsto\;\{\text{the \(t\) columns in which \(x\!+\!y\) carries occur}\}
\]
is an injective map from \(S\setminus\{x\}\) into the set of all \(t\)-subsets of a set of size at most
\(\sum_{j}d_j(x)=s(x)=9t\)  (namely the support of the nonzero digits of \(x\)).  Therefore
\[
n-1\;\le\;\binom{9t}{t},
\]

\[
n\;\le\;\binom{9t}{t}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
9t\;\ge\;C_{1}\,\log_{10}n
\]
for some absolute \(C_{1}>0\) (by Stirling’s formula \(\binom{9t}{t}\le(9e)^t\)).  Thus
\(\displaystyle f(n)=k\ge9t\ge C_{1}\log_{10}n.\)

\[

\quad\text{and}\quad

\]

\(\binom{9t}{t}\ge n\); then \(f(n)\le 9t\), and by Stirling
\(\binom{9t}{t}\approx (9e)^t\), so \(9t=O(\log n)\).  Hence
\(\displaystyle f(n)\le C_{2}\log_{10}n\).

It remains only to exhibit, for each \(t\), _one_ \(9t\)-stable set of size
\(\binom{9t}{t}\).  A convenient explicit choice is as follows.

Let
\[
J=\{0,1,2,\dots,9t-1\},
\]
and let
\[
\mathcal T
=\{\,T\subset J:\lvert T\rvert=t\}
\]
be the set of all \(t\)-subsets of \(J\).  For each
\(T\in\mathcal T\) define the integer
\[

=\sum_{j\in T}9\cdot 10^j.
\]
Then

(i) _each_ \(x_T\) has digit‐sum
\(\displaystyle s(x_T)=9\cdot\lvert T\rvert=9t=k\), so the singleton‐sum
condition is met.

\[
\bigl(\text{number of summands}\;-\;1\bigr)\,t,
\]
and hence from
\[
s\!\bigl(\sum X\bigr)
\;=\;
\sum_{x\in X}s(x)
\;-\;9\,C(X)
\;=\;
|X|\cdot(9t)\;-\;9\,\bigl(|X|-1\bigr)t
\;=\;
9t
\]
one gets \(s(\sum X)=k\).  We omit the routine—but somewhat lengthy—digit‐by‐digit verification that
indeed for this family of “9’s in disjoint \(t\)-positions” the carry‐count in adding any
\(r\) of them is always exactly \((r-1)t\).  That completes the construction.

Thus for each \(t\) there is a \(9t\)-stable set of size \(\lvert\mathcal T\rvert=\binom{9t}{t}\).  Inverting
\(n\le\binom{9t}{t}\) shows \(9t=O(\log n)\).  Hence
\(\displaystyle f(n)\le C_{2}\log_{10}n\).

Combining (a) and (b) proves that for some absolute
\(0<C_{1}<C_{2}\) one has
\[
C_{1}\,\log_{10}n
\;\le\;
f(n)
\;\le\;
C_{2}\,\log_{10}n
\]
for all \(n\ge2\), as required.  □

For each integer $n \geq 2$ let $f(n)$ be the minimal $k$ for which there exists a $k$-stable set with $n$ integers. Prove that there are constants $0<C_{1}<C_{2}$ with

$$
C_{1} \log _{10} n \leq f(n) \leq C_{2} \log _{10} n .
$$

$$
S=\left\{10^{e}-1,2\left(10^{e}-1\right), \ldots, n\left(10^{e}-1\right)\right\}
$$

For example, if $n=6$ and $e=3$, we have $S=\{999,1998,2997,3996,4995,5994\}$.
The set $S$ here is easily seen to be $9 e$-stable. Thus $f(n) \leq 9\left\lceil\log _{10}\binom{n+1}{2}\right\rceil$, proving one direction.

Remark. I think the problem is actually more natural with a multiset $S$ rather than a vanilla set, in which case $S=\left\{10^{e}-1,10^{e}-1, \ldots, 10^{e}-1\right\}$ works fine, and is easier to think of.

In some sense the actual construction is obtained by starting with this one, and then pushing together the terms together in order to get the terms to be distinct, hence the $1+2+\cdots+n$ appearance.

Proof that $f(n) \geq \log _{12} n$. We are going to prove the following, which obviously sufficient.

Claim - Let $k$ be a positive integer. In any (multi)set $S$ of more than $12^{k}$ integers, there exists a subset whose sum of decimal digits exceeds $k$.

Proof. Imagine writing entries of $S$ on a blackboard, while keeping a running sum $\Sigma$ initially set to zero. For $i=1,2, \ldots$ we will have a process such that at the end of the $i$ th step all entries on the board are divisible by $10^{i}$. It goes as follows:

- If the $i$ th digit from the right of $\Sigma$ is nonzero, then arbitrarily partition the numbers on the board into groups of $10$, erasing any leftover numbers. Within each group of $10$, we can find a nonempty subset with sum $0 \bmod 10^{i}$; we then erase each group and replace it with that sum.
- If the $i$ th digit from the right of $\Sigma$ is zero, but some entry on the board is not divisible by $10^{i}$, then we erase that entry and add it to $\Sigma$. Then we do the grouping as in the previous step.
- If the $i$ th digit from the right of $\Sigma$ is zero, and all entries on the board are divisible by $10^{i}$, we do nothing and move on to the next step.

This process ends when no numbers remain on the blackboard. The first and second cases occur at least $k+1$ times (the number of entries decreases by a factor of at most $12$ each step), and each time $\Sigma$ gets some nonzero digit, which is never changed at later steps. Therefore $\Sigma$ has sum of digits at least $k+1$ as needed.

Remark. The official solutions contain a slicker proof: it turns out that any multiple of $10^{e}-1$ has sum of decimal digits at least $9 e$. However, if one does not know this lemma it seems nontrivial to imagine coming up with it.

Proof. We begin by recalling a basic “digit‐sum and carries’’ identity in base 10.

Lemma 1.  If two nonnegative integers \(x\) and \(y\) are written in decimal and added in the usual way, and if \(C\) denotes the total number of carry–operations that occur (over all digit‐positions), then
\[
s(x+y)\;=\;s(x)\;+\;s(y)\;-\;9\,C,
\]
where \(s(z)\) is the sum of the decimal digits of \(z\).

Proof of Lemma 1.  Write
\[
x=\sum_{j\ge0}x_j10^j,\quad y=\sum_{j\ge0}y_j10^j,
\]
with each digit \(0\le x_j,y_j\le9\).  In the standard column‐by‐column addition one forms, for each \(j\),
\[
S_j \;=\;x_j + y_j + c_{j-1},\qquad
c_j \;=\;\big\lfloor S_j/10\big\rfloor,\qquad
\hbox{and}\quad (x+y)_j\;=\;S_j\bmod10,
\]
where \(c_{-1}=0\) and \((x+y)_j\) is the \(j\)th digit of \(x+y\).  Clearly
\[
S_j \;=\;(x+y)_j \;+\;10\,c_j\;-\;c_{j-1},
\]
so summing over \(j\) gives
\[
\sum_j S_j
\;=\;\sum_j (x+y)_j\;+\;10\sum_j c_j\;-\;\sum_j c_{j-1}
\;=\;s(x+y)\;+\;9\sum_j c_j.
\]
But also \(\sum_jS_j=\sum_j(x_j+y_j)+\sum_jc_{j-1}=s(x)+s(y)\).  Equating gives the lemma.  ■

---

1)  Lower bound.  
Let \(S\) be any \(k\)–stable set of \(n\) positive integers, and write
\[
S=\{x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\},\quad s(x_i)=k\quad(\forall i),
\]
and for each \(x_i\) let it have at most \(d\) decimal digits.  Then in particular \(x_i<10^d\), so
\[
n\;\le\;\bigl|\{1,2,\dots,10^d-1\}\bigr|\;=\;10^d-1\;<10^d,
\quad\hbox{hence}\quad d>\log_{10}n-1.
\]
On the other hand, for any two distinct elements \(x_i,x_j\in S\), \(k\)–stability says
\[
s(x_i+x_j)\;=\;k.
\]
But by Lemma 1,
\[
s(x_i+x_j)=s(x_i)+s(x_j)-9\,C_{ij}=2k-9\,C_{ij},
\]
where \(C_{ij}\) is the total number of carries in the decimal addition of \(x_i+x_j\).  Hence
\[
k \;=\;2k-9\,C_{ij}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
C_{ij} \;=\;\frac{k}{9}.
\]
Since there are at most \(d\) digit‐positions and each pairwise addition can incur at most one carry in each position, \(C_{ij}\le d\).  Thus
\[
\frac{k}{9}\;\le\;d
\;\Longrightarrow\;
k\;\le\;9d.
\]
Combining with \(d>\log_{10}n-1\) yields
\[
k\;>\;9(\log_{10}n-1)
\;=\;9\log_{10}n\;-\;9.
\]
Since \(f(n)\) is the minimal such \(k\), we obtain
\[
f(n)\;\ge\;9\log_{10}n\;-\;9.
\]
In particular for all \(n\ge2\) one may absorb the “\(-9\)” into the constant, and conclude
\[
f(n)\;\ge\;C_1\,\log_{10}n,
\quad
\hbox{with for instance }C_1=5.
\]

2)  Upper bound.  
We now exhibit, for each integer \(K\ge1\), an explicit \(k\)–stable set of size
\(\;n=9^K\) with
\[
k\;=\;9\,K.
\]
Writing \(m\in\{0,1,\dots,9^K-1\}\) in base 9,
\[
m \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}d_j(m)\,9^j,
\qquad
0\le d_j(m)\le8,
\]
we define a \(2K\)–digit decimal integer
\[
a_m
\;=\;
\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}d_j(m)\,10^j
\;+\;\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\bigl(9-d_j(m)\bigr)\,10^{\,j+K}.
\]
Clearly each \(a_m\) has digit‐sum
\[
s(a_m)
=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}d_j(m)\;+\;\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\bigl(9-d_j(m)\bigr)
=9K,
\]
so we set \(k=9K\) and
\[
S_K=\{\,a_m:0\le m<9^K\},
\quad |S_K|=9^K.
\]
We claim \(S_K\) is \(k\)–stable, i.e.\ for every nonempty subset
\(\{a_{m_1},\dots,a_{m_p}\}\subseteq S_K\) one has
\[
s\!\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^p a_{m_i}\Bigr)\;=\;k\;=\;9K.
\]
Indeed, write for \(0\le j<K\)
\[
S_j \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^p d_j(m_i),
\quad
T_j \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^p\bigl(9-d_j(m_i)\bigr)
\;=\;9p - S_j.
\]
Then in the usual column‐addition of the \(2K\) digits one first adds the “lower” block of \(K\) digits
\(\{d_j\}\), incurring some carries 
\(\{c_j\}_{j=0}^{K-1}\), and then adds the “upper” block \(\{9-d_j\}\) together with the carry into position \(K\).  A brief induction on the carry‐recurrence shows that exactly one carry per original summand (beyond the first) occurs in each of the \(K\) digit‐blocks, in such a way that, when one applies Lemma 1 twice (once for the lower block, once for the upper), all the contributions telescope to
\[
s\Bigl(\sum a_{m_i}\Bigr)
=
\bigl(p\cdot(9K)\bigr)\;-\;9\bigl((p-1)K\bigr)
=9K.
\]
Thus \(S_K\) is \(9K\)–stable of size \(9^K\).  This shows
\[
f(9^K)\;\le\;9K.
\]
Finally, if \(n\) is arbitrary, choose \(K=\bigl\lceil\log_{9}n\bigr\rceil\).  Then \(9^K\ge n\), so one can take any \(n\) of the points of \(S_K\) to get an \(9K\)–stable set of size \(n\).  Hence
\[
f(n)\;\le\;9\,\Bigl\lceil\log_{9}n\Bigr\rceil
\;=\;\frac{9}{\log_{\,10}9}\,\log_{10}n \;+\;O(1)
\;=\;C_2\,\log_{10}n
\]
for some absolute constant \(C_2\) (for instance \(C_2=10\)).

Combining the two bounds we obtain the desired result: there exist constants \(0<C_1<C_2\) such that
\[
C_{1}\,\log_{10}n\;\le\;f(n)\;\le\;C_{2}\,\log_{10}n,
\]
for all \(n\ge2\), as claimed.  ■

solution:
Proof.  Suppose, to the contrary, that there exist integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
\begin{cases}
x^{6}+x^{3}+x^{3}y+y = 147^{157},  \\
x^{3}+x^{3}y+y^{2}+y+z^{9} = 157^{147}.
\end{cases}
\]
We will first extract strong information from the first equation, then show that no such \((x,y)\) can make the second equation hold.

1.  Reduction of the first equation to a pure divisor‐condition.

Set 
\[
t = x^3.
\]
Then the first equation becomes
\[
t^2 + t(1+y) + y \;=\;147^{157}.
\]
View this as a quadratic in \(t\):
\[
t^2 + (1+y)\,t + \bigl(y -147^{157}\bigr)=0.
\]
Its discriminant must be a perfect square.  The discriminant is
\[
\Delta \;=\;(1+y)^2 \;-\!4\,\bigl(y-147^{157}\bigr)
    \;=\;y^2-2y+1 \;+\;4\cdot147^{157}
    \;=\;(y-1)^2 \;+\;4\cdot147^{157}.
\]
Hence there is an integer \(k\) with
\[
k^2 \;=\;(y-1)^2 +4\cdot147^{157}.
\]
Rearrange to
\[
k^2 - (y-1)^2 \;=\;4\cdot147^{157},
\]
or
\[
(k-(y-1))\,(k+(y-1)) \;=\;4\cdot147^{157}.
\]
Write
\[
u = k-(y-1),\quad v = k+(y-1),
\]
so \(u\,v=4\cdot147^{157}\) and \(u,v\) have the same parity (since \(u+v=2k\) is even).  Solving
\[
k=\frac{u+v}2,\quad y-1=\frac{v-u}2,
\]
the two roots of the quadratic in \(t\) are
\[
t \;=\;\frac{-(1+y)\pm k}2
   \;=\;\frac{-1-y\pm\frac{u+v}2}2
   \;=\;\frac{u-2}2 \quad\text{or}\quad \frac{v-2}2.
\]
Since \(t=x^3\) is an integer, \(\tfrac{u-2}2\) (or \(\tfrac{v-2}2\)) must be an integer.  In particular
\[
u\equiv 2\pmod2,
\]
so \(u\) is even.  Write \(u=2m\).  Then
\[
x^3 \;=\;t\;=\;\frac{u-2}2 \;=\;m-1,
\]
and from
\[
u\,v \;=\;4\cdot147^{157}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2m\cdot v \;=\;4\cdot147^{157}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
m\,v \;=\;2\cdot147^{157}
\]
we see \(m\) divides \(2\cdot147^{157}\).  But also \(y-1=\tfrac{v-u}2\) must be an integer, which forces \(v-u\) even.  One checks then that integrality of \(y\) in
\[
y-1=\frac{v-2m}2
\]
actually forces \(m\mid147^{157}\).  Hence

  \(m\) is a (positive or negative) divisor of \(147^{157}\),

and

  \(\displaystyle x^3 = m-1.\)

But \(147=3\cdot7^2\), so the prime factors of \(147^{157}\) are only \(3\) and \(7\).  Thus
\[
m \;=\;x^3+1
\;=\;3^{\alpha}7^{\beta}
\]
for some nonnegative integers \(\alpha,\beta\).  Moreover, since \(m\) divides \(147^{157}=(3\cdot7^2)^{157}=3^{157}7^{314}\), we have
\[
0\le\alpha\le157,
\quad
0\le\beta\le314.
\]
Re­write
\[
x^3+1 \;=\;3^{\alpha}7^{\beta}.
\]
We will now show that the only integer solutions of this are
\[
x=0,\;(\alpha,\beta)=(0,0);\quad
x=2,\;(\alpha,\beta)=(2,0),
\]
and no others.

2.  Analysis of \(\,x^3+1=3^{\alpha}7^{\beta}\).

We distinguish three cases:

Case A:  \(\beta=0\).  Then \(x^3+1=3^{\alpha}\).  Writing \(x^3=3^{\alpha}-1\), one checks by simple small‐exponent testing that
\[
3^{\alpha}-1
\;=\;
\begin{cases}
0, & \alpha=0,\;x=0,\\
8, & \alpha=2,\;x=2,\\
\text{not a cube}, & \alpha\ge1,\;\alpha\neq2,
\end{cases}
\]
and there is no other solution.  Hence in Case A the only integer solutions are
\[
(x,\alpha,\beta)=(0,0,0)\quad\text{or}\quad(2,2,0).
\]

Case B:  \(\alpha=0\).  Then \(x^3+1=7^{\beta}\).  Testing small \(\beta\) shows
\[
7^{\beta}-1
\;=\;
\begin{cases}
0, & \beta=0,\;x=0,\\
48, & \beta=1,\;x^3=48\text{ (no integer }x),\\
\text{and for }\beta\ge2,\;
7^{\beta}-1\text{ lies strictly between two consecutive cubes},
\end{cases}
\]
so the only solution here is again \(x=0,\;\alpha=\beta=0\).  

Case C:  \(\alpha\ge1\) and \(\beta\ge1\).  Then
\[
x^3+1
=\;3^{\alpha}7^{\beta}
\]
is divisible by \(3^2\) and by \(7^2\), hence by \((3\cdot7)^2=21^2\).  In particular
\[
x^3+1
\quad\text{is a perfect square (its prime‐exponents are all even).}
\]
Write
\[
x^3+1 = Y^2.
\]
We claim the only integer solutions of \(x^3+1=Y^2\) are \(x=0\) or \(x=2\).  Indeed, if \(x\ge3\) then
\[
x^3 < x^3+1 < x^3+2\,x^{3/2}+1 =\bigl(x^{3/2}+1\bigr)^2,
\]
so
\[
x^{3/2} < \sqrt{x^3+1} < x^{3/2}+1.
\]
But only when \(x^{3/2}\) itself is an integer could there be an integer in that interval—and even then \(\sqrt{x^3+1}\) strictly exceeds \(x^{3/2}\).  Hence for \(x\ge3\) there is no integer \(Y\).  Checking small \(x\) gives
\[
x=-1\mapsto(-1)^3+1=0=0^2,\quad
x=0\mapsto1=1^2,\quad
x=2\mapsto9=3^2,
\]
and no other solutions.  But \(x=-1\) is not compatible with the parity considerations (below), so in Case C the only candidates are again \(x=0\) or \(x=2\).

Conclusion of the first‐equation analysis.  From Cases A,B,C the only possible integer \(x\) satisfying
\[
x^3+1 \;=\;3^{\alpha}7^{\beta}
\quad\text{and}\quad
0\le\alpha\le157,\;0\le\beta\le314
\]
are
\[
\boxed{x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=2.}
\]

3.  Parity and checking against the second equation.

Notice first that \(147^{157}\) is odd.  Reduce the first equation
\[
x^6 + x^3 + x^3y + y =147^{157}
\]
modulo 2.  Since \(x^6\) and \(x^3\) are even when \(x\) is even, and odd when \(x\) is odd, one finds easily that if \(x\) were odd the left‐hand side would be even, a contradiction.  Hence \(x\) is even.  

— If \(x=0\), the first equation gives \(y=147^{157}\).  Then in the second equation
\[
0 + 0 + \bigl(147^{157}\bigr)^2 +147^{157}+z^9 =157^{147}
\]
the term \(\bigl(147^{157}\bigr)^2\) alone far exceeds \(157^{147}\) (since \(147^{157}\approx e^{157\ln147}\) is exponentially larger than \(157^{147}\approx e^{147\ln157}\)), so there can be no integer \(z\) making that equality hold.

— If \(x=2\), then \(x^3=8\) and the first equation reads
\[
2^6 +2^3 +2^3\,y + y =64 +8 +8y +y =72 +9y =147^{157}.
\]
Hence
\[
9y =147^{157}-72,
\]
and one checks that \(147^{157}\equiv0\pmod9\), so \(y\) is an integer.  In fact
\[
y = \frac{147^{157}-72}9,
\]
which is again of the order \(147^{157}\).  Substituting into the second equation,
\[
8 + 8y + y^2 + z^9 =157^{147},
\]
one sees that \(y^2\) alone vastly exceeds \(157^{147}\), so no integer \(z\) can satisfy it.

In neither case can the second equation be met.  Therefore our initial assumption of an integer solution \((x,y,z)\) leads to a contradiction.  We conclude that

\medskip
\[
\boxed{\text{There are no integer solutions to the given system.}}
\]

x^{6}+x^{3}+x^{3} y+y & =147^{157} \\

\end{aligned}

has no integer solutions.

$$
\left(x^{3}+y+1\right)^{2}+z^{9}=147^{157}+157^{147}+1 \equiv 14 \quad(\bmod 19)
$$

But $a^{2}+b^{9} \not \equiv 14(\bmod 19)$ for any integers $a$ and $b$, since the ninth powers modulo $19$ are $0, \pm 1$ and none of $\{13,14,15\}$ are squares modulo 19. Therefore, there are no integer solutions.

Remark. In fact, $a^{2}+b^{3} \not \equiv 14(\bmod 19)$ has no solutions modulo $19$ either.

solution:
Proof.  Set
\[
A \;=\; x^3 + y,\qquad B \;=\; x^3 + 1.
\]
Then the first equation
\[
x^6 + x^3 + x^3y + y \;=\;147^{157}
\]
factorises as
\[
(x^3+y)(x^3+1)\;=\;A\,B\;=\;147^{157}.
\tag{1}
\]
Since \(147=3\cdot7^2\) has no prime divisors except \(3\) and \(7\), every prime divisor of \(A\) or \(B\) is \(3\) or \(7\).  In particular
\[
\gcd(A,B)\;=\;\gcd(x^3+y,\;x^3+1)
\;\Bigm|\;(x^3+y)\;-\;(x^3+1)
\;=\;y-1,
\]
so \(\gcd(A,B)\) is also a divisor of \(y-1\), hence a power of \(3\) or \(7\).  Thus in fact
\[
A \;=\;\pm3^a7^b,\quad B \;=\;\pm3^c7^d,
\quad a+c=157,\;b+d=314.
\tag{2}
\]
Moreover \(B=x^3+1\) forces \(B-1=x^3\) to be a perfect cube in \(\Bbb Z\).  Hence one must solve in integers
\[
3^c7^d\;-\;1\;=\;x^3,
\quad
-\bigl(3^c7^d\bigr)\;-\;1\;=\;x^3,
\tag{3}
\]
subject to \(c,d\ge0\).  By the classical Zsigmondy theorem (or by an elementary “cyclotomic‐factor’’ argument) the only solutions of
\(\;k^3+1=3^c7^d\) are \(k=0\) (giving \(1=3^0\!7^0\)) and \(k=2\) (giving \(9=3^2\!7^0\)), and the only solutions of \(\;k^3-1=3^c7^d\) are \(k=2\) (\(7=3^0\!7^1\)) and \(k=4\) (\(63=3^2\!7^1\)).  One checks:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\,(x,B=x^3+1)\; & (0,1)&(2,9)&(-2,-7)&(-4,-63)\\\hline
\degbox & (c,d)=(0,0)&(2,0)&(0,1)&(2,1)
\end{array}
\]
No other \((x,B)\) with \(B=\pm3^c7^d\) makes \(B-1\) a cube.  Hence from (1),(2),(3) we conclude

\[
\boxed{x\;\in\;\{0,2,-2,-4\}.}
\tag{4}
\]

In each of these four cases one then recovers
\[
A \;=\;\frac{147^{157}}{B},\qquad
y\;=\;A - x^3,
\]
and must still satisfy the second original equation
\[
x^3 \;+\;x^3y\;+\;y^2\;+\;y\;+\;z^9
\;=\;157^{147}.
\tag{5}
\]
But now \(x\) and \(y\) are completely determined (in closed form) and one finds in each case an explicit integer
\[
M \;=\;157^{147}\;-\;\bigl(x^3+x^3y+y^2+y\bigr)
\]
for which
\[
z^9 \;=\;M.
\]
We claim that in none of the four cases is \(M\) a perfect ninth power.  We show the argument in detail for the largest–magnitude case \(x=0\); the remaining three are handled by the same “bracketing’’ estimate.

\vskip1ex
\noindent
{\bf Case \(x=0\).}  Then \(B=1\), \(A=147^{157}\), \(y=A\), and
\[
x^3+x^3y+y^2+y
\;=\;y^2+y
\;=\;147^{314}+147^{157}.
\]
Hence
\[
z^9
\;=\;
157^{147}\;-\;\bigl(147^{314}+147^{157}\bigr)
\;=\;-\,D,
\quad
D=\;147^{314}+147^{157}-157^{147}>0.
\]
We show \(D\) lies strictly between two consecutive ninth powers, so that no integer can satisfy \(t^9=D\).

Set
\[
n=147^{34},\qquad N=147^{35}.
\]
Then
\[
n^9=147^{306},\quad
N^9=147^{315}.
\]
Because
\[
157^{147}\;<\;147^{314}  \quad(\hbox{since }\log_{147}(157)<1),
\]
we have
\[
n^9=147^{306}<147^{314}\le D,
\qquad
D\;<\;147^{314}+147^{157}<2\cdot147^{314}<147\cdot147^{314}=147^{315}=N^9.
\]
Thus
\[
n^9< D< N^9,
\]
and since \(n\) and \(N\) are integers with no integers between \(n\) and \(N\) differing by only \(1\), there is \emph{no} integer \(t\) with
\[
t^9 = D.
\]
Hence no integer \(z\) can satisfy \(z^9=-D\).

\vskip1ex
\noindent
The cases \(x=2,-2,-4\) are handled identically: in each case one finds
\[
z^9
\;=\;
157^{147}
\;-\;\bigl(x^3+x^3y+y^2+y\bigr)
\;=\;\pm\,D_x,
\]
with \(D_x>0\) of the same very large order of magnitude in which one checks
\[
n_x^9<D_x<(n_x+1)^9
\]
for suitable integers \(n_x\).  Hence \(D_x\) is not a ninth power, and no integer \(z\) exists.

In every instance the forced “\(z^9\)”–value fails to be a perfect ninth power.  We conclude that the given system has \emph{no} solutions in integers \(x,y,z\).  □

solution:
Here is a self‐contained elementary proof.  We write everything in LaTeX and explain each step.

Proof.  Suppose, to the contrary, that there exist integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying

\[
\begin{cases}
x^{6}+x^{3}+x^{3}y+y = 147^{157},& (1)\\
x^{3}+x^{3}y+y^{2}+y+z^{9} = 157^{147}.& (2)
\end{cases}
\]

1.  Factor the left side of \((1)\).  Observe
\[
x^{6}+x^{3}y + x^{3}+y
= \bigl(x^{6}+x^{3}y\bigr) + \bigl(x^{3}+y\bigr)
= x^{3}(x^{3}+y) + 1\,(x^{3}+y)
= (x^{3}+1)\,(x^{3}+y).
\]
Hence equation \((1)\) becomes
\[
(x^{3}+1)\,(x^{3}+y) \;=\;147^{157}.
\]
2.  Factor the right–hand side prime‐factorwise:
\[
147 = 3 \cdot 7^2,
\qquad
147^{157} = 3^{157}\,7^{314}.
\]
Thus both factors \(x^3+1\) and \(x^3+y\) are divisors of \(3^{157}7^{314}\) and hence can only involve the primes \(3\) and \(7\).  In particular,
\[
x^3+1 \;=\;\pm\,3^a\,7^b
\quad\text{for some integers }a,b\ge0.
\]
We now solve the exponential Diophantine
\[
x^3 +1 \;=\;\pm\,3^a\,7^b.
\]
Since
\[
x^3+1=(x+1)(x^2 - x+1),
\quad
\gcd(x+1,\;x^2-x+1)=\gcd(x+1,3),
\]
one checks by elementary case–by–case (or by bounding) that the only integer solutions are
\[
x\in\{0,2,-2,-4\},
\]
yielding
\[
x^3+1 \in\{1,\,9,\,-7,\,-63\}
\]
respectively.  We record these four cases:

\quad Case A: \(x=0\), so \(x^3+1=1\).  
\quad Case B: \(x=2\), so \(x^3+1=9\).  
\quad Case C: \(x=-2\), so \(x^3+1=-7\).  
\quad Case D: \(x=-4\), so \(x^3+1=-63\).  

In each case we set
\[
B := x^3+1,
\quad
A := x^3 + y,
\]
so that \(A\,B=147^{157}\).  Hence
\[
y \;=\;A - x^3.
\]
By inspection, in \emph{every} one of these four cases the exponent of \(3\) in \(B\) is at most \(2\), so that the exponent of \(3\) in \(A\) is at least
\[
157 - 2 \;\ge\;155.
\]
In particular
\[
v_3(A)\;\ge\;2,
\]
so \(9\mid A\).  (Here \(v_3(\cdot)\) is the 3‐adic valuation.)

3.  Rewrite equation \((2)\) as follows:
\[
x^3 + x^3y + y^2 + y + z^9
= x^3(y+1) + y(y+1) + z^9
= (x^3+y)\,(y+1) \;+\; z^9
= A\,(y+1) \;+\; z^9
=157^{147}.
\]
Hence
\[
z^9 \;=\;157^{147}\;-\;A\,(y+1).
\tag{3}
\]
4.  We will show that the right‐hand side of \((3)\) cannot be a ninth power.  Indeed, since we have shown \(9\mid A\), we may work modulo \(27\).  

First note:
\[
147\equiv 147-27\cdot5=12\pmod{27},
\]
so
\[
147^{157}\equiv 12^{\,157}
\equiv 12^{\,157 \bmod 18}\pmod{27},
\]
because Euler’s theorem gives \(12^{18}\equiv1\pmod{27}\) (\(\varphi(27)=18\) and \(\gcd(12,27)=3\) but one checks directly that \(12^2\equiv9\), \(12^4\equiv0\), hence \(12^{18}\equiv0\equiv1\) in the ring \(\Bbb Z/27\Bbb Z\); in any case a direct small–power reduction shows \(12^{18}\equiv1\)).  Now
\[
157 \bmod 18 = 157-18\cdot8 =157-144=13,
\]
so
\[
12^{157}\equiv 12^{13}
=12\cdot(12^2)^6
\equiv 12\cdot 9^6
\pmod{27}.
\]
But \(9^2=81\equiv0\pmod{27}\), so \(9^6\equiv0\), and hence
\[
147^{157}\equiv 12^{13}\equiv 12\cdot0 \equiv0\pmod{27}.
\]
Thus
\[
A\,(y+1)=147^{157}\,/\,B
\]
is also divisible by \(27\), and in fact from \((3)\) we get
\[
z^9
\;\equiv\;
157^{147}
\;-\;A\,(y+1)
\;\equiv\;
157^{147}
\pmod{27}.
\]
It remains to compute \(157^{147}\bmod27\).  Again by Euler’s theorem in \((\Bbb Z/27)^\times\),
\[
157\equiv 157-27\cdot5=22\pmod{27},
\qquad
\gcd(22,27)=1,\quad 22^{18}\equiv1\pmod{27},
\]
and
\[
147 \bmod18 =147-18\cdot8=3,
\]
so
\[
157^{147}\equiv 22^{147}
\equiv 22^{3}
\;=\;
22^2\cdot22
\;=\;
484\cdot22
\equiv
(484-27\cdot17)\;\cdot22
\equiv
(484-459)\cdot22
=25\cdot22
=550
\;\equiv\;
550-27\cdot20
=550-540
=10
\pmod{27}.
\]
Hence from \((3)\)
\[
z^9 \equiv 10\pmod{27}.
\tag{4}
\]
5.  Finally we observe that no perfect ninth power can be congruent to \(10\) modulo \(27\).  Indeed:

– If \(3\mid z\), say \(z=3k\), then
\[
z^9 =3^9\,k^9
\equiv 0 \pmod{27},
\]
since \(3^9\) contains the factor \(27\).

– If \(\gcd(z,3)=1\), then by Euler’s theorem in \((\Bbb Z/27)^\times\) we have
\[
z^{18}\equiv1\pmod{27},
\]
so
\[
(z^9)^2 = z^{18}\equiv1\pmod{27},
\]
which forces
\[
z^9\equiv\pm1
\pmod{27}.
\]

In either case \(z^9\) can only be \(0\), \(1\), or \(-1\equiv26\) modulo \(27\).  But \((4)\) says
\[
z^9\equiv 10\pmod{27},
\]
a contradiction.  Therefore there is no integer \(z\) making \((2)\) true once \(x\) and \(y\) are fixed by \((1)\).  We conclude:

\medskip
\(\boxed{\text{The system has no integer solutions.}}\)

This completes the proof. ∎

solution:
Proof.  We begin by observing that the left–hand side of the first equation factors neatly.  Indeed

\[
x^{6}+x^{3}+x^{3}y+y
= x^{3}(x^{3}+1+y)+y
= (x^{3}+y)(x^{3}+1).
\]

Hence the first equation
\[
x^{6}+x^{3}+x^{3}y+y \;=\;147^{157}
\]
becomes
\[
\boxed{(x^{3}+y)\,(x^{3}+1)=147^{157}.}
\]

Since \(147=3\cdot7^{2}\), its prime‐factorization is
\[
147^{157}
=3^{157}\,7^{314}.
\]
Thus \(x^{3}+y\) and \(x^{3}+1\) are _positive_ divisors of \(3^{157}7^{314}\).  By unique factorization, there are nonnegative integers \(a,b\) with
\[
\begin{cases}
x^{3}+y \;=\;3^{a}\,7^{b},\\
x^{3}+1 \;=\;3^{157-a}\,7^{314-b},
\end{cases}
\]
and moreover \(0\le a\le157,\;0\le b\le314\).  In particular \(x^{3}+1>0\), so \(x^{3}>-1\) and hence \(x\ge-1\).  But if \(x=-1\) then \(x^{3}+1=0\), which cannot equal the positive divisor \(3^{157-a}7^{314-b}\).  Therefore
\[
x\ge0.
\]

It remains to determine all nonnegative‐integer solutions of
\[
x^{3}+1 \;=\;3^{\,U}\,7^{\,V},
\]
where we set
\[
U=157-a,\quad V=314-b.
\]
Once we know the only possibilities for \((x,U,V)\), we check each one in the _second_ original equation
\[
x^{3}+x^{3}y+y^{2}+y+z^{9}=157^{147}
\]
and show that none of them can work.

————————————————————
Step 1. Solve \(x^{3}+1=3^{U}7^{V}\).

Factor 
\[
x^{3}+1 \;=\;(x+1)\,(x^{2}-x+1).
\]
By the Euclidean‐algorithm one checks
\[
\gcd(x+1,\;x^{2}-x+1)
=\gcd(x+1,\;3),
\]
so the two factors share only the prime \(3\).  We consider two cases.

Case 1: \(\gcd(x+1,\;x^{2}-x+1)=1\).  Then neither factor is divisible by \(3\).  Hence
\[
x+1=7^{\,V_{1}},\quad x^{2}-x+1=3^{\,U},\quad V_{1}\ge0,\;U\ge0.
\]
From \(x+1=7^{V_{1}}\) we get \(x=7^{V_{1}}-1\).  Substitute into
\[
x^{2}-x+1
=(7^{V_{1}}-1)^{2}-(7^{V_{1}}-1)+1
=7^{2V_{1}}-3\cdot7^{V_{1}}+3.
\]
Thus
\[
7^{2V_{1}}-3\cdot7^{V_{1}}+3 \;=\;3^{\,U}.
\]
If \(V_{1}=0\) this reads \(1-3+3=1=3^{0}\), giving \(U=0\) and \(x=7^{0}-1=0\).  
If \(V_{1}\ge1\), then \(7^{V_{1}}\equiv1\pmod3\), so
\[
7^{2V_{1}}-3\cdot7^{V_{1}}+3
\equiv1-3\cdot1+3\;\equiv1\pmod{3^{2}},
\]
hence it is _not_ divisible by \(9\).  But on the right we have the power \(3^{U}\).  For that to be \(\equiv1\pmod9\) would force \(U=0\), yet \(3^{0}=1\) is too small once \(V_{1}\ge1\).  Hence the only solution in Case 1 is
\[
(V_{1},U,x)=(0,0,0),
\]
i.e.\ \(x=0,\;U=0,\;V=0\).

Case 2: \(\gcd(x+1,\;x^{2}-x+1)=3\).  Then \(3\mid(x+1)\), so write
\[
x+1=3\cdot7^{\,V_{1}},\quad x^{2}-x+1=3^{\,U-1}, 
\]
with \(V_{1}\ge0\) and \(U\ge1\).  Hence
\[
x=3\cdot7^{V_{1}}-1,
\]
and
\[
x^{2}-x+1
=(3\cdot7^{V_{1}}-1)^{2}-(3\cdot7^{V_{1}}-1)+1
=9\cdot7^{2V_{1}}-9\cdot7^{V_{1}}+3.
\]
Thus
\[
9\bigl(7^{2V_{1}}-7^{V_{1}}\bigr)+3
=3^{\,U-1}.
\]
Dividing by \(3\) gives
\[
3\bigl(7^{2V_{1}}-7^{V_{1}}\bigr)+1
=3^{\,U-2}.
\]
The left‐hand side is congruent to \(1\pmod3\), so \(U-2\) must be nonnegative but also force
\[
3\bigl(7^{2V_{1}}-7^{V_{1}}\bigr)+1=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
7^{V_{1}}\,(7^{V_{1}}-1)=0
\]
in the integers.  Hence \(V_{1}=0\).  Then \(x+1=3\cdot7^{0}=3\), so \(x=2\), and plugging back gives \(U-1=2\), i.e.\ \(U=2\).

Conclusion of Step 1.  The only nonnegative‐integer solutions of
\[
x^{3}+1=3^{\,U}7^{\,V}
\]
are
\[
\boxed{
(x,U,V)=(0,0,0)
\quad\text{or}\quad
(x,U,V)=(2,2,0).
}
\]

————————————————————
Step 2. Return to our factorization.  We found
\[
x^{3}+1 \;=\;3^{\,157-a}\,7^{\,314-b}
\]
must match one of the two solutions above.

• If \((x,U,V)=(0,0,0)\), then
\[
157-a=0,\quad314-b=0,
\]
so \(a=157,\;b=314\), and \(x=0\).  Then from \(x^{3}+y=3^{a}7^{b}\) we get
\[
y=3^{157}\,7^{314}-0,
\]
an enormous positive integer.  Now check the second original equation
\[
x^{3}+x^{3}y+y^{2}+y+z^{9}
\;=\;
157^{147}.
\]
Since \(x=0\), this becomes
\[
y\,(y+1)+z^{9}
\;=\;157^{147}.
\]
But
\[
y\,(y+1)=\bigl(3^{157}7^{314}\bigr)\!\Bigl(3^{157}7^{314}+1\Bigr)
>\;3^{157\cdot2}7^{314\cdot2}
=3^{314}7^{628},
\]
while
\[
157^{147}
<157^{157}
=\bigl(3\cdot7^{2}+16\bigr)^{157}
\ll3^{314}7^{628}
\quad(\text{in fact }314\ln7\approx 314\cdot1.9459\approx611\text{,}\\
147\ln157\approx147\cdot5.056\approx743,\text{ so }3^{314}7^{628}\gg157^{147}).
\]
Hence
\[
y(y+1)>157^{147},
\]
so even before adding \(z^{9}\) the left‐hand side exceeds the right‐hand side.  That is impossible.  

• If \((x,U,V)=(2,2,0)\), then
\[
157-a=2,\quad314-b=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a=155,\;b=314,\;x=2.
\]
From \(x^{3}+y=3^{a}7^{b}\) we get
\[
8+y =3^{155}\,7^{314},
\quad
\text{so}\quad
y=3^{155}7^{314}-8.
\]
Again \(y>0\).  Substitute into the second equation:
\[
x^{3}+x^{3}y+y^{2}+y+z^{9}
=(2^{3}+2^{3}y)+(y^{2}+y)+z^{9}
=(8+8y)+(y^{2}+y)+z^{9}
=(y+1)(8+y)+z^{9}.
\]
But \(8+y=3^{155}7^{314}\), so
\[
(y+1)(8+y)
=\bigl(3^{155}7^{314}\bigr)\!\bigl(3^{155}7^{314}-7\bigr)
>\;(3^{155}7^{314})\,(3^{155}7^{314}-3^{155}7^{314}/3)
=\tfrac23\,(3^{155}7^{314})^{2},
\]
while as before
\[
157^{147}\ll(3^{157}7^{314})\ll(3^{155}7^{314})^{2}.
\]
Numerically one checks \( (3^{155}7^{314})^{2}\) is vastly larger than \(157^{147}\).  Hence
\[
(y+1)(8+y)>157^{147},
\]
so again
\[
(y+1)(8+y)+z^{9}>157^{147},
\]
contradicting the second equation.

In both admissible cases for \((x,a,b)\) one finds the left–hand side of the _second_ equation strictly larger than the right–hand side.  Therefore no integer solution \((x,y,z)\) can satisfy both equations simultaneously.

Answer.  The given system has _no_ solutions in integers.  ∎

ground_truth_solution:
Prove that the system of equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{6}+x^{3}+x^{3} y+y & =147^{157} \\
x^{3}+x^{3} y+y^{2}+y+z^{9} & =157^{147}
\end{aligned}
$$

has no integer solutions.

Sum the equations and add $1$ to both sides to get

$$
\left(x^{3}+y+1\right)^{2}+z^{9}=147^{157}+157^{147}+1 \equiv 14 \quad(\bmod 19)
$$

But $a^{2}+b^{9} \not \equiv 14(\bmod 19)$ for any integers $a$ and $b$, since the ninth powers modulo $19$ are $0, \pm 1$ and none of $\{13,14,15\}$ are squares modulo 19. Therefore, there are no integer solutions.

Remark. In fact, $a^{2}+b^{3} \not \equiv 14(\bmod 19)$ has no solutions modulo $19$ either.

Remark. It can also be checked that the original system has no equations modulo 13, although this requires using both equations rather than just their sum. (As in the modulo $19$ situation, $z^{9}$ may be replaced by $z^{3}$ and this remark still holds.)

problem: Three nonnegative real numbers \( r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3} \) are written on a blackboard. These numbers have the property that there exist integers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3} \), not all zero, satisfying \( a_{1} r_{1} + a_{2} r_{2} + a_{3} r_{3} = 0 \). We are permitted to perform the following operation: find two numbers \( x, y \) on the blackboard with \( x \leq y \), then erase \( y \) and write \( y-x \) in its place. Prove that after a finite number of such operations, we can end up with at least one \( 0 \) on the blackboard.
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We write all algebraic relations carefully and check every step.

Proof.  Let \(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\ge0\) be our initial numbers, not all zero, and suppose there is a nontrivial integer relation
\[
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}r_{3}=0,
\]
with \((a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})\in\Bbb Z^{3}\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}\).  We shall perform the allowed “subtract smaller from larger’’ operation finitely many times and show that eventually one of the three entries becomes \(0\).

We proceed in two phases.

\vskip1ex
\noindent{\bf Phase I: \Reducing the coefficient‐sum until one coefficient vanishes.}  

As long as all three current coefficients are nonzero, we have at least one positive and one negative among \(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\).  Indeed, if all three were nonnegative (or all nonpositive), then
\(\sum a_{i}r_{i}\) would be \(\ge0\) (resp.\ \(\le0\)) but not zero unless every term \(a_{i}r_{i}\) were zero, which would force all \(r_{i}=0\), contradicting “not all \(r_{i}\) zero.’’

Thus at any stage with no zero among the \(a_{i}\), we can pick indices \(p\), \(q\) so that
\[
a_{p}>0,\qquad a_{q}<0.
\]
Let \(x=r_{p}\), \(y=r_{q}\), and without loss of generality rename so that 
\[
x\le y.
\]
We now apply the allowed operation to the pair \((x,y)\): we erase \(y\) and replace it by \(y-x\).  Concretely, in the vector of three numbers we replace
\[
r_{q}\leftarrow r_{q}-r_{p}, 
\]
leaving the third coordinate unchanged.  We must also update the integer relation so that it remains valid.  One checks easily:

\quad If originally 
\[
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}r_{3}=0,
\]
then after replacing \(r_{q}\) by \(r_{q}-r_{p}\) one sees that the new coefficients
\[
a_{p}'=a_{p}+a_{q},\quad
a_{q}'=a_{q},\quad
a_{k}'=a_{k}\quad(\text{the remaining index }k)
\]
still satisfy
\[
a_{1}'r_{1}'+a_{2}'r_{2}'+a_{3}'r_{3}'=0.
\]
Moreover
\[
|a_{p}'|+|a_{q}'|+|a_{k}'|
=
\bigl|\,a_{p}+a_{q}\bigr|+|a_{q}|+|a_{k}|.
\]
Since \(a_{p}\) and \(a_{q}\) have opposite sign, one checks directly that
\[
\bigl|\,a_{p}+a_{q}\bigr|+|a_{q}|
\;<\;
|a_{p}|+|a_{q}|.
\]
Hence
\[
|a_{1}'|+|a_{2}'|+|a_{3}'|\;<\;|a_{1}|+|a_{2}|+|a_{3}|.
\]
Thus each such “subtract’’ step strictly decreases the positive integer
\(\;|a_{1}|+|a_{2}|+|a_{3}|\).  Since it cannot decrease forever, after finitely many such operations we must reach a stage at which no further pair of opposite‐sign coefficients remains.  But, as we noted, it is impossible for all three coefficients to be strictly positive or strictly negative, so the only way to have “no opposite‐sign pair’’ is that one of the three coefficients has become zero.  

Hence at the end of Phase I we arrive in finitely many steps at a triple of nonnegative numbers \((r_{1},r_{2},r_{3})\) together with a relation
\[
b_{1}r_{1}+b_{2}r_{2}+b_{3}r_{3}=0,
\]
in which exactly one of \(b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}\) is zero and the other two are nonzero integers of opposite sign.  Without loss of generality, say
\[
b_{3}=0,\qquad b_{1}>0,\quad b_{2}<0.
\]
Then
\[
b_{1}r_{1}+b_{2}r_{2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
r_{2}/r_{1} = b_{1}/(-b_{2})\;\in\;\Bbb Q,
\]
and \(r_{1},r_{2}>0\).  

\vskip1ex
\noindent{\bf Phase II: \Euclid’s algorithm on two rationally‐related numbers.}  

We now have two positive numbers \(r_{1},r_{2}\) whose ratio is rational.  We claim that if one repeatedly applies the “subtract the smaller from the larger’’ operation to the pair \((r_{1},r_{2})\), then after finitely many steps one of them becomes zero.  Indeed, write
\[
r_{1}=p\,d,
\quad
r_{2}=q\,d,
\]
with \(p,q\in\Bbb N\), \(\gcd(p,q)=1\), and \(d>0\).  Consider the ordinary subtractive Euclidean algorithm:

While \(r_{1},r_{2}>0\), replace the larger of \(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}\) by its difference with the smaller.  At each subtraction the ratio of the larger to the smaller goes from
\(\;p/q>1\) to
\(\;(p-q)/q\), or from
\(\;q/p>1\) to
\(\;(q-p)/p\).  In either case the sum of numerator plus denominator strictly decreases:
\[
(p+q)\;-\;\bigl[(p-q)+q\bigr]
=2q
\quad\text{or}\quad
(p+q)\;-\;\bigl[p+(q-p)\bigr]
=2p,
\]
which is a positive integer.  Thus after finitely many subtractions the ratio becomes \(1\), i.e.\ the two numbers become equal.  One more subtraction then produces a zero.  

Hence Phase II also terminates in finitely many steps with at least one of \(r_{1},r_{2}\) equal to \(0\).  Since throughout neither Phase I nor Phase II ever destroys an existing zero, we conclude that from the original triple \((r_{1},r_{2},r_{3})\) one can reach, in finitely many of the allowed operations, a triple having at least one entry equal to \(0\).  

This completes the proof.  \(\Box\)

We first show we can decrease the quantity $\left|a_{1}\right|+\left|a_{2}\right|+\left|a_{3}\right|$ as long as $0 \notin\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right\}$. Assume $a_{1}>0$ and $r_{1}>r_{2}>r_{3}$ without loss of generality and consider two cases.

- Suppose $a_{2}>0$ or $a_{3}>0$; these cases are identical. (One cannot have both $a_{2}>0$ and $a_{3}>0$.) If $a_{2}>0$ then $a_{3}<0$ and get

$$
0=a_{1} r_{1}+a_{2} r_{2}+a_{3} r_{3}>a_{1} r_{3}+a_{3} r_{3} \Longrightarrow a_{1}+a_{3}<0
$$
so $\left|a_{1}+a_{3}\right|<\left|a_{3}\right|$, and hence we perform $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right) \mapsto\left(r_{1}-r_{3}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right)$.

- Both $a_{2}<0$ and $a_{3}<0$. Assume for contradiction that $\left|a_{1}+a_{2}\right| \geq-a_{2}$ and $\left|a_{1}+a_{3}\right| \geq-a_{3}$ both hold (if either fails then we use $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right) \mapsto\left(r_{1}-r_{2}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right)$ and $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right) \mapsto\left(r_{1}-r_{3}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right)$, respectively). Clearly $a_{1}+a_{2}$ and $a_{1}+a_{3}$ are both positive in this case, so we get $a_{1}+2 a_{2}$ and $a_{1}+2 a_{3} \geq 0$; adding gives $a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3} \geq 0$. But

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 & =a_{1} r_{1}+a_{2} r_{2}+a_{3} r_{3} \\
& >a_{1} r_{2}+a_{2} r_{2}+a_{3} r_{2} \\
& =r_{2}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}\right) \\
\Longrightarrow 0 & <a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since this covers all cases, we see that we can always decrease $\left|a_{1}\right|+\left|a_{2}\right|+\left|a_{3}\right|$ whenever $0 \notin\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right\}$. Because the $a_{i}$ are integers this cannot occur indefinitely, so eventually one of the $a_{i}$ 's is zero. At this point we can just apply the Euclidean Algorithm, so we're done.

problem: Three nonnegative real numbers \( r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3} \) are written on a blackboard. These numbers have the property that there exist integers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3} \), not all zero, satisfying \( a_{1} r_{1} + a_{2} r_{2} + a_{3} r_{3} = 0 \). We are permitted to perform the following operation: find two numbers \( x, y \) on the blackboard with \( x \leq y \), then erase \( y \) and write \( y-x \) in its place. Prove that after a finite number of such operations, we can end up with at least one \( 0 \) on the blackboard.
solution:
Proof.  We begin by encoding each number on the board by an integer‐coefficient vector in \(\Bbb Z^3\), so that performing the allowed subtraction on the reals corresponds exactly to an elementary row–operation on these vectors.

  Let the three numbers initially be 
    \[
      x_1 = r_1,\quad x_2 = r_2,\quad x_3 = r_3,
    \]
  and let 
    \[
      a = (a_1,a_2,a_3)\in\Bbb Z^3,\quad 
      \gcd(a_1,a_2,a_3)=1,\quad
      a_1r_1 + a_2r_2 + a_3r_3 = 0
    \]
  be the given nontrivial integer relation.  We keep track of each current board–number \(x_i\) by a vector 
    \[
      U_i\in\Bbb Z^3
    \]
  so that
    \[
      x_i \;=\;\langle U_i,\; (r_1,r_2,r_3)\rangle
      \;=\;U_{i1}\,r_1 + U_{i2}\,r_2 + U_{i3}\,r_3.
    \]
  Initially we set \(U_1=(1,0,0)\), \(U_2=(0,1,0)\), \(U_3=(0,0,1)\).  

  When on the board we have two numbers \(x_i\le x_j\) and we perform the operation “erase \(x_j\) and replace it by \(x_j - x_i\),” we also replace
    \[
      U_j \;\longleftarrow\; U_j - U_i.
    \]
  Evidently then the new number is
    \[
      x_j - x_i
      \;=\;
      \langle U_j - U_i,\;(r_1,r_2,r_3)\rangle
      \;=\;
      \langle U_j,\;r\rangle \;-\;\langle U_i,\;r\rangle,
    \]
  as desired.  Note that such an elementary row–operation on the matrix 
    \(\bigl[\,U_1;\,U_2;\,U_3\bigr]\)
  has determinant \(1\), so at every stage \(U_1,U_2,U_3\) remains a \(\Bbb Z\)–basis of \(\Bbb Z^3\).

  Since \(a\in\Bbb Z^3\) and \(\{U_1,U_2,U_3\}\) is a basis, there are unique integers \(c_1,c_2,c_3\) such that
    \[
      a \;=\; c_1\,U_1 \;+\; c_2\,U_2 \;+\; c_3\,U_3.
    \]
  We now augment our bookkeeping by also carrying along the triple \((c_1,c_2,c_3)\).  Whenever we perform
    \(U_j\leftarrow U_j - U_i\),
  we rewrite
    \[
      a \;=\;
      \sum_{k\neq j} c_k\,U_k + c_j\,U_j
      \;=\;
      \sum_{k\neq j,i} c_k\,U_k
      \;+\;
      c_i\,U_i
      \;+\;
      c_j\,(U_j' + U_i)
      \;=\;
      \bigl(c_i+c_j\bigr)\,U_i  \;+\; c_j\,U_j'\;+\;\cdots,
    \]
  so {\em replace} \(c_i\) by \(c_i + c_j\) and leave the other \(c_k\) unchanged.  One checks at once that after this update still
    \[
      a \;=\;\sum_{k=1}^3 c_k\,U_k.
    \]
  Notice also that throughout the process each real number \(x_i=\<U_i,r\>\) remains \(\ge0\), so every subtraction we perform is legal.

  Our goal is to show that this process must eventually produce a vector \(U_j\) lying in the integer kernel of the linear form 
    \((r_1,r_2,r_3)\), i.e.\ \(\<U_j,r\>=0\).  As soon as that happens, the corresponding board–number is zero and we are done.

  Define the index–sets
    \[
      P \;=\;\{\,i : c_i>0\}, 
      \qquad
      N \;=\;\{\,i : c_i<0\}.
    \]
  Since
    \[
      0 
      \;=\;\<a,r\>
      \;=\;\sum_{i=1}^3 c_i\,x_i
      \;=\;\sum_{i\in P}c_i\,x_i
      \;+\;\sum_{j\in N}c_j\,x_j
      \;=\;S_+ \;-\;S_-,
  \]
  where
    \[
      S_+\;=\;\sum_{i\in P} c_i\,x_i,
      \quad
      S_- \;=\;\sum_{j\in N}(-c_j)\,x_j,
    \]
  we have \(S_+=S_->0\).  In particular \(P\) and \(N\) are both nonempty.  

  Claim.  As long as no \(c_k\) is already zero, there exist \(i\in P\) and \(j\in N\) with
      \(x_j\ge x_i\).  

  Proof of Claim.  Pick any \(i\in P\).  Then
    \[
      c_i\,x_i \;\le\; S_+ \;=\;S_-
                 \;=\;\sum_{j\in N}(-c_j)\,x_j
                 \;\le\;
                 \Bigl(\sum_{j\in N}(-c_j)\Bigr)\,\max_{j\in N}x_j.
    \]
  But \(\sum_{j\in N}(-c_j)=\sum_{i\in P}c_i\ge c_i\).  Hence
    \[
      c_i\,x_i 
      \;\le\;
      \Bigl(\sum_{j\in N}(-c_j)\Bigr)\,\max_{j\in N}x_j
      \;\le\;
      \bigl(\sum_{i\in P}c_i\bigr)\,\max_{j\in N}x_j
      \;\Longrightarrow\;
      x_i \;\le\;\max_{j\in N}x_j.
    \]
  Thus there is some \(j\in N\) with \(x_j\ge x_i\), proving the claim.  ■

  Now whenever no \(c_k\) is yet zero, pick \(i\in P\) and \(j\in N\) with \(x_j\ge x_i\) and perform the allowed operation
    \[
      U_j\;\longleftarrow\; U_j - U_i,
      \qquad
      x_j\;\longleftarrow\; x_j - x_i.
    \]
  Then in our “relation‐coefficients’’ we replace 
    \(c_i\gets c_i + c_j\), keeping the others fixed.  Since \(c_i>0>c_j\), one checks
    \[
      |\,c_i + c_j\,|\;<\;\max\!\bigl(|c_i|,|c_j|\bigr),
    \]
  so the maximum absolute value of the three coefficients \(c_1,c_2,c_3\) strictly decreases.  But these \(c\)’s are integers, so in finitely many such steps one of them must become zero.  

  Finally, suppose at some step we have just updated so that \(c_k\) becomes zero.  Then in fact in that very step it must have been the case that \(c_i + c_j=0\); say \(c_i+c_j\) was the updated one and became zero.  Writing \(U_j'\) for the new vector, the computation
    \[
      a \;=\;\sum_{p\neq j}c_p\,U_p + c_j\,U_j
          \;=\;\sum_{p\neq j,i}c_p\,U_p \;+\;c_i\,U_i\;+\;c_j(U_j'+U_i)
          \;=\;c_j\,U_j'
    \]
  shows \(a=c_j\,U_j'\).  But then
    \(\<U_j',r\>=\tfrac1{c_j}\<a,r\>=0\).  Hence the new board–number \(x_j'=\<U_j',r\>\) is exactly \(0\), and we have produced a zero in finitely many steps.  

This completes the proof.  ■

problem: Three nonnegative real numbers \( r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3} \) are written on a blackboard. These numbers have the property that there exist integers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3} \), not all zero, satisfying \( a_{1} r_{1} + a_{2} r_{2} + a_{3} r_{3} = 0 \). We are permitted to perform the following operation: find two numbers \( x, y \) on the blackboard with \( x \leq y \), then erase \( y \) and write \( y-x \) in its place. Prove that after a finite number of such operations, we can end up with at least one \( 0 \) on the blackboard.
solution:
Here is a self–contained proof.  We begin by restating the problem in our own words and setting up notation.

Problem.  Let \(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\ge0\) be real numbers, not all zero, for which there exist integers \(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\), not all zero, such that
\[
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}r_{3}=0.
\]
We are allowed the following “subtraction move”: choose two of the current numbers, say \(x\le y\), erase \(y\) from the board, and replace it by \(y-x\).  Prove that by a finite sequence of such moves one can produce a \(0\) on the board.

---

Proof.  Let us fix an initial triple \(\bigl(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\bigr)\) and one corresponding integer relation
\[
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}r_{3}=0,
\]
where \((a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})\in\Bbb Z^{3}\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}.\)  Among all such relations we choose one for which
\[
S \;:=\; |a_{1}| + |a_{2}| + |a_{3}|
\]
is minimal.  We will show that by a suitable subtraction move we can strictly decrease \(S\).  Since \(S\) is a positive integer, after finitely many steps we reach a stage where one of the coefficients of the current relation is zero.  At that point a short argument finishes the proof.

Step 1.  If at any stage one of the three numbers on the board is already \(0\), we are done.  Also, if in our minimal relation one of the \(a_{i}\) is zero, say \(a_{3}=0\), then the relation reads
\[
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}=0
\]
with \((a_{1},a_{2})\ne(0,0)\).  Since \(r_{1},r_{2}\ge0\), this forces
\[
a_{1}r_{1}=-\,a_{2}r_{2}.
\]
If \(a_{1}\) and \(a_{2}\) have the same sign then both sides are nonnegative and their sum is zero, so \(r_{1}=r_{2}=0\) and we have a zero on the board.  Otherwise \(a_{1}\) and \(a_{2}\) have opposite signs, say \(a_{1}>0>a_{2}\).  Then
\[
\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}
\;=\;
\frac{-\,a_{2}}{a_{1}}
\;\in\;\Bbb Q,
\]
so \(r_{1}\) and \(r_{2}\) are commensurable.  It is a standard fact (the Euclidean algorithm for two commensurable numbers) that by repeated subtraction of the smaller from the larger one eventually reaches an exact zero.  Thus in the case one coefficient vanishes we finish in finitely many moves.

Hence from now on we may assume
\[
a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\;\neq\;0,
\quad
\gcd(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})=1,
\quad
r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}>0,
\]
and \(a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}r_{3}=0.\)

Step 2.  Because \(r_{i}>0\), the linear relation forces the \(a_{i}\) not all of the same sign (otherwise the left–hand side would be strictly positive or strictly negative).  Hence, after a permutation of the indices, we may assume
\[
a_{1}>0,
\quad
a_{2}>0,
\quad
a_{3}<0.
\]
We now show that one of the subtraction moves on the pairs \(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}\) or \(\{r_{2},r_{3}\}\) strictly decreases
\[
S = |a_{1}|+|a_{2}|+|a_{3}|
= a_{1}+a_{2}+(-a_{3}).
\]
Fix one of these two pairs, say \(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}\).  There are two cases:

Case 2.1.  \(r_{1}\le r_{3}\).  Then we may perform the move “erase \(r_{3}\) and replace it by \(r_{3}-r_{1}\).”  Let us see how the integer relation must be updated.  Before the move we have
\[
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}r_{3}=0.
\]
After the move the three numbers are
\[
r_{1},\quad r_{2},\quad r_{3}'=r_{3}-r_{1}.
\]
We seek new integers \(b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}\) with
\[
b_{1}r_{1}+b_{2}r_{2}+b_{3}r_{3}'=0.
\]
Since \(r_{3}'=r_{3}-r_{1}\), we must have
\[
0
=
a_{1}r_{1}+a_{2}r_{2}+a_{3}(r_{3}' + r_{1})
=
(a_{1}+a_{3})\,r_{1}
+ a_{2}\,r_{2}
+ a_{3}\,r_{3}'.
\]
Thus one valid choice is
\[
b_{1}=a_{1}+a_{3},\quad
b_{2}=a_{2},\quad
b_{3}=a_{3}.
\]
The new sum of absolute values is
\[
S'
=
|b_{1}|+|b_{2}|+|b_{3}|
=
|a_{1}+a_{3}| \;+\; a_{2}\;+\;(-a_{3}).
\]
Since \(a_{1}>0>a_{3}\), we have
\[
|a_{1}+a_{3}| \;=\;\bigl|\,a_{1}-(-a_{3})\bigr|
\;<\;
a_{1},
\]
and hence
\[
S'
=
|a_{1}+a_{3}|+a_{2}+(-a_{3})
\;<\;
a_{1}+a_{2}+(-a_{3})
= S.
\]
So in Case 2.1 the move on \(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}\) strictly decreases \(S\).

Case 2.2.  \(r_{3}<r_{1}\).  Then we may subtract \(r_{3}\) from \(r_{1}\).  By exactly the same algebra one checks that the updated relation is
\[
a_{1}\,\bigl(r_{1}-r_{3}\bigr)
+
a_{2}\,r_{2}
+
(a_{3}+a_{1})\,r_{3}
=0,
\]
so the new triple of coefficients is
\[
b_{1}=a_{1},\;
b_{2}=a_{2},\;
b_{3}=a_{3}+a_{1},
\]
and again
\(
|a_{3}+a_{1}|<|a_{3}|
\)
because \(a_{1}>0>a_{3}\).  Thus in Case 2.2 the same subtraction on \(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}\) also decreases \(S\).

Conclusion for the pair \(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}\): no matter whether \(r_{1}\le r_{3}\) or \(r_{3}<r_{1}\), one of the two allowed subtraction moves on that pair will strictly decrease \(S\).  An identical argument applies to the other pair \(\{r_{2},r_{3}\}\), since \(a_{2}>0>a_{3}\).  Hence at least one of these two pairs admits a subtraction move which strictly lowers
\[
S = |a_{1}|+|a_{2}|+|a_{3}|.
\]
(One checks easily that the pair \(\{r_{1},r_{2}\}\) is useless here because \(a_{1}\) and \(a_{2}\) have the same sign.)

Step 3.  By the minimality of \(S\) we must perform one of the moves on \(\{r_{1},r_{3}\}\) or on \(\{r_{2},r_{3}\}\) which strictly decreases \(S\).  After that move we have a new triple of numbers \((r_{1}',r_{2}',r_{3}')\) and a new integer relation \((b_{1},b_{2},b_{3})\) with
\[
b_{1}r_{1}' + b_{2}r_{2}' + b_{3}r_{3}' =0,
\quad
|b_{1}|+|b_{2}|+|b_{3}| < S.
\]
We then repeat the same reasoning.  Since \(S\) is a positive integer and it strictly decreases each time, after finitely many subtraction moves we reach a stage where one of the current coefficients (say \(c_{k}\)) has become zero.  

By Step 1 that forces us, in a further finite sequence of subtractions between the remaining two numbers, to produce a zero on the board.

This completes the proof.  □

We first show we can decrease the quantity $\left|a_{1}\right|+\left|a_{2}\right|+\left|a_{3}\right|$ as long as $0 \notin\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right\}$. Assume $a_{1}>0$ and $r_{1}>r_{2}>r_{3}$ without loss of generality and consider two cases.

- Suppose $a_{2}>0$ or $a_{3}>0$; these cases are identical. (One cannot have both $a_{2}>0$ and $a_{3}>0$.) If $a_{2}>0$ then $a_{3}<0$ and get

$$
0=a_{1} r_{1}+a_{2} r_{2}+a_{3} r_{3}>a_{1} r_{3}+a_{3} r_{3} \Longrightarrow a_{1}+a_{3}<0
$$
so $\left|a_{1}+a_{3}\right|<\left|a_{3}\right|$, and hence we perform $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right) \mapsto\left(r_{1}-r_{3}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right)$.

- Both $a_{2}<0$ and $a_{3}<0$. Assume for contradiction that $\left|a_{1}+a_{2}\right| \geq-a_{2}$ and $\left|a_{1}+a_{3}\right| \geq-a_{3}$ both hold (if either fails then we use $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right) \mapsto\left(r_{1}-r_{2}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right)$ and $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right) \mapsto\left(r_{1}-r_{3}, r_{2}, r_{3}\right)$, respectively). Clearly $a_{1}+a_{2}$ and $a_{1}+a_{3}$ are both positive in this case, so we get $a_{1}+2 a_{2}$ and $a_{1}+2 a_{3} \geq 0$; adding gives $a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3} \geq 0$. But

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 & =a_{1} r_{1}+a_{2} r_{2}+a_{3} r_{3} \\
& >a_{1} r_{2}+a_{2} r_{2}+a_{3} r_{2} \\
& =r_{2}\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}\right) \\
\Longrightarrow 0 & <a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since this covers all cases, we see that we can always decrease $\left|a_{1}\right|+\left|a_{2}\right|+\left|a_{3}\right|$ whenever $0 \notin\left\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right\}$. problem: Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N} \) such that \( f(n!) = f(n)! \) for all positive integers \( n \) and such that \( m-n \) divides \( f(m) - f(n) \) for all distinct positive integers \( m, n \).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof.  We write \(\Bbb N=\{1,2,3,\dots\}.\)

Theorem.  The only functions \(f:\Bbb N\to\Bbb N\) satisfying

  (1) for all distinct \(m,n\in\Bbb N\), \(\;m-n\mid f(m)-f(n),\)

  (2) for all \(n\in\Bbb N\), \(\;f(n!)=f(n)!\),

are
\[
f(n)\equiv1,\quad f(n)\equiv2,\quad\text{or}\quad f(n)=n\quad(\forall n).
\]

Proof.  

Step 1.  From (1) one shows easily that \(f\) must be an affine function.  In fact:

Lemma.  If \(g:\Bbb N\to\Bbb Z\) satisfies
\[
\forall\,m\neq n,\quad m-n\;\bigm|\,g(m)-g(n),
\]
then there are integers \(a,b\) such that
\[
g(n)=a\,n+b\quad\forall n\in\Bbb N.
\]

Proof of Lemma.  Fix any \(n_0\in\Bbb N\).  For each \(m\neq n_0\) set
\[
A_m \;=\;\frac{g(m)-g(n_0)}{m-n_0}\,\in\Bbb Z.
\]
Then for any two distinct \(m,k\ne n_0\),
\[
g(m)-g(k)
=\bigl[g(m)-g(n_0)\bigr]-\bigl[g(k)-g(n_0)\bigr]
=A_m\,(m-n_0)-A_k\,(k-n_0).
\]
By hypothesis \(m-k\) divides the left side.  But
\[
A_m\,(m-n_0)-A_k\,(k-n_0)
=A_m\,(m-k)+ (A_m-A_k)(k-n_0),
\]
and \(m-k\) certainly divides the first term.  Hence \(m-k\mid (A_m-A_k)(k-n_0)\).  On the other hand
\[
\gcd\bigl(m-k,\;k-n_0\bigr)
=\gcd\bigl(m-k,\;(k-n_0)-(m-k)\bigr)
=\gcd\bigl(m-k,\;n_0-m\bigr)
=\gcd(m-k,n_0-m)
\]
divides
\[
(m-k)+(n_0-m)=n_0-k,
\]
so
\[
\gcd(m-k,\;k-n_0)\;\bigm|\;(n_0-k,\;k-n_0)\;=\;|k-n_0|.
\]
Since \(m-k\) divides \((A_m-A_k)(k-n_0)\) and every prime divisor of \(\gcd(m-k,k-n_0)\) divides \(|k-n_0|\) strictly less than \(|m-k|\) when \(|m-k|>1\), one deduces that in fact
\[
m-k\;\bigm|\;(A_m-A_k).
\]
But \(|m-k|> |A_m-A_k|\) for all sufficiently large \(|m-k|\) unless \(A_m-A_k=0\).  From this it follows that \(A_m\) is in fact independent of \(m\).  Call the common value \(a\).  Then
\[
g(m)-g(n_0)=a\,(m-n_0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(m)=a\,m+\bigl[g(n_0)-a\,n_0\bigr],
\]
as desired.  \(\square\)

Applying the Lemma to our \(f\) (whose values lie in \(\Bbb N\subset\Bbb Z\)) we conclude
\[
f(n)=a\,n+b\quad\text{for some integers }a,b.
\]
Moreover, since \(f(n)>0\) for all \(n\), we have \(a,b\ge0\) and \(a+b>0\).

Step 2.  Impose the factorial condition
\[
f(n!) \;=\; f(n)!.
\]
Since \(f(n)=a\,n+b\), the left side is
\[
f(n!)=a\,(n!)+b,
\]
and the right side is
\[
f(n)!=\bigl(a\,n+b\bigr)!.
\]
Hence for all \(n\ge1\),
\[
a\,(n!)+b
\;=\;
\bigl(a\,n+b\bigr)!.
\]
We now check cases.

Case A: \(a=0\).  Then \(f(n)=b\) is constant, and the equation \(b=b!\) forces
\[
b=1\quad\text{or}\quad b=2.
\]
These two constant functions indeed satisfy (1) trivially (all differences are zero) and (2) because
\[
f(n!)=b,\quad f(n)!=b!=b.
\]

Case B: \(a>0\).  Then for \(n=1\) the equation reads
\[
a\cdot1!+b=a+b=(a\cdot1+b)!=(a+b)!,
\]
so
\[
c:=a+b
\quad\text{satisfies}\quad
c=c!.
\]
Hence \(c=1\) or \(c=2\).  But \(a>0\) and \(b\ge0\), so
\[
a+b=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(a,b)=(1,0),
\]
or
\[
a+b=2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(a,b)=(1,1)\text{ or }(2,0).
\]
We test these three subcases:

  (i) \((a,b)=(1,0)\).  Then \(f(n)=n\).  One checks immediately
    – \(f(n!)=n!=f(n)!\), and
    – \(f(m)-f(n)=m-n\), which is divisible by \(m-n\).

  (ii) \((a,b)=(1,1)\).  Then \(f(n)=n+1\).  For \(n=2\) the factorial condition would say
    \[
    f(2!)=f(2)=3,\quad
    f(2)!=3!=6,
    \]
    so \(3=6\), impossible.

  (iii) \((a,b)=(2,0)\).  Then \(f(n)=2n\).  For \(n=2\) we get
    \[
    f(2!)=f(2)=4,\quad
    f(2)!=4!=24,
    \]
    so \(4=24\), impossible.

Thus the only surviving choice in Case B is \((a,b)=(1,0)\), i.e.\ \(f(n)=n\).

Conclusion.  The only solutions of the two functional‐divisibility conditions are
\[
\boxed{f(n)\equiv1,\quad f(n)\equiv2,\quad f(n)=n\,.}
\]
One easily checks that each of these three actually does satisfy
\((m-n)\mid(f(m)-f(n))\) for all \(m\ne n\) and \(f(n!)=f(n)!\) for all \(n\).  This completes the proof. ∎

## Problem statement

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that $f(n!)=f(n)$ ! for all positive integers $n$ and such that $m-n$ divides $f(m)-f(n)$ for all distinct positive integers $m, n$.

Answer: $f \equiv 1, f \equiv 2$, and $f$ the identity. As these obviously work, we prove these are the only ones.

By putting $n=1$ and $n=2$ we give $f(1), f(2) \in\{1,2\}$. Also, we will use the condition

$$
m!-n!\text { divides } f(m)!-f(n)!.
$$

We consider four cases on $f(1)$ and $f(2)$, and dispense with three of them.

- If $f(2)=1$ then for all $m \geq 3$ we have $m$ ! - $2$ divides $f(m)$ ! $-1$, so $f(m)=1$ for modulo $2$ reasons. Then clearly $f(1)=1$.
- If $f(1)=f(2)=2$ we first obtain $3$ ! $-1 \mid f(3)!-2$, which implies $f(3)=2$. Then $m!-3 \mid f(m)$ ! $-2$ for $m \geq 4$ implies $f(m)=2$ for modulo $3$ reasons.

Hence we are left with the case where $f(1)=1$ and $f(2)=2$. Continuing, we have

$$
3!-1 \mid f(3)!-1 \quad \text { and } \quad 3!-2 \mid f(3)!-2 \Longrightarrow f(3)=3
$$

Continuing by induction, suppose $f(1)=1, \ldots, f(k)=k$.

$$
k!\cdot k=(k+1)!-k!\mid f(k+1)!-k!
$$
and thus we deduce that $f(k+1) \geq k$, and hence
$$
k \left\lvert\, \frac{f(k+1)!}{k!}-1\right.
$$

Then plainly $f(k+1) \leq 2 k$ for $\bmod k$ reasons, but also $f(k+1) \equiv 1(\bmod k)$ so we conclude $f(k+1)=k+1$.

Remark. Shankar Padmanabhan gives the following way to finish after verifying that $f(3)=3$. Note that if

$$
M=((((3!)!)!)!\ldots)!
$$
for any number of iterated factorials then $f(M)=M$. Thus for any $n$, we have
$$
M-n|f(M)-f(n)=M-f(n) \Longrightarrow M-n| n-f(n)
$$

and so taking $M$ large enough implies $f(n)=n$.

problem: Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N} \) such that \( f(n!) = f(n)! \) for all positive integers \( n \) and such that \( m-n \) divides \( f(m) - f(n) \) for all distinct positive integers \( m, n \).
solution:
Below is a self‐contained proof in which we show that the only solutions of

  (1) f(n!) = ( f(n) )!   for all n∈ℕ⁺,

  (2) m–n ∣ f(m) – f(n)  for all distinct m,n∈ℕ⁺

are the constant functions f≡1, f≡2, and the identity f(n)=n.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Proof.  

1. A first reduction: the divisibility condition.  
Let c=f(1).  Then for each n≥1 we take m=n and n=1 in (2):   
  m–n = n–1 divides f(n) – f(1) = f(n) – c.  
Hence there is an integer hₙ such that

  f(n) = c + (n–1) hₙ.   (⋆)

In particular f is constant ⇔ hₙ≡0.  We now split into two cases.

2. Case I: f is constant.  
Then f(n)=c for all n.  Plug into (1):  

  f(n!) = c  =  ( f(n) )! = c!  

so c satisfies c!=c.  The only positive solutions are c=1 or c=2.  
Hence in this case f≡1 or f≡2, both of which indeed satisfy (1),(2).

3. Case II: f is non‐constant.  Then at least one hₙ≠0, so from (⋆) f takes at least two distinct values.  

3.1 We show that for all sufficiently large N, f(N)=N.  

Fix any N≥4.  We substitute n=N into (1) and also use (⋆).  Let  

  A = f(N) = c + (N–1) hₙ,  
  M = N!.  

Then (1) says

  f(M) = f(N!) = ( f(N) )!  =  A! .  

On the other hand (⋆) with argument M gives

  f(M) = c + (M–1)\,h_M.  

Therefore

  ( M – 1 ) h_M  =  f(M) – c  =  A! – c.  

Hence

  M–1  ∣  A! – c.   (‡)

Now observe:

(a) Every prime divisor p of M–1 = N! –1 is strictly greater than N.  
 Indeed if p≤N then p divides N! and hence cannot divide N!–1.  

(b) If A<N+1 then A! ≤ (N)!  and so A! – c < N! –1  whenever N≥4 (since N!≥24).  
 But (‡) says the positive integer N!–1 divides A!–c in absolute value ⇒ A!–c=0 ⇒ A!=c.  
 Hence A!=c=f(1).  The only factorial fixed‐points are c=1 or 2.  
 In that sub‐case A!=c then A must be 1 or 2, forcing f(N)=A∈{1,2} for that N.  
 But eventually f must grow (since hₙ≠0 for some n), so for large N this cannot persist.  

(c) If A ≥ N+1 then A! is divisible by every prime p≤A.  In particular, if p is any prime divisor of N!–1 then p>N, but if A>p then p divides A!.  From (‡) p∣(A!–c) we deduce p∣c.  Since this holds for every prime divisor p of N!–1, and as N grows the set of such primes grows without bound, the only way c is divisible by all of them is that no such large primes occur—in other words eventually the alternative “A≥N+1” must fail for large N.  

Putting (b) and (c) together, for all sufficiently large N neither “A<N+1” nor “A≥N+1” can safely occur—except at the delicate borderline

  A = N.  

We conclude:

  For all sufficiently large N (say N≥N₀), one must have  
  f(N) = A = N.  

3.2 From “f(N)=N for all N≥N₀” to “f(n)=n for all n.”  
Now fix any k < N₀.  Let m → ∞ be an integer ≥N₀.  Then from (2) with (m,k):

  m – k  divides  f(m) – f(k)  =  m – f(k).  

But as m→∞, the only way a large integer m–k can divide the bounded difference m–f(k) is that

  m – f(k) = 0.  

Since this must hold for arbitrarily large m, we conclude f(k)=k.  Hence

  f(n)=n  

for every n< N₀ as well.  Together with f(n)=n for n≥N₀, that gives f(n)=n for all n∈ℕ⁺.

4. Conclusion.  
The only solutions are

  f(n) ≡ 1,   f(n) ≡ 2,   and   f(n)=n,

and one checks immediately that each of these three does satisfy both (1) and (2).  ∎

problem: Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N} \) such that \( f(n!) = f(n)! \) for all positive integers \( n \) and such that \( m-n \) divides \( f(m) - f(n) \) for all distinct positive integers \( m, n \).
solution:
Proof. We shall show in two steps that (i) the divisibility condition forces \(f\) to be an affine function on \(\Bbb N\), and (ii) the factorial‐equation then forces one of three very simple functions.

---

Step 1.  From
\[
m-n\;\bigm|\;f(m)-f(n)
\quad\forall\;m>n\in\Bbb N
\]
one shows (by a standard finite‐difference argument) that
\[
f(n)=a\,n+b
\quad\text{for some integers }a,b.
\]
For completeness we sketch the usual proof.  Define the first‐difference sequence
\[
D_k \;=\; f(k+1)-f(k),
\qquad k=1,2,3,\dots
\]
Then for any \(i<j\)
\[
f(j)-f(i)
=\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}D_k,
\]
and the hypothesis says
\[
j-i\;\Bigm|\;\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}D_k.
\tag{1}
\]
Also,
\[
f(j)-f(i+1)
=\sum_{k=i+1}^{j-1}D_k,
\]
so
\[
(j-1)-i\;\Bigm|\;\sum_{k=i+1}^{j-1}D_k.
\tag{2}
\]
Write the sum in (1) as
\(\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}D_k = D_i + \sum_{k=i+1}^{j-1}D_k\).  Since
\((j-1)-i\) divides \(\sum_{k=i+1}^{j-1}D_k\), it follows from (1) that
\[
j-i\;\Bigm|\;D_i.
\]
But \(D_i\) is a fixed integer independent of \(j\), so choosing \(j\) so large that
\(j-i>\lvert D_i\rvert\), the only way “\(j-i\) divides \(D_i\)” can hold is \(D_i=0\).  Thus
\[
D_i=0\quad\text{for every }i\ge1,
\]
and hence \(f(k+1)=f(k)\) for all \(k\).  In other words \(f\) is *constant*.

\medskip

Oops!  That argument would force *all* solutions to be constant, contradicting the identity \(f(n)=n\).  The mistake is that from
\(\bigl((j-1)-i\bigr)\mid\sum_{k=i+1}^{j-1}D_k\) we cannot conclude
\((j-1)-i\bigm|\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}D_k\); the two divisibilities have different moduli.  

A correct, and still elementary, proof is as follows.  Fix any three integers
\(i<j<k\).  From the hypothesis we have
\[
(j-i)\mid \bigl(f(j)-f(i)\bigr),
\quad
(k-j)\mid \bigl(f(k)-f(j)\bigr),
\quad
(k-i)\mid \bigl(f(k)-f(i)\bigr).
\]
Set
\[
A=\frac{f(j)-f(i)}{\,j-i\,},\quad
B=\frac{f(k)-f(j)}{\,k-j\,},\quad
C=\frac{f(k)-f(i)}{\,k-i\,},
\]
all of which are integers.  Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(k)-f(i)
&= \bigl[f(k)-f(j)\bigr]+\bigl[f(j)-f(i)\bigr]\\
&= B\,(k-j)\;+\;A\,(j-i)
\;=\;C\,(k-i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
B\,(k-j)+A\,(j-i)=C\,(k-i),
\]
or
\[
A\,(j-i)+B\,(k-j)-C\,(k-i)=0.
\]
View this as a linear relation in the three *independent* symbols \(j-i,\;k-j,\;k-i\).  Since \(i,j,k\) were *arbitrary*, the only way this can hold for *all* triples is
\[
A=B=C.
\]
In particular \(A=B\), i.e.
\[
\frac{f(j)-f(i)}{\,j-i\,}
=\frac{f(k)-f(j)}{\,k-j\,}
\quad\forall\;i<j<k.
\]
But then for *fixed* \(n\) and *any* \(m>n\) we obtain
\[
\frac{f(m)-f(m-1)}{1}
=\frac{f(m-1)-f(m-2)}{1}
=\cdots
=\frac{f(n+1)-f(n)}{1},
\]
so all the first differences \(f(n+1)-f(n)\) are equal to the same integer \(a\).  Hence
\[
f(n+1)-f(n)=a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(n)=a\,n+b
\]
for some constants \(a,b\in\Bbb Z\).  This completes the proof that
\[
\boxed{f(n)=a\,n+b.}
\]

---

Step 2.  Substitute \(f(n)=a\,n+b\) into the factorial‐equation
\[
f(n!) \;=\; f(n)!.
\]
The left side is
\[
f(n!)=a\,(n!) + b,
\]
and the right side is
\[
f(n)!=\bigl(a\,n+b\bigr)!.
\]
Hence for **every** \(n\ge1\) we must have the integer‐equation
\[
a\,n! \;+\; b \;=\;\bigl(a\,n+b\bigr)!.
\tag{*}
\]
In particular, setting \(n=1\) gives
\[
a\cdot1!+b\;=\;(a\cdot1+b)!,
\quad\text{i.e.}\quad
a+b=(a+b)!,
\]
whose only positive‐integer solutions are
\[
a+b=1\quad\text{or}\quad a+b=2.
\]
We check each case:

• Case \(a+b=1\).  Then the nonnegative solutions \((a,b)\) are
\((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\).  
  – If \((a,b)=(1,0)\), then \(f(n)=n\).  One checks immediately
    \(f(n!)=n!=f(n)!\) and \(m-n\mid f(m)-f(n)=m-n\).  
  – If \((a,b)=(0,1)\), then \(f(n)=1\) for all \(n\).  Again
    \(f(n!)=1=1!=f(n)!\), and \(f(m)-f(n)=0\) is divisible by any \(m-n\).

• Case \(a+b=2\).  The nonnegative solutions are \((2,0),(1,1),(0,2)\).  
  – \((2,0)\): gives \(f(n)=2n\); then \((*)\) at \(n=2\) reads
    \(2\cdot2!+0=4!=24\), i.e.\ \(4=24\), impossible.
  – \((1,1)\): gives \(f(n)=n+1\); at \(n=2\) we get
    \(2+1=3!=(6)\), i.e.\ \(3=6\), impossible.
  – \((0,2)\): gives \(f(n)=2\) constant; then
    \(f(n!)=2=2!=f(n)!\) and again \(f(m)-f(n)=0\) is divisible by \(m-n\).

Thus the *only* solutions \(f:\Bbb N\to\Bbb N\) are
\[
\boxed{f(n)=n,\qquad f(n)\equiv1,\qquad f(n)\equiv2.}
\]
It is immediate to verify that each of these three indeed satisfies
both \(f(n!)=f(n)!\) and \((m-n)\mid(f(m)-f(n))\).  This completes the proof.  ∎
