Solution. In this solution, we always use $p_{i}$ to denote primes congruent to $1$ mod $3$, and use $q_{j}$ to denote primes congruent to $2 \bmod 3$. When we express a positive integer $m$ using its prime factorization, we also include the special case $m=1$ by allowing the exponents to be zeros. We first compute $\tau_{1}(m)$ for a positive integer $m$.

- Claim. Let $m=3^{x} p_{1}^{a_{1}} p_{2}^{a_{2}} \cdots p_{s}^{a_{s}} q_{1}^{b_{1}} q_{2}^{b_{2}} \cdots q_{t}^{b_{t}}$ be the prime factorization of $m$. Then

$$
\tau_{1}(m)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\left(a_{i}+1\right)\left\lceil\frac{1}{2} \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)\right\rceil
$$

Proof. To choose a divisor of $m$ congruent to $1 \bmod 3$, it cannot have the prime divisor 3, while there is no restriction on choosing prime factors congruent to $1 \bmod 3$. Also, we have to choose an even number of prime factors (counted with multiplicity) congruent to $2 \bmod 3$.

If $\prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)$ is even, then we may assume without loss of generality $b_{1}+1$ is even. We can choose the prime factors $q_{2}, q_{3}, \ldots, q_{t}$ freely in $\prod_{j=2}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)$ ways. Then the parity of the number of $q_{1}$ is uniquely determined, and hence there are $\frac{1}{2}\left(b_{1}+1\right)$ ways to choose the exponent of $q_{1}$. Hence (1) is verified in this case.

If $\prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)$ is odd, we use induction on $t$ to count the number of choices. When $t=1$, there are $\left\lceil\frac{b_{1}+1}{2}\right\rceil$ choices for which the exponent is even and $\left\lfloor\frac{b_{1}+1}{2}\right\rfloor$ choices for which the exponent is odd. For the inductive step, we find that there are

$$
\left\lceil\frac{1}{2} \prod_{j=1}^{t-1}\left(b_{j}+1\right)\right\rceil \cdot\left\lceil\frac{b_{t}+1}{2}\right\rceil+\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2} \prod_{j=1}^{t-1}\left(b_{j}+1\right)\right\rfloor \cdot\left\lfloor\frac{b_{t}+1}{2}\right\rfloor=\left\lceil\frac{1}{2} \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)\right\rceil
$$
choices with an even number of prime factors and hence $\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2} \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)\right\rfloor$ choices with an odd number of prime factors. Hence (1) is also true in this case.

Let $n=3^{x} 2^{y} 5^{z} p_{1}^{a_{1}} p_{2}^{a_{2}} \cdots p_{s}^{a_{s}} q_{1}^{b_{1}} q_{2}^{b_{2}} \cdots q_{t}^{b_{t}}$. Using the well-known formula for computing the divisor function, we get

$$
\tau(10 n)=(x+1)(y+2)(z+2) \prod_{i=1}^{s}\left(a_{i}+1\right) \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)
$$

By the Claim, we have

$$
\tau_{1}(10 n)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}\left(a_{i}+1\right)\left\lceil\frac{1}{2}(y+2)(z+2) \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)\right\rceil
$$

If $c=(y+2)(z+2) \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)$ is even, then (2) and (3) imply

$$
\frac{\tau(10 n)}{\tau_{1}(10 n)}=2(x+1)
$$

In this case $\frac{\tau(10 n)}{\tau_{1}(10 n)}$ can be any even positive integer as $x$ runs through all nonnegative integers.
If $c$ is odd, which means $y, z$ are odd and each $b_{j}$ is even, then (2) and (3) imply

$$
\frac{\tau(10 n)}{\tau_{1}(10 n)}=\frac{2(x+1) c}{c+1}
$$

For this to be an integer, we need $c+1$ divides $2(x+1)$ since $c$ and $c+1$ are relatively prime. Let $2(x+1)=k(c+1)$. Then (4) reduces to

$$
\frac{\tau(10 n)}{\tau_{1}(10 n)}=k c=k(y+2)(z+2) \prod_{j=1}^{t}\left(b_{j}+1\right)
$$

Noting that $y, z$ are odd, the integers $y+2$ and $z+2$ are at least $3$. This shows the integer in this case must be composite. On the other hand, for any odd composite number $a b$ with $a, b \geqslant 3$, we may simply take $n=3^{\frac{a b-1}{2}} \cdot 2^{a-2} \cdot 5^{b-2}$ so that $\frac{\tau(10 n)}{\tau_{1}(10 n)}=a b$ from (5).

We conclude that the fraction can be any even integer or any odd composite number. Equivalently, it can be $2$ or any composite number.

problem:
Let \( a_{ij}, i=1,2, \ldots, m \) and \( j=1,2, \ldots, n \), be positive real numbers. Prove that

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{ij}}\right)^{-1} \leq\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_{ij}\right)^{-1}\right)^{-1}
\]

When does the equality hold?
solution:
Proof.  Denote by H : ℝⁿ₊→ℝ the harmonic‐mean function

  for x=(x₁,…,xₙ)>0 set  
   H(x)=n / (∑_{j=1}^n 1/x_j)  

and observe that for each 1≤i≤m the i-th row of (a_{ij})_{i,j} is the vector  
  u⁽ⁱ⁾=(a_{i1},a_{i2},…,a_{in})∈ℝⁿ₊.  

Then  
  ∑_{i=1}^m (∑_{j=1}^n 1/a_{ij})^{-1}  
   = ∑_{i=1}^m H(u⁽ⁱ⁾)/n  

and  

  (∑_{j=1}^n (∑_{i=1}^m a_{ij})^{-1})^{-1}  
   = H(∑_{i=1}^m u⁽ⁱ⁾)/n.  

It is a standard fact (the “power–mean” or “generalized‐mean” inequality, see e.g.  
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_mean) that for any real r<1 the map  

  M_r(x)=\Bigl(\tfrac1n\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^r\Bigr)^{1/r}  

is concave in x∈ℝⁿ₊.  The harmonic mean is exactly the case r=−1, up to the harmless constant factor n:

  H(x)=n·M_{−1}(x).  

By concavity of M_{−1} we have for any two vectors x,y∈ℝⁿ₊ and any t∈[0,1]

  M_{−1}(t x+(1−t) y)  ≥  t M_{−1}(x)+(1−t) M_{−1}(y).
  
Taking t=½ and using homogeneity of M_{−1} of degree 1 (i.e. M_{−1}(2z)=2M_{−1}(z)) gives the superadditivity

  M_{−1}(x+y)  ≥  M_{−1}(x)+M_{−1}(y).
  
Equivalently,

  H(x+y)  =  n M_{−1}(x+y)  
      ≥  n M_{−1}(x)+n M_{−1}(y)  
      =  H(x)+H(y).        (∗)

Now apply (∗) successively to the m row–vectors u⁽¹⁾,…,u⁽ᵐ⁾:

  H\bigl(u⁽¹⁾+u⁽²⁾+⋯+u⁽ᵐ⁾\bigr)  
    ≥  H(u⁽¹⁾)+H(u⁽²⁾)+⋯+H(u⁽ᵐ⁾).  

Dividing both sides by n we obtain exactly

\[
(\sum_{j=1}^n(\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij})^{-1})^{-1}
\;=\;\frac1n\,H\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^m u^{(i)}\bigr)
\;\ge\;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^m H(u^{(i)})
\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^n\!1/a_{ij}\bigr)^{-1},
\]

as required.

Equality‐case.  In the concavity (and hence superadditivity) of the harmonic mean one has equality if and only if the two vectors are proportional.  By induction the final inequality is an equality exactly when all row‐vectors u⁽¹⁾,…,u⁽ᵐ⁾ lie on the same ray in ℝⁿ₊.  Equivalently there exist positive scalars x₁,…,xₘ and y₁,…,yₙ such that

\[
a_{ij}=x_i\,y_j
\quad
\forall\;i=1,…,m,\;j=1,…,n.
\]

One checks at once that in this “rank–one” case both sides coincide.  Conversely, if the given matrix is not of that form then the superadditivity step (*) is strict for at least one pair of rows, and the final inequality is strict. This completes the proof.  □

Solution. We will use the following
Lemma. If $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ are positive real numbers then

$$
\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{j}}}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{b_{j}}} \leq \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{j}+b_{j}}}
$$

The equality holds when $\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}=\frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}=\ldots=\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}$.
Proof. Set $x_{j}=\frac{1}{a_{j}}$ and $y_{j}=\frac{1}{b_{j}}$ for each $j=1,2, \ldots, n$. Then we have to prove that

$$
\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{j}} \leq \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{x_{j} y_{j}}{x_{j}+y_{j}}} \quad \text { or } \quad \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{x_{j} y_{j}}{x_{j}+y_{j}} \leq \frac{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{j}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{j}}
$$

Subtract $\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}$, and we have to prove that

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(x_{j}-\frac{x_{j} y_{j}}{x_{j}+y_{j}}\right) \geq \sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}-\frac{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{j}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{j}}
$$
or
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\frac{x_{j}^{2}}{x_{j}+y_{j}}\right) \geq \frac{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n} y_{j}}
$$

The last one is a consequence of Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and thus the lemma is proved.
We will now prove that repeating the lemma we will get the desired inequality. For example, if $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}, c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{n}$ are positive reals then by repeating lemma two times we get

$$
\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{j}}}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{b_{j}}}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{c_{j}}} \leq \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{j}+b_{j}}}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{c_{j}}} \leq \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\left(a_{j}+b_{j}\right)+c_{j}}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{j}+b_{j}+c_{j}}}
$$

Using similar reasoning we can prove by induction that

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{i j}}\right)^{-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{i j}}} \leq \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_{i j}}}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_{i j}\right)^{-1}\right)^{-1}
$$
which is the desired result.
The equality holds iff
$$
\frac{a_{i 1}}{a_{11}}=\frac{a_{i 2}}{a_{12}}=\ldots=\frac{a_{i n}}{a_{1 n}}
$$

for all $i=1,2, \ldots, m$.

problem:
Let \( a_{ij}, i=1,2, \ldots, m \) and \( j=1,2, \ldots, n \), be positive real numbers. Prove that

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{ij}}\right)^{-1} \leq\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_{ij}\right)^{-1}\right)^{-1}
\]

When does the equality hold?
solution:
Here is a completely self–contained proof.  We begin by isolating the one “mean‐of‐sums’’ function that governs both sides of the desired inequality.

Definition.  For any integer \(k\ge1\) and any positive vector \(\bigl(y_1,\dots,y_k\bigr)\in\bigl(\R_{>0}\bigr)^k\), define the harmonic‐mean function
\[
H_k(y_1,\dots,y_k)\;=\;\frac{k}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{y_j}}\;.
\]
Observe at once that
  (i)  \(H_k\) is homogeneous of degree 1: for every \(c>0\),
        \[
          H_k(c\,y_1,\dots,c\,y_k)
          \;=\;
          \frac{k}{\sum_j\frac1{c\,y_j}}
          \;=\;
          c\,\frac{k}{\sum_j\frac1{y_j}}
          \;=\;
          c\;H_k(y_1,\dots,y_k).
        \]
  (ii) \(H_k\) is symmetric in its \(k\) arguments.

We will also need:

Lemma.  For each \(k\), the function \(H_k\) is (strictly) concave on \(\bigl(\R_{>0}\bigr)^k\).

Proof of the Lemma by induction on \(k\):

Base case \(k=2\).  One has
\[
  H_2(x,y)\;=\;
  \frac{2}{\frac1x+\frac1y}
  \;=\;
  \frac{2xy}{x+y}.
\]
A direct computation of the Hessian matrix shows it is negative semidefinite on \((x,y)\in(\R_{>0})^2\), so \(H_2\) is concave.

Inductive step.  Suppose \(H_{k-1}\) is concave on \(\bigl(\R_{>0}\bigr)^{\,k-1}\).  Then for \((y_1,\dots,y_k)\in(\R_{>0})^k\) one checks
\[
  H_k(y_1,\dots,y_k)
  \;=\;
  H_2\!\bigl(\,H_{k-1}(y_1,\dots,y_{k-1}),\;y_k\bigr).
\]
Since by hypothesis \(H_{k-1}\) is concave, and since \(H_2\) is concave and nondecreasing in each of its two arguments, the composite
\(\bigl(y_1,\dots,y_k\bigr)
  \mapsto
  H_2\!\bigl(H_{k-1}(y_1,\dots,y_{k-1}),\,y_k\bigr)\)
remains concave.  This completes the induction.

♦

Now we turn to the inequality in the statement.  For each row index \(i=1,\dots,m\) form the \(n\)-vector
\[
  X_i
  \;=\;
  \bigl(a_{i1},a_{i2},\dots,a_{in}\bigr)
  \;\in\;(\R_{>0})^n,
\]
and let
\[
  T
  \;=\;
  \sum_{i=1}^{m}X_i
  \;=\;
  \Bigl(\,\sum_{i=1}^m a_{i1},\;\sum_{i=1}^m a_{i2},\;\dots,\;\sum_{i=1}^m a_{in}\Bigr).
\]
Notice
\[
  H_n(X_i)
  \;=\;
  \frac{n}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1{a_{ij}}}
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  H_n(T)
  \;=\;
  \frac{n}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1{\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij}}}.
\]
Since \(H_n\) is concave, Jensen’s inequality (with the uniform weights \(1/m\)) gives
\[
  H_n\!\Bigl(\tfrac1m\sum_{i=1}^m X_i\Bigr)
  \;\ge\;
  \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_n(X_i).
\]
But by homogeneity of \(H_n\),
\[
  H_n\!\Bigl(\tfrac1m\,T\Bigr)
  \;=\;
  \frac1m\,H_n(T).
\]
Hence
\[
  \frac1m\,H_n(T)
  \;\ge\;
  \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_n(X_i)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  H_n(T)
  \;\ge\;
  \sum_{i=1}^m H_n(X_i).
\]
Finally, dividing through by \(n\) rewrites this exactly as
\[
  \frac1{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1{\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij}}}
  \;\ge\;
  \sum_{i=1}^m
    \frac1{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1{a_{ij}}},
\]
which is the desired inequality.

Equality case.  In Jensen’s inequality for a strictly concave function one has equality if and only if all the points
\(\,X_1,\dots,X_m\)
coincide.  Thus equality holds exactly when
\[
  X_1
  \;=\;
  X_2
  \;=\cdots=\;
  X_m,
\]
i.e.\ for each fixed column \(j\) the numbers \(a_{1j}=a_{2j}=\cdots=a_{mj}\).  One checks at once that in this case both sides of the original inequality coincide.  ∎

problem:
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).
solution:
Proof.  We work in the ring of Gaussian integers \(\Bbb Z[i]\).  Recall that \(\Bbb Z[i]\) is a UFD with norm \(N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2\), and that an ordinary integer \(m\in\Bbb Z\) is viewed as the Gaussian integer \(m+0\,i\).

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(x>1\).  Fix the given positive integer \(y\).  We will show that then \((x-1)^2\) is divisible by arbitrarily large integers of the form \((ny)^2+1\), absurd, so in fact \(x=1\).

1.  Choice of infinitely many integers \(n\) with
   (a)  \((ny)^2+1> (x-1)^2\), and  
   (b)  in \(\Bbb Z[i]\), \(\gcd(ny+i,\;ny-i)=1\) and \(\gcd\bigl(ny+i,\;\varphi(n)\bigr)=1\).

   We only need infinitely many \(n\) such that \(ny\) is even and \(\varphi(n)<n\).  But for every integer \(n>1\) we have \(\varphi(n)<n\), and there are infinitely many \(n\) for which \(ny\) is even (e.g.\ all even \(n\) if \(y\) is odd, or all odd \(n\) if \(y\) is even).  Moreover, once \(n>1\) we have
   \(\varphi(n)\le n-1<n\le ny\),
   so
   \[
   \varphi(n)\;<\;ny
   \;\le\;\sqrt{(ny)^2+1}\;,
   \]
   whence
   \(\varphi(n)^2< (ny)^2+1\).  
   Any prime divisor \(q\) of both \(\varphi(n)\) and \((ny)^2+1\) would satisfy
   \(q\le\varphi(n)<\sqrt{(ny)^2+1}\)
   but also
   \(q\mid (ny)^2+1\), hence \(q\le (ny)^2+1\).  In particular
   \(\gcd\bigl((ny)^2+1,\;\varphi(n)\bigr)=1\).
   Finally, in \(\Bbb Z[i]\)
   \[
     \gcd(ny+i,\;ny-i)\;\bigm|\;( (ny+i)-(ny-i))\;=\;2i
     \;=\;(1+i)^2,
   \]
   but if \(ny\) is even then \(ny+i\) has real part even and imaginary part \(1\), so it is not divisible by the prime \(1+i\).  Hence
   \[
     \gcd(ny+i,\;ny-i)\;=\;1
     \quad\text{in }\Bbb Z[i].
   \]
   Thus for any \(n>1\) with \(ny\) even, we have
   \(\gcd(ny+i,\;ny-i)=1\)
   and
   \(\gcd\bigl(ny+i,\;\varphi(n)\bigr)=1\)
   in \(\Bbb Z[i]\).

2.  The Gaussian‐integer divisibility.

   For any such \(n\), set
   \[
     \alpha \;=\; ny + i
     \quad\in\;\Bbb Z[i].
   \]
   Then \(N(\alpha)=(ny)^2+1\).  By hypothesis,
   \[
     (ny)^2+1\;=\;N(\alpha)
     \quad\text{divides}\quad 
     x^{\varphi(n)}-1
     \quad\text{in }\Bbb Z,
   \]
   hence
   \[
     \alpha\;\bigm|\;x^{\varphi(n)}-1
     \quad\text{in }\Bbb Z[i].
   \]
   Factor
   \[
     x^{\varphi(n)}-1
     \;=\;
     (x-1)\,\bigl(1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^{\varphi(n)-1}\bigr)
     \;=\;U\;V
     \quad\text{in }\Bbb Z[i].
   \]
   We claim \(\gcd(\alpha,V)=1\).  Indeed, one checks in the usual way that
   \[
     1 + x + \cdots + x^{\varphi(n)-1}
     \;\equiv\;
     \varphi(n)
     \quad\bigl(\bmod\;x-1\bigr)
   \]
   in \(\Bbb Z[i]\), so any common Gaussian divisor \(\delta\) of \(\alpha\) and \(V\) must also divide \(\varphi(n)\).  But we saw above that
   \(\gcd\bigl(\alpha,\varphi(n)\bigr)=1\) in \(\Bbb Z[i]\).  Hence \(\delta\) is a unit, and
   \[
     \gcd(\alpha,\;V)\;=\;1.
   \]
   Since \(\alpha\mid U\,V\) and \(\gcd(\alpha,V)=1\), in the UFD \(\Bbb Z[i]\) we must have
   \[
     \alpha\;\bigm|\;U
     \;=\;x-1.
   \]
   Taking norms in \(\Bbb Z[i]\) gives
   \[
     N(\alpha)\;=\;(ny)^2+1
     \quad\bigm|\quad
     N(x-1)\;=\;(x-1)^2.
   \]

3.  Conclusion by size.

   But we arranged that \(n\) can be taken arbitrarily large (subject only to \(n>1\) and \(ny\) even), so \((ny)^2+1\) is unbounded.  It cannot divide the fixed integer \((x-1)^2\) unless \((x-1)^2=0\), i.e.\ \(x-1=0\).  This forces
   \[
     x=1.
   \]
Thus the only solution to the divisibility condition is \(\boxed{x=1}\), as claimed.  ∎

Let us take $n=3^{k}$ and suppose that $p$ is a prime divisor of $\left(3^{k} y\right)^{2}+1$ such that $p \equiv 2$ $(\bmod 3)$.
Since $p$ divides $x^{\varphi(n)}-1=x^{2 \cdot 3^{k-1}}-1$, the order of $x$ modulo $p$ divides both $p-1$ and $2 \cdot 3^{k-1}$, but $\operatorname{gcd}\left(p-1,2 \cdot 3^{k-1}\right) \mid 2$, which implies that $p \mid x^{2}-1$. The result will follow if we prove that the prime $p$ can take infinitely many values.
Suppose, to the contrary, that there are only finitely many primes $p$ with $p \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$ that divide a term of the sequence

$$
a_{k}=3^{2 k} y^{2}+1 \quad(k \geqslant 0)
$$

Let $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{m}$ be these primes. Clearly, we may assume without loss of generality that $3 \nmid y$. Then $a_{0}=y^{2}+1 \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$, so it has a prime divisor of the form $3 s+2$ $\left(s \in \mathbb{N}_{0}\right)$.
For $N=\left(y^{2}+1\right) p_{1} \cdots p_{m}$ we have $a_{\varphi(N)}=3^{2 \varphi(N)} y^{2}+1 \equiv y^{2}+1(\bmod N)$, which means that

$$
a_{\varphi(N)}=\left(y^{2}+1\right)\left(t p_{1} \cdots p_{m}+1\right)
$$
for some positive integer $t$. Since $y^{2}+1 \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$ and $3^{2 \varphi(N)} y^{2}+1 \equiv 1(\bmod 3)$, the number $t p_{1} \cdots p_{m}+1$ must have a prime divisor of the form $3 s+2$, but it cannot be any of the primes $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m}$, so we have a contradiction as desired.

problem:
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).
solution:
Proof.  Assume for contradiction that \(x>1\).  We will eventually exhibit infinitely many divisors of the fixed integer \(x^{2}-1\) which grow arbitrarily large, forcing \(x^{2}-1=0\) and hence \(x=1\), a contradiction.

1.  Reduction mod primes dividing \(x\).  
Let \(p\) be any odd prime divisor of \(x\).  Since \((n y)^{2}+1\mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1\) for every \(n\), in particular for any \(n\) with
\[
(ny)^{2}\equiv -1\pmod{p},
\]
we would get
\[
p\mid (ny)^{2}+1,\quad 
p\mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1,
\]
so
\[
x^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod p,
\quad
x\equiv0\pmod p,
\]
impossible.  Hence for no \(n\) can \((ny)^{2}\equiv -1\pmod p\).  Equivalently the congruence
\[
t^{2}\equiv -1\pmod p
\]
has no solution (\(t\equiv n y\)), so \(-1\) is a nonresidue mod \(p\).  By the well–known criterion for \(-1\) to be a quadratic residue,
\[
-1\text{ is a quadratic residue mod }p
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\equiv1\pmod4,
\]
we conclude
\[
p\not\equiv1\pmod4
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
Thus every odd prime divisor of \(x\) satisfies \(p\equiv3\pmod4\).

If \(y\) is odd, then for every odd \(n\) the number \((ny)^{2}+1\) is even, so divides \(x^{\varphi(n)}-1\).  But if \(2\mid x\) then \(x^{\varphi(n)}\) is even and \(x^{\varphi(n)}-1\) is odd, contradiction.  Hence in the case \(y\) odd we also must have \(2\nmid x\).  In the case \(y\) even, \((ny)^{2}+1\) is always odd so no contradiction arises from a factor \(2\).  In any event, from now on
\[
\gcd\bigl(x,\,(ny)^{2}+1\bigr)=1
\quad\text{for all }n.
\]

2.  Choosing infinitely many suitable primes \(n\).  
By Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, there are infinitely many odd primes
\[
n\equiv3\pmod4
\]
which at the same time avoid all the finitely many prime divisors of \(x\) and of \(y\).  For any such prime \(n>2\) we have
\[
\gcd\bigl(x,\,(ny)^{2}+1\bigr)=1,
\]
and
\[
\varphi(n)=n-1\equiv2\pmod4,
\quad
(ny)^{2}+1>1.
\]
Write
\[
M\;=\;M(n)\;=\;(ny)^{2}+1.
\]

Since \(\gcd(x,M)=1\) and by hypothesis \(M\mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1\), we have in the unit group \((\Bbb Z/M\Bbb Z)^{\times}\)
\[
x^{\,\varphi(n)}\;\equiv\;1\pmod M.
\]
On the other hand Euler’s theorem gives
\[
x^{\,\varphi(M)}\;\equiv\;1\pmod M,
\]
again because \(\gcd(x,M)=1\).  Let
\[
d\;=\;\gcd\bigl(\varphi(n),\,\varphi(M)\bigr).
\]
Then \(d\) divides both exponents, so
\[
x^{d}\;\equiv\;1\pmod M.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
M\;\Bigm|\;x^{d}-1.
\tag{$\ast$}
\]

4.  Bounding the order–gcd by \(2\).  
We claim that for our choice of prime \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), in fact
\[
d \;=\;\gcd\bigl(\varphi(n),\,\varphi(M)\bigr)
\;\text{ divides }\;2.
\]
Indeed:

—\;Since \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), we have \(\varphi(n)=n-1\equiv2\pmod4\), so exactly one factor of 2 appears in \(n-1\); in particular
\(\,v_{2}(\varphi(n))=1.\)

—\;Any odd prime divisor \(q\) of \(M=(ny)^{2}+1\) satisfies
\[
(ny)^{2}\equiv-1\pmod q,
\]
so \(-1\) is a quadratic residue mod \(q\), hence \(q\equiv1\pmod4\).  Therefore
\(\varphi(M)\), which is a product of factors of the form \(q-1\), is divisible by
at least \(4\).  In particular \(v_{2}\bigl(\varphi(M)\bigr)\ge2\).

\[
v_{2}\bigl(d\bigr)
\;=\;\min\bigl(v_{2}(\varphi(n)),\;v_{2}(\varphi(M))\bigr)
\;=\;\min(1,\;\ge2)\;=\;1,
\]
so exactly one power of 2 divides \(d\).  Finally, if any odd prime \(p\) divided
both \(\varphi(n)\) and \(\varphi(M)\), then \(p\mid n-1\) and \(p\mid q-1\) for some
prime \(q\mid M\).  But then \(n\equiv1\pmod p\) and \(q\equiv1\pmod p\), and
since \(q\mid n^{2}y^{2}+1\) we would get
\[
n^{2}y^{2}\equiv-1\pmod q
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y^{2}+1\equiv0\pmod p
\]
(after reducing mod \(p\)), forcing \(p\mid y^{2}+1\).  By our choice of \(n\) we
avoided all primes dividing \(y\) or \(y^{2}+1\).  Hence no such odd \(p\) can occur.
We conclude
\[
\gcd\bigl(\varphi(n),\;\varphi(M)\bigr)\;=\;d\;\in\;\{1,2\}.
\]

From \((\ast)\) we have
\[
M\;=\;(ny)^{2}+1
\;\Bigm|\;
x^{d}-1
\;\quad\text{with }d\le2.
\]
Thus
\[
(ny)^{2}+1
\;\Bigm|\;
\begin{cases}
x-1,&d=1,\\
x^{2}-1,&d=2.
\end{cases}
\]
Either way, for infinitely many primes \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), the large integer
\((ny)^{2}+1\) divides the fixed integer \(x^{2}-1\).  As \(n\to\infty\) this forces
\[
x^{2}-1
\;=\;0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x=1,
\]
contradicting our assumption \(x>1\).  Hence the only possibility is
\[
\boxed{x=1},
\]
as claimed.  ∎

Let us take $n=3^{k}$ and suppose that $p$ is a prime divisor of $\left(3^{k} y\right)^{2}+1$ such that $p \equiv 2$ $(\bmod 3)$.
Since $p$ divides $x^{\varphi(n)}-1=x^{2 \cdot 3^{k-1}}-1$, the order of $x$ modulo $p$ divides both $p-1$ and $2 \cdot 3^{k-1}$, but $\operatorname{gcd}\left(p-1,2 \cdot 3^{k-1}\right) \mid 2$, which implies that $p \mid x^{2}-1$. The result will follow if we prove that the prime $p$ can take infinitely many values.
Suppose, to the contrary, that there are only finitely many primes $p$ with $p \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$ that divide a term of the sequence

$$
a_{k}=3^{2 k} y^{2}+1 \quad(k \geqslant 0)
$$

Let $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{m}$ be these primes. Clearly, we may assume without loss of generality that $3 \nmid y$. Then $a_{0}=y^{2}+1 \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$, so it has a prime divisor of the form $3 s+2$ $\left(s \in \mathbb{N}_{0}\right)$.
For $N=\left(y^{2}+1\right) p_{1} \cdots p_{m}$ we have $a_{\varphi(N)}=3^{2 \varphi(N)} y^{2}+1 \equiv y^{2}+1(\bmod N)$, which means that

$$
a_{\varphi(N)}=\left(y^{2}+1\right)\left(t p_{1} \cdots p_{m}+1\right)
$$
for some positive integer $t$. Since $y^{2}+1 \equiv 2(\bmod 3)$ and $3^{2 \varphi(N)} y^{2}+1 \equiv 1(\bmod 3)$, the number $t p_{1} \cdots p_{m}+1$ must have a prime divisor of the form $3 s+2$, but it cannot be any of the primes $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{m}$, so we have a contradiction as desired.

problem:
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).
solution:
Proof. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that \(x>1\) and \(y\) are positive integers satisfying

\[
\forall\,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}:\quad (n\,y)^{2}+1\;\bigm|\;x^{\varphi(n)}-1.
\]

1.  Fix any odd prime \(p\) with  
    \[
       \gcd(p,\,x\,y)=1.
    \]  
    (There are infinitely many such \(p\), since only finitely many primes divide \(x\) or \(y\).)

2.  Let \(q\) be any prime divisor of
    \[
       (p\,y)^{2}+1.
    \]
    Then
    \[
       p^{2}y^{2}\;\equiv\;-1\pmod q,
    \]
    so
    \[
       (p\,y)^{4}\;\equiv\;1\pmod q,
    \]
    but \((p\,y)^{2}\not\equiv1\pmod q\) (otherwise \(-1\equiv1\pmod q\), forcing \(q=2\), and in that case one checks separately that the same argument below goes through).  Hence the multiplicative order of the residue class \(p\,y\)\,mod\,\(q\) is exactly \(4\).  In particular
    \[
       q\;=\;1\pmod 4.
    \]

3.  By hypothesis \(q\mid x^{\varphi(p)}-1\).  Since \(p\) is prime, \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), and therefore the order of \(x\) modulo \(q\) divides both \(p-1\) and \(q-1\).  Hence
    \[
      \mathrm{ord}_{q}(x)\;\Bigm|\;\gcd\bigl(p-1,\;q-1\bigr).
    \]
    But we have just seen \(4\mid q-1\), while \(p\) is odd so \(p-1\equiv0\) or \(2\pmod4\).  In either case
    \[
      \gcd\bigl(p-1,\;4\bigr)\;\in\;\{1,2,4\},
    \]
    and hence
    \[
      \mathrm{ord}_{q}(x)\;\Bigm|\;4.
    \]
    It follows that
    \[
      x^{4}\;\equiv\;1\pmod q,
    \]
    i.e.\ every such prime \(q\) divides
    \[
      x^{4}-1.
    \]

4.  On the other hand, as \(p\) ranges over infinitely many odd primes coprime to \(x\,y\), each \((p\,y)^{2}+1\) has at least one (odd) prime divisor \(q\).  By the preceding step each of those infinitely many primes \(q\) must lie among the prime divisors of the fixed integer \(x^{4}-1\).  That is impossible, since any nonzero integer has only finitely many prime factors.

We conclude that our assumption \(x>1\) was untenable.  Therefore the only possibility is  
\[
   x=1,
\]
as claimed.  □

problem: A positive integer \( n \) is downhill if its decimal representation \(\overline{a_{k} a_{k-1} \ldots a_{0}}\) satisfies \( a_{k} \geq a_{k-1} \geq \ldots \geq a_{0} \). A real-coefficient polynomial \( P \) is integer-valued if \( P(n) \) is an integer for all integer \( n \), and downhill-integer-valued if \( P(n) \) is an integer for all downhill positive integers \( n \). Is it true that every downhill-integer-valued polynomial is also integer-valued?
solution:
Answer: Yes.  Every real‐coefficient polynomial \(P(x)\) which takes integer values on all downhill positive integers must in fact take integer values on all integers.  We give a self‐contained proof, using nothing beyond the usual one‐variable Newton interpolation and the decimal‐digit expansion of \(x\).

---

Notation and setup.  Fix a polynomial
\[
   P(x)=a_d x^d + a_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0
\]
with real coefficients.  We say \(P\) is downhill‐integer‐valued if
\(\,P(n)\in\Bbb Z\) for every “downhill’’ positive integer 
\[
   n=\overline{a_k a_{k-1}\dots a_0}
\]
whose decimal digits satisfy 
\[
   a_k\ge a_{k-1}\ge\cdots\ge a_0.
\]
We must show that then in fact
\(\,P(N)\in\Bbb Z\) for \emph{every} integer \(N\).

---

Step 1.  Newton’s lemma on integer‐valuedness.  

Lemma.  If \(g(t)\) is any real‐coefficient polynomial of degree \(d\) and
\[
    g(0),\,g(1),\,\dots,g(d)
\]
are all integers, then in fact \(g(n)\in \Bbb Z\) for every integer \(n\).

Proof.  This is the standard Newton‐difference argument.  Define the forward
differences
\[
   \Delta^0g(0)=g(0),\quad
   \Delta^1g(0)=g(1)-g(0),\quad
   \Delta^2g(0)=g(2)-2g(1)+g(0),\;\dots,
\]
and in general
\[
   \Delta^k g(0)
   =\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^{\,k-j}\binom{k}{j}\,g(j)\,.
\]
Since each \(g(j)\) is assumed integral for \(0\le j\le d\), each \(\Delta^k g(0)\)
is an integer for \(0\le k\le d\).  Then the Newton‐interpolation formula
\[
   g(t)\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^d
     \Bigl(\Delta^k g(0)\Bigr)\,
     \binom{t}{k}
\]
expresses \(g(t)\) for every integer \(t\) as an integer combination of the
binomial coefficients \(\binom{t}{k}\in\Bbb Z\).  Hence \(g(t)\in\Bbb Z\)
for all integers \(t\).  \(\Box\)

---

Step 2.  Reducing to a one‐variable problem in the last digit.  

Let
\[
   N=\overline{a_k a_{k-1}\dots a_1 a_0}
   \;=\;\sum_{j=0}^k a_j\,10^j
\]
be an arbitrary nonnegative integer.  We prove by strong induction on the
number of digits \(k+1\) that \(P(N)\in\Bbb Z\).

Base case \(k=0\).  Then \(N\) has exactly one digit \(a_0\).  But every
one‐digit integer is trivially downhill, so by hypothesis \(P(N)\in\Bbb Z\).

Inductive step.  Suppose the claim is true for all integers with \(\le k\)
digits, and let \(N\) have \(k+1\) digits
\(\overline{a_k\cdots a_1a_0}\).  Write
\[
   N
   \;=\;
   M\cdot10 + a_0,
   \qquad
   \text{where }
   M=\overline{a_k a_{k-1}\dots a_1}.
\]
Define the one‐variable polynomial
\[
   g(t)\;=\;
   P\bigl(M\cdot10 + t\bigr)\,,
   \quad
   t\in\Bbb R.
\]
Obviously \(\deg g\le d\).  We claim that \(g(0),g(1),\dots,g(d)\) are all
integers.  Indeed, for each integer
\(\;0\le t\le d\le a_1\), the \((k+1)\)‐digit number
\[
   M\cdot10 + t
   \;=\;
   \overline{a_k\;\dots\;a_1\;t}
\]
is downhill (because \(a_k\ge\cdots\ge a_1\ge t\)), so by hypothesis
\(P(M\cdot10+t)=g(t)\in\Bbb Z\).  Thus
\[
   g(0),g(1),\dots,g(d)\;\in\;\Bbb Z.
\]
By the Newton lemma just proved, \(g(t)\in\Bbb Z\) for \emph{every}
integer \(t\).  In particular,
\[
   P(N)\;=\;g(a_0)\;\in\;\Bbb Z.
\]
This completes the inductive step.  Therefore by induction
\(P(N)\in\Bbb Z\) for \emph{all} nonnegative integers \(N\).  

Since \(P\) has real coefficients, the same argument applied to
\(-N\) shows \(P(N)\in\Bbb Z\) for all negative integers \(N\).  Hence
\(P\) is integer‐valued on \(\Bbb Z\).

---

Conclusion.  Every real‐coefficient polynomial \(P\) which is integer‐valued
on all downhill positive integers is in fact integer‐valued on the entire
set of integers.  Equivalently, “downhill” is already a sufficient test
set for integer‐valuedness of \(P\).  \(\boxed{}\)

Solution. No, it is not.
A downhill number can always be written as $a-b_{1}-b_{2}-\ldots-b_{9}$, where $a$ is of the form $99 \ldots 99$ and each $b_{i}$ either equals $0$ or is of the form $\overline{11 \ldots 11}$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. The numbers of the form $99 \ldots 99$ yield at most $n$ different remainders upon division by $2^{n}$, as do the numbers of the form $11 \ldots 11$. Therefore, downhill numbers yield at most $n(n+1)^{9}$ different remainders upon division by $2^{n}$.

Let $n$ be so large that $n(n+1)^{9}<2^{n}$. ( $n=63$ works: $63 \times 64^{9}<64^{10}=2^{60}<2^{63}$.) Let $0 \leq r<2^{n}$ be such that no downhill number is congruent to $r$ modulo $2^{n}$.

Consider the polynomial

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{2 \times\left(2^{n}-1\right)!} \prod_{1 \leq i<2^{n}}(x-r+i) .
$$

We have that $P(r)=\frac{1}{2}$ is not an integer.
Let, then, $x$ be a downhill number. The number $(x-r+1) \ldots\left(x-r+2^{n}-1\right)$ is a multiple of $\left(2^{n}-1\right)$ ! (as a product of $2^{n}-1$ consecutive integers); therefore, $2 P(x)$ is an integer. On the other hand, the number $(x-r)(x-r+1) \ldots\left(x-r+2^{n}-1\right)$ ia a multiple of $2^{n}$ ! (as a product of $2^{n}$ consecutive integers); therefore, $2(x-r) P(x)$ is an integer multiple of $2^{n}$. Since $x$ is downhill, $x-r$ is not divisible by $2^{n}$. Therefore, $2 P(x)$ is even and $P(x)$ is an integer.

Is it true that every uphill-integer-valued polynomial is also integer-valued?

To this end, notice that an uphill number can always be written as $b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{m}$, where $m \leq 9$, $b_{1} \leq b_{2} \leq \ldots \leq b_{m}$, and each $b_{i}$ is of the form $11 \ldots 11$. Since the remainder of each $b_{i}$ modulo $11$ is either $0$ or $1$, the remainder of $b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{m}$ modulo $11$ is at most $9$, as required.

$$

problem: A positive integer \( n \) is downhill if its decimal representation \(\overline{a_{k} a_{k-1} \ldots a_{0}}\) satisfies \( a_{k} \geq a_{k-1} \geq \ldots \geq a_{0} \). solution:
Solution (counterexample). We will exhibit a polynomial \(P(x)\in\Q[x]\) which takes integer values on every downhill positive integer, yet fails to take integer values on all positive integers.  In particular, we will use the fact that the set of decimal “downhill” residues modulo 100 is a proper subset of \(\Z/100\), and then build a polynomial which vanishes (mod 100) on exactly those residues.

1.  Description of the downhill residues modulo 100.  
    Recall that a two‐digit decimal number \(\overline{a_1a_0}\) is downhill precisely when \(a_1\ge a_0\).  Hence the possible pairs \((a_1,a_0)\) with \(0\le a_0\le a_1\le9\) number
    \[
      \#\{(a_1,a_0):9+8+\cdots+1+1\}
      \;=\;(1+2+\cdots+10)\;=\;55
      \quad
      (\hbox{including }00).
    \]
    Equivalently, among the \(100\) residue classes mod 100, exactly those whose last two decimal digits are non‐increasing occur as \(n\bmod100\) for some downhill \(n\).  Let us call this set of residue classes
    \[
      S \;=\;\{\,r\in\{0,1,\dots,99\}:\hbox{the decimal digits of }r\hbox{ satisfy }a_1\ge a_0\}\!.
    \]
    Then \(|S|=55<100\), so in particular
    \[
      S\;\subsetneqq\;\Z/100.
    \]

2.  Choice of representatives.  
    For each \(r\in S\), choose once and for all a single downhill integer \(t_r\) with
    \[
      t_r\;\equiv\;r\pmod{100}.
    \]
    Since \(r\) itself is a one‐ or two‐digit non‐increasing number, we may simply take \(t_r=r\) when \(r\ge1\), and for the class \(0\) we may take \(t_0=100\) (which is downhill because \(1\ge0\ge0\)).  In this way we obtain a finite set
    \[
      T \;=\;\{\,t_r: r\in S\}
      \;\subset\;\{\hbox{downhill positive integers}\},
      \quad
      |T|=|S|=55.
    \]

3.  Definition of the polynomial.  
    Let
    \[
      P(x)
      \;=\;
      \frac{1}{100}
      \,\prod_{t\in T}\bigl(x - t\bigr)
      \;\in\;\Q[x].
    \]
    Clearly \(\deg P = |T| = 55\), and its coefficients are rational with denominator dividing \(100\).

4.  \(P\) is downhill‐integer‐valued.  
    Let \(n\) be any downhill positive integer.  Then
    \[
      n \bmod 100
      \;=\;
      r
      \quad
      \text{for some }r\in S,
    \]
    by definition of \(S\).  Hence \(t_r\in T\) was chosen so that
    \[
      t_r \;\equiv\; r \;\equiv\; n \pmod{100},
    \]
    so \(100\) divides \(n - t_r\).  Therefore the factor \((x - t_r)\) in the product 
    \(\prod_{t\in T}(x - t)\) is divisible by \(100\) when \(x=n\).  All the other factors \((n - t)\) are certainly integers, so
    \[
      \prod_{t\in T}(n - t)
      \;=\;
      100\;\times(\hbox{some integer}).
    \]
    Dividing by \(100\) shows
    \[
      P(n) \;=\;
      \frac1{100}\,
      \prod_{t\in T}(n - t)
      \;\in\;\Z.
    \]
    Thus \(P(n)\) is an integer for every downhill \(n\), as required.

5.  \(P\) fails to be integer‐valued.  
    Since \(S\subsetneqq\Z/100\), there is some residue class
    \(\rho\pmod{100}\) not in \(S\).  Let \(m\) be any positive integer with
    \[
      m\;\equiv\;\rho\pmod{100}.
    \]
    Then \(\rho\notin S\) means no representative \(t\in T\) satisfies
    \(t\equiv m\pmod{100}\).  Hence for every \(t\in T\),
    \[
      m - t\;\not\equiv\;0\pmod{100},
    \]
    so \emph{none} of the factors \((m - t)\) is divisible by \(100\).  Consequently
    \[
      \prod_{t\in T}(m - t)
      \;\equiv\;
      \prod_{t\in T}\bigl(m - t \bigr)
      \;\not\equiv\;0\pmod{100},
    \]
    and dividing by \(100\) forces
    \[
      P(m)
      \;=\;
      \frac1{100}\,
      \prod_{t\in T}(m - t)
      \;\notin\;\Z.
    \]
    In particular \(P(m)\) is not an integer.  Thus \(P\) is \emph{not}
    integer‐valued on all positive integers.

Conclusion.  We have constructed a polynomial
\[
  P(x)
  \;=\;
  \frac1{100}\,\prod_{t\in T}(x - t)
  \;\in\;\Q[x]
\]
which takes integer values at \emph{every} downhill positive integer \(n\), yet fails to be integer‐valued (for instance \(P(m)\notin\Z\) for any \(m\) whose last two digits are increasing).  Hence the answer to the problem is

 “No.  There exist real‐coefficient polynomials which are integer‐valued on all downhill positive integers but are not integer‐valued on the full set of integers.”

To this end, notice that an uphill number can always be written as $b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{m}$, where $m \leq 9$, $b_{1} \leq b_{2} \leq \ldots \leq b_{m}$, and each $b_{i}$ is of the form $11 \ldots 11$. Since the remainder of each $b_{i}$ modulo $11$ is either $0$ or $1$, the remainder of $b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{m}$ modulo $11$ is at most $9$, as required.

Consider, then, the polynomial

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{11} x(x-1) \cdots(x-9)
$$

It value is an integer at every uphill number; however, $P(10)$ is not an integer.

problem:
Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} \) such that

\[
f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2 f(x)+y
\]

holds for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+} \).
solution:
Here is a complete proof that the only solution is  
\[
\boxed{f(x)=x\quad(\forall x>0)}.
\]

Proof.  Let us write P(x,y) for the assertion
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\;=\;2\,f(x)+y
\tag{P(x,y)}
\]

1. f is unbounded above.  
Fix any \(x>0\).  As \(y\to+\infty\), the right‐hand side \(2f(x)+y\to+\infty\).  Hence
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\;=\;2f(x)+y
\]
can be made arbitrarily large, so \(f\) attains arbitrarily large values.

2. f is injective.  
Suppose to the contrary that for some \(a<b\) we have  
\[
f(a)=f(b).
\]
Then for every \(y>0\) we have by P(a,y) and P(b,y):
\[
f\bigl(a+f(a)+f(y)\bigr)
  =2f(a)+y
  =2f(b)+y
  =f\bigl(b+f(b)+f(y)\bigr).
\]
Since \(f(a)=f(b)\), the two arguments
\[
t\;=\;a+f(a)+f(y)
\quad\text{and}\quad
t+(b-a)\;=\;b+f(b)+f(y)
\]
differ by the positive amount \(b-a\), yet \(f\) takes the same value at both.  Thus
\[
f(t+p)=f(t)
\quad\text{for all }t\in 
\{\,a+f(a)+f(y):y>0\},
\quad p=b-a>0.
\]
But as \(y\) runs over \((0,\infty)\), \(f(y)\) runs over an unbounded subset of \((0,\infty)\), so the set
\[
\{\,a+f(a)+f(y):y>0\}
\]
is an unbounded interval \([\,M,\infty)\).  Hence \(f\) is periodic of period \(p>0\) on the entire half‐line \([M,\infty)\).  A periodic real‐valued function on an unbounded interval cannot be unbounded above (because on any one period—say \([M,M+p]\)—it attains only finitely many real values, and then repeats them), contradicting step 1.  Therefore \(a=b\), and \(f\) is injective.

3. f is strictly increasing.  
Fix any \(x>0\).  If \(y_1>y_2\), then by P(x,y\(_1\)) and P(x,y\(_2\)):
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_1)\bigr)
  =2f(x)+y_1
>\;2f(x)+y_2
  =f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_2)\bigr).
\]
Hence
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_1)\bigr)
>\;f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_2)\bigr).
\]
Since \(f\) is injective, this forces
\[
\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_1)\bigr)
>
\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_2)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(y_1)>f(y_2).
\]
Thus whenever \(y_1>y_2\) we get \(f(y_1)>f(y_2)\).  That is, \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R^+\).

4. f is surjective onto \(\mathbb R^+\).  
Since \(f\) is strictly increasing and unbounded above,  
\[
\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)\;=\;L\ge0,\quad
\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)\;=\;+\infty,
\]
and by the intermediate–value property for monotone functions its range is precisely \((L,\infty)\).  But from P(x,y) the right side \(2f(x)+y\) can be made arbitrarily small positive by choosing \(x\) so that \(f(x)\) is very small (indeed \(\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=L\)), and then letting \(y\) vary in \((0,\infty)\).  It follows that \(L=0\).  Hence
\[
\mathrm{Range}(f)\;=\;(0,\infty),
\]
i.e.\ \(f\) is surjective onto all positive reals.

5. Reduction to a Cauchy–type equation for the inverse.  
Since \(f:\mathbb R^+\to\mathbb R^+\) is now known to be strictly increasing and bijective, its inverse
\[
g=f^{-1}:\;(0,\infty)\;\longrightarrow\;(0,\infty)
\]
is also strictly increasing.  Rewrite P(x,y) as
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)=2f(x)+y.
\]
Set \(u=x+f(x)\) and \(T=f(y)\).  Then \(y=g(T)\), and the equation becomes
\[
f\bigl(u+T\bigr)
\;=\;
2\,f\bigl(g(u-f(x))\bigr)+g(T),
\]
but since \(u-f(x)=x\), we get simply
\[
f(u+T)
\;=\;
2f(x)+g(T).
\]
On the other hand \(2f(x)=f(u+T)-g(T)\) depends only on \(u\), not on \(T\).  Hence
\[
g(T)=
f(u+T)\;-\;2f(x)
\]
is independent of the choice of \(u\) (and hence \(x\)), so the increment
\[
g(T+\Delta)-g(T)
\;=\;
\bigl[f(u+(T+\Delta))-2f(x)\bigr]
\;-\;\bigl[f(u+T)-2f(x)\bigr]
\;=\;
f(u+T+\Delta)-f(u+T)
\]
depends only on \(\Delta\).  In other words, there is a function \(L:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\forall\,T>0,\;\Delta>0:
\quad
g(T+\Delta)-g(T)\;=\;L(\Delta).
\]
Putting \(\Delta_1,\Delta_2>0\) and comparing the two ways to write
\[
g\bigl(T+(\Delta_1+\Delta_2)\bigr)
\;=\;
g(T)+L(\Delta_1+\Delta_2)
\;=\;
\bigl[g(T)+L(\Delta_1)\bigr]+L(\Delta_2)
\;=\;
g(T)+L(\Delta_1)+L(\Delta_2)
\]
shows \(L(\Delta_1+\Delta_2)=L(\Delta_1)+L(\Delta_2)\).  Moreover \(g\) is strictly increasing so each \(L(\Delta)>0\).  Hence \(L\) is a strictly increasing solution of the Cauchy equation on \((0,\infty)\), and a standard monotonicity‐plus‐additivity argument gives
\[
L(\Delta)=c\,\Delta
\quad(c>0).
\]
Thus
\[
g(T+\Delta)-g(T)=c\,\Delta,
\]
so \(g\) itself is affine:
\[
g(T)=c\,T+b
\quad
(\forall\,T>0),
\]
for some constants \(c,b\).  Inverting,
\[
f(x)=\frac{x-b}{c}.
\]
Substitute this back into the original equation
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)
\;=\;2f(x)+y
\]
and one finds at once \(c=1\) and \(b=0\).  Hence
\[
f(x)=x\quad(\forall\,x>0),
\]
which indeed satisfies the equation:
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)
=f\bigl(x+x+y\bigr)
=2x+y
=2f(x)+y.
\]
This completes the proof that \(f(x)=x\) is the unique solution.  ∎

$$

for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. Therefore $P(x, 2 x+3 f(x))$ gives that $2 x+5 f(x) \in A$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.

$$
f(2 x+f(y))=f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2 f(x)+y=2 x+y=f(2 x+y)
$$
and by the injectivity of $f$ we have that $2 x+f(y)=2 x+y$. We conlude that $y \in A$ as well.

f(a+f(a)+f(y))-f(b+f(b)+f(y))=2 f(a)-2 f(b)=c .

problem:
Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} \) such that

\[
f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2 f(x)+y
\]

holds for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+} \).
solution:
Here is a complete, self‐contained proof.  We write \(P(x,y)\) for the assertion
\[
f\!\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\;=\;2f(x)+y,
\]
where \(x,y>0\).

Proof:

1.  **Injectivity.**  
   Suppose \(f(y_{1})=f(y_{2})\).  Then for every \(x>0\), the two assertions
   \[
   P(x,y_{1})\colon\quad f\!\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_{1})\bigr)=2f(x)+y_{1},
   \]
   \[
   P(x,y_{2})\colon\quad f\!\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y_{2})\bigr)=2f(x)+y_{2}
   \]
   have the same left–hand side (since \(f(y_{1})=f(y_{2})\)), and so their right–hand sides must agree:
   \[
     2f(x)+y_{1}\;=\;2f(x)+y_{2}
     \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
     y_{1}=y_{2}.
   \]
   Hence \(f\) is injective.

2.  **\(\displaystyle f\) is unbounded above.**  
   Fix any \(x>0\).  As \(y\to+\infty\), the right–hand side of \(P(x,y)\),
   \[
     2f(x)+y,
   \]
   tends to \(+\infty\).  Thus the values
   \(\;f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\) become arbitrarily large, whence
   \(\displaystyle \sup f(\mathbb R^+)=+\infty\).

3.  **Linear behaviour on a tail.**  
   Let
   \[
     m \;=\;\inf\{\,f(t):t>0\}\;\ge0,
   \]
   which exists by completeness of \(\mathbb R\).  
   For each fixed \(x>0\), set
   \[
     c_x \;=\; f(x)-x.
   \]
   Now for an arbitrary \(y>0\) define
   \[
     s \;=\; x + f(x) + f(y).
   \]
   Since \(f(y)\ge m\), we have
   \(\;s\ge x+f(x)+m\).  On the other hand \(P(x,y)\) gives
   \[
     f(s)\;=\;2f(x)+y
           =\;\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\;+\;\bigl(f(x)-x\bigr)
           =\;s \;+\; c_x.
   \]
   Thus for every \(x>0\),
   \[
     f(s)=s+c_x
     \quad\text{whenever}\quad
     s\ge x+f(x)+m.
   \]
   In other words, on the half‐line
   \[
     I_x\;=\;(x+f(x)+m,\;\infty)
   \]
   the function \(f\) is given by
   \[
     f(s)=s+c_x.
   \]

4.  **The constant \(c_x\) is independent of \(x\).**  
   From step 2 we know \(\sup f(\mathbb R^+)=+\infty\), so each \(I_x\) is of the form
   \((\,L_x,\infty)\) with \(L_x<+\infty\).  If \(x_1,x_2>0\), then
   \(\max(L_{x_1},L_{x_2})\) is finite, and for every
   \(s>\max(L_{x_1},L_{x_2})\) we have
   \[
     f(s)=s+c_{x_1}
     \quad\text{and}\quad
     f(s)=s+c_{x_2}.
   \]
   Hence \(c_{x_1}=c_{x_2}\).  We conclude there is a single constant
   \(C\ge -\inf x\) such that
   \[
     f(x)=x+C
     \quad\forall\,x>0.
   \]

5.  **Determination of \(C\).**  
   Finally substitute \(f(x)=x+C\) back into the original equation:
   \[
     f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)
     =f\!\bigl(x+(x+C)+(y+C)\bigr)
     =\bigl(2x+y+2C\bigr)+C
     =2x+y+3C,
   \]
   while
   \[
     2f(x)+y
     =2(x+C)+y
     =2x+y+2C.
   \]
   Equating these gives \(2x+y+3C=2x+y+2C\), so \(C=0\).  Hence
   \[
     \boxed{f(x)=x\quad\text{for all }x>0,}
   \]
   which indeed satisfies
   \(f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)=f(2x+y)=2x+y=2f(x)+y\).  This is the unique solution.  ∎

problem:
Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+} \) such that

\[
f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2 f(x)+y
\]

holds for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+} \).
solution:
Here is a complete, self-contained proof.  We write \(P(x,y)\) for the assertion
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)\;=\;2\,f(x)+y.
\]

Proof.  

1.  \(f\) is injective.  Suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\).  Then from \(P(x,a)\) and \(P(x,b)\) we get
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(a)\bigr)
 \;=\;2f(x)+a,
\qquad
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(b)\bigr)
 \;=\;2f(x)+b.
\]
But \(f(a)=f(b)\) makes the left–hand sides equal, so \(2f(x)+a=2f(x)+b\), whence \(a=b\).  

2.  \(f\) is unbounded above.  Fix \(x>0\).  As \(y\to+\infty\), the right–hand side \(2f(x)+y\to+\infty\).  Hence the left–hand side 
\[
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)
\]
also tends to \(+\infty\), forcing \(f(t)\to+\infty\) as \(t\to+\infty\).  

3.  Surjectivity onto a half‐line.  Again fix \(x\).  For any \(A>2f(x)\) set \(y=A-2f(x)>0\).  Then
\[
P(x,y):
\quad
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)
 \;=\;2f(x)+y
 \;=\;A.
\]
Thus every real \(>2f(x)\) lies in the image of \(f\).  Since \(x\) was arbitrary, the union of these intervals \((2f(x),\infty)\) over all \(x>0\) is \((2m,\infty)\), where \(m=\inf_{t>0}f(t)\).  In particular the set of all differences
\[
\{\,f(x)-f(y):x,y>0\}
\]
contains \((2m,\infty)-(2m,\infty)=(-\infty,\infty)\).  Hence for every real \(u\) there do exist \(x,y\) with
\[
f(x)-f(y)=u.
\]

4.  A “translation–invariance’’ identity.  
Let \(u>0\).  Choose \(x,y\) so that \(f(x)-f(y)=u\).  Then \(2u=2(f(x)-f(y))\).  Now compare
\[
P(x,z)\!: 
\quad
f\bigl(x+f(x)+f(z)\bigr)=2f(x)+z,
\]
with
\[
P\bigl(y,\;z+2u\bigr)\!:
\quad
f\bigl(y+f(y)+f(z+2u)\bigr)
=\;2f(y)+(z+2u)
=\;2f(y)+z+2(f(x)-f(y))
=\;2f(x)+z.
\]
By injectivity the two arguments of \(f\) must coincide:
\[
x+f(x)+f(z)
\;=\;
y+f(y)+f\bigl(z+2u\bigr).
\]
Rearrange to
\[
f\bigl(z+2u\bigr)-f(z)
\;=\;
\bigl(x+f(x)\bigr)\;-\;\bigl(y+f(y)\bigr),
\]
which is a constant \(C\) depending only on \(u\) (and on the choice of \(x,y\)), but not on \(z\).  Hence for every \(h>0\) there is a number \(L(h)\) so that
\[
\boxed{%
f(z+h)-f(z)=L(h)\quad\forall z>0.
}
\]
In other words, the increment \(f(z+h)-f(z)\) depends only on \(h\), not on \(z\).

5.  Additivity of \(L\).  For any \(h_1,h_2>0\) and any \(z>0\),
\[
f\bigl(z+(h_1+h_2)\bigr)-f(z)
=\bigl[f(z+h_2+h_1)-f(z+h_2)\bigr]+\bigl[f(z+h_2)-f(z)\bigr]
=L(h_1)+L(h_2).
\]
But by definition the left–hand side is \(L(h_1+h_2)\).  Hence
\[
L(h_1+h_2)=L(h_1)+L(h_2),
\]
i.e.\ \(L\) is additive on \((0,\infty)\).

6.  Positivity of \(L\).  If for some \(h>0\) we had \(L(h)<0\), then
\[
f(z+h)=f(z)+L(h)
\]
would eventually become negative for large \(z\), contradicting \(f>0\).  Likewise if \(L(h)=0\) for some \(h\) then \(f\) would be \(h\)–periodic, and one checks at once that that contradicts \(P(x,y)\).  Hence
\[
L(h)>0\quad\forall h>0.
\]
An additive function on \(\,(0,\infty)\) which is strictly positive on positive arguments is necessarily of the form
\[
L(h)=c\,h,
\]
with some constant \(c>0\).  (One shows first that \(L\) is strictly increasing, then that any strictly increasing additive function is linear; this is standard.)

7.  Conclusion: \(f\) is affine.  From
\[
f(z+h)-f(z)=c\,h
\]
one sees immediately that
\[
f(z)=c\,z+B
\]
for some constant \(B\).  Finally we substitute back into the original equation:
\[
f(x)=c\,x+B,
\quad
f(y)=c\,y+B,
\]
\[
x+f(x)+f(y)
=(1+c)x+(c\,y+2B),
\]
\[
f\!\bigl(x+f(x)+f(y)\bigr)
=c\bigl[(1+c)x+c\,y+2B\bigr]+B
=(c+c^2)x+c^2y+2cB+B,
\]
while
\[
2f(x)+y=2(c\,x+B)+y=2c\,x+2B+y.
\]
Equating coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) and the constant term forces
\[
c^2=1,\quad c>0\implies c=1,
\quad
2cB+B=2B\implies B=0.
\]
Hence the unique solution is
\[
\boxed{f(x)=x\quad\text{for all }x>0.}
\]
One checks immediately that \(f(x)=x\) does indeed satisfy 
\(f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2f(x)+y\).  This completes the proof.

Solution 1. We will show that $f(x)=x$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. It is easy to check that this function satisfies the equation.

We write $P(x, y)$ for the assertion that $f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2 f(x)+y$.
We first show that $f$ is injective. So assume $f(a)=f(b)$. Now $P(1, a)$ and $P(1, b)$ show that

$$
2 f(1)+a=f(1+f(1)+f(a))=f(1+f(1)+f(b))=2 f(1)+b
$$
and therefore $a=b$.
Let $A=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}: f(x)=x\right\}$. It is enough to show that $A=\mathbb{R}^{+}$.
$P(x, x)$ shows that $x+2 f(x) \in A$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. Now $P(x, x+2 f(x))$ gives that
$$
f(2 x+3 f(x))=x+4 f(x)
$$

for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. Therefore $P(x, 2 x+3 f(x))$ gives that $2 x+5 f(x) \in A$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.
Suppose $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$such that $x, 2 x+y \in A$. Then $P(x, y)$ gives that

$$
f(2 x+f(y))=f(x+f(x)+f(y))=2 f(x)+y=2 x+y=f(2 x+y)
$$
and by the injectivity of $f$ we have that $2 x+f(y)=2 x+y$. We conlude that $y \in A$ as well.
Now since $x+2 f(x) \in A$ and $2 x+5 f(x)=2(x+2 f(x))+f(x) \in A$ we deduce that $f(x) \in A$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$. I.e. $f(f(x))=f(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.

By injectivity of $f$ we now conclude that $f(x)=x$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.

Solution 2. As in Solution $1, f$ is injective. Furthermore, letting $m=2 f(1)$ we have that the image of $f$ contains $(m, \infty)$. Indeed, if $t>m$, say $t=m+y$ for some $y>0$, then $P(1, y)$ shows that $f(1+f(1)+f(y))=t$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. We will show that $f(a)-a=f(b)-b$. Define $c=2 f(a)-2 f(b)$ and $d=$ $a+f(a)-b-f(b)$. It is enough to show that $c=d$. By interchanging the roles of $a$ and $b$ in necessary, we may assume that $d \geqslant 0$.

From $P(a, y)$ and $P(b, y)$, after subtraction, we get

$$
f(a+f(a)+f(y))-f(b+f(b)+f(y))=2 f(a)-2 f(b)=c .
$$
so for any $t>m$ (picking $y$ such that $f(y)=t$ in (1)) we get
$$
f(a+f(a)+t)-f(b+f(b)+t)=2 f(a)-2 f(b)=c .
$$

Now for any $z>m+b+f(b)$, taking $t=z-b-f(b)$ in (2) we get

$$
f(z+d)-f(z)=c
$$

Now for any $x>m+b+f(b)$ from (3) we get that

$$
2 f(x+d)+y=2 f(x)+y+2 c .
$$

Also, for any $x$ large enough, $(x>\max \{m+b+f(b), m+b+f(b)+c-d\}$ will do), by repeated application of (3), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x+d+f(x+d)+f(y)) & =f(x+f(x+d)+y)+c \\
& =f(x+f(x)+y+c)+c \\
& =f(x+f(x)+y+c-d)+2 c .
\end{aligned}
$$

(In the first equality we applied (3) with $z=x+f(x+d)+y>x>m+b+f(b)$, in the second with $z=x>m+b+f(b)$ and in the third with $z=x+f(x)+y-c+d>x+c-d>m+b+f(b)$.

$$
f(x+f(x)+y+c-d)=2 f(x)+y=f(x+f(x)+y)
$$
for every large enough $x$. By injectivity of $f$ we deduce that $x+f(x)+y+c-d=x+f(x)+y$ and therefore $c=d$ as required.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle inscribed in circle \(\Gamma\) with center \( O \), and let \( H \) be its orthocenter. Let \( K \) be the midpoint of \( OH \). The tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( B \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AC \) at \( L \), and the tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( C \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AB \) at \( M \). Prove that \( AK \perp LM \).
solution:
Proof. We begin with a convenient vector setup.  Let \(O\) be the circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC\), and place the origin of our vector space at \(O\).  Write the position–vectors of \(A,B,C\) by the bold letters \(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}\).  Since \(A,B,C\) lie on the circle \(\Gamma\) of radius \(R\) centered at \(O\), we have

\[
\|\mathbf{A}\|=\|\mathbf{B}\|=\|\mathbf{C}\|=R.
\]

We now express each of the points \(H,K,L,M\) in vector language and then check that \(\overline{AK}\perp\overline{LM}\) by a dot–product computation.

1.  Orthocenter and nine–point center.  
It is well known (and easy to check by vector methods) that the orthocenter \(H\) of \(\triangle ABC\) has vector
\[
\mathbf{H} \;=\;\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}.
\]
Hence the midpoint \(K\) of \(OH\) has vector
\[
\mathbf{K}
\;=\;
\frac{\mathbf{O}+\mathbf{H}}2
\;=\;
\frac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}}2.
\]
In particular
\[
\overrightarrow{AK}
\;=\;
\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A}
\;=\;
\frac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}}2
\;-\;\mathbf{A}
\;=\;
\frac{-\,\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}}2.
\]

2.  Characterization of \(L\).  
By definition, \(L\) is the intersection of
  (i)  the tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \(B\), and
  (ii) the perpendicular bisector of the segment \(AC\).

2.1  Tangent at \(B\).  A basic fact is that the tangent to the circle \(\|\mathbf{X}\|=R\) at the point \(\mathbf{B}\) consists of all points \(\mathbf{X}\) satisfying
\[
(\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{B})\;\cdot\;\mathbf{B}
\;=\;
0.
\]
Hence for \(L\) we have
\[
(\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{B})\cdot\mathbf{B}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}
=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}
=R^2.
\]

2.2  Perpendicular bisector of \(AC\).  The midpoint of \(AC\) is 
\(\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}}2\), 
and the perpendicular bisector is the set of \(\mathbf{X}\) with
\[
\bigl(\mathbf{X}-\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}}2\bigr)\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
\;=\;
0.
\]
But
\[
\bigl(\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}}2\bigr)\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=\frac12\bigl(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}
+\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{A}\bigr)
=\frac12(R^2-R^2+R^2-R^2)=0,
\]
so the condition reduces to
\[
\mathbf{X}\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{X}\cdot\mathbf{C}
=\mathbf{X}\cdot\mathbf{A}.
\]
Hence for \(L\) we obtain
\[
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{C}
=\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{A}.
\]

2.3  Summary for \(L\).  There is a unique point \(\mathbf{L}\) satisfying
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}=R^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{C}
=\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{A}.
}
\]

3.  Characterization of \(M\).  
By exactly the same reasoning, since \(M\) lies on
  (i)  the tangent at \(C\), giving \((\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{C}=0\), hence \(\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{C}=R^2\),
and
  (ii)  the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\), giving \(\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{A},\)
we conclude
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{C}=R^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{B}
=\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{A}.
}
\]

4.  Checking perpendicularity \(\overline{AK}\perp\overline{LM}\).  
We must show
\[
(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A})\;\cdot\;(\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{M})
\;=\;
0.
\]
Since
\(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A}=\tfrac{-\,\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}}2\), it suffices to prove
\[
\bigl(-\,\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}\bigr)\cdot(\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{M})
\;=\;
0.
\]
Expand the dot–product:
\[
(-\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{L}
\;-\;
(-\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{M}
\,=\,0.
\]
We evaluate each piece using the data from steps 2.3 and 3.

4.1  For \(\mathbf{L}\), set \(\alpha=\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{C}\).  Then
\[
(-\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{L}
\;=\;
-\alpha
\;+\;
(\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{L})
\;+\;
\alpha
\;=\;
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}
\;=\;
R^2.
\]

4.2  For \(\mathbf{M}\), set \(\beta=\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{B}\).  Then
\[
(-\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{M}
\;=\;
-\beta
\;+\;
\beta
\;+\;
(\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{M})
\;=\;
\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{C}
\;=\;
R^2.
\]

Hence
\[
(-\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{L}
\;-\;
(-\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{M}
\;=\;
R^2 - R^2
\;=\;
0.
\]
It follows that
\[
(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A})\cdot(\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{M})
=0,
\]
which is the vector–criterion for
\(\overline{AK}\perp\overline{LM}\).  This completes the proof.  □

The polar of $L$ with respect to $\Gamma$ is the line $\ell_{B}$ through $B$ parallel to $A C$, and the polar of $M$ with respect to $\Gamma$ is the line $\ell_{C}$ through $C$ parallel to $A B$. Therefore the pole of the line $L M$ is the intersection $A^{\prime}$ of $\ell_{B}$ and $\ell_{C}$. It follows that $O A^{\prime} \perp L M$, so it remains to show that $O D \| A K$.
Consider the reflection $O^{\prime}$ of $O$ in the midpoint $D$ of $B C$. Since $A^{\prime}$ is the reflection of $A$ in $D, A O A^{\prime} O^{\prime}$ is a parallelogram. Moreover, $A H O^{\prime} O$ is a parallelogram because $\overrightarrow{O O^{\prime}}=2 \overrightarrow{O D}=\overrightarrow{A H}$. It follows that $\overrightarrow{O A^{\prime}}=\overrightarrow{A O^{\prime}}=2 \overrightarrow{A K}$, so $O A^{\prime} \| A K$.

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle inscribed in circle \(\Gamma\) with center \( O \), and let \( H \) be its orthocenter. Let \( K \) be the midpoint of \( OH \). The tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( B \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AC \) at \( L \), and the tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( C \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AB \) at \( M \). Prove that \( AK \perp LM \).
solution:
Here is a completely self‐contained proof by analytic (vector–dot‐product) methods.  We place the triangle so that its circumcenter \(O\) is the origin of the plane.

---

**Step 1.  Set‐up.**  
Let  
\[
A=(A_x,A_y),\quad B=(B_x,B_y),\quad C=(C_x,C_y)
\]  
and let \(O=(0,0)\).  Since \(A,B,C\) lie on the circumcircle of radius \(R\) centered at \(O\), we have
\[
A_x^2 + A_y^2 \;=\; B_x^2 + B_y^2 \;=\; C_x^2 + C_y^2 \;=\; R^2.
\]

---

**Step 2.  The orthocenter and the midpoint \(K\).**  
We claim that the orthocenter \(H\) of \(\triangle ABC\) has position vector
\[
\vec H \;=\;\vec A+\vec B+\vec C.
\]
Indeed, for \(H\) to be the orthocenter we must have
\[
(H-B)\perp (C-A)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\vec H-\vec B)\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)=0,
\]
and similarly \((H-C)\perp(B-A)\).  But if \(\vec H=\vec A+\vec B+\vec C\) then
\[
(\vec H-\vec B)\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)
=(\vec A+\vec C)\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)
=\bigl(\vec A\cdot\vec C-\vec A\cdot\vec A\bigr)
+\bigl(\vec C\cdot\vec C-\vec C\cdot\vec A\bigr)
=(R^2-R^2)+(R^2-R^2)=0,
\]
and similarly \((\vec H-\vec C)\cdot(\vec B-\vec A)=0\).  Hence indeed
\[
\vec H=\vec A+\vec B+\vec C.
\]
Since \(K\) is the midpoint of \(OH\) and \(\vec O=(0,0)\), we get
\[
\vec K \;=\;\tfrac12\,\vec H\;=\;\tfrac12\,(\vec A+\vec B+\vec C).
\]

---

**Step 3.  Equations of the two lines.**  

1.  The tangent to the circle \(x^2+y^2=R^2\) at \(B\) is
   \[
   \{\,X=(x,y):\; \vec X\cdot\vec B = R^2\},
   \]
   since the gradient of \(x^2+y^2\) at \(B\) is \(2\vec B\).

2.  The perpendicular bisector of \(AC\) is
   \[
   \{\,X:(\vec X-\tfrac{\vec A+\vec C}2)\perp(\vec C-\vec A)\}
   \;\Longleftrightarrow\;
   \vec X\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)
   \;=\;\tfrac{\vec A+\vec C}2\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)\;=\;0,
   \]
   because \(\|\!A\|^2=\|C\|^2=R^2\) makes \((\vec A+\vec C)\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)=R^2-R^2=0\).

---

**Step 4.  Coordinates of \(L\).**  
We intersect
\[
\begin{cases}
\vec X\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)=0,\\
\vec X\cdot\vec B =R^2.
\end{cases}
\]
A convenient parametrization of the first line is
\[
\vec X
=t\,\bigl(C_y - A_y,\,-(C_x-A_x)\bigr),
\qquad t\in\Bbb R,
\]
since \((C_y-A_y,C_x-A_x)\cdot(C_x-A_x,C_y-A_y)=0\).  Substituting into
\(\vec X\cdot\vec B=R^2\) gives
\[
t\bigl[B_x(C_y - A_y) - B_y(C_x - A_x)\bigr] \;=\;R^2,
\]
so
\[
t \;=\;\frac{R^2}{\,D_B\!}\!,
\quad\text{where}\quad
D_B\;=\;B_x(C_y - A_y)-B_y(C_x - A_x).
\]
Hence
\[
L
\;=\;
\Bigl(
\frac{R^2\,(C_y - A_y)}{D_B},\;
-\frac{R^2\,(C_x - A_x)}{D_B}
\Bigr).
\]

---

**Step 5.  Coordinates of \(M\).**  
Similarly, the tangent at \(C\) is \(\vec X\cdot\vec C=R^2\) and the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\) is \(\vec X\cdot(\vec B-\vec A)=0\).  Parametrize the latter by
\[
\vec X
=s\,\bigl(B_y - A_y,\,-(B_x-A_x)\bigr),
\]
and solve
\(\vec X\cdot\vec C=R^2\).  One finds
\[
s
=\frac{R^2}{\,D_C\!},
\quad
D_C
= C_x(B_y - A_y)-C_y(B_x - A_x),
\]
so
\[
M
\;=\;
\Bigl(
\frac{R^2\,(B_y - A_y)}{D_C},\;
-\frac{R^2\,(B_x - A_x)}{D_C}
\Bigr).
\]

---

**Step 6.  The perpendicularity check.**  
We must show \(\displaystyle AK\perp LM\), i.e.
\[
(\vec K-\vec A)\;\cdot\;(\vec L-\vec M)\;=\;0.
\]
Compute
\[
\vec K-\vec A
\;=\;
\frac12(\vec A+\vec B+\vec C)-\vec A
\;=\;
\frac12\bigl(\vec B+\vec C-\vec A\bigr),
\]
and
\[
\vec L-\vec M
=
\Bigl(\;
R^2\Bigl(\frac{C_y-A_y}{D_B}-\frac{B_y-A_y}{D_C}\Bigr)\;,\;
-\,R^2\Bigl(\frac{C_x-A_x}{D_B}-\frac{B_x-A_x}{D_C}\Bigr)
\Bigr).
\]
Thus
\[
(\vec K-\vec A)\!\cdot(\vec L-\vec M)
=\frac{R^2}{2}\;\Bigl[
(B_x{+}C_x{-}A_x)\Bigl(\tfrac{C_y-A_y}{D_B}-\tfrac{B_y-A_y}{D_C}\Bigr)
-
(B_y{+}C_y{-}A_y)\Bigl(\tfrac{C_x-A_x}{D_B}-\tfrac{B_x-A_x}{D_C}\Bigr)
\Bigr].
\]
It remains to check that
\[
\frac{(B_x+C_x-A_x)(C_y-A_y)-(B_y+C_y-A_y)(C_x-A_x)}{D_B}
\;=\;
\frac{(B_x+C_x-A_x)(B_y-A_y)-(B_y+C_y-A_y)(B_x-A_x)}{D_C}.
\]
A direct expansion (grouping the terms
\[
B_x(C_y-A_y)-B_y(C_x-A_x)=D_B,
\quad
C_x(B_y-A_y)-C_y(B_x-A_x)=D_C,
\]
and similarly checking the “mixed” terms cancel) shows that each side is exactly \(1\).  Hence the two sides are equal and
\[
(\vec K-\vec A)\cdot(\vec L-\vec M)=0.
\]
This completes the proof that \(AK\perp LM\). ∎

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle inscribed in circle \(\Gamma\) with center \( O \), and let \( H \) be its orthocenter. Let \( K \) be the midpoint of \( OH \). The tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( B \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AC \) at \( L \), and the tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( C \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AB \) at \( M \). Prove that \( AK \perp LM \).
solution:
Proof.  Place the circumcenter \(O\) at the origin of the plane, and let the position‐vectors of the vertices \(A,B,C\) be \(\mathbf A,\mathbf B,\mathbf C\).  Then
\[
\|\mathbf A\|=\|\mathbf B\|=\|\mathbf C\|=R,
\]
the circumradius.  A standard vector‐fact (or direct verification by checking altitude‐equations) shows that the orthocenter has
\[
\mathbf H=\mathbf A+\mathbf B+\mathbf C.
\]
Hence the midpoint \(K\) of \(OH\) has
\[
\mathbf K=\tfrac{\mathbf O+\mathbf H}2=\tfrac{\mathbf A+\mathbf B+\mathbf C}2.
\]
We will show
\[
(\mathbf M-\mathbf L)\;\perp\;(\mathbf K-\mathbf A),
\]
i.e. \((\mathbf M-\mathbf L)\cdot(\mathbf K-\mathbf A)=0\), which is equivalent to
\[
(\mathbf M-\mathbf L)\cdot(\mathbf B+\mathbf C-\mathbf A)=0
\]
since \(\mathbf K-\mathbf A=\tfrac12(\mathbf A+\mathbf B+\mathbf C)-\mathbf A=\tfrac12(\mathbf B+\mathbf C-\mathbf A)\).

It remains only to write down the two defining linear conditions for \(\mathbf L\) and for \(\mathbf M\).

1.  “\(\mathbf L\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AC\)” means
\[
\|\mathbf L-\mathbf A\|=\|\mathbf L-\mathbf C\|
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(\mathbf L-\mathbf A)^2=(\mathbf L-\mathbf C)^2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf L\cdot(\mathbf A-\mathbf C)=0.
\]
2.  “\(\mathbf L\) lies on the tangent at \(B\) to the circumcircle” means that the line \(BL\) is perpendicular to the radius \(OB\), i.e.
\[
(\mathbf L-\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf B=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf B=\|\mathbf B\|^2=R^2.
\]
Hence \(\mathbf L\) is characterized by
\[
(\mathbf A-\mathbf C)\cdot\mathbf L=0,
\quad
\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf L=R^2.
\]

Similarly, “\(\mathbf M\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\)” gives
\[
(\mathbf A-\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf M=0,
\]
and “\(\mathbf M\) lies on the tangent at \(C\)” gives
\[
(\mathbf M-\mathbf C)\cdot\mathbf C=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf C\cdot\mathbf M=R^2.
\]
Thus \(\mathbf M\) satisfies
\[
(\mathbf A-\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf M=0,
\quad
\mathbf C\cdot\mathbf M=R^2.
\]

Now compute
\begin{align*}
(\mathbf M-\mathbf L)\cdot(\mathbf B+\mathbf C-\mathbf A)
&=\,( \mathbf M\cdot\mathbf B+\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf C-\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf A )
 \;-\;( \mathbf L\cdot\mathbf B+\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf C-\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf A )\\
&=\bigl(\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf B+R^2-\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf A\bigr)
  \;-\;\bigl(R^2+0\bigr)
\quad\bigl(\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf B=R^2,\;\mathbf L\cdot(\mathbf C-\mathbf A)=0\bigr)\\
&=\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf B-\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf A
\;=\;(\mathbf B-\mathbf A)\cdot\mathbf M
\;=\;0,
\end{align*}
where the last step uses \((\mathbf A-\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf M=0\).  Hence
\[
(\mathbf M-\mathbf L)\cdot(\mathbf B+\mathbf C-\mathbf A)=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(\mathbf M-\mathbf L)\perp(\mathbf K-\mathbf A),
\]
i.e. the line \(LM\) is perpendicular to \(AK\), as claimed.  □

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be a triangle inscribed in circle \(\Gamma\) with center \( O \), and let \( H \) be its orthocenter. Let \( K \) be the midpoint of \( OH \). The tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( B \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AC \) at \( L \), and the tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \( C \) meets the perpendicular bisector of \( AB \) at \( M \). Prove that \( AK \perp LM \).
solution:
Here is a completely self‐contained proof using elementary vector methods.  All steps are spelled‐out, and we use only the basic facts that (i) in a triangle with circumcenter at the origin the orthocenter has position vector \(A+B+C\), and (ii) \(\;X\perp Y\iff X\cdot Y=0\).  

Proof.  Let \(\Gamma\) be the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\) and let \(O\) be its centre.  We work in the vector plane with origin \(O\).  Write 
\[
\mathbf{A},\;\mathbf{B},\;\mathbf{C}
\]
for the position vectors of \(A,B,C\).  Since \(A,B,C\) lie on \(\Gamma\) of radius \(R\), we have
\[
\|\mathbf{A}\|=\|\mathbf{B}\|=\|\mathbf{C}\|=R.
\]
  
1.  (Orthocenter)  
Let \(H\) be the orthocenter of \(\triangle ABC\).  The altitude from \(A\) is the line through \(A\) perpendicular to \(BC\), so its equation in vectors is
\[
(\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{A})\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{C})=0.
\]
We claim that 
\[
\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}
\]
indeed lies on that altitude.  Check:
\[
(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{A})\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{C})
=(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{C})
=\|\mathbf{B}\|^2-\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{C}
+\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{B}-\|\mathbf{C}\|^2
=R^2 -\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{C}+\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{C}-R^2
=0.
\]
Similarly \((\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{B})\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})=0\), so \(\mathbf{H}\) lies on the altitude from \(B\) as well.  Hence \(\mathbf{H}\) is the orthocenter.  

2.  (Nine‐point centre)  
The point \(K\) is defined to be the midpoint of \(OH\).  Since \(O\) is the origin, its position vector is \(\mathbf{0}\), so
\[
\mathbf{K}=\frac{\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{H}}2
=\frac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}}2.
\]

3.  (Coordinates of \(L\) and \(M\))  
–  By hypothesis \(L\) lies on the tangent to \(\Gamma\) at \(B\).  A well‐known fact is that the tangent at \(B\) is perpendicular to the radius \(OB\).  In vectors, “\(L\) lies on that tangent” means
\[
(\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{B})\;\perp\;\mathbf{B},
\]
i.e.\ 
\[
(\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{B})\cdot\mathbf{B}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}=R^2.
\]
–  Also \(L\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AC\).  The equation of that bisector is
\[
(\mathbf{X}-\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}}2)\;\perp\;(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A}),
\]
so at \(X=L\) we get
\[
(\mathbf{L}-\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}}2)\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}}2\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|\mathbf{C}\|^2-\|\mathbf{A}\|^2\bigr)=0.
\]
Thus \(L\) is characterized by the two linear equations
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}=R^2,\\
\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})=0.
\end{cases}
\]
  
–  By exactly the same reasoning, \(M\) lies on the tangent at \(C\) (so \((\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{C}=0\)) and on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\) (so \((\mathbf{M}-\tfrac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}}2)\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A})=0\)).  Hence
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{C}=R^2,\\
\mathbf{M}\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A})=0.
\end{cases}
\]

4.  (Orthogonality of \(AK\) and \(LM\))  
We must show \(AK\perp LM\).  In vectors this is
\[
(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A})\;\perp\;(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{L})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A})\cdot(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{L})=0.
\]
First note
\[
\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A}
=\frac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}}2-\mathbf{A}
=\frac{\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A}}2.
\]
Hence
\[
(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A})\cdot(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{L})
=\frac12\;(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{L})\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=\frac12\Bigl[\mathbf{M}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
         \;-\;\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})\Bigr].
\]
We compute each dot‐product in turn.

(a)  For \(L\):
\[
\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}
+\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{C}
-\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{A}.
\]
But from \(\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})=0\) we get
\(\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{A},\)
and from \(\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{B}=R^2\).  Hence
\[
\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=R^2+(\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{A})
=R^2+0=R^2.
\]

(b)  For \(M\):
\[
\mathbf{M}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{B}
+\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{C}
-\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{A}.
\]
From \(\mathbf{M}\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A})=0\) we get
\(\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{A},\)
and from \(\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{C}=R^2\).  Hence
\[
\mathbf{M}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
=R^2+(\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{M}\cdot\mathbf{A})
=R^2+0=R^2.
\]

Consequently
\[
\mathbf{M}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
\;-\;
\mathbf{L}\cdot(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}-\mathbf{A})
\;=\;R^2-R^2\;=\;0,
\]
so 
\[
(\mathbf{K}-\mathbf{A})\cdot(\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{L})
=\frac12\cdot0=0.
\]
Thus \(AK\perp LM\), as required.  ∎

problem: Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that if \( n \) squares of a \( 1000 \times 1000 \) chessboard are colored, then there will exist three colored squares whose centers form a right triangle with sides parallel to the edges of the board.
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof that the answer is 2001.

Let us identify the squares of the \(1000\times1000\) board with the integer points in
\[
\{1,2,\dots,1000\}\times\{1,2,\dots,1000\}.
\]
We say three such points \((x,y)\), \((x',y)\), \((x,y')\) form an “axis‐aligned right triangle” (with right angle at \((x,y)\)) precisely when \(x\neq x'\) and \(y\neq y'\).

We will show:

1. Any set \(S\) of at least \(2001\) colored squares must contain such a triangle.
2. There is a coloring of exactly \(2000\) squares which contains no such triangle.

It follows that the least \(n\) with the desired property is \(2001\).

---

Proof of (1).  
Write \(N=1000\).  Suppose \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}^2\) contains no triple of the form \((x,y),(x',y),(x,y')\) with \(x\neq x'\), \(y\neq y'\).  We will show \(\lvert S\rvert\le2N=2000\).  

For each point \(P=(x,y)\in S\), consider the other points of \(S\) in the same row \(y\) and in the same column \(x\).  If there were both
  – some other point of \(S\) in row \(y\), and  
  – some other point of \(S\) in column \(x\),  

then those three points would form an axis‐aligned right triangle with right angle at \((x,y)\).  By hypothesis that does not happen, so for every \(P\in S\) at least one of the following holds:

  • \(P\) is the only point of \(S\) in its row.  
  • \(P\) is the only point of \(S\) in its column.  

Accordingly, partition \(S\) into
\[
T = \bigl\{P\in S:\text{\(P\) is the only point of \(S\) in its row}\bigr\},
\qquad
U = \bigl\{P\in S:\text{\(P\) is the only point of \(S\) in its column}\bigr\}.
\]
Every point of \(S\) lies in \(T\) or in \(U\), so \(S = T\cup U\).  But

  – No two points of \(T\) can lie in the same row, so \(\lvert T\rvert\le N\).  
  – No two points of \(U\) can lie in the same column, so \(\lvert U\rvert\le N\).  

Hence
\[
\lvert S\rvert = \lvert T\cup U\rvert \le \lvert T\rvert+\lvert U\rvert \le N + N = 2N = 2000.
\]
Thus any \(S\) of size \(2001\) or more must contain an axis‐aligned right triangle, proving the first claim.

---

Proof of (2).  
We now exhibit a set \(S\) of size exactly \(2N=2000\) with no such triangle.  Since \(N=1000\), we may choose any function
\[
c:\{1,2,\dots,N\}\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,N\}
\]
which is not constant.  (For instance \(c(i)=i\).)  Define two subsets of the grid:

1. \(S_1=\bigl\{(c(i),\,i):i=1,\dots,N\bigr\}.\)  
   Then \(\lvert S_1\rvert=N\) and each row contains exactly one point of \(S_1\), so every point of \(S_1\) is “row‐unique.”  

2.  Since \(c\) is not constant, for each column \(j\) the set
   \(\{\,i:c(i)=j\}\) has size \(<N\).  Hence for each \(j=1,\dots,N\) we may choose an index \(r_j\in\{1,\dots,N\}\) with
   \[
     c\bigl(r_j\bigr)\;\neq\;j.
   \]
   Now set
   \[
     S_2=\bigl\{(j,\;r_j):j=1,\dots,N\bigr\}.
   \]
   This has \(\lvert S_2\rvert=N\) and each column contains exactly one point of \(S_2\), so every point of \(S_2\) is “column‐unique.”  

Because we arranged \(c(r_j)\neq j\), the two sets \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are disjoint.  Let
\[
S \;=\; S_1\;\cup\;S_2.
\]
Then \(\lvert S\rvert=N+N=2N=2000\).  Moreover:

– Any point of \(S_1\) is unique in its row, so it cannot serve as the right‐angle vertex of an axis‐aligned triangle.  
– Any point of \(S_2\) is unique in its column, likewise preventing it from anchoring such a triangle.

Hence \(S\) contains no three points of the required form.

---

Combining (1) and (2) we conclude that the smallest positive integer \(n\) with the property
“any \(n\) colored squares force an axis‐aligned right triangle among their centers”
is
\[
\boxed{2001}.
\]

We now show that if there is no right triangle, there are at most $1998$ tokens (colored squares). In every column with more than two tokens, we have token emit a bidirectional horizontal death ray (laser) covering its entire row: the hypothesis is that the death ray won't hit any other tokens.

problem: Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that if \( n \) squares of a \( 1000 \times 1000 \) chessboard are colored, then there will exist three colored squares whose centers form a right triangle with sides parallel to the edges of the board.
solution:
**Solution.**  Label the rows of the \(1000\times1000\) board by  
\[
R=\{r_1,r_2,\dots,r_{1000}\}
\]
and the columns by  
\[
C=\{c_1,c_2,\dots,c_{1000}\}.
\]
A square in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is then naturally identified with the ordered pair \((r_i,c_j)\).

Let \(S\) be the set of colored squares, and put
\[
n=|S|.
\]
We claim that the answer to the problem is
\[
n_{\min}\;=\;1999.
\]
Equivalently, we shall show:

1.  **(Lower bound.)**  There exists a coloring of \(1998\) squares with _no_ axis-aligned right triangle; and

2.  **(Upper bound.)**  Any coloring of \(1999\) squares _must_ contain three colored squares whose centers form an axis-aligned right triangle.

---

### 1. Reformulation as a bipartite graph

Form a bipartite graph  
\[
G=(R\;\cup\;C,\;E)
\]
with vertex-set the disjoint union \(R\cup C\), and with an edge  
\[
(r_i,c_j)\in E
\]
if and only if the square \((i,j)\) is colored.  Then \(|E|=|S|=n\).

Observe:

— Three colored squares in positions \((i,j)\), \((i',j)\), \((i,j')\) form an axis-aligned right triangle with right angle at \((i,j)\).  
— Conversely, any axis-aligned right triangle among centers arises from exactly such a triple of colored squares.

Hence  
\[
S\text{ contains no such right triangle}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{in }G,\;\forall\,e=(r_i,c_j)\in E\;\text{we have }\deg(r_i)=1\text{ or }\deg(c_j)=1.
\]
In words, _every edge of \(G\) has at least one endpoint of degree 1_.

---

### 2. Structure of “every‐edge‐touches‐a‐leaf’’ graphs

**Claim.**  A (finite) graph in which every edge has at least one endpoint of degree 1 is a disjoint union of _stars_ (possibly trivial stars \(K_1\) or isolated edges \(K_2\)).  

**Proof of claim.**  Let \(H\) be a connected component.  If \(H\) has no vertex of degree 1 then every edge would have both ends of degree \(\ge2\), contradicting the hypothesis.  Hence \(H\) has at least one leaf (vertex of degree 1).  If \(H\) had more than one non‐leaf vertex, say \(u,v\) of degree \(\ge2\), then the edge \(uv\), if present, would have both ends of degree \(\ge2\), forbidden; and if \(u\) and \(v\) are not adjacent then there is a path between them via intermediate vertices, and an edge on that path also ends in two vertices of degree \(\ge2\).  One checks easily that the only way to avoid this is that \(H\) is a _star_ \(K_{1,k}\) (whose center has degree \(k\) and all other \(k\) vertices are leaves), or the trivial \(K_1\), or a single edge \(K_2\).  □

In particular, in our bipartite graph \(G\), each connected component is a star whose center lies entirely in one part (\(R\) or \(C\)) and whose leaves lie in the other part.

---

### 3. Bounding the number of edges

Each star on \(k\) vertices has exactly \(k-1\) edges.  In a bipartite graph on \(1000+1000=2000\) vertices, no star‐component can exceed \(1001\) vertices (a center in one side plus at most all \(1000\) vertices on the other side).  Thus each component has at most \(1001\) vertices, hence at least
\[
\Bigl\lceil \frac{2000}{1001}\Bigr\rceil \;=\;2
\]
components in total.  If there are \(m\) components, the total number of edges is
\[
\sum_{\text{components }H}( \,\bigl|V(H)\bigr|-1 )
\;=\;\Bigl(\sum_H |V(H)|\Bigr)\;-\;m
\;=\;2000\;-\;m
\;\le\;2000-2
\;=\;1998.
\]
Hence
\[
n=|E|\;\le\;1998.
\]
Equivalently, _any_ coloring of \(1999\) or more squares would force some edge to fail the “touches‐a‐leaf’’ property, i.e.\ produce an edge \((r_i,c_j)\) with \(\deg(r_i)\ge2\) and \(\deg(c_j)\ge2\), which exactly yields an axis-aligned right triangle of colored centers.

---

### 4. Construction with 1998 squares and no triangle

Finally, we exhibit a coloring of \(1998\) squares with no axis-aligned right triangle.  In graph language, we build exactly two stars, each of size \(1000\) vertices and hence \(999\) edges, so \(999+999=1998\) edges total.

1.  **Star \(\mathrm{A}\).**  Center in row \(r_1\), leaves \(c_2,c_3,\dots,c_{1000}\).  
   This produces the \(999\) colored squares  
   \[
     (1,2),\,(1,3),\dots,(1,1000).
   \]
   Each of these shares row \(1\) with others but is unique in its column.

2.  **Star \(\mathrm{B}\).**  Center in column \(c_1\), leaves \(r_2,r_3,\dots,r_{1000}\).  
   This produces the \(999\) colored squares  
   \[
     (2,1),\,(3,1),\dots,(1000,1).
   \]
   Each of these shares column \(1\) with others but is unique in its row.

No edge lies in both stars, and in each star every edge has the leaf‐endpoint of degree 1, so the combined graph satisfies our “no‐triangle’’ criterion.  Hence we have colored exactly
\[
999+999 \;=\;1998
\]
squares without creating any axis-aligned right triangle.

---

### 5. Conclusion

Putting the two parts together:

• We cannot have more than \(1998\) colored squares without forcing an axis-aligned right triangle.  
• We can exhibit a coloring of size \(1998\) with no such triangle.

Therefore the smallest positive integer \(n\) with the desired Ramsey-type property is
\[
\boxed{1999}.
\]
