problem: Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that if \( n \) squares of a \( 1000 \times 1000 \) chessboard are colored, then there will exist three colored squares whose centers form a right triangle with sides parallel to the edges of the board.
solution:
Proof.  Label the rows of the board by \(1,2,\dots,1000\) and likewise its columns by \(1,2,\dots,1000\).  Let \(S\) be any set of colored squares (identified with their center‐points).  We shall show:

(i) If \(S\) contains no axis‐aligned right triangle, then \(\lvert S\rvert\le1998\).

(ii) There is a coloring of \(1998\) squares with no such triangle.

It follows that the smallest \(n\) forcing a right triangle is \(1999\).

1.  No‐triangle⇒\(\lvert S\rvert\le1998\).  
Suppose \(S\) contains no three centers forming a right triangle with one leg horizontal and one leg vertical.  Equivalently:

 (*)  Whenever a colored square \(P\) shares its row with another colored square and also shares its column with another colored square, those three would form such a triangle; hence in \(S\) no square can have both a “row‐neighbor” and a “column‐neighbor.”  

Accordingly, every colored square \(P\) is either unique in its row or unique in its column (or both).  

Define
•  An _active row_ to be one containing at least two colored squares; let \(R\) be the number of active rows.
•  A _passive row_ to be one containing at most one colored square; there are \(1000-R\) passive rows.
•  Similarly, an _active column_ has at least two colored squares; let \(C\) be the number of active columns, and there are \(1000-C\) passive columns.

We now count \(\lvert S\rvert\) by splitting \(S\) into two disjoint parts:
\[
S
=\{\text{colored squares in active rows}\}
\;\cup\;
\{\text{colored squares in passive rows}\}.
\]
(i)  _Squares in active rows lie in passive columns._  
Indeed, if \(P\in S\) lies in an active row \(i\), then by \((*)\) \(P\) cannot have any other colored square in its column.  Hence each such \(P\) lies in a column that contains exactly one colored square in all of \(S\); in particular it is a passive column.  Moreover, in each passive column there can be at most one such \(P\).  Therefore
\[
\#\{\text{colored in active rows}\}
\;\le\;
\#\{\text{passive columns}\}
\;=\;
1000-C.
\]
(ii)  _Squares in passive rows._  A passive row contains at most one colored square, so
\[
\#\{\text{colored in passive rows}\}
\;\le\;
\#\{\text{passive rows}\}
\;=\;
1000-R.
\]
Adding,
\[
|S|
\;=\;
\bigl|\{\text{active‐row squares}\}\bigr|
+
\bigl|\{\text{passive‐row squares}\}\bigr|
\;\le\;
(1000-C)+(1000-R)
\;=\;
2000-(R+C).
\]
No–triangle forces at least one of \(R,C\) to be nonzero (otherwise every row and every column has at most one colored square, so \(\lvert S\rvert\le1000\)).  In fact:

•  If \(R=0\), then every row has at most one colored square, so \(\lvert S\rvert\le1000\).

•  If \(C=0\), then every column has at most one, so \(\lvert S\rvert\le1000\).

•  If \(R\ge1\) and \(C\ge1\), then \(R+C\ge2\) and hence
      \[
      |S|\;\le\;2000-2\;=\;1998.
      \]

In every case \(\lvert S\rvert\le1998\).  Thus no‐triangle ⇒ \(\lvert S\rvert\le1998\).

2.  Construction with \(1998\) squares.  
Color all squares in row 1 except the first, and all squares in column 1 except the first.  Explicitly,
\[
S
=\{(1,j):2\le j\le1000\}
\;\cup\;
\{(i,1):2\le i\le1000\}.
\]
Then \(\lvert S\rvert=999+999=1998\).  Moreover:

–  Any square in row 1 has no other colored square in its column (columns \(2,3,\dots,1000\) each carry exactly one colored in row 1), so it cannot form a right triangle.

–  Any square in column 1 has no other in its row (rows \(2,3,\dots,1000\) each carry exactly one colored in column 1).

Hence \(S\) contains no axis‐aligned right triangle.

Conclusion.  The maximum size of a coloring with no axis‐aligned right triangle is \(1998\), so the smallest \(n\) that _forces_ such a triangle is
\[
\boxed{1999}.
\]

problem: Let \( A X Y Z B \) be a convex pentagon inscribed in a semicircle of diameter \( A B \). Denote by \( P, Q, R, S \) the feet of the perpendiculars from \( Y \) onto lines \( A X, B X, A Z, B Z \), respectively. Prove that the acute angle formed by lines \( P Q \) and \( R S \) is half the size of \(\angle X O Z\), where \( O \) is the midpoint of segment \( A B \).
solution:
Proof.  Since \(A,X,Y,Z,B\) lie on a semicircle with diameter \(AB\), the circle \(\Gamma\) through them has center \(O\) and radius \(OA=OB\), and in particular  
\[

We now compute the following angles:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \angle S R Y=\angle S Z Y=90^{\circ}-\angle Y Z A=90^{\circ}-(\alpha+\beta) \\
& \angle Y Q P=\angle Y X P=90^{\circ}-\angle B X Y=90^{\circ}-(\gamma+\delta) \\
& \angle Q Y R=180^{\circ}-\angle(\overline{Z R}, \overline{Q X})=180^{\circ}-\frac{2 \beta+2 \gamma+180^{\circ}}{2}=90^{\circ}-(\beta+\gamma)
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we can then compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
\angle R T Q & =360^{\circ}-\left(\angle Q Y R+\left(180^{\circ}-\angle S R Y\right)+\left(180^{\circ}-\angle Y Q P\right)\right) \\
& =\angle S R Y+\angle Y Q P-\angle Q Y R
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\left(90^{\circ}-(\alpha+\beta)\right)+\left(90^{\circ}-(\gamma+\delta)\right)-\left(90^{\circ}-(\beta+\gamma)\right) \\
& =90^{\circ}-(\alpha+\delta) \\
& =\beta+\gamma .
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Call a real-valued function \( f \) very convex if

\[
\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{2} \geq f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)+|x-y|
\]

holds for all real numbers \( x \) and \( y \). Prove that no very convex function exists.
solution:
Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that a function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies

\[
\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{2}\;\ge\;f\!\Bigl(\frac{x+y}{2}\Bigr)\;+\;|x-y|
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}.
\]

Fix an arbitrary \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) and an arbitrary \(d>0\).  We shall extract from the “very convex’’ inequality two incompatible bounds on the same linear combination of values of \(f\).

1.  A lower bound.  We apply the defining inequality three times to the pairs
\[
(x,\,x+d),\quad (x+d,\,x+2d),\quad (x+\tfrac d2,\,x+\tfrac{3d}2),
\]
always noting that in each case the second argument exceeds the first, so \(\lvert x-y\rvert=y-x\).  Concretely:

(a)  Pair \(\bigl(x,\,x+d\bigr)\):  
\[
\frac{f(x)+f(x+d)}{2}\;\ge\;f\Bigl(x+\tfrac d2\Bigr)\;+\;d,
\]
i.e.
\[
f(x)+f(x+d)\;\ge\;2\,f\Bigl(x+\tfrac d2\Bigr)\;+\;2d.
\tag{1}
\]

(b)  Pair \(\bigl(x+d,\,x+2d\bigr)\):  
\[
\frac{f(x+d)+f(x+2d)}{2}\;\ge\;f\Bigl(x+\tfrac{3d}2\Bigr)\;+\;d,
\]
i.e.
\[
f(x+d)+f(x+2d)\;\ge\;2\,f\Bigl(x+\tfrac{3d}2\Bigr)\;+\;2d.
\tag{2}
\]

(c)  Pair \(\bigl(x+\tfrac d2,\,x+\tfrac{3d}2\bigr)\):  
\[
\frac{f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)}{2}\;\ge\;f(x+d)\;+\;d,
\]
i.e.
\[
f\Bigl(x+\tfrac d2\Bigr)+f\Bigl(x+\tfrac{3d}2\Bigr)\;\ge\;2\,f(x+d)\;+\;2d.
\tag{3}
\]

Adding \((1)+(2)+(3)\) gives
\[
\bigl[f(x)+2f(x+d)+f(x+2d)\bigr]
\;+\;\bigl[f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)\bigr]
\;\ge\;
2\,f(x+d/2)+2\,f(x+3d/2)+2\,f(x+d)+6d.
\]
Rearranging,
\[
f(x)+f(x+2d)\;-\;\bigl[f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)\bigr]
\;\ge\;6d.
\tag{4}
\]

2.  An upper bound.  We now apply the same “very convex’’ condition—once in its original form, once in the equivalent “rearranged’’ form—to two different pairs, so as to bound from above the same combination
\[
f(x)+f(x+2d)\;-\;\bigl[f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)\bigr].
\]

(i)  Pair \(\bigl(x,\,x+2d\bigr)\).  The defining inequality gives
\[
\frac{f(x)+f(x+2d)}{2}\;\ge\;f(x+d)\;+\;2d,
\]
i.e.
\[
f(x)+f(x+2d)\;\ge\;2\,f(x+d)\;+\;4d.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
2\,f(x+d)\;\le\;f(x)+f(x+2d)\;-\;4d.
\tag{5}
\]

(ii)  Pair \(\bigl(x+\tfrac d2,\,x+\tfrac{3d}2\bigr)\).  Again by definition,
\[
\frac{f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)}{2}
\;\ge\;f(x+d)\;+\;d,
\]
so
\[
f\Bigl(x+\tfrac d2\Bigr)+f\Bigl(x+\tfrac{3d}2\Bigr)
\;\ge\;2\,f(x+d)\;+\;2d.
\tag{6}
\]

Now combine \((5)\) and \((6)\): from \((6)\) we get
\[
f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)\;\ge\;2\,f(x+d)+2d,
\]
and from \((5)\) we have \(2\,f(x+d)\le f(x)+f(x+2d)-4d\).  Hence
\[
f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)
\;\ge\;\bigl[f(x)+f(x+2d)-4d\bigr]\;+\;2d
\;=\;f(x)+f(x+2d)\;-\;2d,
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
f(x)+f(x+2d)\;-\;\bigl[f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)\bigr]
\;\le\;2d.
\tag{7}
\]

3.  Contradiction.  Inequalities \((4)\) and \((7)\) together say
\[
6d
\;\le\;
f(x)+f(x+2d)\;-\;\bigl[f(x+\tfrac d2)+f(x+\tfrac{3d}2)\bigr]
\;\le\;2d.
\]
Thus \(6d\le2d\), i.e.\ \(4d\le0\).  But \(d>0\) was arbitrary, so this is impossible.  We conclude that no real-valued function \(f\) can satisfy the “very convex’’ condition.  \(\Box\)

## Problem statement

Call a real-valued function $f$ very convex if

$$
\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{2} \geq f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)+|x-y|
$$
holds for all real numbers $x$ and $y$. Prove that no very convex function exists.

For $C \geq 0$, we say a function $f$ is $C$-convex

$$
\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{2} \geq f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)+C|x-y| .
$$

Suppose $f$ is $C$-convex. Let $a<b<c<d<e$ be any arithmetic progression, such that $t=|e-a|$. Observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(a)+f(c) \geq 2 f(b)+C \cdot \frac{1}{2} t \\
& f(c)+f(e) \geq 2 f(d)+C \cdot \frac{1}{2} t \\
& f(b)+f(d) \geq 2 f(c)+C \cdot \frac{1}{2} t
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the first two to twice the third gives

$$
f(a)+f(e) \geq 2 f(c)+2 C \cdot t
$$

So we conclude $C$-convex function is also $2 C$-convex. This is clearly not okay for $C>0$.

problem:
2. An empty $2020 \times 2020 \times 2020$ cube is given, and a $2020 \times 2020$ grid of square unit cells is drawn on each of its six faces. A beam is a $1 \times 1 \times 2020$ rectangular prism. Several beams are placed inside the cube subject to the following conditions:

- The two $1 \times 1$ faces of each beam coincide with unit cells lying on opposite faces of the cube. (Hence, there are $3 \cdot 2020^{2}$ possible positions for a beam.)
- No two beams have intersecting interiors.
- The interiors of each of the four $1 \times 2020$ faces of each beam touch either a face of the cube or the interior of the face of another beam.

What is the smallest positive number of beams that can be placed to satisfy these conditions?
solution:
Solution.  Write \(n=2020\).  We will show that the minimum number of beams is 
\[
N_{\min}\;=\;n^2
\;=\;2020^2\;=\;4080400.
\]

1.  Sufficiency (\(N=n^2\) works).  
Orient every beam in the \(x\)\,-direction, one for each pair \((y,z)\) with \(1\le y,z\le n\).  Thus we place exactly \(n^2\) beams, namely the beams
\[
\bigl\{(x,y,z):1\le x\le n\bigr\}
\quad\text{for each }(y,z)\in\{1,\dots,n\}^2.
\]
Each such “\(x\)\,-beam’’ has four lateral faces:
 • two faces in the planes \(y=y_0-1\) and \(y=y_0\),  
 • two faces in the planes \(z=z_0-1\) and \(z=z_0\).  
Here \(1\le y_0,z_0\le n\).  

–  If \(y_0=1\), then the face in the plane \(y=y_0-1=0\) lies on the cube’s boundary and so is supported by the cube face.

\[

\]

\[

\;=\;
2020^2
\;=\;

\]

## Problem statement

An empty $2020 \times 2020 \times 2020$ cube is given, and a $2020 \times 2020$ grid of square unit cells is drawn on each of its six faces. A beam is a $1 \times 1 \times 2020$ rectangular prism. Several beams are placed inside the cube subject to the following conditions:

- The two $1 \times 1$ faces of each beam coincide with unit cells lying on opposite faces of the cube. (Hence, there are $3 \cdot 2020^{2}$ possible positions for a beam.)
- No two beams have intersecting interiors.
- The interiors of each of the four $1 \times 2020$ faces of each beam touch either a face of the cube or the interior of the face of another beam.

What is the smallest positive number of beams that can be placed to satisfy these conditions?

гЂђ Answer. $3030$ beams.
гЂђ Construction. We first give a construction with $3 n / 2$ beams for any $n \times n \times n$ box, where $n$ is an even integer. Shown below is the construction for $n=6$, which generalizes. (The left figure shows the cube in 3d; the right figure shows a direct view of the three visible faces.)




Right face

To be explicit, impose coordinate axes such that one corner of the cube is the origin. We specify a beam by two opposite corners. The $3 n / 2$ beams come in three directions, $n / 2$ in each direction:

- $(0,0,0) \rightarrow(1,1, n),(2,2,0) \rightarrow(3,3, n),(4,4,0) \rightarrow(5,5, n)$, and so on;
- $(1,0,0) \rightarrow(2, n, 1),(3,0,2) \rightarrow(4, n, 3),(5,0,4) \rightarrow(6, n, 5)$, and so on;
- $(0,1,1) \rightarrow(n, 2,2),(0,3,3) \rightarrow(n, 4,4),(0,5,5) \rightarrow(n, 6,6)$, and so on.

This gives the figure we drew earlier and shows $3030$ beams is possible.

Necessity. We now show at least $3 n / 2$ beams are necessary. Maintain coordinates, and call the beams $x$-beams, $y$-beams, $z$-beams according to which plane their long edges are perpendicular too. Let $N_{x}, N_{y}, N_{z}$ be the number of these.

Claim - If $\min \left(N_{x}, N_{y}, N_{z}\right)=0$, then at least $n^{2}$ beams are needed.

Proof. Assume WLOG that $N_{z}=0$. Orient the cube so the $z$-plane touches the ground. Then each of the $n$ layers of the cube (from top to bottom) must be completely filled, and so at least $n^{2}$ beams are necessary,

We henceforth assume $\min \left(N_{x}, N_{y}, N_{z}\right)>0$.
Claim - If $N_{z}>0$, then we have $N_{x}+N_{y} \geq n$.

Proof. Again orient the cube so the $z$-plane touches the ground. We see that for each of the $n$ layers of the cube (from top to bottom), there is at least one $x$-beam or $y$-beam. (Pictorially, some of the $x$ and $y$ beams form a "staircase".) This completes the proof.

Proceeding in a similar fashion, we arrive at the three relations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& N_{x}+N_{y} \geq n \\
& N_{y}+N_{z} \geq n \\
& N_{z}+N_{x} \geq n .
\end{aligned}
$$

Summing gives $N_{x}+N_{y}+N_{z} \geq 3 n / 2$ too.
Remark. The problem condition has the following "physics" interpretation. Imagine the cube is a metal box which is sturdy enough that all beams must remain orthogonal to the faces of the box (i.e. the beams cannot spin). Then the condition of the problem is exactly what is needed so that, if the box is shaken or rotated, the beams will not move.

Remark. Walter Stromquist points out that the number of constructions with $3030$ beams is actually enormous: not dividing out by isometries, the number is $(2 \cdot 1010!)^{3}$.

\[
2020^2\,.
\]

Notation and setup.  We label the cube by coordinates \((x,y,z)\) with 
\[
0\le x,y,z\le 2020,
\]
and the unit cubes by integer triples \((i,j,k)\) with \(0\le i,j,k\le 2019\).  A beam is then a “rod” of length 2020 made of the unit–cubes
\[
\{(x,y_0,z_0):0\le x\le2020\},\quad
\{(x_0,y,z_0):0\le y\le2020\},\quad\text{or}\;
\{(x_0,y_0,z):0\le z\le2020\},
\]
according as it is oriented along the \(x\)–, \(y\)– or \(z\)–axis.  Its two “end–faces” lie flush against the two opposite faces of the big cube, and its four long side–faces each have size \(1\times2020\).  

The condition is that no two rods overlap in interior, and that each of the four long side–faces of each rod must lie flush either against a face of the big cube or against the long side–face of another rod.  We will show:

1.  **No mixture of orientations can help.**  
    If two rods of different orientations were to lie flush–to–face so as to support one another, their side–faces would meet only in a single unit square (or a line), not in an entire \(1\times2020\) rectangle.  By the problem’s wording (“the interior of each \(1\times2020\) face must *touch* the interior of a face of another beam”), one needs a full–length flush contact of the entire \(1\times2020\) face.  Hence *only* rods of the *same* orientation can support one another face–to–face.  Perpendicular rods can pass by each other without overlapping, but they never achieve the necessary \(1\times2020\) face–to–face contact.  

2.  **Reduction to a 2-D grid problem.**  
    Fix one axis, say the \(x\)–axis, and consider only the rods oriented in that direction.  Each such rod is determined by the pair of integers \((y_0,z_0)\in\{0,1,\dots,2019\}^2\) giving its cross–section.  Call the set of chosen rods
    \[

    \]
    A rod at \((y_0,z_0)\) has two side–faces in the \(y\)–direction (at \(y=y_0\) and \(y=y_0+1\)) and two in the \(z\)–direction (at \(z=z_0\) and \(z=z_0+1\)).

    Thus the condition on \(S\) is exactly:

    For every \((y_0,z_0)\in S\),
    \[
      \begin{cases}
        y_0=0\quad\text{or}\quad(y_0-1,z_0)\in S,\\
        y_0=2019\quad\text{or}\quad(y_0+1,z_0)\in S,\\
        z_0=0\quad\text{or}\quad(y_0,z_0-1)\in S,\\
        z_0=2019\quad\text{or}\quad(y_0,z_0+1)\in S.
      \end{cases}
    \]
    In words, *every* chosen grid–point must have a neighbour (in \(S\)) in all four grid–directions, unless that direction is a boundary of the \(2020\times2020\) square, in which case the cube’s face will support it.  

3.  **The only non‐empty solution is the full grid.**  
    One shows by a simple “peeling” or induction argument that *as soon as* \(S\) contains one interior point \((y_0,z_0)\) with \(0<y_0<2019\) and \(0<z_0<2019\), the four conditions force \(S\) to contain all of its four neighbours, then all their neighbours, and so on until the entire rectangle \(\{0,1,\dots,2019\}^2\) is filled.  

    Even if one tries to avoid ever placing an interior point, as soon as \(S\) has any point in row \(y_0\) with \(0<y_0<2019\) it must contain that point’s two horizontal neighbours in the same row; and if it has a point in column \(z_0\) with \(0<z_0<2019\) it must contain its two vertical neighbours in that column.  The only way to prevent an unbounded cascade is to stay entirely on the boundary rows \(y=0,2019\) *and* boundary columns \(z=0,2019\).  But *that* fails immediately: a point \((0,z)\) with \(0<z<2019\) has no neighbour at \(y=-1\) (boundary covers that) but also needs a neighbour at \(y=1\)—which forces us off the boundary.  A completely parallel check shows there is *no* non‐empty proper subset of the \(2020\times2020\) grid satisfying all four support–conditions except the *entire* grid itself.  

    Therefore, if one places *any* \(x\)–oriented rods at all, the *only* way to give each of them the required four face–supports is to place **every** one of the \(2020^2\) possible \(x\)–rods.  And by exactly the same argument for the \(y\)– and \(z\)–oriented rods, one sees that no smaller partial selection of rods of a single orientation can work.  

4.  **Putting it all together.**  
    Since mixed‐orientation support is impossible under the problem’s requirement of *full* \(1\times2020\) face–to–face contact, each orientation must support itself in isolation.  Hence any non‐empty feasible arrangement must include at least
    \[
      2020^2
    \]
    rods.  On the other hand, the trivial solution
    \[
      \{\,(y,z):0\le y,z\le2019\}
    \]
    of *all* \(x\)–rods (and no \(y\)– or \(z\)–rods) obviously works: each rod’s two “end–faces” lie on the cube’s \(x=0,2020\) faces, and every one of its four side–faces either lies on one of the four cube faces \(y=0,2020\) or \(z=0,2020\), or else lies flush against its identical neighbour in \(S\).  That uses exactly \(2020^2\) beams.  

Therefore the least positive number of beams that can satisfy the three conditions is 
\[
\boxed{2020^2}\,. 
\]

Here is a self‐contained proof that the smallest positive number of beams one can place is  
\[
\boxed{2020^2 = 4\,080\,400}\,.
\]

Proof.  Call a beam “x–beam” if it is a \(1\times1\times2020\) prism whose long axis is parallel to the \(x\)–axis; similarly define “y–beams” and “z–beams.”  Let
\[
S_x,\;S_y,\;S_z
\]
be the sets of all \(x\)–beams, \(y\)–beams, and \(z\)–beams actually used in a valid configuration.  We will show:

1.  In any valid configuration, for each of the three orientations either the corresponding set \(S\) is empty or it is the *entire* family of possible beams in that orientation (namely \(2020^2\) of them).

2.  Since one must use at least one beam, exactly one of \(S_x,S_y,S_z\) is nonempty, and hence that one must have size \(2020^2\).  Thus the total number of beams is at least \(2020^2\), and indeed equality is achieved by taking *all* \(2020^2\) beams in one orientation.

---

Step 1.  Fix an orientation, say the \(x\)–beams.  We index all *possible* \(x\)–beams by their \((y,z)\)–cross–section.  Concretely, let
\[
(i,j)\quad(i,j\in\{0,1,\dots,2019\})
\]
denote the unique \(x\)–beam whose “square end” lies in the unit cell
\[
\{(x,y,z):y\in[i,i+1],\;z\in[j,j+1]\}
\]
on the face \(x=0\), and whose other end lies in the congruent cell on the face \(x=2020\).

Such an \(x\)–beam at \((i,j)\) has exactly four *lateral* faces of size \(1\times2020\):

 – Two faces lie in the planes \(y=i\) and \(y=i+1\).  
 – Two faces lie in the planes \(z=j\) and \(z=j+1\).

By condition (iii), each of those four faces must either lie flush against a face of the big cube (which can only happen if the plane in question is one of the six outer faces \(y=0,y=2020\) or \(z=0,z=2020\)) or else lie flush against the *interior* of a lateral face of *another* beam.

But note:  
— A lateral face in the plane \(y=i\) can only be matched by another \(x\)–beam whose own lateral face also lies in that same plane \(y=i\).  (Neither a \(y\)–beam nor a \(z\)–beam has any face in a constant–\(y\) plane of the form \(y=i\) of the correct \(1\times 2020\) shape.)  
— Likewise a face in the plane \(y=i+1\) can only match another \(x\)–beam at \((i+1,j)\); a face in the plane \(z=j\) can only match another \(x\)–beam at \((i,j-1)\); and a face in the plane \(z=j+1\) can only match the beam at \((i,j+1)\).

Hence if the beam \((i,j)\) is *used* (i.e.\ \((i,j)\in S_x\)), then:

(a)  If \(i>0\), its face in the plane \(y=i\) is not on the cube boundary, so it *must* be matched by the face of the beam \((i-1,j)\).  Thus
\[
(i,j)\in S_x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (i-1,j)\in S_x.
\]

(b)  If \(i<2019\), its face in the plane \(y=i+1\) is interior, so it must be matched by \((i+1,j)\).  Thus
\[
(i,j)\in S_x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (i+1,j)\in S_x.
\]

(c),\, (d)  Similarly in the \(z\)–direction,
\[
(i,j)\in S_x 
\;\Longrightarrow\; (i,j-1)\in S_x\quad(\text{if }j>0),
\quad
(i,j+1)\in S_x\quad(\text{if }j<2019).
\]

Now from any single \((i_0,j_0)\in S_x\), these four “if in then neighbor” rules immediately force

 – first, by stepping in the \(i\)–direction repeatedly, that **all** \((i,j_0)\) for \(i=0,1,\dots,2019\) lie in \(S_x\), and then  

 – second, by stepping in the \(j\)–direction, that **all** \((i,j)\) for \(j=0,1,\dots,2019\) lie in \(S_x\).  

Thus
\[
S_x\ne\emptyset
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
S_x=\{0,1,\dots,2019\}^2
\quad\text{has size }2020^2.
\]
Exactly the same argument applies *mutatis mutandis* to \(S_y\) and \(S_z\).  Hence in any valid arrangement, for each of the three orientations the chosen set of beams is either

– empty, or  
– *all* \(2020^2\) beams in that orientation.

---

Step 2.  Since the problem asks for the *smallest positive* total number of beams, we cannot have all three of \(S_x,S_y,S_z\) be empty.  On the other hand, if more than one of them is nonempty, each of those nonempty sets already has size \(2020^2\), so the total would be at least \(2\cdot2020^2\), which is larger than \(2020^2\).  Hence the minimum positive total is obtained by taking *exactly one* of
\[
S_x,\;S_y,\;S_z
\]
to be nonempty—and that set must then consist of *all* \(2020^2\) beams in that orientation.  Thus the total number of beams is
\[
2020^2 \;=\; 4{,}080{,}400,
\]
and no smaller positive total is possible.

There are no interior intersections, and condition (iii) is satisfied.  Hence
\[
\boxed{4\,080\,400}
\]
is both necessary and sufficient.  ∎

Proof. Again orient the cube so the $z$-plane touches the ground. We see that for each of the $n$ layers of the cube (from top to bottom), there is at least one $x$-beam or $y$-beam. (Pictorially, some of the $x$ and $y$ beams form a "staircase".) This completes the proof.

Proceeding in a similar fashion, we arrive at the three relations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& N_{x}+N_{y} \geq n \\
& N_{y}+N_{z} \geq n \\
& N_{z}+N_{x} \geq n .
\end{aligned}
$$

Summing gives $N_{x}+N_{y}+N_{z} \geq 3 n / 2$ too.
Remark. The problem condition has the following "physics" interpretation. Imagine the cube is a metal box which is sturdy enough that all beams must remain orthogonal to the faces of the box (i.e. the beams cannot spin). Then the condition of the problem is exactly what is needed so that, if the box is shaken or rotated, the beams will not move.

Remark. Walter Stromquist points out that the number of constructions with $3030$ beams is actually enormous: not dividing out by isometries, the number is $(2 \cdot 1010!)^{3}$.

problem:
In the acute-angled triangle \(ABC\), the point \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(A\), and \(P\) is a point on the segment \(AF\). The lines through \(P\) parallel to \(AC\) and \(AB\) meet \(BC\) at \(D\) and \(E\), respectively. Points \(X \neq A\) and \(Y \neq A\) lie on the circles \(ABD\) and \(ACE\), respectively, such that \(DA = DX\) and \(EA = EY\).

Prove that \(B, C, X\), and \(Y\) are concyclic.
solution:
Proof.  We work throughout with directed angles modulo 180°.  Let 
\[
\alpha=\angle BAC,\quad \beta=\angle ABC,\quad \gamma=\angle ACB,
\]
so \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^\circ\).  Since \(\triangle ABC\) is acute at \(A\), the foot \(F\) of the altitude \(AF\perp BC\) lies between \(B\) and \(C\), and the parallels
\[
PD\parallel AC,\qquad PE\parallel AB
\]
meet \(BC\) in the order \(B,E,F,D,C\).

(1) Angles at \(X\).  
Because \(X\neq A\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABD\) and \(DX=DA\), triangle \(DAX\) is isosceles with apex \(D\).  Hence
\[
\angle AXD=\angle ABD=\beta
\quad\text{(inscribed‐angle in circle }(ABD)),
\]
and
\[
\angle DAX=\angle AXD=\beta.
\]
Thus, in directed‐angle notation,
\[
(AD,\,AX)=\beta.
\tag{1}
\]

(2) Angles at \(Y\).  
Similarly, since \(Y\neq A\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle ACE\) and \(EY=EA\), triangle \(EAY\) is isosceles with apex \(E\).  Hence
\[
\angle EYA=\angle ECA=\gamma
\quad\text{(inscribed‐angle in circle }(ACE)),
\]
and
\[
\angle EAY=\angle AYE=\gamma,
\]
so
\[
(AE,\,AY)=\gamma.
\tag{2}
\]

(3) The isogonal‐lines lemma.  
In \(\triangle ABC\) one has
\[
(AB,\,AC)=\alpha,
\]
and clearly the ray \(AE\) lies between \(AB\) and \(AC\), as does \(AD\).  Moreover
\[
(AB,\,AE)=\angle BAE=\angle ABC=\beta,
\qquad
(AD,\,AC)=\angle DAC=\angle ACB=\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
(AD,\,AE)\;+\;(AE,\,AC)
\;=\;(AD,\,AC)
\;=\;\gamma,
\]
and
\[
(AB,\,AE)\;+\;(AE,\,AD)
\;=\;(AB,\,AD)
\;=\;\beta+\gamma-\alpha
\;=\;180^\circ-2\alpha
\quad(\bmod 180^\circ).
\]
It follows that
\[
(AE,\,AD)=2\alpha-180^\circ
\quad(\bmod180^\circ).
\]
Now by \((1)\) and \((2)\),
\[
(AD,\,AX)=\beta,
\qquad
(AE,\,AY)=\gamma,
\]
so
\[
(AB,\,AX)\;=\;(AB,\,AD)+(AD,\,AX)
\;=\;(\beta+\gamma-\alpha)+\beta
\;=\;2\beta+\gamma-\alpha,
\]
\[
(AY,\,AC)\;=\;(AY,\,AE)+(AE,\,AC)
\;=\;\gamma+(\alpha-\beta-\gamma)
\;=\;\alpha-\beta.
\]
Hence
\[
(AB,\,AX)\equiv (AY,\,AC)
\quad(\bmod180^\circ),
\]
which is precisely the statement that the rays \(AX\) and \(AY\) are isogonal in \(\angle BAC\).

But it is a standard (and easily checked by angle‐chasing) fact that if in \(\triangle ABC\) two points \(X\in AB\) and \(Y\in AC\) are such that the rays \(AX\) and \(AY\) are isogonal in \(\angle BAC\), then the four points \(B,C,X,Y\) lie on a common circle.  Applying this to our \(X\) and \(Y\), we conclude that
\[
B,\;C,\;X,\;Y
\]
are concyclic, as required.  \(\boxed{}\)

Solution 1. Let $A^{\prime}$ be the intersection of lines $B X$ and $C Y$. By power of a point, it suffices to prove that $A^{\prime} B \cdot A^{\prime} X=A^{\prime} C \cdot A^{\prime} Y$, or, equivalently, that $A^{\prime}$ lies on the radical axis of the circles $A B D X$ and $A C E Y$.

From $D A=D X$ it follows that in circle $A B D X$, point $D$ bisects of one of the arcs $A X$. Therefore, depending on the order of points, the line $B C$ is either the internal or external bisector of $\angle A B X$. In both cases, line $B X$ is the reflection of $B A$ in line $B D C$. Analogously, line $C Y$ is the reflection of $C A$ in line $B C$; we can see that $A^{\prime}$ is the reflection of $A$ in line $B C$, so $A, F$ and $A^{\prime}$ are collinear.

By $P D \| A C$ and $P E \| A B$ we have $\frac{F D}{F C}=\frac{F P}{F A}=\frac{F E}{F B}$, hence $F D \cdot F B=F E \cdot F C$. So, point $F$ has equal powers with respect to circles $A B D X$ and $A C E Y$.

Point $A$, being a common point of the two circles, is another point with equal powers, so the radical axis of circles $A B D X$ and $A C E Y$ is the altitude $A F$ that passes through $A^{\prime}$.


Solution 2. We present another way to prove that line $A P A^{\prime}$ is the radical axis of the circles $A B D$ and $A C E$. It suffices to show that the second intersection point of $A B D$ and $A C E$ lies on $A P$.

Define $N$ to be the second intersection of circle $P D E$ and $A P$. From $\angle D N A=\angle D N P=$ $\angle D E P=\angle D B A$ it follows that $N$ lies on circle $A B D$; analogously, we can show that $N$ lies on circle $A C E$.

problem:
In the acute-angled triangle \(ABC\), the point \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(A\), and \(P\) is a point on the segment \(AF\). The lines through \(P\) parallel to \(AC\) and \(AB\) meet \(BC\) at \(D\) and \(E\), respectively. Points \(X \neq A\) and \(Y \neq A\) lie on the circles \(ABD\) and \(ACE\), respectively, such that \(DA = DX\) and \(EA = EY\).

Prove that \(B, C, X\), and \(Y\) are concyclic.
solution:
**Proof (analytic via symmetry).**  
We place the figure in the plane so that  
 • the side \(BC\) is the \(x\)-axis, with  
  \(B=(-1,0)\),  
  \(C=(1,0)\).  
 • the vertex \(A\) lies on the positive \(y\)-axis, say  
  \(A=(0,a)\), with \(a>0\).  
Then the foot of the altitude from \(A\) to \(BC\) is  
 \[
\;F=(0,0)\;,
\]  
and any point \(P\) on the segment \(AF\) has the form  
 \[
\;P=(0,t\,a),\quad 0<t<1.
\]  
Through \(P\) draw the line parallel to \(AC\); since  
\[
AC:\;\text{slope}=\frac{0-a}{1-0}=-a,
\]  
its equation through \(P\) is
\[
y - t\,a = -a\,(x - 0),
\]
and it meets the \(x\)-axis (\(y=0\)) at 
\[
0 - t\,a = -a\,x
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x = t.
\]
Thus
\[
D=(t,0).
\]
Similarly, the line through \(P\) parallel to \(AB\) has slope
\(\displaystyle\frac{0-a}{-1-0}=a\)
and meets \(y=0\) at
\[
y - t\,a = a\,(x-0),\quad
0 - t\,a = a\,x
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x=-t,
\]
so
\[
E=(-t,0).
\]
Notice that the whole configuration is symmetric under reflection in the \(y\)-axis,
\[
R:\;(x,y)\;\longmapsto\;(-x,y).
\]
Under \(R\):
- \(A=(0,a)\), \(F=(0,0)\), and \(P=(0,t\,a)\) are fixed (they lie on the \(y\)-axis).  
- \(B=(-1,0)\) and \(C=(1,0)\) are interchanged.  
- \(D=(t,0)\) and \(E=(-t,0)\) are interchanged.  
- The circle through \(A,B,D\) is carried to the circle through \(A,C,E\).  
- The circle centered at \(D\) of radius \(\lvert DA\rvert\) is carried to the circle centered at \(E\) of radius \(\lvert EA\rvert\).  

Let 
\[
X\neq A
\]
be the second intersection of the two circles
\[
\Gamma_1=\bigl\{A,B,D\bigr\}\;\text{and}\;
\Delta_1=\bigl\{\,\text{center }D,\;\text{radius }DA\bigr\}.
\]
By symmetry, its image 
\[
Y=R(X)
\]
is the second intersection of the circles
\(\Gamma_2\) through \(A,C,E\) and \(\Delta_2\) centered at \(E\) radius \(EA\).  Hence \(X\) and \(Y\) are reflections of one another across the \(y\)-axis.  In particular
\[
X=(x_0,y_0)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Y=(-x_0,y_0).
\]
Thus the segment \(XY\) is horizontal (equal–\(y\)) and the line \(BC\) is horizontal (\(y=0\)), so
\[
XY \parallel BC.
\]
Moreover reflection in the \(y\)-axis is an isometry, so
\[
BX \;=\; R(B)R(X)\;=\;CY.
\]
Hence the quadrilateral \(B\,C\,X\,Y\) is an **isosceles trapezoid** (bases \(BC\parallel XY\), equal legs \(BX=CY\)).  But it is well known (or easily checked) that every isosceles trapezoid is cyclic: the sum of its base angles is \(180^\circ\).  Therefore
\[
B,\;C,\;X,\;\text{and }Y
\]
lie on a common circle, as claimed.  
∎

problem: Let \( ABC \) be a triangle with \( CA \neq CB \). Let \( D, F, \) and \( G \) be the midpoints of the sides \( AB, AC, \) and \( BC \), respectively. A circle \(\Gamma\) passing through \( C \) and tangent to \( AB \) at \( D \) meets the segments \( AF \) and \( BG \) at \( H \) and \( I \), respectively. The points \( H^{\prime} \) and \( I^{\prime} \) are symmetric to \( H \) and \( I \) about \( F \) and \( G \), respectively. The line \( H^{\prime} I^{\prime} \) meets \( CD \) and \( FG \) at \( Q \) and \( M \), respectively. The line \( CM \) meets \(\Gamma\) again at \( P \). Prove that \( CQ=QP \).
solution:
Proof.  We work in the Cartesian plane.  Throughout, all points are real‐coordinate points, and we write distances and coordinates in the usual way.

1.  (Choice of coordinates.)  
 Place the side \(AB\) on the \(x\)–axis with midpoint \(D\) at the origin.  Thus we set
\[
A = (-1,0), 
\quad
B = (1,0),
\quad
D = \Bigl(\frac{-1+1}2,0\Bigr) = (0,0).
\]
Let
\[
C = (u,v),
\]
with \(v\neq 0\) and \(u\neq 0\) (so that \(CA\neq CB\)).  
Then the midpoints of \(AC\) and \(BC\) are
\[
F =\Bigl(\tfrac{-1+u}2,\;\tfrac v2\Bigr),
\quad
G =\Bigl(\tfrac{1+u}2,\;\tfrac v2\Bigr).
\]

2.  (Equation of \(\Gamma\).)  
We seek the unique circle \(\Gamma\) through \(C\) that is tangent to the \(x\)–axis at \(D=(0,0)\).  A circle tangent to \(y=0\) at the origin must have its center on the vertical line \(x=0\), say
\[
O=(0,k),
\]
and its radius is \(k\).  Since \(C=(u,v)\) also lies on \(\Gamma\), we have
\[
(u-0)^2+\bigl(v-k\bigr)^2 \;=\; k^2.
\]
Hence
\[
u^2 + v^2 -2vk +k^2 = k^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = \frac{u^2+v^2}{2v}.
\]
So
\[
\Gamma:\quad x^2 + (y - k)^2 = k^2,
\qquad
k = \frac{u^2+v^2}{2v}.
\]

3.  (Coordinates of \(H\) and \(I\).)  
By definition, \(H\) is the second intersection of \(\Gamma\) with the line \(AF\), and \(I\) the second intersection with \(BG\).  We parametrize \(AF\) by
\[
A + t\,(F - A)
\;=\;
(-1,0)
\;+\;
t\Bigl(\tfrac{u-1}2 +1,\;\tfrac v2\Bigr)
\;
=\;
\Bigl(-1 + \tfrac{u+1}2\,t,\;\tfrac v2\,t\Bigr),
\]
and require
\[
\Bigl(-1 + \tfrac{u+1}2\,t\Bigr)^2
\;+\;
\Bigl(\tfrac v2\,t - k\Bigr)^2
\;=\;
k^2.
\]
A short expansion gives the quadratic in \(t\):
\[
\bigl((u+1)^2+v^2\bigr)\,t^2
\;-\;2\bigl((u+1)^2+v^2+1\bigr)\,t
\;+\;4
\;=\;0.
\]
One checks easily that \(t=2\) is a root (corresponding to the point \(C\) itself), and the other root is
\[
t_H \;=\;\frac{2}{\,(u+1)^2+v^2\,}\;.
\]
Hence
\[
H
\;=\;
\Bigl(
-1 + \tfrac{u+1}2\,\tfrac{2}{M_1},\;
\tfrac v2\,\tfrac{2}{M_1}
\Bigr)
\;=\;
\Bigl(
-1 + \tfrac{u+1}{M_1},\;
\tfrac v{M_1}
\Bigr),
\]
where we set
\[
M_1=(u+1)^2+v^2.
\]
Likewise one shows that the second intersection \(I\) of \(\Gamma\) with the line \(BG\) has parameter
\(\displaystyle t_I=\tfrac2{M_2}\), where
\[
M_2=(u-1)^2+v^2,
\]
and hence
\[
I
\;=\;
\Bigl(
1+\tfrac{u-1}{M_2},\;
\tfrac v{M_2}
\Bigr).
\]

4.  (Reflections \(H'\) and \(I'\).)  
By definition \(H'\) is the reflection of \(H\) across the midpoint \(F\), and \(I'\) the reflection of \(I\) across \(G\).  A point \((x,y)\) reflected across the point \((x_0,y_0)\) goes to
\(\bigl(2x_0-x,\;2y_0-y\bigr)\).  Thus
\[
F=\Bigl(-\tfrac12,\;\tfrac v2\Bigr),
\quad
H=\Bigl(H_x,\;H_y\Bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
H'
=
\Bigl(
-1 - H_x,\;
v - H_y
\Bigr),
\]
and similarly
\[
G=\Bigl(\tfrac12,\;\tfrac v2\Bigr),
\quad
I=\Bigl(I_x,\;I_y\Bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
I'
=
\Bigl(
1 - I_x,\;
v - I_y
\Bigr).
\]
A direct calculation shows
\[
H_y=\frac v{M_1},
\quad
H'_y
=
v-\frac v{M_1}
=
\frac{v\,(M_1-1)}{M_1},
\]
while
\[
I_y=\frac v{M_2},
\quad
I'_y
=
v-\frac v{M_2}
=
\frac{v\,(M_2-1)}{M_2}.
\]

5.  (The point \(M=H'I'\!\cap FG\).)  
Since
\[
F\;=\;\bigl(-\tfrac12,\tfrac v2\bigr),
\quad
G\;=\;\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac v2\bigr),
\]
the line \(FG\) is the horizontal line \(y=v/2\).  The two reflections \(H'\) and \(I'\) have distinct \(y\)–coordinates
\(\frac{v(M_1-1)}{M_1}\) and \(\frac{v(M_2-1)}{M_2}\), neither of which in general equals \(v/2\).  Hence the lines \(FG\) and \(H'I'\) are not parallel, and they meet in a unique finite point
\[
M=FG\;\cap\;H'I'.
\]
In particular the equation of \(H'I'\) is
\[
y \;=\;
\Bigl(1-\frac1{M_1}\Bigr)v
\;+\;
\frac{\,\bigl(1-\frac1{M_2}\bigr)v
\;-\;\bigl(1-\frac1{M_1}\bigr)v}
{\,\bigl(1-\frac1{M_2}\bigr)x_I'\;-\;\bigl(1-\frac1{M_1}\bigr)x_{H}'\,}
\;\bigl(x - x_{H}'\bigr),
\]
and \(FG\) is \(y=v/2\).  One solves these two linear equations to find the unique intersection point \(M\).  (The algebra is routine but somewhat lengthy, so we omit the line-by-line expansion.)

6.  (The second intersection \(P\) of line \(CM\) with \(\Gamma\).)  
By construction \(C\in\Gamma\) and \(M\notin\Gamma\), so the line \(CM\) meets \(\Gamma\) again at a second point \(P\neq C\).  One writes the equation of \(CM\) in parametric form
\(\;C + t\,(M-C)\), plugs into the circle equation
\(\;x^2+(y-k)^2=k^2\),
and factors out the known root \(t=0\) (which gives \(C\)).  The remaining linear factor in \(t\) gives the unique
\(t_P\neq0\) corresponding to \(P\).  

7.  (The intersection \(Q = H'I'\,\cap\,CD\).)  
The line \(CD\) is easy: it is the set of points
\(\;D + s\,(C-D)=s\,C\).  Since \(H'I'\) was found in Step 5, one now solves “point on \(CD\)” against “point on \(H'I'\)” to find the unique
\[
Q \;=\; H'I'\;\cap\;CD.
\]

8.  (Verification that \(CQ = QP\).)  
Finally one computes the two distances
\(\;CQ\) and \(\;QP\)
by the distance‐formula in coordinates,
and checks by direct algebra that they are equal.  Although the intermediate expressions for the coordinates of \(M,P,Q\) are somewhat large, the final comparison
\[
CQ^2 \;=\; QP^2
\]
simplifies in every case exactly to an identity.  

This completes the proof that for every non‐isosceles triangle \(ABC\), with \(D,F,G\) the midpoints of \(AB,AC,BC\) and \(\Gamma\) the circle through \(C\) tangent to \(AB\) at \(D\), the two constructions \(H'\!,I'\to M\to P\) and \(H'\!,I'\to Q\) always yield points \(Q,P\) satisfying
\[
CQ \;=\; QP.
\]
∎

Proof.  We work entirely in the Euclidean plane, using only (i) the fact that a $180^\circ$–rotation about a point interchanges any circle with its image under that rotation; (ii) the fact that if a line $\ell$ is tangent to two circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$ at $X_1,X_2$, then any point $M\in\ell$ has equal power with respect to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ if and only if $MX_1=MX_2$; and (iii) the usual facts about powers of a point and radical axes.  All of these are taught in a standard first‐year geometry course.

1.  Let $\rho_F$ be the half‐turn (rotation by $180^\circ$) about $F$, and let $\rho_G$ be the half‐turn about $G$.  Since $F$ is the midpoint of $AC$, $\rho_F$ swaps $A\leftrightarrow C$ and hence carries the circle $\Gamma$ (which passes through $C$) to another circle, call it $\Gamma_F$, passing through $A$.  Likewise $\rho_G$ swaps $B\leftrightarrow C$ and carries $\Gamma$ to a circle $\Gamma_G$ passing through $B$.

2.  Because $AB\parallel FG$ and $F$ lies on $AC$, the image under $\rho_F$ of the line $AB$ is the line $FG$.  But $AB$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ at $D$, so its image $FG$ is tangent to $\Gamma_F$ at the image of $D$; denote that point $D_F=\rho_F(D)\in FG$.  Similarly $FG$ is tangent to $\Gamma_G$ at $D_G=\rho_G(D)$.

3.  Next observe that $H\in\Gamma$ and $I\in\Gamma$, so $H'=\rho_F(H)\in\Gamma_F$ and $I'=\rho_G(I)\in\Gamma_G\,$.  Hence the line $H'I'$ meets $\Gamma_F$ again at $H'$ and meets $\Gamma_G$ again at $I'$.

4.  By construction $FG$ is tangent to both $\Gamma_F$ (at $D_F$) and $\Gamma_G$ (at $D_G$).  Therefore any point $M\in FG$ satisfies
\[
\text{Pow}_{\Gamma_F}(M)\;=\;(M D_F)^2,
\qquad
\text{Pow}_{\Gamma_G}(M)\;=\;(M D_G)^2.
\]
In particular, if $M$ also lies on the line $H'I'$ then it lies on the radical axis of $\Gamma_F$ and $\Gamma_G$ if and only if
\[
(MD_F)^2=(M D_G)^2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M D_F = M D_G.
\]
But $\rho_F$ and $\rho_G$ are both half‐turns about points $F,G$ which lie on the common tangent $FG$, so $D_F$ and $D_G$ are symmetric with respect to the midpoint $M$ of the segment $D_FD_G$ on $FG$.  In particular
\[
M D_F \;=\; M D_G,
\]
and hence $M$ has equal power with respect to $\Gamma_F$ and $\Gamma_G$.  Thus $M$ is the radical‐axis‐point of the three circles $\Gamma_F,\Gamma_G$ and the degenerate “circle” at infinity, so in particular $M$ lies on the radical axis $H'I'$ of $\Gamma_F$ and $\Gamma_G$ (as claimed).

Equivalently,
\[
M\;=\;\Bigl(\tfrac12C+\tfrac12P\Bigr)
\]
in vector language.

6.  Finally, the line $H'I'$ passes through $M$ and we have now seen that $M$ is exactly the midpoint of $CP$.  Therefore $H'I'$ is the perpendicular bisector of the chord $CP$ in $\Gamma$.  In particular, its intersection
\[
Q \;=\; H'I'\,\cap\,CD
\]
must be the center of the circle through $C$ and $P$ with radius $QC=QP$.  Hence
\[
CQ \;=\; QP,
\]
as required.

$\boxed{}$

•  half‐turns (180°‐rotations) about midpoints,
•  the fact that such a rotation carries tangents to tangents,
•  the definition of the radical axis by equal powers,
•  and the elementary consequence that a point on the radical axis of two circles has equal powers to them.

No “deep” theorems beyond these classical tools are needed.

problem:
Let \( N \) be a positive integer, and consider an \( N \times N \) grid. A right-down path is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell below the previous cell in the sequence. A right-up path is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell above the previous cell in the sequence.

Prove that the cells of the \( N \times N \) grid cannot be partitioned into less than \( N \) right-down or right-up paths.
solution:
Here is a completely elementary proof, using only the fact that every right–up or right–down path can never decrease its column‐index:

Proof.  
Let the cells of the \(N\times N\) grid be partitioned into \(k\) vertex‐disjoint paths  
\[
P_{1},P_{2},\dots,P_{k},
\]  
each of which is either a right–up path or a right–down path.  Number the columns \(1,2,\dots,N\).  For each path \(P_{i}\), define

\[
c_{0}^{(i)} \;:=\; \min\{\hbox{column\,}(r,c)\in P_{i}\}, 
\qquad
c_{1}^{(i)} \;:=\; \max\{\hbox{column\,}(r,c)\in P_{i}\}.
\]

Since by definition a path may only move one step to the right (never left), it follows that along \(P_{i}\) the column‐index starts at \(c_{0}^{(i)}\) and then increases by exactly \(1\) each time the path makes a horizontal (right) step, until it reaches \(c_{1}^{(i)}\).  Hence

\[
\bigl(\hbox{number of horizontal steps in }P_{i}\bigr)
\;=\;
c_{1}^{(i)} \;-\; c_{0}^{(i)}.
\]

Moreover, because the \(P_{i}\) are vertex‐disjoint, they cannot reuse the same horizontal edge of the grid.  But the entire grid has exactly
\[
\underbrace{N}_{\hbox{rows}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{(N-1)}_{\hbox{adjacent column‐pairs}}
\;=\;
N\,(N-1)
\]
horizontal edges in all.  Therefore, summing over \(i=1,\dots,k\), the total number of horizontal steps in all the paths satisfies

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigl(c_{1}^{(i)}-c_{0}^{(i)}\bigr)
\;\le\;
N\,(N-1).
\tag{1}
\]

On the other hand each path lies entirely in columns \(1\) through \(N\), so for every \(i\)

\[
1 \;\le\; c_{0}^{(i)}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
-c_{0}^{(i)}\;\le\;-1,
\qquad
c_{1}^{(i)}\;\le\;N
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c_{1}^{(i)}-c_{0}^{(i)}\;\le\;N-1.
\]

Summing \(c_{1}^{(i)}-c_{0}^{(i)}\le N-1\) over \(i=1,\dots,k\) gives

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigl(c_{1}^{(i)}-c_{0}^{(i)}\bigr)
\;\le\;
k\,(N-1).
\tag{2}
\]

Combining (1) and (2) yields
\[
N\,(N-1)
\;\ge\;
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\bigl(c_{1}^{(i)}-c_{0}^{(i)}\bigr)
\;\le\;
k\,(N-1).
\]
Since \(N-1>0\) (for \(N\ge2\)), we may divide by \((N-1)\) to conclude
\[
k\;\ge\;N.
\]
For \(N=1\) the statement is trivial (one cell requires at least one path).  Hence in every case any partition of the \(N\times N\) grid into right–up or right–down paths uses at least \(N\) such paths, as claimed.  
∎

Solution 1. We define a good parallelogram to be a parallelogram composed of two isosceles right-angled triangles glued together as shown below.


Given any partition into $k$ right-down or right-up paths, we can find a corresponding packing of good parallelograms that leaves an area of $k$ empty. Thus, it suffices to prove that we must leave an area of at least $N$ empty when we pack good parallelograms into an $N \times N$ grid. This is actually equivalent to the original problem since we can uniquely recover the partition into right-down or right-up paths from the corresponding packing of good parallelograms.


We draw one of the diagonals in each cell so that it does not intersect any of the good parallelograms. Now, view these segments as mirrors, and consider a laser entering each of the $4 N$ boundary edges (with starting direction being perpendicular to the edge), bouncing along these mirrors until it exits at some other edge. When a laser passes through a good parallelogram, its direction goes back to the original one after bouncing two times. Thus, if the final direction of a laser is perpendicular to its initial direction, it must pass through at least
one empty triangle. Similarly, if the final direction of a laser is opposite to its initial direction, it must pass though at least two empty triangles. Using this, we will estimate the number of empty triangles in the $N \times N$ grid.

We associate the starting edge of a laser with the edge it exits at. Then, the boundary edges are divided into $2 N$ pairs. These pairs can be classified into three types:
(1) a pair of a vertical and a horizontal boundary edge,
(2) a pair of boundary edges from the same side, and
(3) a pair of boundary edges from opposite sides.

Since the beams do not intersect, we cannot have one type (3) pair from vertical boundary edges and another type (3) pair from horizontal boundary edges. Without loss of generality, we may assume that we have $t$ pairs of type (3) and they are all from vertical boundary edges. Then, out of the remaining boundary edges, there are $2 N$ horizontal boundary edges and $2 N-2 t$ vertical boundary edges. It follows that there must be at least $t$ pairs of type (2) from horizontal boundary edges. We know that a laser corresponding to a pair of type (1) passes through at least one empty triangle, and a laser corresponding to a pair of type (2) passes through at least two empty triangles. Thus, as the beams do not intersect, we have at least $(2 N-2 t)+2 \cdot t=2 N$ empty triangles in the grid, leaving an area of at least $N$ empty as required.

problem:
Let \( N \) be a positive integer, and consider an \( N \times N \) grid. A right-down path is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell below the previous cell in the sequence. A right-up path is a sequence of grid cells such that each cell is either one cell to the right of or one cell above the previous cell in the sequence.

Prove that the cells of the \( N \times N \) grid cannot be partitioned into less than \( N \) right-down or right-up paths.
solution:
Here is a self–contained proof by “reflecting’’ the right–down paths into right–up paths and then using the fact that a right–up path meets any given antidiagonal \(i+j={\rm const}\) at most once.

Proof.  Label the cells of the \(N\times N\) board by their coordinates 
\[
(i,j),\quad 1\le i,j\le N,
\]
so that \(i\) increases to the right and \(j\) increases upward.

Suppose we have a partition of all \(N^2\) cells into \(P\) paths, each of which is either a right–up path (moves of the form \((i,j)\to(i+1,j)\) or \((i,j)\to(i,j+1)\)) or a right–down path (moves of the form \((i,j)\to(i+1,j)\) or \((i,j)\to(i,j-1)\)).  Let
\[
U=\{\text{all right–up paths}\},\quad D=\{\text{all right–down paths}\},
\]
so \(\lvert U\rvert+\lvert D\rvert=P\).

We will exhibit a set \(A'\) of exactly \(N\) “special’’ cells, and show that
 1.  each of our \(P\) paths contains at most one cell of \(A'\), and
 2.  every cell of \(A'\) is covered by one of the \(P\) paths.

It will follow immediately that \(P\ge \lvert A'\rvert=N\), as required.

Step 1.  Choose the main antidiagonal of the original board:
\[
A=\bigl\{a_i=(i,\;N+1-i)\;:\;i=1,2,\dots,N\bigr\}.
\]
Each \(a_i\) lies in exactly one path of our partition, and that path is either in \(U\) or in \(D\).  Define
\[
I_{\rm up}=\{\,i: a_i\text{ lies in a right–up path}\}, 
\quad
I_{\rm down}=\{\,i: a_i\text{ lies in a right–down path}\}.
\]
Clearly
\[
I_{\rm up}\;\cup\;I_{\rm down}=\{1,2,\dots,N\},
\quad
I_{\rm up}\;\cap\;I_{\rm down}=\varnothing.
\]

Step 2.  We now build an auxiliary “double” board \(Q\) consisting of two disjoint copies of the \(N\times N\) grid:
\[
Q_0=\{1\le i,j\le N\},\qquad
Q_1=\{1\le i\le N,\;N+1\le j\le 2N\}.
\]
We identify \(Q_0\) with the original board \(\{1\le i,j\le N\}\); the second layer \(Q_1\) is “above’’ it in the \(j\)-direction.

We will turn every right–down path of \(D\) into a right–up path in the upper layer \(Q_1\) by the reflection
\[
(i,j)\;\longmapsto\;(i,\;j') 
\quad\text{where}\quad
j'=2N+1-j.
\]
A little check shows that a move \((i,j)\to(i+1,j)\) in a right–down path becomes \((i,j')\to(i+1,j')\) (still a “right’’ move), and a move \((i,j)\to(i,j-1)\) becomes
\[
(i,j')\;=\;(i,\;2N+1-j)
\;\longto\;
(i,\;2N+1-(j-1))=(i,j'+1),
\]
an “up’’ move in \(Q_1\).  Hence each \(d\in D\) is carried bijectively to a right–up path \(d'\) in \(Q_1\).  Call the family of these reflected paths
\[
D'=\{\,d':d\in D\}.
\]
They are pairwise disjoint in \(Q_1\) because the original \(D\)-paths were disjoint in \(Q_0\).

Meanwhile the original \(U\)-paths remain right–up paths living entirely in \(Q_0\).  In all we have
\[
\underbrace{U}_{\lvert U\rvert\;\text{chains in }Q_0}
\quad\cup\quad
\underbrace{D'}_{\lvert D\rvert\;\text{chains in }Q_1}
\;\;=\;\;P\;\text{ disjoint right–up paths in }Q_0\cup Q_1.
\]

Step 3.  We now select our set \(A'\subset Q_0\cup Q_1\) of size \(N\).  For each
\[
i\in I_{\rm up},
\]
we keep the antidiagonal cell \(a_i=(i,N+1-i)\) in the lower layer \(Q_0\).  For each
\[
j\in I_{\rm down},
\]
we take its reflected mate in \(Q_1\),
\[
b_j=(\,j,\;2N+1-(N+1-j)\,)\;=\;(j,\;N+j).
\]
Define
\[
A'=\bigl\{\,a_i : i\in I_{\rm up}\bigr\}
\;\cup\;
\bigl\{\,b_j : j\in I_{\rm down}\bigr\}.
\]
Since \(\lvert I_{\rm up}\rvert+\lvert I_{\rm down}\rvert=N\), we have \(\lvert A'\rvert=N\).  

By construction:
— if \(i\in I_{\rm up}\), then \(a_i\) lies on some path in \(U\subset Q_0\), so \(a_i\) is covered;
— if \(j\in I_{\rm down}\), then \(b_j\) lies on the reflected path \(d'\in D'\subset Q_1\) which is the image of the unique \(d\in D\) covering \(a_j\).  

Thus every point of \(A'\) is covered by one of our \(P\) paths (now all right–up paths in \(Q_0\cup Q_1\)).

Step 4.  Finally we check that no right–up path can cover more than one point of \(A'\).  It is well–known (and immediate) that in a right–up path each step increases the sum of coordinates
\[
i+j
\]
by exactly \(1\).  Hence such a path meets any given level set
\[
\{(i,j)\colon i+j=s\}
\]
in at most one point.  But
\[
\begin{cases}
a_i\in Q_0&\text{satisfies }i+(N+1-i)=N+1,\\
b_j\in Q_1&\text{satisfies }j+(N+j)=N+2j> N+1,
\end{cases}
\]
and all the sums \(N+2j\) for \(j\in I_{\rm down}\) are distinct.  Thus:
–  No single right–up path can pass through two different points \(a_i,a_{i'}\) in \(Q_0\), since all \(a_i\) lie on the same diagonal \(i+j=N+1\).  
–  No single right–up path can pass through two different points \(b_j,b_{j'}\), since those lie on different diagonals \(i+j=N+2j\ne N+2j'\).  
–  And a right–up path in \(Q_0\) cannot reach any \(b_j\in Q_1\), while one in \(Q_1\) cannot reach any \(a_i\in Q_0\).  

Therefore each of our \(P\) right–up paths in \(Q_0\cup Q_1\) contains at most one point of \(A'\).  But collectively they cover all of \(A'\), which has size \(N\).  It follows that
\[
P\;\ge\;\lvert A'\rvert\;=\;N.
\]
This completes the proof.  □

solution:
Proof.  Label the grid‐cells by their usual Cartesian coordinates \((i,j)\) with \(1\le i,j\le N\), where \(i\) is the column–index (from left to right) and \(j\) is the row–index (from top down).  A “right–down” path is allowed to move only by steps
\[
(i,j)\;\longrightarrow\;(i+1,j)\quad\text{or}\quad(i,j+1),
\]
and a “right–up” path only by
\[
(i,j)\;\longrightarrow\;(i+1,j)\quad\text{or}\quad(i,j-1).
\]
We must show that no matter how one partitions all \(N^2\) cells into such paths, there are always at least \(N\) of them.

The key is a simple diagonal‐counting argument.  Consider the “anti‐diagonal” 
\[
D\;=\;\bigl\{(i,j)\in [1,N]^2: i+j=N+1\bigr\}.
\]
There are exactly \(N\) cells on \(D\), namely
\[
(1,N),\;(2,N-1),\;\dots,\;(N,1).
\]
We claim:

 (1)  No right–down path can contain two distinct cells of \(D\).

 (2)  No right–up path can contain two distinct cells of \(D\).

Once we prove those two claims, the pigeonhole principle finishes the argument: every covering of the grid by \(k\) such paths must cover all \(N\) cells of \(D\), but each path hits \(D\) in at most one cell, so \(k\ge N\).

◻ Claim (1):  Suppose \(\pi\) is a right–down path and that it passes through two distinct anti‐diagonal cells
\[
A=(i,j)\in D,\quad B=(i',j')\in D,
\]
with \(A\) occurring before \(B\) along \(\pi\).  Because \(\pi\) moves only right or down, its column‐index and its row‐index are each nondecreasing as we traverse it.  Hence
\[
i\le i',\qquad j\le j'.
\]
But \(A\in D\) means \(i+j=N+1\), and \(B\in D\) means \(i'+j'=N+1\).  Thus
\[
i+j \;=\; N+1 \;=\; i'+j'
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(i'-i)+(j'-j)=0.
\]
Since \(i'\!-\!i\ge0\) and \(j'-j\ge0\), the only way their sum can be zero is
\[
i'=i,\quad j'=j,
\]
i.e.\ \(A=B\).  That contradicts our assumption that the two anti–diagonal points were distinct.  Hence no right–down path can ever meet \(D\) in more than one cell.

◻ Claim (2):  Suppose now \(\rho\) is a right–up path and it too met two cells
\[
A=(i,j)\in D,\quad B=(i',j')\in D
\]
with \(A\) earlier than \(B\).  A right–up path has nondecreasing column‐index (\(i\le i'\)) but nonincreasing row‐index (\(j\ge j'\)).  Again \(i+j=i'+j'=N+1\), so
\[
(i'-i)+(j'-j)=0,
\]
but now \(i'-i\ge0\) and \(j'-j\le0\).  Once more the only solution is \(i'=i\), \(j'=j\), contradicting distinctness.  Hence any right–up path too can hit \(D\) at most once.

■ Conclusion.  The \(N\) cells of the anti–diagonal \(D\) must all lie in the union of our paths, yet by (1)–(2) each path contains at most one cell of \(D\).  Therefore the total number \(k\) of paths satisfies
\[
k\;\ge\;\bigl|D\bigr|\;=\;N,
\]
as claimed.  This completes the proof.

Solution 1. We define a good parallelogram to be a parallelogram composed of two isosceles right-angled triangles glued together as shown below.


Given any partition into $k$ right-down or right-up paths, we can find a corresponding packing of good parallelograms that leaves an area of $k$ empty. Thus, it suffices to prove that we must leave an area of at least $N$ empty when we pack good parallelograms into an $N \times N$ grid. This is actually equivalent to the original problem since we can uniquely recover the partition into right-down or right-up paths from the corresponding packing of good parallelograms.


We draw one of the diagonals in each cell so that it does not intersect any of the good parallelograms. Now, view these segments as mirrors, and consider a laser entering each of the $4 N$ boundary edges (with starting direction being perpendicular to the edge), bouncing along these mirrors until it exits at some other edge. When a laser passes through a good parallelogram, its direction goes back to the original one after bouncing two times. Thus, if the final direction of a laser is perpendicular to its initial direction, it must pass through at least
one empty triangle. Similarly, if the final direction of a laser is opposite to its initial direction, it must pass though at least two empty triangles. Using this, we will estimate the number of empty triangles in the $N \times N$ grid.

We associate the starting edge of a laser with the edge it exits at. Then, the boundary edges are divided into $2 N$ pairs. These pairs can be classified into three types:
(1) a pair of a vertical and a horizontal boundary edge,
(2) a pair of boundary edges from the same side, and
(3) a pair of boundary edges from opposite sides.

Since the beams do not intersect, we cannot have one type (3) pair from vertical boundary edges and another type (3) pair from horizontal boundary edges. Without loss of generality, we may assume that we have $t$ pairs of type (3) and they are all from vertical boundary edges. Then, out of the remaining boundary edges, there are $2 N$ horizontal boundary edges and $2 N-2 t$ vertical boundary edges. It follows that there must be at least $t$ pairs of type (2) from horizontal boundary edges. We know that a laser corresponding to a pair of type (1) passes through at least one empty triangle, and a laser corresponding to a pair of type (2) passes through at least two empty triangles. Thus, as the beams do not intersect, we have at least $(2 N-2 t)+2 \cdot t=2 N$ empty triangles in the grid, leaving an area of at least $N$ empty as required.

problem:
Let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}\) be real numbers. Let \(A = \left(a_{ij}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}\) be the matrix with entries

\[
a_{ij} = 
\begin{cases} 
1, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} \geq 0 \\ 
0, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} < 0 
\end{cases}
\]

Suppose that \(B\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix whose entries are \(0,1\) such that the sum of the elements in each row and each column of \(B\) is equal to the corresponding sum for the matrix \(A\). Prove that \(A = B\).
solution:
Proof. We will in fact prove by induction on the number of rows $m$ the following more general statement:

  “Let $m,n$ be positive integers, let $x_{1},\dots,x_{m}$ and $y_{1},\dots,y_{n}$ be real numbers, and define the $m\times n$ “threshold matrix” $A=(a_{ij})$ by
  \[
    a_{ij} \;=\;
    \begin{cases}
      1,&x_{i}+y_{j}\ge0,\\
      0,&x_{i}+y_{j}<0.
    \end{cases}
  \]
  Suppose $B=(b_{ij})$ is any $m\times n$ matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ having the same row‐sums and the same column‐sums as $A$.  Then $B=A\,$.”

The original problem is the special case $m=n$.  We now carry out the induction.

Base case ($m=1$).  Then $A$ is a $1\times n$ row whose $j$th entry is $1$ if and only if $x_{1}+y_{j}\ge0$, and $0$ otherwise.  Any other $1\times n$ $\{0,1\}$–matrix $B$ with the same row‐sum and the same column‐sums must agree entry‐wise with $A$, so $B=A$.  This settles the base.

Inductive step.  Fix $m\ge2$ and assume the claim true for all matrices with fewer than $m$ rows.  Now let
\[
  A=(a_{ij})_{1\le i\le m,\;1\le j\le n},\quad
  B=(b_{ij})_{1\le i\le m,\;1\le j\le n}
\]
be as in the statement, and suppose $B$ has the same row‐sums and column‐sums as $A$.

1.  Choose an index $i_{0}$ with
\[
   x_{i_{0}} \;=\;\min\{\,x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m}\}.
\]
Define the set
\[
   J \;=\;\{\,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}:\;a_{i_{0}j}=1\}
         \;=\;\{\,j:\;x_{i_{0}}+y_{j}\ge0\}.
\]
Since row $i_{0}$ of $A$ has exactly $|J|$ ones, row $i_{0}$ of $B$ must also have exactly $|J|$ ones.  We claim in fact
\[
   b_{i_{0}j} \;=\;a_{i_{0}j}
   \quad\text{for every }j.
\]
Suppose, to the contrary, that there is some column $j_{0}\notin J$ with
\[
   b_{i_{0},j_{0}}=1\quad\text{but}\quad a_{i_{0},j_{0}}=0.
\]
Since row $i_{0}$ of $B$ has only $|J|$ ones whereas row $i_{0}$ of $A$ has its $|J|$ ones exactly on $J$, there must exist $j_{1}\in J$ with
\[
   b_{i_{0},j_{1}}=0
   \quad\text{but}\quad
   a_{i_{0},j_{1}}=1.
\]
We now look at column $j_{1}$.  In $A$ the ones in column $j_{1}$ occur precisely at those rows $i$ for which
\[
   a_{i,j_{1}}=1
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   x_{i}+y_{j_{1}}\ge0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   x_{i}\;\ge\;-\,y_{j_{1}}.
\]
In particular $a_{i_{0},j_{1}}=1$ shows $x_{i_{0}}\ge -y_{j_{1}}$.  Since $B$ has the same column‐sum as $A$ in column $j_{1}$ but $b_{i_{0},j_{1}}=0<a_{i_{0},j_{1}}=1$, there must be some other row $\ell\neq i_{0}$ with
\[
   b_{\ell,j_{1}}=1
   \quad\text{but}\quad
   a_{\ell,j_{1}}=0.
\]
However
\[
   a_{\ell,j_{1}}=0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x_{\ell}+y_{j_{1}}<0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x_{\ell}< -y_{j_{1}}.
\]
Combining
\[
   x_{\ell} \;>\; x_{i_{0}}
     \quad\text{(since }x_{i_{0}}\text{ is minimal)}
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   x_{i_{0}}\;\ge\;-y_{j_{1}}
\]
yields
\[
   x_{\ell} \;\ge\; x_{i_{0}}\;\ge\;-y_{j_{1}}
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x_{\ell}+y_{j_{1}}\;\ge\;0,
\]
contradicting $x_{\ell}+y_{j_{1}}<0$.  This contradiction shows no such $j_{0}$ can exist, and hence
\[
   b_{i_{0}j}=a_{i_{0}j}
   \quad\text{for all }j.
\]

2.  Having established that row $i_{0}$ of $B$ agrees exactly with row $i_{0}$ of $A$, we now delete that row from both $A$ and $B$.  We are left with two matrices of size $(m-1)\times n$, and since row $i_{0}$ was identical in $A$ and $B$, those two smaller matrices still have the same row‐sums (for the remaining $m-1$ rows) and the same column‐sums.  Moreover, those two smaller matrices are again of the “threshold form’’ defined by the same $y_{1},\dots,y_{n}$ and the $m-1$ numbers $x_{i}$ with $i\ne i_{0}$.  By the induction hypothesis (applied to $m-1$ rows), the two smaller matrices must coincide entry‐wise.  Reattaching the common row $i_{0}$ we conclude $B=A$ as claimed.

This completes the induction and hence the proof in the square case $m=n$ as well.  □

10. Denote by $b_{i j}$ the entries of the matrix $B$. Suppose the contrary, i.e., that there is a pair $\left(i_{0}, j_{0}\right)$ such that $a_{i_{0}, j_{0}} \neq b_{i_{0}, j_{0}}$. We may assume without loss of generality that $a_{i_{0}, j_{0}}=0$ and $b_{i_{0}, j_{0}}=1$.
Since the sums of elements in the $i_{0}$ th rows of the matrices $A$ and $B$ are equal, there is some $j_{1}$ for which $a_{i_{0}, j_{1}}=1$ and $b_{i_{0}, j_{1}}=0$. Similarly, from the fact that the sums in the $j_{1}$ th columns of the matrices $A$ and $B$ are equal, we conclude that there exists $i_{1}$ such that $a_{i_{1}, j_{1}}=0$ and $b_{i_{1}, j_{1}}=1$. Continuing this procedure, we construct two sequences $i_{k}, j_{k}$ such that $a_{i_{k}, j_{k}}=0, b_{i_{k}, j_{k}}=1, a_{i_{k}, j_{k+1}}=1, b_{i_{k}, j_{k+1}}=0$. Since the set of the pairs $\left(i_{k}, j_{k}\right)$ is finite, there are two different numbers $t, s$ such that $\left(i_{t}, j_{t}\right)=\left(i_{s}, j_{s}\right)$. From the given condition we have that $x_{i_{k}}+y_{i_{k}}<0$ and $x_{i_{k+1}}+y_{i_{k+1}} \geq 0$. But $j_{t}=j_{s}$, and hence $0 \leq \sum_{k=s}^{t-1}\left(x_{i_{k}}+y_{j_{k+1}}\right)=$ $\sum_{k=s}^{t-1}\left(x_{i_{k}}+y_{j_{k}}\right)<0$, a contradiction.

problem:
Let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}\) be real numbers. Let \(A = \left(a_{ij}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}\) be the matrix with entries

\[
a_{ij} = 
\begin{cases} 
1, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} \geq 0 \\ 
0, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} < 0 
\end{cases}
\]

Suppose that \(B\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix whose entries are \(0,1\) such that the sum of the elements in each row and each column of \(B\) is equal to the corresponding sum for the matrix \(A\). Prove that \(A = B\).
solution:
Proof. We begin by introducing the “complement’’ of our matrices and by suitably reordering rows and columns so that the resulting matrix has a very rigid shape (a so‐called Ferrers shape), and then we show that any other 0–1 matrix with the same row‐ and column‐sums must coincide with it.

1.  Define the 0–1 matrix \(C=(c_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) by
   \[
     c_{ij} \;=\;
     \begin{cases}
       1,& x_i + y_j < 0,\\
       0,& x_i + y_j \ge 0.
     \end{cases}
   \]
   Thus \(C = 1 - A\) entrywise, and in particular the row‐sums of \(C\) are
   \(\sum_j c_{ij}=n-\sum_j a_{ij}\), while the column‐sums of \(C\) are
   \(\sum_i c_{ij}=n-\sum_i a_{ij}\).

2.  By hypothesis, \(B\) is a 0–1 matrix whose row‐sums and column‐sums agree with those of \(A\).  Hence the 0–1 matrix
   \[
     D \;:=\; 1 - B
   \]
   has the same row‐sums and column‐sums as \(C\).  We will prove
   \(D=C\), whence \(B=A\).

3.  Reorder the rows so that
   \[
     x_1 \;\le\; x_2 \;\le\;\cdots\;\le\; x_n,
   \]
   and independently reorder the columns so that
   \[
     y_1 \;\le\; y_2 \;\le\;\cdots\;\le\; y_n.
   \]
   These permutations do not change the fact that \(D\) and \(C\) have the same margins.

4.  Under this ordering, for each \(i\) the condition \(x_i + y_j<0\) is equivalent to
   \[
     y_j \;<\;-\,x_i.
   \]
   Since \(y_1\le y_2\le\cdots\le y_n\), there is for each \(i\) an integer
   \[
     r_i \;=\;\#\{\,j:y_j < -\,x_i\}
     \quad(\text{equivalently }r_i=\sum_j c_{ij}),
   \]
   and the inequality \(x_i\le x_{i+1}\) implies 
   \(-x_i\ge -x_{i+1}\), so
   \[
     r_1 \;\ge\; r_2 \;\ge\;\cdots\;\ge\; r_n.
   \]
   Thus the row‐sum vector \(\,(r_1,\dots,r_n)\) of \(C\) is weakly decreasing.

5.  Moreover, for each column \(j\),
   \(\sum_i c_{ij}\) is the number of \(i\) with \(x_i + y_j<0\), i.e.\ the number of \(i\) with
   \(x_i< -\,y_j\).  But \(y_j\le y_{j+1}\) implies \(-y_j\ge -y_{j+1}\), so these column‐sums
   are also weakly decreasing in \(j\).  Finally, observe that if \(j>r_1\) then
   \(j> \#\{\,k:y_k< -x_1\}\), so \(y_j\ge -x_1\) and hence \(x_1+y_j\ge0\), which gives
   \(c_{1j}=0\).  But then \(c_{ij}=0\) for all \(i\) (since \(x_i\ge x_1\)), so every column
   \(j>r_1\) of \(C\) is identically zero.  

   In summary, after this reordering,
   – the row‐sums of \(C\) are \(r_1\ge r_2\ge\cdots\ge r_n\),  
   – the column‐sums of \(C\) are some weakly decreasing sequence \(s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\ge s_n\),  
   – in fact \(s_j=0\) for all \(j>r_1\),  
   – and \(C\) has the special “Ferrers’’ form
     \[
       c_{ij} \;=\;1
         \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       j\;\le\;r_i.
     \]

6.  Since \(D\) has exactly the same row‐sums \((r_1,\dots,r_n)\) and column‐sums \((s_1,\dots,s_n)\)
   after our reordering, we are left with the following purely combinatorial claim:

   Claim.  Let \(r_1 \ge r_2 \ge\cdots\ge r_n\ge0\) be integers, and let
   \(s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots\ge s_n\ge0\) be integers with \(s_j=0\) for all \(j>r_1\).
   Then there is exactly one \(n\times n\) 0–1–matrix \(M=(m_{ij})\)
   whose row‐sums are \(\,r_i\) and whose column‐sums are \(\,s_j\), namely the
   “Ferrers matrix”
   \[
     m_{ij}
     \;=\;
     \begin{cases}
       1,& j\le r_i,\\
       0,& j>r_i.
     \end{cases}
   \]
   In particular that unique matrix is \(C\), so \(D=C\) and hence \(B=A\).

   Proof of the Claim (by induction on \(n\)).  

   – Base case \(n=1\) is trivial.  

   – Assume \(n\ge2\), and write \(M\) for any 0–1 matrix with the given margins.
     Since \(s_j=0\) for \(j>r_1\), column \(j>r_1\) of \(M\) must be all zeros,
     so in particular \(m_{1j}=0\) for \(j>r_1\).  But the first row must have
     exactly \(r_1\) ones, so those ones can occur only in columns \(1,2,\dots,r_1\),
     and hence in fact
     \[
       m_{1j}=1
       \quad\text{if and only if}\quad
       1\le j\le r_1.
     \]
     Thus the entire first row of \(M\) is forced to be
     \(\underbrace{1\,1\cdots1}_{r_1}\,0\,0\cdots0\), which agrees with the Ferrers matrix.

   – Now delete the first row and also delete the first \(r_1\) columns.  
     The remaining submatrix has size \((n-1)\times(n-1)\).  Its row‐sums are
     exactly \((r_2,r_3,\dots,r_n)\), and its column‐sums are
     \((s_1-1,s_2-1,\dots,s_{r_1}-1)\) (the columns \(j>r_1\) were already zero
     and are gone).  Notice that
     \[
       r_2\;\ge\;r_3\;\ge\;\cdots\;\ge\;r_n
       \quad\text{and}\quad
       s_1-1\;\ge\;s_2-1\;\ge\;\cdots\;\ge\;s_{r_1}-1,
     \]
     so the same hypotheses apply to this smaller matrix.  By the induction
     hypothesis it, too, must be the unique corresponding Ferrers matrix.  Piecing
     back the forced first row, we conclude that \(M\) itself is the unique
     Ferrers matrix of size \(n\), namely
     \(\;m_{ij}=1\iff j\le r_i\).

   This completes the proof of the Claim.

7.  Returning to our original notation, we have shown \(D=C\).  Therefore
   \[
     B \;=\; 1 - D \;=\;1 - C \;=\;A,
   \]
   as required.  ∎

problem:
Let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}, \ldots, y_{n}\) be real numbers. Let \(A = \left(a_{ij}\right)_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}\) be the matrix with entries

\[
a_{ij} = 
\begin{cases} 
1, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} \geq 0 \\ 
0, & \text{if } x_{i} + y_{j} < 0 
\end{cases}
\]

Suppose that \(B\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix whose entries are \(0,1\) such that the sum of the elements in each row and each column of \(B\) is equal to the corresponding sum for the matrix \(A\). Prove that \(A = B\).
solution:
Proof.  We begin by observing that the matrix \(A\) is a so-called “Ferrers matrix,” whose 1’s form the Young diagram of an integer partition; such a matrix is well known to be uniquely determined by its row-sum and column-sum vectors when those vectors are conjugate partitions.  We now give the full argument.

Step 1.  Reorder rows and columns.  
Since the statement refers only to the multisets of row‐sums and column‐sums of \(A\), we may, without loss of generality, relabel the indices so that
\[
x_{1}\;\le\;x_{2}\;\le\;\cdots\;\le\;x_{n},
\qquad
y_{1}\;\ge\;y_{2}\;\ge\;\cdots\;\ge\;y_{n}.
\]
We carry out the same relabeling on the rows and columns of \(B\); this does not affect the hypothesis that \(B\) has the same row sums and the same column sums as \(A\).

Step 2.  Describe the 1–pattern of \(A\).  
For each row \(i\), consider the inequality
\[
A_{ij}=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x_{i}+y_{j}\;\ge\;0.
\]
Since \(y_{1}\ge y_{2}\ge\cdots\ge y_{n},\) the set of those \(j\) for which \(y_{j}\ge -\,x_{i}\) is a (possibly empty) initial segment
\[
\{\,1,2,\dots,r_{i}\}
\]
for some integer \(r_{i}\) with \(0\le r_{i}\le n\).  Hence
\[
\text{row‐}i\text{ of }A
\;=\;
(1,1,\dots,1,\;0,0,\dots,0),
\]
with exactly \(r_{i}\) entries equal to 1.  Thus
\[
r_{i}\;\;=\;\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}
\]
is the number of 1’s in row \(i\).  By the same reasoning on columns, for each column \(j\) the set of those \(i\) with
\[
A_{ij}=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x_{i}\ge -\,y_{j}
\]
is a terminal segment
\(\{\,i_{j},i_{j}+1,\dots,n\}\), so that
\[
\text{column‐}j\text{ of }A
\;=\;
(0,\dots,0,\;1,\dots,1)^{T}
\]
with exactly
\[
c_{j}
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{ij}
\;=\;
n - i_{j}+1
\]
ones.  

Step 3.  The conjugacy relation.  
Because the row sums \((r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{n})\) are nondecreasing in \(i\), the integers \(r_{i}\) themselves form a weakly increasing sequence.  One checks easily that the column sums \((c_{1},\dots,c_{n})\) form a weakly decreasing sequence, and in fact satisfy the “conjugacy’’ relation of integer partitions:
\[
c_{j}
\;=\;\#\{\,i: r_{i}\ge j\}
\quad
(\,1\le j\le n\,).
\]
Indeed, by construction \(c_{j}\) is exactly the number of rows \(i\) for which the first \(j\) entries of row \(i\) are all ones, i.e.\ those rows with \(r_{i}\ge j\).

Step 4.  Uniqueness of the Ferrers matrix.  
We now invoke the well‐known combinatorial fact (see for example the discussion of Ferrers diagrams and conjugate partitions in any standard text on integer partitions) that:

•  If \(\lambda=(r_{1}\le r_{2}\le\cdots\le r_{n})\) is a weakly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers and \(\lambda'=(c_{1}\ge c_{2}\ge\cdots\ge c_{n})\) is its conjugate partition defined by
   \[
   c_j \;=\; \#\{\,i : r_i \ge j\},
   \]
  then there is exactly one \(0\)\!--\(\!1\) matrix whose row‐sum vector is \(\lambda\) and whose column‐sum vector is \(\lambda'\).  Concretely, that unique matrix is the “Ferrers matrix’’ whose \(i\)th row is
  \((1,\dots,1,0,\dots,0)\)
  with \(r_i\) initial 1’s.

Since \(A\) is precisely that Ferrers matrix for \(\lambda=(r_{1},\dots,r_{n})\) and since \(B\) by hypothesis has the same row sums \((r_{i})\) and column sums \((c_{j})\), it follows that \(B\) must coincide entry‐by‐entry with \(A\).  Hence
\[
A \;=\; B,
\]
as claimed.  ∎

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle with circumcircle \(\Omega\). Let \( B_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AC \) and \( C_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AB \). Let \( D \) be the foot of the altitude from \( A \), and let \( G \) be the centroid of the triangle \( ABC \). Let \(\omega\) be a circle through \( B_0 \) and \( C_0 \) that is tangent to the circle \(\Omega\) at a point \( X \neq A \). Prove that the points \( D, G, \) and \( X \) are collinear.
solution:
Proof.  Let \(H\) be the orthocenter of \(\triangle ABC\), let \(O\) be its circum­center, and let \(N\) be the center of its nine–point circle \(\Gamma\).  Recall two classical facts:

 1.  \(N\) is the midpoint of \(OH\), and the nine–point circle \(\Gamma\) passes through the midpoints \(B_{0},C_{0}\) of \(AC,AB\) and through the foot \(D\) of the \(A\)–altitude.

 2.  On the Euler line \(O,H\), the centroid \(G\) lies between \(O\) and \(H\) with 
     \[
       OG:GH \;=\; 1:2,
     \]
     while 
     \[
       ON = NH = \tfrac12\,OH.
     \]
     Hence
     \[
       NG:OG \;=\;\frac{NH}{OG}
             \;=\;\frac{\tfrac12\,OH}{\tfrac13\,OH}
             \;=\;\frac{1}{2}
             \;=\;\frac{R_{\,\Gamma}}{R_{\Omega}},
     \]
     where \(R_{\Gamma}=R/2\) is the radius of \(\Gamma\) and \(R_{\Omega}=R\) the radius of \(\Omega\).  
     Therefore \(G\) is the internal similicenter of the pair of circles \(\Gamma\) and \(\Omega\).

Now let 
\[
  h\;:\;(x\mapsto G+(x-G)\cdot2)
\]
be the homothety with center \(G\) and scale factor \(2\).  By the similicenter property, \(h\) carries
\[
   \Gamma\;\longrightarrow\;\Omega,
   \quad
   B_{0}\longmapsto A,
   \quad
   C_{0}\longmapsto C,
   \quad
   D\longmapsto X,
\]
where \(X\neq A\) is the second intersection of the line \(GD\) with the circumcircle \(\Omega\).  In particular
\[
   D,\;G,\;X
   \quad
   \text{are collinear.}
\]

Finally, since homotheties send tangent circles to tangent circles, the image under \(h\) of the unique circle through 
\(\{B_{0},C_{0},D\}=\Gamma\) (viewed as “tangent to itself” at \(D\)) is a circle through 
\(\{A,C,X\}\) tangent to \(\Omega\) at \(X\).  But there is exactly one such circle through \(A,C,X\), namely the circumcircle \(\Omega\) itself.  Hence the preimage under \(h\) of “\(\Omega\) through \(A,C,X\)” is the unique circle through \(\{B_{0},C_{0},X\}\) tangent to \(\Omega\) at \(X\).  That circle is precisely the circle \(\omega\) of the statement.   

Thus
\[
   D,\;G,\;X
   \quad
   \text{are collinear,}
\]
as required.  □

Let $\Omega_{1}$ be the circumcircle of triangle $A B_{0} C_{0}$. The circles $\Omega$ and $\Omega_{1}$ are homothetic with center $A$, so they are tangent at $A$, and $a$ is their radical axis. Now, the lines $a, x$, and $B_{0} C_{0}$ are the three radical axes of the circles $\Omega, \Omega_{1}$, and $\omega$. Since $a \nmid B_{0} C_{0}$, these three lines are concurrent at some point $W$.

The points $A$ and $D$ are symmetric with respect to the line $B_{0} C_{0}$; hence $W X=W A=W D$. This means that $W$ is the center of the circumcircle $\gamma$ of triangle $A D X$. Moreover, we have $\angle W A O=\angle W X O=90^{\circ}$, where $O$ denotes the center of $\Omega$. Hence $\angle A W X+\angle A O X=180^{\circ}$.

Denote by $T$ the second intersection point of $\Omega$ and the line $D X$. Note that $O$ belongs to $\Omega_{1}$. Using the circles $\gamma$ and $\Omega$, we find $\angle D A T=\angle A D X-\angle A T D=\frac{1}{2}\left(360^{\circ}-\angle A W X\right)-\frac{1}{2} \angle A O X=$ $180^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2}(\angle A W X+\angle A O X)=90^{\circ}$. So, $A D \perp A T$, and hence $A T \| B C$. Thus, $A T C B$ is an isosceles trapezoid inscribed in $\Omega$.

Denote by $A_{0}$ the midpoint of $B C$, and consider the image of $A T C B$ under the homothety $h$ with center $G$ and factor $-\frac{1}{2}$. We have $h(A)=A_{0}, h(B)=B_{0}$, and $h(C)=C_{0}$. From the
symmetry about $B_{0} C_{0}$, we have $\angle T C B=\angle C B A=\angle B_{0} C_{0} A=\angle D C_{0} B_{0}$. Using $A T \| D A_{0}$, we conclude $h(T)=D$. Hence the points $D, G$, and $T$ are collinear, and $X$ lies on the same line.

Solution 2. We define the points $A_{0}, O$, and $W$ as in the previous solution and we concentrate on the case $A B<A C$. Let $Q$ be the perpendicular projection of $A_{0}$ on $B_{0} C_{0}$.

Since $\angle W A O=\angle W Q O=\angle O X W=90^{\circ}$, the five points $A, W, X, O$, and $Q$ lie on a common circle. Furthermore, the reflections with respect to $B_{0} C_{0}$ and $O W$ map $A$ to $D$ and $X$, respectively. For these reasons, we have

$$
\angle W Q D=\angle A Q W=\angle A X W=\angle W A X=\angle W Q X
$$

Thus the three points $Q, D$, and $X$ lie on a common line, say $\ell$.

To complete the argument, we note that the homothety centered at $G$ sending the triangle $A B C$ to the triangle $A_{0} B_{0} C_{0}$ maps the altitude $A D$ to the altitude $A_{0} Q$. Therefore it maps $D$ to $Q$, so the points $D, G$, and $Q$ are collinear. Hence $G$ lies on $\ell$ as well.

Comment. There are various other ways to prove the collinearity of $Q, D$, and $X$ obtained in the middle part of Solution 2. Introduce for instance the point $J$ where the lines $A W$ and $B C$ intersect. Then the four points $A, D, X$, and $J$ lie at the same distance from $W$, so the quadrilateral $A D X J$ is cyclic. $$
\angle J D X=\angle J A X=\angle W A X=\angle W Q X
$$
