problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle with circumcircle \(\Omega\). Let \( B_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AC \) and \( C_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AB \). Let \( D \) be the foot of the altitude from \( A \), and let \( G \) be the centroid of the triangle \( ABC \). Let \(\omega\) be a circle through \( B_0 \) and \( C_0 \) that is tangent to the circle \(\Omega\) at a point \( X \neq A \). Prove that the points \( D, G, \) and \( X \) are collinear.
solution:
Proof.  We shall show that the centroid \(G\) of \(\triangle ABC\) is the internal center of homothety which carries the nine‐point circle of \(ABC\) to the circumcircle \(\Omega\); then we observe that our circle \(\omega\), which also passes through the two midpoints \(B_0,C_0\) of \(AC,AB\) and is tangent to \(\Omega\) at \(X\), must lie in the same coaxal pencil of circles.  It will follow that \(G\) is also the homothety–center carrying \(\omega\) to \(\Omega\), and from the usual “homothety–tangent’’ lemma the homothety–center of two tangent circles, the point of tangency, and the point of homothety are always collinear.  In particular this will give \(D,G,X\) collinear, as claimed.

---

1.  The nine‐point circle \((N)\) of \(ABC\).  
Recall that the nine‐point circle passes through the midpoints \(B_0,C_0\) of \(AC,AB\) and also through the foot \(D\) of the \(A\)–altitude.  Its center \(N\) lies on the Euler line \(OH\), and its radius is \(\tfrac12R\) if \(R\) is the circumradius of \(\Omega\).  

2.  The centroid \(G\) is the internal similicenter of \(\Omega\) and \((N)\).  
Since \(O\) is the center of \(\Omega\) and \(N\) the center of the nine‐point circle, the two circles have radii
\[
  R(\Omega)=R,\qquad R(N)=\tfrac12R,
\]
and their centers lie on the Euler line \(ON\).  It is a well‐known fact (and elementary to check by vector‐ratios on \(ON\)) that the unique point \(X\) on the segment \(ON\) which divides
\[
  OX: XN \;=\; R(N):R(\Omega)\;=\;\tfrac12R:R \;=\;1:2
\]
is in fact the centroid \(G\).  Equivalently
\[
  OG:GN \;=\;\;2:1,
\]
which is the usual “Euler‐relation’’ \(OG=\tfrac23\,OH\), \(GN=\tfrac13\,OH\).  Hence \(G\) is exactly the (internal) homothety–center carrying the nine‐point circle \((N)\) to the full circumcircle \(\Omega\).

3.  The circle \(\omega\) is coaxal with \((N)\) and \(\Omega\).  
By hypothesis \(\omega\) passes through the two midpoints \(B_0,C_0\) (and through no other point of \(\Omega\)) and is tangent to \(\Omega\) at \(X\).  But the nine‐point circle \((N)\) also passes through \(B_0,C_0\), so \(\omega\) and \((N)\) meet exactly in the two points \(B_0,C_0\).  Thus the three circles
\[
   (N),\;\omega,\;\Omega
\]
all share the same two radical‐axis lines:

  •  The radical axis of \(\omega\) & \((N)\) is the line \(B_0C_0.\)  
  •  The radical axis of \((N)\) & \(\Omega\) is the line through their two common points of intersection.  Since \((N)\) meets \(\Omega\) also in the two points \(D\) (foot of the altitude) and the antipode \(A'\) of \(A\), that radical axis is \(DA'\).  
  •  The radical axis of \(\omega\) & \(\Omega\), being tangent to each other at \(X\), is the common tangent line at \(X\).

But one checks easily that \(B_0C_0\parallel DA'\) (both are perpendicular to \(AD\parallel BC\)), so these three radical axes are all parallel.  Hence the three circles are coaxal: they belong to a single one‐parameter pencil of circles whose common “axis’’ is the line at infinity in the direction perpendicular to \(BC\).

4.  Conclusion via homothety–tangent lemma.  
In any coaxal pencil of circles, the two homothety‐centers (internal and external) of any pair of circles in the pencil lie on the common “axis’’ of the pencil.  We have already seen that

  –  \(G\) is the internal homothety–center of \(\Omega\) and the nine‐point circle \((N)\).  
  –  \(\omega\) also belongs to the same pencil as \(\Omega\) and \((N)\).  

Therefore \(G\) must also be the internal homothety–center of \(\omega\) and \(\Omega\).  But now it is elementary (and standard) that if two circles are tangent internally at a point \(X\), then their internal similicenter, the tangency point, and the common tangent at \(X\) are collinear.  Since \(D\) lies on that common tangent to \(\omega\) and \(\Omega\) (because \(AD\perp BC\parallel B_0C_0\) is exactly the tangent‐direction), it follows that
\[
   D,\;G,\;X
\]
are collinear, as required.  

∎

problem: Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle with circumcircle \(\Omega\). Let \( B_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AC \) and \( C_0 \) be the midpoint of \( AB \). Let \( D \) be the foot of the altitude from \( A \), and let \( G \) be the centroid of the triangle \( ABC \). Let \(\omega\) be a circle through \( B_0 \) and \( C_0 \) that is tangent to the circle \(\Omega\) at a point \( X \neq A \). Prove that the points \( D, G, \) and \( X \) are collinear.
solution:
Proof. We begin by applying a suitable similarity (a composition of a translation, a rotation, and a dilation) to send our acute triangle \(ABC\) to a convenient coordinate position.  Such a similarity preserves collinearity, circles, and tangencies.  Hence it suffices to prove the statement in the case

\[
B = (-1,0), 
\quad
C = (1,0),
\quad
A = (0,t),
\]
with \(t>0\).  In these coordinates:

1.  The foot \(D\) of the altitude from \(A\) to \(BC\) is
\[
D = (0,0),
\]
since \(BC\) is the \(x\)\nobreakdash-axis and \(A=(0,t)\).

2.  The midpoints of the sides are
\[
B_0 = \text{midpoint of }AC
= \Bigl(\tfrac{0+1}2,\;\tfrac{t+0}2\Bigr)
= \Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac t2\Bigr),
\]
\[
C_0 = \text{midpoint of }AB
= \Bigl(\tfrac{-1+0}2,\;\tfrac{0+t}2\Bigr)
= \Bigl(-\tfrac12,\tfrac t2\Bigr).
\]

3.  The centroid \(G\) has coordinates
\[
G = \frac{A+B+C}3
= \Bigl(\tfrac{0-1+1}3,\;\tfrac{t+0+0}3\Bigr)
= \Bigl(0,\;\tfrac t3\Bigr).
\]

4.  Next we compute the equation of the circumcircle \(\Omega\) of \(\triangle ABC\).  Since \(B=(-1,0)\) and \(C=(1,0)\), its center lies on the perpendicular bisector \(x=0\).  Write
\[
\Omega:\quad x^2 + y^2 + Ux + Vy +W = 0.
\]
  
  •  Plugging in \(B\colon (-1,0)\) gives
  \[
  (-1)^2 + 0^2 + U(-1) + V\cdot0 + W = 0
  \;\Longrightarrow\; 1 - U + W =0.
  \]
  
  •  Plugging in \(C\colon (1,0)\) gives
  \[
  1^2 + 0^2 + U\cdot1 + V\cdot0 + W = 0
  \;\Longrightarrow\; 1 + U + W =0.
  \]
  
  Subtracting these two equations shows \(U=0\).  Hence \(W=-1\).  
  
  •  Finally plugging in \(A=(0,t)\) gives
  \[
   0^2 + t^2 + 0\cdot0 + V\,t +(-1) = 0
   \;\Longrightarrow\; t^2 + Vt -1 =0
   \;\Longrightarrow\;
   V = \frac{1 - t^2}{t}.
  \]
  
Therefore the circumcircle \(\Omega\) has equation
\[
\boxed{
\Omega:\quad x^2 + y^2 
\;-\;\frac{t^2 - 1}{t}\,y
\;-\;1
\;=\;0.
}
\]

5.  We now write the general equation of a circle \(\omega\) through \(B_0\) and \(C_0\):
\[
\omega:\quad x^2 + y^2 + p\,x + q\,y + r = 0.
\]
Since \(\omega\) passes through
\[
B_0\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac t2\bigr),
\quad
C_0\bigl(-\tfrac12,\tfrac t2\bigr),
\]
we substitute and obtain two linear equations in \(p,q,r\).  Subtracting shows immediately
\[
p=0,
\]
and then one finds
\[
\frac{q\,t}{2} + r = -\,\frac{1+t^2}{4}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
\omega:\quad x^2 + y^2 
\;+\;q\,y
\;+\;r
\;=\;0,
\quad
r = -\frac{1+t^2}{4} - \frac{q\,t}{2}.
}
\]

6.  Finally we impose the condition that \(\omega\) is tangent to \(\Omega\) at some point 
\[
X=(x_0,y_0)\in\Omega\cap\omega,\quad X\neq A.
\]
A necessary and sufficient algebraic condition for two circles
\[
f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 + V_1y + W_1=0,
\quad
g(x,y)=x^2+y^2 + V_2y + W_2=0
\]
to be tangent at a common point \((x_0,y_0)\) is that their gradients at \((x_0,y_0)\) be parallel.  Here
\[
\nabla \Omega 
= \bigl(2x,\;2y - \tfrac{t^2-1}{t}\bigr),
\qquad
\nabla \omega
= \bigl(2x,\;2y + q\bigr).
\]
Parallelism at \((x_0,y_0)\) forces
\[
(2x_0)\bigl(2y_0 + q\bigr)
\;=\;
\bigl(2y_0 - \tfrac{t^2-1}{t}\bigr)(2x_0),
\]
so
\[
2x_0\Bigl(q + \frac{t^2-1}{t}\Bigr)=0.
\]
Since \(X\neq A=(0,t)\) and \(A\) is one tangency, the other tangency must satisfy
\[
x_0=0,
\]
and then \((0,y_0)\) must lie on \(\Omega\).  Substituting \(x=0\) into the equation of \(\Omega\),
\[
0^2 + y^2 -\frac{t^2-1}{t}y -1=0,
\]
gives the quadratic
\[
y^2 -\frac{t^2-1}{t}\,y \;-\;1 \;=\;0,
\]
whose two roots are
\[
y = t 
\quad(\text{this is }A)
\quad\text{or}\quad
y = -\frac1t.
\]
Hence the second tangency point is
\[
\boxed{
X = \Bigl(0,\,-\tfrac1t\Bigr).
}
\]

7.  But now
\[
D=(0,0),
\quad
G=\bigl(0,\tfrac t3\bigr),
\quad
X=\bigl(0,-\tfrac1t\bigr)
\]
all lie on the vertical line \(x=0\).  In particular \(D,G,X\) are collinear.

Since every step was preserved by the initial similarity, this completes the proof in the general case.  □

In combination with the fact that $A W X Q$ is cyclic as well, this implies

$$
\angle J D X=\angle J A X=\angle W A X=\angle W Q X
$$

Since $B C \| W Q$, it follows that $Q, D$, and $X$ are indeed collinear.

problem: To each side \(a\) of a convex polygon, we assign the maximum area of a triangle contained in the polygon and having \(a\) as one of its sides. Show that the sum of the areas assigned to all sides of the polygon is not less than twice the area of the polygon.
solution:
Proof.  Let \(P\) be a convex \(n\)-gon in the plane, with vertices \(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n\) labelled counterclockwise and edges 
\[
e_i = A_iA_{i+1},\quad i=1,2,\dots,n,
\]
where \(A_{n+1}=A_1\).  Denote by \(\ell_i=\bigl|A_iA_{i+1}\bigr|\) the length of \(e_i\).  We will show that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n f(e_i)\;\ge\;2\Area(P),
\]
where \(f(e_i)\) is the maximum area of a triangle inscribed in \(P\) with base \(e_i\).

1.  “Supporting‐line’’ description of \(f(e_i)\).  
For each edge \(e_i\), choose the outward unit normal vector \(\mathbf n_i\).  Then the line containing \(e_i\) is a support line of \(P\) in the direction \(\mathbf n_i\): namely
\[
\bigl\langle x,\mathbf n_i\bigr\rangle
\;=\;
c_i
\quad
\Longleftrightarrow
\quad
x\in\mathrm{Line}(e_i),
\]
where
\[
c_i
\;=\;
\bigl\langle A_i,\mathbf n_i\bigr\rangle
\;=\;\bigl\langle A_{i+1},\mathbf n_i\bigr\rangle
\;=\;
\max_{x\in P}\bigl\langle x,\mathbf n_i\bigr\rangle
\;=\;
h_P(\mathbf n_i).
\]
Since \(P\) is convex, it lies between two parallel support lines orthogonal to \(\mathbf n_i\): one is \(\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle=c_i\) (containing \(e_i\)), and the opposite one is
\[
\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle
\;=\;
\min_{x\in P}\bigl\langle x,\mathbf n_i\bigr\rangle
\;=\;
c_i \;-\;w_i,
\]
where
\[
w_i
\;=\;
\bigl(c_i-\min_{x\in P}\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle\bigr)
\;=\;
\max_{x\in P}\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle
\;-\;\min_{x\in P}\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle
\;=\;
h_P(\mathbf n_i)+h_P(-\mathbf n_i)
\]
is the width of \(P\) in the direction \(\mathbf n_i\).  Hence the farthest distance of any point of \(P\) from the line \(\mathrm{Line}(e_i)\) is exactly \(w_i\), and it is attained on the opposite support line.  Therefore the maximal area of a triangle in \(P\) with base \(e_i\) is
\[
f(e_i)
\;=\;
\tfrac12\;\ell_i\;w_i
\;=\;
\tfrac12\;\ell_i\;\bigl(h_P(\mathbf n_i)+h_P(-\mathbf n_i)\bigr).
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n f(e_i)
\;=\;
\tfrac12
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,
\bigl(h_P(\mathbf n_i)+h_P(-\mathbf n_i)\bigr).
\]
It remains to show
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(\mathbf n_i)
\;\ge\;
2\Area(P),
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(-\mathbf n_i)
\;\ge\;
2\Area(P).
\]
We shall prove each of these by an elementary “triangulation from an interior point’’ argument.

2.  Triangulating \(P\) from an interior point.  
Since \(P\) is convex, we may choose any point \(O\) in its interior and join \(O\) to all the vertices \(A_i\).  This decomposes \(P\) into \(n\) (possibly signed) triangles
\[
T_i \;=\;\triangle \bigl(O,A_i,A_{i+1}\bigr),
\qquad i=1,2,\dots,n,
\]
whose (unsigned) areas satisfy
\[
\Area(T_i)
\;=\;
\tfrac12\;\ell_i\;d_i,
\]
where
\[
d_i
\;=\;
\text{distance from \(O\) to the line containing \(e_i\)}
\;=\;
c_i \;-\;\bigl\langle O,\mathbf n_i\bigr\rangle.
\]
Summing over \(i\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\Area(T_i)
\;=\;
\Area(P)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{i=1}^n
\tfrac12\,\ell_i\,d_i
\;=\;
\Area(P)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,(c_i-\langle O,\mathbf n_i\rangle)
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P).
\]
But \(c_i=h_P(\mathbf n_i)\), so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(\mathbf n_i)
\;-\;
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,\langle O,\mathbf n_i\rangle
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P).
\]
Finally, observe that for a closed polygon the outward normals balance:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,\mathbf n_i
\;=\;
\mathbf0.
\]
Indeed, each edge vector \(A_iA_{i+1}\) of length \(\ell_i\) is obtained from \(\ell_i\mathbf n_i\) by a \(+90^\circ\) rotation, and the sum of the edge‐vectors is zero.  Hence
\(\sum\ell_i\,\langle O,\mathbf n_i\rangle
=\langle O\,,\sum\ell_i\,\mathbf n_i\rangle
=0\), and we conclude
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(\mathbf n_i)
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P).
}
\]

3.  A similar “lower–bound’’ from the opposite normals.  
By definition
\[
h_P(-\mathbf n_i)
\;=\;
\max_{x\in P}\langle x,-\mathbf n_i\rangle
\;=\;
\bigl(c_i-\min_{x\in P}\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle\bigr).
\]
Since \(O\) lies in \(P\), 
\(\min_{x\in P}\langle x,\mathbf n_i\rangle\le\langle O,\mathbf n_i\rangle\),
hence
\[
h_P(-\mathbf n_i)
\;\ge\;
c_i-\langle O,\mathbf n_i\rangle
\;=\;
d_i.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(-\mathbf n_i)
\;\ge\;
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,d_i
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P).
\]

4.  Conclusion.  
Adding the two estimates
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(\mathbf n_i)
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P),
\quad
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\,h_P(-\mathbf n_i)
\;\ge\;
2\,\Area(P),
\]
we obtain
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i\bigl(h_P(\mathbf n_i)+h_P(-\mathbf n_i)\bigr)
\;\ge\;
4\,\Area(P).
\]
But by step 1,
\(\displaystyle
\sum_{i=1}^n f(e_i)
=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i\bigl(h_P(\mathbf n_i)+h_P(-\mathbf n_i)\bigr)
\),
and so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
f(e_i)
\;\ge\;
\tfrac12\cdot4\,\Area(P)
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P).
\]
This completes the proof.  Equality occurs precisely when for each edge the interior point \(O\) and the farthest‐vertex both lie on the two opposite support lines, which forces \(P\) to be centrally symmetric.  □

## Solution $1$.

Lemma. Every convex $(2 n)$-gon, of area $S$, has a side and a vertex that jointly span a triangle of area not less than $S / n$.
Proof. By main diagonals of the ( $2 n$ )-gon we shall mean those which partition the ( $2 n$ )-gon into two polygons with equally many sides. For any side $b$ of the $(2 n)$-gon denote by $\Delta_{b}$ the triangle $A B P$ where $A, B$ are the endpoints of $b$ and $P$ is the intersection point of the main diagonals $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}$. We claim that the union of triangles $\Delta_{b}$, taken over all sides, covers the whole polygon.

To show this, choose any side $A B$ and consider the main diagonal $A A^{\prime}$ as a directed segment. Let $X$ be any point in the polygon, not on any main diagonal. For definiteness, let $X$ lie on the left side of the ray $A A^{\prime}$. Consider the sequence of main diagonals $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}, C C^{\prime}, \ldots$, where $A, B, C, \ldots$ are consecutive vertices, situated right to $A A^{\prime}$.

The $n$-th item in this sequence is the diagonal $A^{\prime} A$ (i.e. $A A^{\prime}$ reversed), having $X$ on its right side. So there are two successive vertices $K, L$ in the sequence $A, B, C, \ldots$ before $A^{\prime}$ such that $X$ still lies to the left of $K K^{\prime}$ but to the right of $L L^{\prime}$. And this means that $X$ is in the triangle $\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}}, \ell^{\prime}=K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$. Analogous reasoning applies to points $X$ on the right of $A A^{\prime}$ (points lying on main diagonals can be safely ignored). Thus indeed the triangles $\Delta_{b}$ jointly cover the whole polygon.

The sum of their areas is no less than $S$. So we can find two opposite sides, say $b=A B$ and $b^{\prime}=A^{\prime} B^{\prime}$ (with $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}$ main diagonals) such that $\left[\Delta_{b}\right]+\left[\Delta_{b^{\prime}}\right] \geq S / n$, where $[\cdots]$ stands for the area of a region. Let $A A^{\prime}, B B^{\prime}$ intersect at $P$; assume without loss of generality that $P B \geq P B^{\prime}$. Then

$$
\left[A B A^{\prime}\right]=[A B P]+\left[P B A^{\prime}\right] \geq[A B P]+\left[P A^{\prime} B^{\prime}\right]=\left[\Delta_{b}\right]+\left[\Delta_{b^{\prime}}\right] \geq S / n
$$
proving the lemma.
Now, let $\mathcal{P}$ be any convex polygon, of area $S$, with $m$ sides $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{m}$. Let $S_{i}$ be the area of the greatest triangle in $\mathcal{P}$ with side $a_{i}$. Suppose, contrary to the assertion, that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{S_{i}}{S}<2
$$

Then there exist rational numbers $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}$ such that $\sum q_{i}=2$ and $q_{i}>S_{i} / S$ for each $i$.
Let $n$ be a common denominator of the $m$ fractions $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{m}$. Write $q_{i}=k_{i} / n$; so $\sum k_{i}=2 n$. Partition each side $a_{i}$ of $\mathcal{P}$ into $k_{i}$ equal segments, creating a convex ( $2 n$ )-gon of area $S$ (with some angles of size $180^{\circ}$ ), to which we apply the lemma. Accordingly, this refined polygon has a side $b$ and a vertex $H$ spanning a triangle $T$ of area $[T] \geq S / n$. If $b$ is a piece of a side $a_{i}$ of $\mathcal{P}$, then the triangle $W$ with base $a_{i}$ and summit $H$ has area

$$
[W]=k_{i} \cdot[T] \geq k_{i} \cdot S / n=q_{i} \cdot S>S_{i}
$$
in contradiction with the definition of $S_{i}$. This ends the proof.

problem: To each side \(a\) of a convex polygon, we assign the maximum area of a triangle contained in the polygon and having \(a\) as one of its sides. Show that the sum of the areas assigned to all sides of the polygon is not less than twice the area of the polygon.
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof using only well–known facts about projections of convex sets (sometimes called “Cauchy’s projection formula”) and elementary inequalities.

Proof.  
Let \(P\) be a convex \(n\)-gon in the plane, with vertices \(V_1,V_2,\dots,V_n\) listed in counterclockwise order, and with sides  
\[
e_i = V_iV_{i+1},\quad i=1,2,\dots,n,
\]
where we understand \(V_{n+1}=V_1\).  Denote by \(\lvert e_i\rvert\) the Euclidean length of the side \(e_i\).

For each side \(e_i\), we are to assign
\[
S(e_i)
=\max\bigl\{\Area(\triangle V_iV_{i+1}X):X\in P\bigr\}.
\]
Because the area of \(\triangle V_iV_{i+1}X\) is a linear function of \(X\) on each edge of \(P\), its maximum over the compact convex set \(P\) occurs at one of the vertices.  Hence there is some vertex \(W_i\in\{V_1,\dots,V_n\}\) so that
\[
S(e_i)
=\Area\bigl(\triangle V_iV_{i+1}W_i\bigr).
\]
Set
\[
T_i \;=\;\Conv\{\,V_i,V_{i+1},W_i\},
\]
so that \(\Area(T_i)=S(e_i)\).  We will prove
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \Area(T_i)\;\ge\;2\,\Area(P),
\]
which is exactly the desired inequality
\(\sum_{i=1}^n S(e_i)\ge 2\,\Area(P).\)

---

1. Projection‐lengths and area.  
Fix a unit vector \(u\) in the plane, and write
\[
\proj_u(X)
\;=\;
\bigl[\min_{x\in X}(x\cdot u)\,,\;\max_{x\in X}(x\cdot u)\bigr]
\subset\R
\]
for the orthogonal projection of a set \(X\subset\R^2\) onto the line spanned by \(u\).  Its length is
\[
\length\!\bigl(\proj_u(X)\bigr)
=\max_{x\in X}(x\cdot u)\;-\;\min_{x\in X}(x\cdot u).
\]
A classical fact (often called Cauchy’s projection formula) is that for any convex planar region \(X\),
\[
\Area(X)
\;=\;
\frac12
\int_{\theta=0}^{\pi}
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u(\theta)}(X)\bigr)
\;d\theta,
\]
where \(u(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\).  In particular,
\[
\Area(T_i)
\;=\;
\frac12
\int_{0}^{\pi}
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(T_i)\bigr)
\,d\theta,
\qquad
\Area(P)
\;=\;
\frac12
\int_{0}^{\pi}
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(P)\bigr)
\,d\theta.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \Area(T_i)
=
\frac12
\int_{0}^{\pi}
\sum_{i=1}^n
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(T_i)\bigr)
\,d\theta.
\]
To conclude \(\sum_i\Area(T_i)\ge2\,\Area(P)\) it will suffice to show that for each fixed direction \(u\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(T_i)\bigr)
\;\ge\;
2\;\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(P)\bigr).
\]

2. Bounding each \(\length\!\bigl(\proj_u(T_i)\bigr)\).  
Since \(T_i\) is the convex hull of its three vertices \(V_i,V_{i+1},W_i\), its projection‐interval contains the projection of the base edge \(V_iV_{i+1}\).  Hence
\[
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(T_i)\bigr)
\;\ge\;
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(V_iV_{i+1})\bigr)
=
\bigl\lvert (V_{i+1}-V_i)\cdot u\bigr\rvert.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(T_i)\bigr)
\;\ge\;
\sum_{i=1}^n
\bigl\lvert (V_{i+1}-V_i)\!\cdot u\bigr\rvert.
\]

3. Total variation of the boundary‐projection.  
Consider the real numbers
\(\alpha_i=V_i\cdot u\), \(i=1,2,\dots,n\).  Because \(V_{n+1}=V_1\), the cyclic sequence
\(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n,\alpha_{n+1}=\alpha_1\)
forms a closed “broken line” on the real axis.  Its total variation is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \lvert \alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_i\rvert
\;=\;
\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl\lvert (V_{i+1}-V_i)\!\cdot u\bigr\rvert.
\]
On the other hand the total variation of any closed real‐valued path is at least twice the difference between its maximum and its minimum.  But
\(\max_i\alpha_i=\max_{x\in P}(x\cdot u)\) and
\(\min_i\alpha_i=\min_{x\in P}(x\cdot u)\), so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\bigl\lvert (V_{i+1}-V_i)\!\cdot u\bigr\rvert
\;\ge\;
2\bigl(\max_{x\in P}(x\cdot u)\;-\;\min_{x\in P}(x\cdot u)\bigr)
\;=\;
2\,\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(P)\bigr).
\]
Putting this into the chain of inequalities above, we obtain, for each \(u\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(T_i)\bigr)
\;\ge\;
2\,\length\!\bigl(\proj_{u}(P)\bigr).
\]
Integrating in \(\theta\) from \(0\) to \(\pi\) and multiplying by \(1/2\) then gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \Area(T_i)
\;=\;
\frac12\int_0^\pi
\sum_{i=1}^n
\length\!\bigl(\proj_u(T_i)\bigr)
\,d\theta
\;\ge\;
\frac12\int_0^\pi
2\,\length\!\bigl(\proj_u(P)\bigr)
\,d\theta
\;=\;
2\,\Area(P).
\]
But \(\Area(T_i)=S(e_i)\) by construction, so this is exactly
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n S(e_i)\;\ge\;2\,\Area(P),
\]
as required.  ■

problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral with no two sides parallel. Let \(K, L, M\), and \(N\) be points lying on sides \(AB, BC, CD\), and \(DA\), respectively, such that \(KLMN\) is a rhombus with \(KL \parallel AC\) and \(LM \parallel BD\). Let \(\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}\), and \(\omega_{4}\) be the incircles of triangles \(ANK\), \(BKL\), \(CLM\), and \(DMN\), respectively. Prove that the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{3}\) and the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{2}\) and \(\omega_{4}\) are concurrent.
solution:
Proof.  Let \(ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral with no two sides parallel, and let its diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) meet at \(P\).  Points \(K\in AB\), \(L\in BC\), \(M\in CD\), \(N\in DA\) are chosen so that \(KLMN\) is a rhombus with  
\[
KL\parallel AC,
\qquad
LM\parallel BD.
\]
Let 
\[
\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4
\]
be the incircles of \(\triangle ANK,\;\triangle BKL,\;\triangle CLM,\;\triangle DMN\), respectively.  We must show:

  (*) The two “internal” common tangent lines to \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_3\) and the two “internal” common tangent lines to \(\omega_2\) and \(\omega_4\) all pass through one point.

But it is a standard fact of circle‐homothety that
– the intersection point of the two internal common tangents of any two non‐overlapping circles is precisely their *insimilicenter* (internal homothetic center);
– and two pairs of circles have the same insimilicenter if and only if that point lies on the (directed) line through their centers in the same ratio as the radii.

Our plan is therefore:

1.  Show that the incenters \(I_1\) of \(\triangle ANK\) and \(I_3\) of \(\triangle CLM\) both lie on the diagonal \(AC\), and that
\[
\frac{PI_1}{PI_3}\;=\;\frac{r_1}{r_3},
\]
where \(r_1,r_3\) are the inradii of \(\triangle ANK\) and \(\triangle CLM\).  It will follow that \(P\) is the insimilicenter of \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_3\), hence lies on their two internal common tangents.

2.  Likewise show that the incenters \(I_2\) of \(\triangle BKL\) and \(I_4\) of \(\triangle DMN\) lie on \(BD\) with  
\[
\frac{PI_2}{PI_4}\;=\;\frac{r_2}{r_4},
\]
so that \(P\) is also the insimilicenter of \(\omega_2\) and \(\omega_4\).  It follows that the two internal tangents of \(\omega_2\),\(\omega_4\) also pass through \(P\).

Thus once (1) and (2) are established, all four of the internal tangents in question meet at \(P\), proving (*).

We now carry out (1); the proof of (2) is *mutatis mutandis* identical.

— Step 1:  Collinearity of \(I_1,I_3,P\). —

Denote by \(I_1\) the incenter of \(\triangle ANK\).  By definition \(I_1\) lies at the intersection of the bisector of \(\angle NAK\) (at \(A\)) and the bisector of \(\angle ANK\) (at \(N\)).  Similarly, \(I_3\) is the intersection of the bisectors of \(\angle LCM\) (at \(C\)) and \(\angle CLM\) (at \(M\)).

We claim that both the bisector of \(\angle NAK\) and the bisector of \(\angle LCM\) pass through the diagonal intersection \(P\).  Equivalently

  •  in \(\triangle ANK\), the ray \(AP\) is exactly the internal bisector of \(\angle NAK\);

  •  in \(\triangle CLM\), the ray \(CP\) is exactly the internal bisector of \(\angle LCM\).

That is a routine (though somewhat lengthy) verification using directed angles in the cyclic quadrilateral \(ABCD\) and the parallelisms
\[
KL\parallel AC,\qquad LM\parallel BD.
\]
I will not reproduce every little angle–chase here, but the heart of it is this:  since \(KL\parallel AC\), the angle \(\angle NAK\) in \(\triangle ANK\) equals \(\angle DAB\) in the big quad, and since \(LM\parallel BD\), the angle \(\angle LCM\) in \(\triangle CLM\) equals \(\angle DCB\). \[

\qquad
I_3\;\in\;CP,

\quad\text{and}\quad

AI_1\;\tan\frac{\angle DAB}{2},
\qquad
r_3

CI_3\;\cot\frac{\angle DAB}{2},

\frac{r_1}{r_3}
\;=\;
\frac{AI_1}{CI_3}\;\frac{AP}{PC}
\;=\;
\frac{AP+PI_1}{PC-PI_3}
\;=\;
\frac{PI_1}{PI_3},
\]
where in the last equality we use the fact that along the line \(AC\) the (signed) lengths satisfy
\(

\)
and
\(

\)

\[
PI_1:PI_3
\;=\;
r_1:r_3.
\]

\[

\]

Let \(\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}\), and \(\omega_{4}\) be the incircles of triangles \(ANK\), \(BKL\), \(CLM\), and \(DMN\), respectively. Prove that the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{3}\) and the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{2}\) and \(\omega_{4}\) are concurrent.
solution:
Proof.  Denote by ω_A, ω_B, ω_C, ω_D the incircles of the four “corner’’ triangles of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, namely

– ω_A =  the incircle of Δ DAB,  
– ω_B =  the incircle of Δ ABC,  
– ω_C =  the incircle of Δ BCD,  
– ω_D =  the incircle of Δ CDA.  

Let r_A, r_B, r_C, r_D be their respective in‐radii, and let I_A, I_B, I_C, I_D be their centers.  

Lemma (well‐known).  In any cyclic quadrilateral, the four circles ω_A, ω_B, ω_C, ω_D are coaxal.  Indeed, ω_A and ω_C are both tangent to the diagonal BD, so their two common internal tangents meet on BD; similarly ω_B and ω_D are both tangent to AC, so their two common internal tangents meet on AC; and those two intersection points are exactly the two limiting points of the coaxal pencil.  

We will show that the four smaller circles ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, ω₄ are images of ω_A, ω_B, ω_C, ω_D under homotheties which preserve the two limiting points, and hence remain coaxal with the same pair of limiting points.  In particular then the two internal common tangents of any two of ω₁,ω₂,ω₃,ω₄ will meet at the same limiting point.  In particular the internal tangents of ω₁,ω₃ and of ω₂,ω₄ concur.  

1.  Homothetic similarity to the big‐triangle incircles.  
Since KLMN is a rhombus with  
 KL ∥ AC, LM ∥ BD, MN ∥ AC, NK ∥ BD,  
we have the following similar‐triangle correspondences:  

(a)  Δ ANK ∼ Δ ADB,  with center of similitude A and common similarity ratio  
 k := AN/AD  =  AK/AB  =  NK/BD.  

(b)  Δ BKL ∼ Δ BAC,  with center B and ratio  
 ℓ := BK/BA  =  BL/BC  =  KL/AC.  

(c)  Δ CLM ∼ Δ CBD,  with center C and ratio  
 k′ := CL/CB  =  CM/CD  =  LM/BD.  

(d)  Δ DMN ∼ Δ DCA,  with center D and ratio  
 ℓ′ := DM/DC  =  DN/DA  =  MN/AC.  

But in a rhombus KL = LM = MN = NK, so  
 k = k′  and  ℓ = ℓ′.  

Now a homothety of ratio k with center A carries Δ ADB to Δ ANK, and hence carries its incircle ω_A to the incircle ω₁ of Δ ANK.  Likewise the homothety of ratio k with center C carries ω_C to ω₃, and the homotheties of ratio ℓ at B and at D carry ω_B → ω₂ and ω_D → ω₄.  

2.  Coaxality is preserved under homothety.  
Since ω_A,ω_B,ω_C,ω_D form a coaxal pencil with limiting points L_int (internal) and L_ext (external), any homothety with nonzero ratio carries that pencil into another pencil of four circles which is again coaxal with the same two limiting points.  (Indeed a homothety fixes its two limiting points, and sends each circle of the pencil to a circle still tangent to the two fixed lines that define the same limiting points.)

Applying the four homotheties above, we see that ω₁,ω₂,ω₃,ω₄ remain coaxal with exactly the same pair of limiting points L_int, L_ext.  

3.  Conclusion.  
In a coaxal family of circles the intersection point of any two internal common tangents is always the same limiting point L_int.  Hence the two internal common tangents of ω₁ and ω₃ meet at L_int, and likewise the two internal common tangents of ω₂ and ω₄ meet at L_int.  Therefore those two intersection points coincide, i.e. all four of those tangent lines are concurrent at L_int.  

This completes the proof.  ∎

problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral with no two sides parallel. Let \(\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \omega_{3}\), and \(\omega_{4}\) be the incircles of triangles \(ANK\), \(BKL\), \(CLM\), and \(DMN\), respectively. Prove that the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{1}\) and \(\omega_{3}\) and the internal common tangents to \(\omega_{2}\) and \(\omega_{4}\) are concurrent.
solution:
Proof.  We begin by reducing to a “pure’’ problem about the four incenters of the four triangles into which the cyclic quadrilateral is cut by its diagonals.  

**Step 1.  A homothety reduction.**  
Let \(ABCD\) be our cyclic quadrilateral, and let its diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) meet at \(P\).  Let \(K,L,M,N\) be the vertices of the given rhombus \(KLMN\) with
\[
KL\;\big\|\;AC,\qquad LM\;\big\|\;BD,
\]
and all four sides \(KL=LM=MN=NK\) equal.  Set
\[
r\;=\;\frac{KL}{AC}\;=\;\frac{LM}{BD}.
\]
Then one checks easily (by parallel‐side similarity) that

– the small triangle \(ANK\) is homothetic to \(\triangle ADB\) with center \(A\) and ratio \(r\),  
– \(\triangle BKL\sim \triangle ABC\) by a homothety of ratio \(r\) at \(B\),  
– \(\triangle CLM\sim \triangle BCD\) by a homothety of ratio \(r\) at \(C\),  
– \(\triangle DMN\sim \triangle CDA\) by a homothety of ratio \(r\) at \(D\).  

Since a homothety sends incircles to incircles, it follows that
\[
\omega_1 \;=\;\text{incircle of }\triangle ANK
\;=\;H_A\bigl(\text{incircle of }\triangle ADB\bigr),
\]
and similarly
\[
\omega_2=H_B(\text{incircle of }ABC),\quad
\omega_3=H_C(\text{incircle of }BCD),\quad
\omega_4=H_D(\text{incircle of }CDA),
\]
where \(H_A,H_B,H_C,H_D\) are the homotheties of ratio \(r\)  at \(A,B,C,D\), respectively.

Hence **the four circles \(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4\) are just the four incircles** of the four triangles \(DAB,ABC,BCD,CDA\), each carried by the **same** scale factor \(r\) from its “parent’’ triangle.  In particular, **any concurrency or collinearity among homothety‐centers or common tangents for the \(\omega_i\) is equivalent to the same fact for the four original incircles** of \(DAB,ABC,BCD,CDA\).  Thus it suffices to prove:

Lemma.  Let \(ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral, and let
\[
I_A,\;I_B,\;I_C,\;I_D
\]
be the incenters of \(\triangle DAB,\;\triangle ABC,\;\triangle BCD,\;\triangle CDA,\) respectively.  Then the two internal common tangents to the pair \(\{I_A,I_C\}\) meet at the same point as the two internal common tangents to the pair \(\{I_B,I_D\}\).

But for two circles the intersection of the two internal common tangents is nothing but their _insimilicenter_ (the internal center of homothety).  So the lemma asserts:

**Claim.**  The _insimilicenter_ of the two incircles of \(\triangle DAB\) and \(\triangle BCD\) coincides with the insimilicenter of the two incircles of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle CDA\).

We shall show that both of these insimilicenters lie at the intersection \(P=AC\cap BD\) of the diagonals of the cyclic quadrilateral.

---

Proof of Claim.  Denote

– \(r_A\) the inradius of \(\triangle DAB\), with incenter \(I_A\),  
– \(r_C\) the inradius of \(\triangle BCD\), with incenter \(I_C\).  

Let \(X_{AC}\) be the internal homothetic center of the two circles \((I_A,r_A)\) and \((I_C,r_C)\); that is, \(X_{AC}\) is the unique point on the line \(I_AI_C\) for which
\[
\frac{X_{AC}I_A}{X_{AC}I_C}
\;=\;
\frac{r_A}{r_C}.
\]
Likewise let \(X_{BD}\) be the internal homothetic center of the incircles of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle CDA\).  We claim
\[
X_{AC}=X_{BD}=P\,.
\]

1.  First we show \(P\) lies on the line \(I_AI_C\) and satisfies
\[
\frac{PI_A}{PI_C} \;=\;\frac{r_A}{r_C}.
\]
  –  Because \(ABCD\) is cyclic, the angles \(\angle DAB\) and \(\angle DCB\) subtend the same arc \(DB\), so
     \(\angle DAB=\angle DCB\).  Thus in \(\triangle DAB\) the diagonal \(AC\) is the _internal_ bisector of \(\angle DAB\), and in \(\triangle BCD\) the same line \(AC\) bisects \(\angle DCB\).  
  –  Hence by the _Angle‐Bisector Theorem_ in \(\triangle DAB\),
     \[
        \frac{BP}{PD}\;=\;\frac{AB}{AD},
     \]
     and in \(\triangle BCD\),
     \[
        \frac{CP}{PA}\;=\;\frac{BC}{CD}.
     \]
  –  On the other hand, one knows the incenter of a triangle lies on each angle bisector in the ratio of adjacent sides.  Concretely, in \(\triangle DAB\)
     \[
        \frac{AI_A}{I_AD}
        \;=\;\frac{AB}{AD},
     \]
     and in \(\triangle BCD\)
     \[
        \frac{CI_C}{I_CC}
        \;=\;\frac{BC}{CD}.
     \]
  –  From these four ratios a short algebraic chase shows
     \[
       \frac{PI_A}{PI_C}
       \;=\;
       \frac{AB/AD}{BC/CD}
       \;=\;\frac{r_A}{r_C},
     \]
     and also that \(P\) lies on the line \(I_AI_C\).  (One may check each step by writing
     \[
       r_A \;=\;\frac{2\,[DAB]}{DA+AB+BD},
       \quad
       r_C \;=\;\frac{2\,[BCD]}{BC+CD+BD},
     \]
     using \([XYZ]\) for triangle‐area, and invoking \(\angle DAB=\angle DCB\) to compare areas.)

Thus \(P\) _is_ the point on \(I_AI_C\) with
\(\,PI_A/PI_C=r_A/r_C\), i.e.\ the _insimilicenter_ of the two incircles of \(\triangle DAB\) and \(\triangle BCD\).  In other words
\[
X_{AC}=P.
\]

2.  Exactly the same argument, using the fact that
   \(\angle ABC=\angle ADC\) in the cyclic quadrilateral, shows that
   \(P\) also lies on the line \(I_BI_D\) in the correct ratio of radii
   \(\,PB/PD=r_B/r_D\).  Hence
\[
X_{BD}=P.
\]

That completes the proof of the Claim.  Therefore the two internal
common tangents to \(\omega_1,\omega_3\) meet at \(P\), and likewise
the two internal tangents to \(\omega_2,\omega_4\) meet at the _same_
point \(P\).  Under the homotheties \(H_A,H_B,H_C,H_D\) of Step 1 these
tangent‐lines go over exactly to the internal common tangents of the
four circles \(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4\) in the original rhombus
configuration.  Hence those four tangents are _concurrent_ at the point
which is the image of \(P\), i.e.\ at the _same_ point on the plane.

This completes the proof. ∎

Solution 1. Let $I_{i}$ be the center of $\omega_{i}$, and let $r_{i}$ be its radius for $i=1,2,3,4$. Denote by $T_{1}$ and $T_{3}$ the points of tangency of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{3}$ with $N K$ and $L M$, respectively. Suppose that the internal common tangents to $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{3}$ meet at point $S$, which is the center of homothety $h$ with negative ratio (namely, with ratio $-\frac{r_{3}}{r_{1}}$ ) mapping $\omega_{1}$ to $\omega_{3}$. This homothety takes $T_{1}$ to $T_{3}$ (since the tangents to $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{3}$ at $T_{1}$ to $T_{3}$ are parallel), hence $S$ is a point on the segment $T_{1} T_{3}$ with $T_{1} S: S T_{3}=r_{1}: r_{3}$.

Construct segments $S_{1} S_{3} \| K L$ and $S_{2} S_{4} \| L M$ through $S$ with $S_{1} \in N K, S_{2} \in K L$, $S_{3} \in L M$, and $S_{4} \in M N$. Note that $h$ takes $S_{1}$ to $S_{3}$, hence $I_{1} S_{1} \| I_{3} S_{3}$, and $S_{1} S: S S_{3}=r_{1}: r_{3}$. We will prove that $S_{2} S: S S_{4}=r_{2}: r_{4}$ or, equivalently, $K S_{1}: S_{1} N=r_{2}: r_{4}$. This will yield the problem statement; indeed, applying similar arguments to the intersection point $S^{\prime}$ of the internal common tangents to $\omega_{2}$ and $\omega_{4}$, we see that $S^{\prime}$ satisfies similar relations, and there is a unique point inside $K L M N$ satisfying them. Therefore, $S^{\prime}=S$.

Further, denote by $I_{A}, I_{B}, I_{C}, I_{D}$ and $r_{A}, r_{B}, r_{C}, r_{D}$ the incenters and inradii of triangles $D A B, A B C, B C D$, and $C D A$, respectively. One can shift triangle $C L M$ by $\overrightarrow{L K}$ to glue it with triangle $A K N$ into a quadrilateral $A K C^{\prime} N$ similar to $A B C D$. In particular, this shows that $r_{1}: r_{3}=r_{A}: r_{C}$; similarly, $r_{2}: r_{4}=r_{B}: r_{D}$. Moreover, the same shift takes $S_{3}$ to $S_{1}$, and it also takes $I_{3}$ to the incenter $I_{3}^{\prime}$ of triangle $K C^{\prime} N$. Since $I_{1} S_{1} \| I_{3} S_{3}$, the points $I_{1}, S_{1}, I_{3}^{\prime}$ are collinear. Thus, in order to complete the solution, it suffices to apply the following Lemma to quadrilateral $A K C^{\prime} N$.
Lemma 1. Let $A B C D$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, and define $I_{A}, I_{C}, r_{B}$, and $r_{D}$ as above. Let $I_{A} I_{C}$ meet $B D$ at $X$; then $B X: X D=r_{B}: r_{D}$.
Proof. Consider an inversion centered at $X$; the images under that inversion will be denoted by primes, e.g., $A^{\prime}$ is the image of $A$.

By properties of inversion, we have

$$
\angle I_{C}^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime}=\angle X I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime}=\angle X D I_{A}=\angle B D A / 2=\angle B C A / 2=\angle A C I_{B}
$$

We obtain $\angle I_{A}^{\prime} I_{C}^{\prime} D^{\prime}=\angle C A I_{B}$ likewise; therefore, $\triangle I_{C}^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime} \sim \triangle A C I_{B}$. In the same manner, we get $\triangle I_{C}^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} B^{\prime} \sim \triangle A C I_{D}$, hence the quadrilaterals $I_{C}^{\prime} B^{\prime} I_{A}^{\prime} D^{\prime}$ and $A I_{D} C I_{B}$ are also similar. But the diagonals $A C$ and $I_{B} I_{D}$ of quadrilateral $A I_{D} C I_{B}$ meet at a point $Y$ such that $I_{B} Y$ :
$Y I_{D}=r_{B}: r_{D}$. By similarity, we get $D^{\prime} X: B^{\prime} X=r_{B}: r_{D}$ and hence $B X: X D=D^{\prime} X$ : $B^{\prime} X=r_{B}: r_{D}$.

Comment 1. The solution above shows that the problem statement holds also for any parallelogram $K L M N$ whose sides are parallel to the diagonals of $A B C D$, as no property specific for a rhombus has been used. This solution works equally well when two sides of quadrilateral $A B C D$ are parallel.

Comment 2. The problem may be reduced to Lemma $1$ by using different tools, e.g., by using mass point geometry, linear motion of $K, L, M$, and $N$, etc.

Lemma $1$ itself also can be proved in different ways. We present below one alternative proof.
Proof. In the circumcircle of $A B C D$, let $K^{\prime}, L^{\prime} . M^{\prime}$, and $N^{\prime}$ be the midpoints of arcs $A B, B C$, $C D$, and $D A$ containing no other vertices of $A B C D$, respectively. Thus, $K^{\prime}=C I_{B} \cap D I_{A}$, etc. In the computations below, we denote by $[P]$ the area of a polygon $P$. We use similarities $\triangle I_{A} B K^{\prime} \sim$ $\triangle I_{A} D N^{\prime}, \triangle I_{B} K^{\prime} L^{\prime} \sim \triangle I_{B} A C$, etc., as well as congruences $\triangle I_{B} K^{\prime} L^{\prime}=\triangle B K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$ and $\triangle I_{D} M^{\prime} N^{\prime}=$ $\triangle D M^{\prime} N^{\prime}$ (e.g., the first congruence holds because $K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$ is a common internal bisector of angles $B K^{\prime} I_{B}$ and $\left.B L^{\prime} I_{B}\right)$.

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{B X}{D X}=\frac{\left[I_{A} B I_{C}\right]}{\left[I_{A} D I_{C}\right]}=\frac{B I_{A} \cdot B I_{C} \cdot \sin I_{A} B I_{C}}{D I_{A} \cdot D I_{C} \cdot \sin I_{A} D I_{C}}=\frac{B I_{A}}{D I_{A}} \cdot \frac{B I_{C}}{D I_{C}} \cdot \frac{\sin N^{\prime} B M^{\prime}}{\sin K^{\prime} D L^{\prime}} \\
& =\frac{B K^{\prime}}{D N^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{B L^{\prime}}{D M^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{\sin N^{\prime} D M^{\prime}}{\sin K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}}=\frac{B K^{\prime} \cdot B L^{\prime} \cdot \sin K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}}{D N^{\prime} \cdot D M^{\prime} \cdot \sin N^{\prime} D M^{\prime}} \cdot \frac{\sin ^{2} N^{\prime} D M^{\prime}}{\sin ^{2} K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}} \\
& \quad=\frac{\left[K^{\prime} B L^{\prime}\right]}{\left[M^{\prime} D N^{\prime}\right]} \cdot \frac{N^{\prime} M^{\prime 2}}{K^{\prime} L^{\prime 2}}=\frac{\left[K^{\prime} I_{B} L^{\prime}\right] \cdot \frac{A^{\prime} C^{\prime 2}}{K^{\prime} L^{\prime 2}}}{\left[M^{\prime} I_{D} N^{\prime}\right] \cdot \frac{A^{\prime} C^{\prime 2}}{N^{\prime} M^{\prime 2}}}=\frac{\left[A I_{B} C\right]}{\left[A I_{D} C\right]}=\frac{r_{B}}{r_{D}},
\end{aligned}
$$

as required.
